Mississippi Cannabis & Hemp Research — Audited Final Report

Parts 0–12, corrected in place. Audit by a separate fact-checking pass; the original writers were not the auditors.

Last audited: 28 October 2026  |  Original research dates: 25 October 2026  |  Status: This file supersedes the 25 October 2026 combined file as the corrected dossier. The original file is left untouched elsewhere.

Federal baseline — given, not re-audited

Scheduling is split. Under a final rule at 91 FR 22714 (effective 28 April 2026), FDA-approved cannabis products and state-licensed medical marijuana are in Schedule III. All other marijuana, including all adult-use, remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is NOT final. IRS 280E: Treasury has said rescheduling generally removes 280E as a bar for businesses no longer dealing in Schedule I/II substances (guidance forthcoming); adult-use activity remains fully subject to 280E. Hemp: Public Law 119-37 §781 takes legal effect 12 November 2026, but Public Law 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026 to only the provisions excluding cannabinoids that are not naturally produced or are synthesized; the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap apply after 11 December 2026. USDA has delayed enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement until 31 December 2026. The federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider is in force through 11 December 2026. No federal cannabis banking law has been enacted.

Mississippi application, as corrected: Schedule III and the 280E change apply to Mississippi's MSDH/MDOR-licensed medical licensees only. Non-medical possession remains Schedule I federally. A future Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians tribal programme is not "state-licensed" on the rule text: 21 CFR 1300.01 defines "state medical marijuana license" as a licence issued by a state entity (or a District of Columbia or federal territorial entity). A tribal licence is not listed, so tribal marijuana would remain Schedule I federally, with §280E still applying, unless new DEA guidance, a rule amendment, or a court ruling changes that [VERIFY — none located]. The report's former "three readings, none adopted" neutrality is superseded by that textual conclusion.

Trap avoided: the MSDH CY2025 Annual Report (January 2026, predating the April 2026 rule) says marijuana "continues to be classified as a Schedule I substance until a final rule is published" — that passage is superseded by the baseline above and must not be carried forward as current law.

Reconciliation — figures adopted everywhere in the rewritten report

  • Tier 6 cultivation: 100,000–150,000 sq ft, maximum 2 locations, combined canopy ≤150,000 sq ft (§41-137-35, capped by HB 1158 (2023)). The MSDH FAQ/rule wording "100,000 sq ft or more" does not override the statute and is removed as the adopted figure.
  • CY2025 retail sales: $138,863,945.64, 1 Jan–29 Dec 2025 for sales/finance tables (MSDH CY2025 Annual Report, direct PDF). Monthly table: Jan $9,752,393.73; Feb $9,165,751.60; Mar $10,826,903.33; Apr $11,033,721.47; May $11,834,733.89; Jun $10,827,062.44; Jul $12,263,999.69; Aug $12,787,641.43; Sep $12,149,233.81; Oct $13,453,864.79; Nov $12,559,884.63; Dec $12,208,754.83. Quarters: Q1 $29,745,048.66; Q2 $33,695,517.80; Q3 $37,200,874.93; Q4 $38,222,504.25. The DistrictCannaMetrics November figure $10.70M is wrong and deleted.
  • Fiscal-year sales (MDOR, Metrc quarterly reports): FY2025 $118,696,744; FY2026 $158,763,559. Pot Culture's ~$118.7M is the FY2025 figure, not a competing CY2025 figure, and is rejected as a CY2025 measure.
  • Licences, patients, practitioners (Dec 2025, MSDH CY2025 Annual Report, direct PDF): 342 licences total — 171 dispensaries, 53 cultivation, 57 micro-cultivation, 17 processing, 20 micro-processing, 16 transport, 5 disposal, 2 testing, 1 research (Dec 2024 research = 0, resolved); 5,862 work permits; 66,041 patients at 15 Dec 2025; 259 practitioners (117 physicians, 137 nurse practitioners, 5 optometrists). Caregiver stock 247 is not in that report's text and stays Official-via-secondary [VERIFY]. Secondary counts 361 businesses / 188 dispensaries (Oct 2026) and ~175/~190 dispensaries (Jan 2026 press) are superseded — different dates/definitions.
  • Tax collections CY2025 (MSDH report, direct): excise $2,180,141.31; cannabis sales tax (Rate Code 83) $9,002,940.86; business licence/patient registration fees $8,935,649 (fees table 1/1–12/29/2025); MSDH fines $135,000; MDOR fines $23,500; MSDH expenses $6,716,483.64.
  • Local opt-outs (MDOR list as opened 28 Oct 2026): 80 municipalities + 17 counties, dispensaries only, undated, "informational only". Lauderdale County, Lucedale, Horn Lake and Greenwood are absent from that list — do not state them as currently opted out; no opt-back record was located for Lucedale/Horn Lake/Greenwood, so that absence is unexplained, not proof of a recorded opt-back.
  • Initiative 65/65A results: no presentation is adopted as the certified total. The court-record (68%/74%), certified-summary (68.52%/73.7%) and all-ballots (61.65%/57.89%) presentations are preserved by denominator only; the Secretary of State 2020 page now redirects and the certified table was not retrieved.
  • Decriminalisation year: unresolved, 1977 vs 1978. Do not quote either year as settled.
  • Choctaw referendum: 1,415–1,164 = 54.9%–45.1%, computed from secondary-reported counts, not a tribal-certified figure. "57%–43%" and "57% to 47%" are secondary misprints and are not quoted as results.

Scope and limits — read before relying on this file

Primary sources only were used to confirm or correct: the Mississippi Code and bill pages on the Legislature's official site, the Mississippi Administrative Code (Secretary of State), MSDH Medical Cannabis Program, MDOR, MDAC, Mississippi Bureau of Narcotics, Mississippi Supreme Court opinions, Secretary of State election records, official Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians government sources, official county/city sites, and (for federal hemp/USDA rules) eCFR/Cornell LII and USDA AMS. Where a claim rested only on news, law-firm blogs, trade press, listing sites, LegiScan/BillTrack50 trackers, or Justia/FindLaw reproductions, it is marked Unverified, even if several secondary sources agree. Justia/FindLaw are reproductions of the 2025 Code, not the Legislature's official compilation — every Code quotation not corroborated by an official bill text still needs a final re-check against legislature.ms.gov / billstatus.ls.state.ms.us before a filing. No live-browser work was done in the Parts 11–12 audit; the MSDH Business Search, HeMP tool and other JavaScript-rendered dashboards could not be run live there, so their live behaviour stays flagged. No personal phone number or email for any individual licence holder is reproduced in this file; where the original listed one, the name and a link to the official source are kept instead. Programme/agency public mailboxes and phones are not personal details.

Federal baseline — given, not re-researched

  • Split scheduling: state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). All adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is not final.
  • IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to §280E.
  • Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026. After 11 December 2026, the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply.
  • USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026.
  • The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026.
  • There is no federal cannabis banking law.
  • Mississippi application: Mississippi's medical programme is state-licensed, so the Schedule III / §280E change is explained as applying to its cultivators, processors, dispensaries and other licensees. Any non-medical possession remains Schedule I federally. Whether a future Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians tribal programme would count as “state-licensed” under the federal rule is marked [VERIFY] throughout — it is not asserted, and no tribal programme, ordinance, regulator, licence or operation was located in Run 2.

Run 1 — Parts 0–1: Headlines and Laws

Mississippi — Cannabis and Hemp Research, Run 1: Parts 0 and 1

State: Mississippi only. This file covers Part 0 (Headlines) and Part 1 (Laws) only. Parts 2–6 are not covered here except for brief cross-references needed for consistency; they belong to later work in this Run 1 commission. Date accessed for all facts in this file: 25 October 2026, unless a different publication or effective date is stated for the fact itself. In this session the following official pages were opened and read directly: MSDH Medical Cannabis Program (MMCP) FAQ pages at mmcp.ms.gov, and the Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce (MDAC) hemp page. Mississippi Code text was read in full through the Justia reproduction of the 2025 Mississippi Code, which reproduces the session-law history line for each section; the Legislature's official bill-status PDFs for SB 2095 (2022), SB 2748 (2025), HB 895 (2026) and HB 1152 (2026) were located in search results but the full official Code text on legislature.ms.gov / billstatus.ls.state.ms.us was not opened page-by-page in this session. Every statute quotation below is therefore labelled with its Justia URL as the page actually read, and the official Legislature source that must be re-checked before publication is named alongside it. Federal baseline applied in this file (given, fixed — not re-researched)

  • Split scheduling: state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). All adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is not final.
  • IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to §280E.
  • Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026. After 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply.
  • USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026.
  • The federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026. There is no federal cannabis banking law.
  • No contradiction with the federal baseline was found in Mississippi law in this research. Mississippi's programme is state-licensed (MSDH/MDOR), so on the given baseline its cultivators, processors, dispensaries and other licensees operating in compliance with the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act fall on the medical / Schedule III side of the split, while any non-medical possession remains Schedule I federally. This is an application of the given baseline, not a new federal finding, and it does not change any Mississippi state penalty in §1.3 below.

Under § 41-29-139(c)(2)(A)1, ≤30 g marijuana / ≤10 g synthetic cannabinoids, first conviction: fine $100–$250, enforceable by summons if the offender shows satisfactory ID and gives a written promise to appear. Second conviction within 2 years is a misdemeanour ($250, ≤60 days, mandatory drug education); third+ within 2 years is a misdemeanour ($250–$1,000, ≤6 months). First/second records are private, nonpublic, and expunged after 2 years. The bill that would have made the first offence a civil offence (HB 196, 2026) died in committee — it is NOT law. § 41-29-139 opened directly, https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-29/article-3/section-41-29-139/ ; HB 196 summary, https://www.billtrack50.com/billdetail/1923380

The Mississippi Hemp Cultivation Act (SB 2725, signed 29 June 2020) authorised a state plan, but the Legislature never appropriated funding, so MDAC states verbatim: "The Mississippi Department of Agriculture & Commerce does not issue hemp licenses." The only legal cultivation route is a USDA licence under the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program (3-year licence; no licence if convicted of a controlled-substance felony in the last 10 years). The Fifth Circuit upheld the ban 22 Nov 2024 (Cocroft v. PART 1 — LAWS

1.1 Legal status: medical only

Current law, in one paragraph. Mississippi is a medical-only state. A person may lawfully possess and use medical cannabis only if (a) diagnosed by a practitioner with whom they have a bona fide practitioner-patient relationship as having a debilitating medical condition, (b) they have received a written certification, and (c) they have been issued a registry identification card by the Mississippi State Department of Health (MSDH, called "MDOH" in the Code). Anything outside that chain — including any purchase from an unlicensed seller, any possession above the MMCEU limits, any home cultivation, and any use by a non-cardholder — falls under the Uniform Controlled Substances Law penalties in §1.3. There is no adult-use licence, no adult-use retail sale, and no reciprocity that lets an out-of-state card alone authorise purchase: a nonresident must obtain a Mississippi nonresident card (see §1.4.6).

What IS legal (state law): - Registered qualifying patient / designated caregiver possession and use within MMCEU limits, from a licensed dispensary, in a non-public place, not in a motor vehicle, not while operating a vehicle/vessel/aircraft in violation of state or federal law. - Licensed cultivation, processing, testing, transportation, disposal, research and dispensary activity, in-state only, under MSDH/MDOR licences, tracked in the seed-to-sale system. - Non-ingested topical cannabis products sold by a dispensary to a person 21+ who is not a cardholder, from a part of the dispensary not requiring a card (§ 41-137-39(21) — see §1.3.4). - Hemp cultivation only under a USDA licence (no state licence exists), and hemp / hemp products as defined in §§ 69-25-201 et seq. — subject to the AG consumable-product opinion in §1.6, which is the main uncertainty in the whole hemp section. - FDA-approved cannabinoid drugs (e.g. Epidiolex-type legend drugs) under the § 41-29-113 exemption — see §1.2, row 4.

What is NOT legal (state law): - Adult-use / recreational possession, purchase, sale, or use by any person, at any amount, even ≤30 g — the ≤30 g first-offence rule is a penalty rule, not a permission (see §1.3.1). - Home cultivation by patients, caregivers, or anyone unlicensed; cultivation only by a licensed cultivation facility in an enclosed, locked, secure facility (§ 41-137-39(5)). - Public smoking/vaping, smoking/vaping in a motor vehicle, open containers in public places (see §1.3.4). - Delivery, drive-through, or curbside sale by a dispensary (§ 41-137-39(21)). - Transport of Mississippi-grown medical cannabis outside Mississippi, and purchase/grow/use of cannabis grown outside Mississippi by a Mississippi establishment (§ 41-137-39(18)). - Sale or possession of a hemp-derived product designed for human ingestion/consumption that is not FDA-approved, outside the Medical Cannabis Act — on the AG's 11 June 2025 reading (opinion, not statute; see §1.6.4). Non-consumable hemp products (fibre, sterilised-seed personal-care products not causing THC to enter the body, industrial products) are expressly exempted in § 41-29-113 — see §1.2.

Federal overlay (given baseline, applied): Federally, state-licensed medical activity moved to Schedule III on 28 April 2026, while non-medical marijuana remains Schedule I. That does not make adult-use possession legal in Mississippi, does not create a federal defence to a Mississippi § 41-29-139 charge, and does not authorise interstate transport. The Mississippi statute itself, § 41-137-39(18), separately forbids taking Mississippi medical cannabis out of state.

Miss. Code §§ 41-137-1 to -67 (cited as §§ 41-137-1 et seq.) Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act The whole medical programme: definitions, who may use, practitioner certification, cards, licensing, local rules, seed-to-sale, fees, taxes (cross-ref Part 2), protections and limits, violations. MSDH has "ultimate authority for oversight"; MDOR licenses dispensaries. Title of SB 2095: "AN ACT TO ENACT THE MISSISSIPPI MEDICAL CANNABIS ACT; TO AUTHORIZE MEDICAL CANNABIS USE BY CERTAIN PATIENTS WHO HAVE DEBILITATING MEDICAL CONDITIONS…" (full title in the enrolled bill). Enacted Laws 2022, ch. 303, eff. on passage (approved 2 Feb 2022). Amended 2023 ch. 436 (27 Mar 2023); 2024 ch. 495 (eff. 1 July 2024, § 41-137-39); 2025 ch. 425 (eff. 1 July 2025, § 41-137-5) and SB 2748 (eff. 1 July 2025, §§ 41-137-3, -5, -37). Full amendment map is [VERIFY — official history] — individual sections below give their own history lines. Enrolled bill (official Legislature PDF): https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2022/pdf/SB/2001-2099/SB2095IN.pdf ; SB 2748: https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2025/pdf/SB/2700-2799/SB2748SG.pdf
§ 41-137-3 Definitions Defines every programme term, including "debilitating medical condition", "MMCEU", "medical cannabis establishment", "artificially derived cannabinoid", "THC" concepts. The MMCEU definition is the quantity engine of the programme. "(r) 'Debilitating medical condition' means: (i) Cancer, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, muscular dystrophy, glaucoma, spastic quadriplegia, positive status for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), hepatitis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, sickle-cell anemia, Alzheimer's disease, agitation of dementia, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), autism, pain refractory to appropriate opioid management, diabetic/peripheral neuropathy, spinal cord disease or severe injury, or the treatment of these conditions; (ii) A chronic, terminal or debilitating disease or medical condition, or its treatment, that produces one or more of the following: cachexia or wasting syndrome, chronic pain, severe or intractable nausea, seizures, or severe and persistent muscle spasms, including, but not limited to, those characteristic of multiple sclerosis; or (iii) Any other serious medical condition or its treatment added by the Mississippi Department of Health, as provided for in Section 41-137-17." — and — "(w) 'MMCEU' means Mississippi Medical Cannabis Equivalency Unit. One unit of MMCEU shall be considered equal to: (i) Three and one-half (3.5) grams of medical cannabis flower; (ii) One (1) gram of total THC in a medical cannabis concentrate; or (iii) One (1) gram of total THC in an infused product." As printed 2025, incorporating SB 2748 (2025). [VERIFY — official history] Page read: https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-3/
§ 41-137-5 Authorisation to use; practitioner certification The gate: diagnosis + written certification + card. Certification 12 months unless shorter; in-person assessment, except homebound/bedbound telemedicine; minors only by MD/DO with parent/guardian present and consenting; 6-month follow-up visit still mandatory (HB 895 would have removed it — vetoed); practitioner registration: 8 hours CE first year, 5 hours/year after; no drug-test condition may be imposed by an agency, though a practitioner may require one within scope of practice. "(1) No person shall be authorized to use medical cannabis in this state unless the person (a) has been diagnosed by a practitioner, with whom the person has a bona fide practitioner-patient relationship within his or her scope of practice, as having a debilitating medical condition for which the practitioner believes, in his or her professional opinion, that the person would likely receive medical or palliative benefit from the medical use of medical cannabis to treat or alleviate the person's debilitating medical condition or symptoms associated with the person's debilitating medical condition, (b) has received a written certification of that diagnosis from the practitioner, and (c) has been issued a registry identification card from the MDOH under Section 41-137-23." […] "(2)(b) Remain current for twelve (12) months, unless the practitioner specifies a shorter period of time; (c) Be issued after an in-person assessment of the patient by a practitioner, or after a telemedicine evaluation for patients who are homebound or bedbound as certified by a practitioner with whom the patient has a bona fide practitioner-patient relationship within his or her scope of practice other than the practitioner making the written certification." […] "(5) After a qualifying patient receives a written certification from a practitioner, the patient shall be required to make a follow-up visit with the practitioner not less than six (6) months after the date of issuance of the certification…" […] "(8) Only physicians and doctors of osteopathic medicine may issue written certifications to registered qualifying patients who are minors." Laws 2022, ch. 303, § 3, eff. on passage (approved 2 Feb 2022); Laws 2023, ch. 436, § 1, eff. on passage (approved 27 Mar 2023); Laws 2025, ch. 425, § 2, eff. 1 July 2025 (history line as printed). Page read: https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-5/

§ 41-137-9 Protections for medical use Cardholders, practitioners, establishments protected from state prosecution / professional discipline for conduct within the Act; no denial of custody/visitation solely for cardholder status; schools/landlords/employers may not be penalised under state law merely for enrolling/leasing to/employing a cardholder — but § 41-137-13 then removes employment protection in substance (see §1.9). Read §§ 41-137-9 and -13 together; quoting one without the other misleads. Full verbatim text not opened in this session. Enrolled bill: https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2022/pdf/SB/2001-2099/SB2095IN.pdf
§ 41-137-11 Statewide seed-to-sale tracking system Every establishment must use the MSDH-certified statewide system from seed/immature plant until purchase by a patient/caregiver or destruction; daily beginning inventory, harvests, acquisitions, sales, disbursements, remediations, disposals, transfers, ending inventory. Dispensaries must check the system before dispensing (see § 41-137-5(6)). Vendor name (Metrc) is not in the statute text; it is the operational system identified by secondary sources and by MSDH materials — see §1.8. "(1) Each medical cannabis establishment shall use a statewide seed-to-sale tracking system certified by the MDOH to track medical cannabis from seed or immature plant stage until the medical cannabis is purchased by a registered qualifying patient or registered designated caregiver or destroyed. Records entered into the seed-to-sale tracking system shall include each day's beginning inventory, harvests, acquisitions, sales, disbursements, remediations, disposals, transfers, ending inventory, and any other data necessary for inventory control records in the statewide seed-to-sale tracking system." 2022 [VERIFY — history]. Page read: https://codes.findlaw.com/ms/title-41-public-health/ms-code-sect-41-137-11/
§ 41-137-13 Limitations — what the Act does NOT do The anti-protection section. No reimbursement duty; no employer accommodation duty; employers expressly may refuse to hire / discharge / discipline for medical use regardless of impairment; drug-testing policies untouched; no private right of action against an employer; federal (incl. DOT) restrictions untouched; workers'-comp drug-free-workplace discount and defences untouched. "(1) This chapter shall not be construed to do any of the following: (a) Require an organization for managed care, health benefit plan, private health insurer, government medical assistance program, employer, property and casualty, or workers' compensation insurer or self-insured group providing coverage for a medical, pharmacy or health care service to pay for or reimburse any other individual or entity for costs associated with the medical use of cannabis; (b) Require any employer to permit, accommodate, or allow the medical use of medical cannabis, or to modify any job or working conditions of any employee who engages in the medical use of medical cannabis…; (c) Prohibit any employer from refusing to hire, discharging, disciplining, or otherwise taking an adverse employment action against an individual… as a result, in whole or in part, of that individual's medical use of medical cannabis, regardless of the individual's impairment or lack of impairment…; (d) Prohibit or limit the ability of any employer from establishing or enforcing a drug-testing policy; (e) Interfere with, impair or impede any federal restrictions or requirements on employment or contracting, including, but not limited to, regulations adopted by the United States Department of Transportation in Title 49, Code of Federal Regulations; (f) Permit, authorize, or establish any individual's right to commence or undertake any legal action against an employer for refusing to hire, discharging, disciplining or otherwise taking an adverse employment action…" 2022 [VERIFY — history]. Page read: https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-13/

§ 41-137-23 Registry identification cards What MSDH must collect, 10-day approval/denial of a completed application, card within 5 days of approval, caregiver background checks, minor safeguards, denial grounds (incomplete, prior revocation, false information, failure to meet chapter), judicial review under § 41-137-59. "(3)(a) Verify the information contained in an application or renewal submitted under this section and approve or deny an application or renewal within ten (10) days of receiving a completed application or renewal application; and (b) Issue registry identification cards to a qualifying patient and his or her designated caregiver(s), if any, within five (5) days of approving the application or renewal." […] "(5) The MDOH shall not issue a registry identification card to a qualifying patient who is younger than eighteen (18) years of age, unless: (a) The qualifying patient's practitioner has explained the potential risks and benefits… to the custodial parent or legal guardian…; and (b) The custodial parent or legal guardian… consents in writing to: (i) Acknowledge the potential harms…; (ii) Allow the qualifying patient's medical use…; (iii) Serve as the qualifying patient's designated caregiver; and (iv) Control the acquisition…, the dosage and the frequency of the use…" Laws 2022, ch. 303, § 12, eff. on passage (approved 2 Feb 2022); Laws 2023, ch. 436, § 2, eff. on passage (approved 27 Mar 2023). § 41-137-29 Conduct NOT authorised; penalties preserved The "does not authorise" list: negligence/recklessness/professional-standard breach; possession/use in a correctional facility unless it elects to allow it; smoking (including vaping/inhalation) in a public place or motor vehicle; operating/navigating/being in actual physical control of a vehicle/aircraft/train/motorboat in violation of §§ 59-23-7, 63-11-30 or federal law as a result of medical use; possession above the allowable amount; caregiver consumption of a patient's cannabis. MMCP's paraphrase: "The law does not authorize you to use medical cannabis in a public place or in a motor vehicle." Verbatim text via SB 2095 § 7 as reproduced: "(2) This chapter does not authorize any individual to engage in, and does not prevent the imposition of any civil, criminal or other penalties for engaging in, the following conduct: … (c) Smoking medical cannabis in a public place or in a motor vehicle; for purposes of this paragraph (c), the term 'smoking' includes vaping and any other method of inhalation of medical cannabis; (d) Operating, navigating, or being in actual physical control of any motor vehicle, aircraft, train, motorboat or other conveyance in a manner that would violate Section 59-23-7, Section 63-11-30 or federal law as a result, in whole or in part, of that individual's medical use of medical cannabis; (e) Possessing medical cannabis in excess of the allowable amount of medical cannabis; or (f) Consumption, by a registered designated caregiver, of cannabis provided for use to a registered qualifying patient." [VERIFY against official § 41-137-29 text.] 2022 [VERIFY]. MMCP paraphrase: https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/node/16 ; SB 2095 reproduction: https://www.scribd.com/document/568505039/Mississippi-Medical-Cannabis-Act
§ 41-137-35 Licensing of establishments; zoning; buffers; dispensary spacing MSDH licenses cultivation/processing/transportation/disposal/research/testing; MDOR licenses dispensaries. Zoning: dispensary/research/testing in commercial zones; cultivation/processing in agricultural/industrial zones (or commercial with variance). 1,000-ft buffer from school/church/child-care property boundary (waiver possible, but main entry never within 500 ft). Dispensaries 1,500 ft apart (main entry to main entry). Local licence/permit allowed at a fee consistent with non-cannabis businesses. Residency: original 3-year / 35% / 100%-micro rules in § 41-137-35(11)–(12) — the general rule "shall stand repealed on December 31, 2022" in the enrolled bill; current residency position is [VERIFY] and is a Part 4 question, not resolved here. "(16)(a)(ii) The physical address of the prospective medical cannabis establishment, which shall not be within one thousand (1,000) feet of the nearest property boundary line of a school, church or child care facility which exists or has acquired necessary real property for the operation of such facility before the date of the medical cannabis establishment application unless the entity has received approval from the school, church or child care facility and received the applicable waiver from their licensing agency, provided that the main point of entry of the cannabis establishment is not located within five hundred (500) feet of the nearest property boundary line of any school, church or child care facility" — and — "(5) No medical cannabis dispensary may be located within a one-thousand-five-hundred-feet radius from the main point of entry of the dispensary to the main point of entry of another medical cannabis dispensary." (subsection numbering as in the 2025 SB 2748 reproduction; confirm numbering in the official Code — [VERIFY].) 2022; amended 2023 (HB 1158, ch. 436); SB 2748 (2025) restates the 1,500-ft rule. Page read (2025 reproduction): https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2025/pdf/SB/2700-2799/SB2748IN.pdf ; § 41-137-35 summary: https://www.casemine.com/act/us/65b0f4d3121ace78b84d7558
§ 41-137-37 Local ordinances; opt-out (summary here; full treatment is Part 3) A municipality/county may enact time/place/manner ordinances not in conflict with the Act, and may charge a reasonable local licence fee — but may NOT prohibit dispensaries expressly or by ordinances making operation impracticable, except through the 90-day opt-out in the Act (opt-out window closed 3 May 2022; opt-back-in by petition/election). SB 2748 (2025) added: no zoning/permitting application to a locality until after the state licence issues. "(1) A municipality or county may enact ordinances or regulations not in conflict with this chapter, or with regulations enacted under this chapter, governing the time, place, and manner of medical cannabis establishment operations in the locality." […] "(2) No municipality or county may prohibit dispensaries either expressly or through the enactment of ordinances or regulations that make their operation impracticable in the jurisdiction." (SB 2095 § 19, via enrolled-bill reproduction — [VERIFY] against current § 41-137-37.) 2022; SB 2748 eff. 1 July 2025 [VERIFY]. § 41-137-39 Requirements, prohibitions, penalties (establishments & cardholders) The operational core: background checks, no employment of under-21s or persons with a disqualifying felony, enclosed/locked/secure facilities, only processors/researchers may make concentrates, no shared office space with / referrals to a practitioner, inspection, dispensary verification duties, MMCEU purchase/possession limits, potency caps, labelling, nonresident rules, 18–25 two-practitioner rule, under-21 entry rule, in-state-only rule, $25/5-year work permits, no plant-growth-regulator cannabis, in-store-only sales, no data-sharing with federal entities. See §1.3 and §1.4 for the operative quotations, each tied to its subsection. §§ 41-29-101 et seq. — Uniform Controlled Substances Law, esp. §§ 41-29-113, -139, -136 Controlled substances; penalties The criminal backdrop. Marijuana and tetrahydrocannabinols are Schedule I (with the hemp / FDA-drug / industrial exemptions in § 41-29-113). § 41-29-139 sets every possession / transfer / manufacture penalty in §1.3. § 41-29-136 (Harper Grace's Law) is the narrow, now largely superseded CBD-solution research defence — see row below. § 41-29-113 tetrahydrocannabinols paragraph (as reproduced in the 2019 HB 1547 and 2025 SB 2314 bill texts, which restate current § 41-29-113): "tetrahydrocannabinols, meaning tetrahydrocannabinols contained in a plant of the genus Cannabis (cannabis plant), as well as the synthetic equivalents of the substances contained in the cannabis plant, or in the resinous extractives of such plant, and/or synthetic substances, derivatives, and their isomers with similar chemical structure and pharmacological activity to those substances contained in the plant such as the following: (A) 1 cis or trans tetrahydrocannabinol; (B) 6 cis or trans tetrahydrocannabinol; (C) 3,4 cis or trans tetrahydrocannabinol. (Since nomenclature of these substances is not internationally standardized, compounds of these structures, regardless of atomic positions, are covered.) ('Tetrahydrocannabinols' excludes dronabinol and nabilone.) For purposes of this paragraph, tetrahydrocannabinols do not include hemp or hemp products regulated under Sections 69-25-201 through 69-25-221. However, the following products are exempted from control: (i) THC-containing industrial products made from cannabis stalks…; (ii) Processed cannabis plant materials used for industrial purposes…; (iii) Animal feed mixtures that contain sterilized cannabis seeds…; (iv) Personal care products that contain oil from sterilized cannabis seeds… (if the products do not cause THC to enter the human body); (v) Hemp as regulated under Sections 69-25-201 through 69-25-221; and (vi) Any product derived from the hemp plant designed for human ingestion and/or consumption that is approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration". Note the tension: clause (vi) exempts only FDA-approved ingestible hemp products; clause (v) exempts "hemp as regulated under" §§ 69-25-201 et seq. — and Mississippi has never funded/operated that state hemp programme (see §1.6). That tension is exactly what the AG's 2025 opinion exploits, and why secondary claims that "delta-8 is banned by HB 1547" are wrong: HB 1547 is a 2019 bill text restating § 41-29-113, not a 2023 delta-8 ban. The delta-8 question is governed by the § 41-29-113 exemption language + the AG opinion, not by a standalone ban statute — [VERIFY] against the current official § 41-29-113. § 41-29-113 as restated in 2019 HB 1547, https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2019/pdf/HB/1500-1599/HB1547PS.pdf ; and 2025 SB 2314, https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2025/pdf/SB/2300-2399/SB2314IN.pdf (SB 2314 would have added "certain hemp products" to Schedule I — it did NOT become law; do not cite it as law). Page read for penalties: https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-29/article-3/section-41-29-139/
§ 41-29-136 — Harper Grace's Law CBD solution for debilitating epileptic conditions Narrow research defence: CBD solution prepared from University of Mississippi National Center for Natural Products Research extract, dispensed by UMMC Pharmacy, on a physician's order, with a hold-harmless agreement; affirmative complete defence to marijuana-possession prosecution for the patient/parent/guardian/custodian; no child-removal proceeding based solely on authorised CBD-solution possession/use. Extended by SB 2340 (2024) to repeal from and after 1 July 2027 (earlier 2021 / 2024 prints superseded) — the current status is [VERIFY] and internally conflicting in secondary reproductions; do not state a repeal date without checking the current official Code. It is in any event largely superseded for patients by the Medical Cannabis Act, and § 41-29-136(4) in the FindLaw print says it "does not apply to any of the actions that are lawful under the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act". "(3)(a) In a prosecution for the unlawful possession of marijuana under the laws of this state, it is an affirmative and complete defense to prosecution that: (i) The defendant suffered from a debilitating epileptic condition or related illness and the use or possession of CBD solution was pursuant to the order of a physician as authorized under this section; or (ii) The defendant is the parent, guardian or custodian of an individual who suffered from a debilitating epileptic condition or related illness and the use or possession of CBD solution was pursuant to the order of a physician as authorized under this section." Enacted 2014; repeal dates in prints conflict (2021 / 2024 / 2027) — [VERIFY]. https://codes.findlaw.com/ms/title-41-public-health/ms-code-sect-41-29-136/ ; https://pharm.olemiss.edu/marijuana/faq/
§§ 69-25-201 to -221 — Mississippi Hemp Cultivation Act (SB 2725, 2020) Hemp cultivation, processing, transportation Legalises hemp (0.3% delta-9 THC, dry weight) under a state plan to be created by the Commissioner of Agriculture and Commerce — a plan that was never funded or implemented. Defines hemp, requires licensing/regulation in theory, but in practice MDAC issues nothing and USDA licenses. The Act's own definitions are the anchor for the § 41-29-113 hemp exemption. MDAC's operative summary (official agency page, opened directly): "Senate Bill 2725, also known as the Mississippi Hemp Cultivation Act, was signed into law on June 29, 2020. This act legalized the cultivation of hemp under a state plan to be created and implemented by the Commissioner of Agriculture and Commerce. Although the act allowed for a state hemp cultivation program, the necessary funding to implement the program was not appropriated by the Mississippi Legislature." Full §§ 69-25-201 et seq. text was not opened in this session — [VERIFY — quote the definition section before publication.] Secondary restatement of the definition: "the plant Cannabis sativa L. and any part of that plant, including the seeds thereof and all derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts, and salts of isomers, whether growing or not, with a delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) concentration of not more than three-tenths percent (0.3%) on a dry weight basis that is grown or processed under [the Hemp Cultivation Act]" (via AG-opinion reporting, https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=7ceef611-389a-4fac-bca0-5a8f937bb423 — secondary, [VERIFY]). Signed 29 June 2020; never funded/implemented. No later amendment located — [VERIFY]. MDAC page opened directly: https://www.mdac.ms.gov/programs/hemp-cultivation-in-ms/
§ 97-31-5 Sale of intoxicating drugs/elixirs Old general statute invoked in one AG opinion on hemp beverages: unlawful, unless otherwise legalised under state law, to sell any drug/elixir/compound that "when drunk to excess, in the form sold, will produce intoxication", except for medicinal/household/cooking purposes. It is not a cannabis statute and must not be presented as one; its application to hemp beverages is AG-opinion reasoning only, with no confirmed court holding located. "It shall be unlawful for any person, firm, corporation or association, to sell, barter, or give away, or keep for such purposes any sweet spirits of nitre, liquid ginger preparation, elixir of orange peel, pear extract, or any like drug, compound, bitters, elixir or preparation of any kind whatsoever, except where otherwise legalized under the laws of this state, which when drunk to excess, in the form sold, will produce intoxication, except when the same is kept, sold, bartered or given away for either medicinal, or household purposes, or for uses in cooking, baking, and purposes incidental to the treatment of disease." (via Lexology summary of the AG opinion — [VERIFY] against official § 97-31-5.) Pre-existing statute; AG beverage opinion date [VERIFY — the Lexology piece is undated in the snippet; do not date it]. https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=7ceef611-389a-4fac-bca0-5a8f937bb423

15 Miss. Admin. Code Part 22 — MSDH Medical Cannabis Program (Subparts 1–7 as adopted) MSDH The MSDH programme rules: definitions, licensing of cultivation/processing/testing/research/transportation/disposal, product safety/laboratory requirements, advertising/marketing (Subpart 3), tracking/labelling (Subpart 4 in the 2021 proposal numbering; Subpart 6 in the adopted processing rules — numbering has shifted between drafts, so cite the rule number, not the subpart name, and [VERIFY] the current SOS compilation), packaging, facility rules. The adopted compilation referenced in this research is the Board-adopted 11 Oct 2023 revision (with a 12 Jan 2024 blackline). Whether a later amendment has superseded it is [VERIFY] against the Secretary of State's Administrative Code. Packaging (Rule 6.1.4, adopted rules): "Labels, packages, and containers shall not be attractive to minors and shall not contain any content that reasonably appears to target children, including toys, cartoon characters, or any color scheme, image, graphic, or feature that might reasonably be expected to make the product label, package, or container entice or appealing to children." […] "Packages and labels shall not contain product names related to candy or candies or any spellings thereof (e.g., kandy, kandies, etc.) or feature images that look like candy." […] "Packaging must shall contain a label that reads: 'Keep out of reach of children'." […] "All usable medical cannabis and cannabis products must shall be packaged in childresistant containers at the point of sale or other transfer to a patient…" — Labelling contents (MMCP FAQ restating Subpart 6): name, batch number, seed-to-sale unique identifier, net quantity/weight + MMCEU equivalency, onset time, ingredients/allergens, nutrition panel (ingested products), total THC and CBD as verified by the testing facility, terpenoid profile if applicable, harm notice, and for edibles when practicable the Mississippi standard cannabis symbol (required on packaging as of 1 July 2023). Buffer rule (Rule 7.4.3, transportation-entity rules, same 1,000-ft / 500-ft-entry test as the statute): "A medical cannabis establishment, inclusive of a cannabis transportation entity, shall not be within 1,000 feet of the nearest property boundary line of a school, church or child care facility which exists or has acquired necessary real property for the operation of such facility before the date of the medical cannabis establishment application unless the entity has received approval from the school, church or child care facility and received the applicable waiver from their licensing agency, provided that the main point of entry of the cannabis establishment is not located within five hundred (500) feet of the nearest property boundary line of any school, church or child care facility." Board-adopted 11 Oct 2023; blackline 12 Jan 2024. Current SOS compilation [VERIFY].

Title 30 (licensing-board rules incorporating the Act) Various boards (e.g. Nursing) Board rules restating § 41-137-3(r) for practitioner scope — e.g. the Nursing board print restating the debilitating-condition list. These are restatements, not independent cannabis law; cite the statute, not the board rule, for the condition list. See § 41-137-3(r) quotation above. [VERIFY] per board.

Regulations NOT found / not applicable: No Mississippi regulation was located that (a) sets a minimum age, permit, registration, testing or labelling regime for hemp-derived cannabinoid products sold outside the medical programme; (b) sets a THC-beverage rule; or (c) responds to PL 119-37/PL 119-103. Those gaps are substantive findings, not omissions — see §1.6.
