1.3 Penalties, cultivation, consumption, product forms and potency caps

1.3.1 Possession penalties for non-patients — Miss. Code § 41-29-139(c) (simple possession)

Source opened directly: https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-29/article-3/section-41-29-139/ (2025 Code reproduction; [VERIFY] against official Code).

First-offence fine-only threshold — YES, but narrow and not a civil offence. The threshold is 30 grams or less of marijuana, or 10 grams or less of synthetic cannabinoids.

Amount / circumstance Classification in the statute text Penalty (verbatim substance)
≤30 g marijuana or ≤10 g synthetic cannabinoids, first conviction Fine only as written (the statute does not call it a misdemeanour or a civil offence in this paragraph; secondary sources variously call it "civil", "misdemeanour with fine only", or "decriminalised" — do not adopt any of those labels without noting the statute's own silence. The "decriminalisation" label (year disputed, 1977 vs 1978 - Secondary sources only, Verify) in secondary sources refers to this fine-only, summons-enforceable treatment, not to legalisation.) "by a fine of not less than One Hundred Dollars ($100.00) nor more than Two Hundred Fifty Dollars ($250.00). The provisions of this paragraph (2)(A) may be enforceable by summons if the offender provides proof of identity satisfactory to the arresting officer and gives written promise to appear in court satisfactory to the arresting officer, as directed by the summons."
Same amount, second conviction within 2 years Misdemeanour "a fine of Two Hundred Fifty Dollars ($250.00), not more than sixty (60) days in the county jail, and mandatory participation in a drug education program approved by the Division of Alcohol and Drug Abuse of the State Department of Mental Health, unless the court enters a written finding that a drug education program is inappropriate." (The 2025 print of § 41-29-139(c)(2)(A) contains no five-day minimum for second or third ≤30 g convictions; the 5-60 days / 5 days-6 months figures in older prints and secondary guides must not be quoted for current law.)
Same amount, third or subsequent conviction within 2 years Misdemeanour "a fine of not less than Two Hundred Fifty Dollars ($250.00) nor more than One Thousand Dollars ($1,000.00) and confinement for not more than six (6) months in the county jail." (Older prints add "not less than five days" — same [VERIFY] note.)
First/second conviction record Private, nonpublic record, expunged "the courts shall forward a report of the conviction to the Mississippi Bureau of Narcotics which shall make and maintain a private, nonpublic record for a period not to exceed two (2) years from the date of conviction. The private, nonpublic record shall be solely for the use of the courts in determining the penalties which attach upon conviction under this paragraph (2)(A) and shall not constitute a criminal record for the purpose of private or administrative inquiry and the record of each conviction shall be expunged at the end of the period of two (2) years following the date of such conviction"
>1 g but ≤30 g marijuana (or ≤10 g synthetic) in a motor vehicle, in the area normally occupied by driver/passengers (trunk excluded; glove/utility compartment counts as occupied area), operator of the vehicle Misdemeanour "may be fined not more than One Thousand Dollars ($1,000.00) or confined for not more than ninety (90) days in the county jail, or both." This is the trap secondary sources flag: the same 8 g that draws a $100–$250 fine at home can draw up to 90 days in jail in a console.
>30 g to <250 g Felony (simple possession tier) "by a fine of not more than One Thousand Dollars ($1,000.00), or confinement in the county jail for not more than one (1) year, or both; or by a fine of not more than Three Thousand Dollars ($3,000.00), or imprisonment in the custody of the Department of Corrections for not more than three (3) years, or both"
250 g to <500 g Felony "by imprisonment for not less than two (2) years nor more than eight (8) years or by a fine of not more than Fifty Thousand Dollars ($50,000.00), or both"
500 g to <1 kg Felony "by imprisonment for not less than four (4) years nor more than sixteen (16) years or a fine of not more than Two Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars ($250,000.00), or both"
1 kg to <5 kg Felony "by imprisonment for not less than six (6) years nor more than twenty-four (24) years or a fine of not more than Five Hundred Thousand Dollars ($500,000.00), or both"
≥5 kg Felony "by imprisonment for not less than ten (10) years nor more than thirty (30) years or a fine of not more than One Million Dollars ($1,000,000.00), or both"

Other § 41-29-139 penalties that apply to non-patients (transfer / possession with intent / manufacture — § 41-29-139(a)–(b)): For marijuana, transfer/possession-with-intent/manufacture tiers are lower than simple-possession felony tiers at the same weight in some bands and must not be conflated with them: - ≤30 g: ≤3 years or ≤$3,000, or both; - >30 g to <250 g: ≤5 years or ≤$5,000, or both; - 250 g to <500 g: 3–10 years or ≤$15,000, or both; - 500 g to <1 kg: 5–20 years or ≤$20,000, or both. The statute as opened stops the marijuana transfer tier at <1 kg; penalties for ≥1 kg on a transfer/manufacture charge are [VERIFY] — do not extrapolate the simple-possession tiers to transfer charges. Source: same § 41-29-139 page, § (b)(2)(A).

Driver's-licence consequence: Secondary sources state any drug conviction results in a 6-month driver's-licence suspension. The statutory basis (§ 63-1-71 or § 41-29-139(i) in older prints) was not opened in this session — [VERIFY] before stating it as law.

Paraphernalia: Secondary sources state up to 6 months / $1,000 for paraphernalia possession. The paraphernalia statute (§ 41-29-139(d) / § 41-29-153 in some prints) was not opened — [VERIFY]. Do not quote a paraphernalia penalty as confirmed.

1.3.2 Cultivation penalties — home grow is PROHIBITED

Confirmed: home grow is prohibited for everyone — patients, caregivers, and non-patients alike. The Act's definition of "medical use" "does not include: 1) The cultivation of cannabis unless the cultivation is done by a cannabis cultivation facility" (§ 41-137-3(dd), via the 2025 definition print). MSDH's toolkit lists as a prohibited use: "Growing cannabis for personal use (home cultivation is not permitted)". All cultivation, harvesting, processing and packaging must take place in an enclosed, locked, secure licensed facility (§ 41-137-39(5)).

Penalty for unlicensed cultivation: There is no separate "home grow" penalty section. Unlicensed cultivation is "manufacture" under § 41-29-139(a)(1) ("manufacture, distribute, dispense or possess with intent to… manufacture…"), punishable under the transfer/manufacture tiers in §1.3.1 above, by weight of marijuana produced/possessed. Plant-count thresholds (as opposed to weight) for cultivation were not located in § 41-29-139 as opened — [VERIFY] whether any plant-count provision exists elsewhere (e.g. § 41-29-139(f) enhancement provisions, not opened). Do not state a plant-count penalty.

1.3.3 Public consumption and smoking rules

  • Smoking (including vaping and any inhalation) in a public place or in a motor vehicle is not authorised (§ 41-137-29(2)(c), quoted in §1.2.1). MMCP's paraphrase, opened directly: "The law does not authorize you to use medical cannabis in a public place or in a motor vehicle." (https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/node/16)
  • Private residence is the permitted setting in MSDH guidance; MSDH regulations define "public place" broadly (churches, areas open to the general public, government-owned/controlled property including streets and sidewalks) — that regulatory definition was reported by a secondary source and is [VERIFY] against 15 Miss. Admin. Code Part 22 before quoting.
  • Open containers: A secondary bill text (HB 1572, 2024, not enacted as quoted) would have made open-container possession in a public place a $100–$200 misdemeanour; it is not presented here as law. Whether a current open-container offence exists for medical cannabis is [VERIFY].
  • Impaired operation: Operating/navigating/being in actual physical control of a motor vehicle, aircraft, train, motorboat or other conveyance in violation of §§ 59-23-7, 63-11-30 or federal law as a result of medical use is not authorised (§ 41-137-29(2)(d)). No per se THC blood limit for driving was located in this research; Mississippi's DUI law is impairment-based as applied to cannabis on the sources found — [VERIFY] against §§ 63-11-30 and 59-23-7 before stating a numeric limit or its absence as settled law. (Full driving/expungement treatment belongs to Part 12, not this file.)
  • Correctional facilities: Possession/use in a correctional facility is not authorised unless the facility elects to allow it (§ 41-137-29(2)(b)).

1.3.4 Allowed medical product forms and THC potency caps

Forms allowed (statute + MSDH): The Act allows flower, concentrates/extracts, oils, tinctures, edibles (including beverages as a form of edible cannabis product — § 41-137-3(u)(iii) lists "foodstuffs, beverages, extracts, oils, tinctures, lozenges and other similar products"), topicals/ointments/soaps/lotions, suppositories, and other cannabis products made only by a licensed processing (or research) facility. Smoking/vaping by a cardholder in a private place is permitted — the Act restricts where smoking occurs, not whether flower may be smoked, unlike Initiative 65A's terminal-only smoking limit (which never became law).

Forms NOT allowed outside the programme: Any intoxicating hemp-derived form (delta-8/10 gummies, THCA flower/vapes, HHC products) sold outside a licensed dispensary — on the AG's reading (§1.6.4). Inside the programme, a product's cannabinoid origin (cannabis-derived vs hemp-derived) is irrelevant; what matters is that it was made by a licensed processor, tested, tracked, and sold by a licensed dispensary within caps.

Potency caps — § 41-137-39(11) (verbatim, opened directly):

"For purposes of this chapter, total THC is defined as THCA multiplied by .877 plus THC Delta 9 and all other psychoactive forms or isomers of THC added together. A medical cannabis establishment shall not sell cannabis flower or trim that has a potency of greater than thirty percent (30%) total THC. A medical cannabis dispensary shall not sell cannabis tinctures, oils or concentrates that have a potency of greater than sixty percent (60%) total THC. Cannabis products that have a potency of over thirty percent (30%) total THC shall be clearly labeled as 'extremely potent.' Edible cannabis products, including food or drink products, that have been combined with usable cannabis or cannabis products shall be physically demarked and labeled with a clear determination of how much total THC is in a single-serving size and how much THC is in the entire package." "A medical cannabis product shall contain a notice of harm regarding the use of cannabis products. Edible cannabis products shall be homogenized to ensure uniform disbursement of cannabinoids throughout the product. All molded edible cannabis products shall be presented in the form of geometric shapes and shall not be molded to contain any images or characters designed or likely to appeal to minors, such as cartoons, toys, animals or children."

Product type Cap (current law) Notes
Flower / trim 30% total THC (hard cap — may not be sold above it) Total THC = THCA×0.877 + delta-9 + all other psychoactive THC forms/isomers.
Tinctures, oils, concentrates 60% total THC (hard cap) HB 895 (2026) would have removed this cap — vetoed 26 Mar 2026, so the cap stands.
Edibles / infused products No separate % cap in § 41-137-39(11); controlled by (a) the MMCEU quantity limit (1 MMCEU = 1 g total THC since 1 July 2025), (b) demarcation + per-serving / per-package labelling, (c) homogenisation, (d) geometric-shape rule, (e) ±10% label-accuracy rule in MSDH rules (see §1.7.1). Any secondary claim of a "10 mg per serving / 100 mg per package" Mississippi medical-edible cap was not found in the statute and must not be quoted — that figure appears in other states' laws and in a failed Mississippi hemp bill proposal (see §1.6.5), not in § 41-137-39.
Topicals / suppositories / ointments / soaps / lotions (nonconsumable) No potency cap stated in § 41-137-39(11); no possession limit (§ 41-137-39(10): "There shall not be a possession limit on nonconsumable medical cannabis, including, but not limited to, suppositories, ointments, soaps, and lotions or other topical agents.") Non-cardholder 21+ topical sale allowed (§ 41-137-39(21)) — the only non-cardholder medical-cannabis sale in the Act.
Vapes / inhalables Governed by the underlying product's cap (flower 30% / concentrate 60%) — no separate vape cap in the statute text opened. Smoking/vaping location rules in §1.3.3 apply.
Plant-growth-regulator cannabis Prohibited entirely — a cultivation facility shall not cultivate it and a dispensary shall not sell/transfer/provide it (§ 41-137-39(20)). Definition: a plant whose growth/structure was modified using plant growth hormones.

1.4 Medical programme

1.4.1 Qualifying conditions (verbatim list)

Miss. Code § 41-137-3(r) (see §1.2.1 for the full verbatim definition). Named conditions (count them as 20 named items, plus the symptom-based route): 1. Cancer; 2. Parkinson's disease; 3. Huntington's disease; 4. Muscular dystrophy; 5. Glaucoma; 6. Spastic quadriplegia; 7. Positive status for HIV; 8. AIDS; 9. Hepatitis; 10. ALS; 11. Crohn's disease; 12. Ulcerative colitis; 13. Sickle-cell anemia; 14. Alzheimer's disease; 15. Agitation of dementia; 16. PTSD; 17. Autism; 18. Pain refractory to appropriate opioid management; 19. Diabetic/peripheral neuropathy; 20. Spinal cord disease or severe injury — plus treatment of any of these. Symptom-based route (§ 41-137-3(r)(ii)): "A chronic, terminal or debilitating disease or medical condition, or its treatment, that produces one or more of the following: cachexia or wasting syndrome, chronic pain, severe or intractable nausea, seizures, or severe and persistent muscle spasms, including, but not limited to, those characteristic of multiple sclerosis." Note: multiple sclerosis is not itself a named condition; it qualifies only via the muscle-spasm symptom route. Secondary lists that name "multiple sclerosis" or "epilepsy" or "seizures" as standalone named conditions are imprecise — seizures qualify via (r)(ii), epilepsy only insofar as it produces seizures. Petition route (§ 41-137-3(r)(iii) + § 41-137-17): Any other serious condition added by MSDH on petition by any Mississippi resident; MSDH to approve/deny within 60 days (MMCP FAQ). No granted petition / added condition was confirmed in this research — [VERIFY] before listing any. Comparison to Initiative 65: Initiative 65 listed 22 conditions in secondary summaries; the Act's list is a legislative list, not the initiative list. Do not present the initiative list as current law.

1.4.2 Practitioner registration and certification

  • Who may certify: A "practitioner" registered with MSDH: MD, DO, nurse practitioner, physician assistant, or optometrist, acting within scope of practice and in a bona fide practitioner-patient relationship (MMCP FAQ, opened via search result: https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/node/21 — "they must be a licensed practitioner (MD, DO, Nurse Practitioner, Physician Assistant, or Optometrist) that has been registered with the Mississippi State Department of Health"). Practitioners do not write a prescription; they issue a written certification. No practitioner is required to issue one.
  • Education: Minimum 8 hours of continuing education in medical cannabis to register; 5 hours annually after the first year to maintain registration (§ 41-137-5(7)(a)).
  • Certification validity: 12 months unless the practitioner specifies shorter (§ 41-137-5(2)(b)). HB 895's 24-month extension was vetoed.
  • Assessment: In-person assessment required, except telemedicine for homebound/bedbound patients as certified by a different practitioner with a bona fide relationship (§ 41-137-5(2)(c), as amended by SB 2748). Renewal-by-telemedicine rules beyond the homebound/bedbound exception are [VERIFY] — secondary sources describe a "same practitioner previously seen in person" renewal route that was not confirmed in the statute text opened.
  • Six-month follow-up: Mandatory — "not less than six (6) months after the date of issuance" (§ 41-137-5(5)). May be with a different registered practitioner. HB 895 would have made it discretionary — vetoed.
  • Drug testing of patients: No agency/board may require a practitioner to require a drug test as a condition of certification; a practitioner may require one within scope of practice (§ 41-137-5(3)).
  • Minors: Only MD/DO may certify a minor (§ 41-137-5(8)); parent/guardian must be present and sign consent (§ 41-137-5(2)(d)); see §1.4.7.
  • Ages 18–25: A patient aged 18 to 25 is not eligible unless two practitioners from separate medical practices have diagnosed the condition after in-person consultation, one of whom must be an MD/DO; the separate-practice requirement does not apply if the patient is homebound or held a card before age 18 (§ 41-137-39(16)). The practitioner reviewing records: if a recommending practitioner is not the patient's primary-care practitioner, they must review the diagnosing practitioner's records.
  • Dispensary staff may not certify: "A medical cannabis dispensary agent or employee shall not issue a written certification" (§ 41-137-39(15)); dispensary employees need 8 hours CE first year, 5 hours/year after, as regulated by MDOR, to be certified to work in a dispensary.

1.4.3 Patient and caregiver cards

  • Application (resident patient): Written certification issued within the 6 months immediately preceding application; application/renewal fee; name, address, Social Security number, date of birth; practitioner's name/address/telephone; caregiver(s)' name/address/SSN/date of birth; documentation if more than one caregiver is needed due to age/medical condition (§ 41-137-23(1)). If the patient cannot submit due to age/medical condition, the person responsible for medical decisions may submit on their behalf (§ 41-137-23(2)).
  • Timeline: MSDH must approve or deny a completed application/renewal within 10 days; card issued within 5 days of approval (§ 41-137-23(3)). MMCP states the same 10-day review / 5-day card availability in its FAQ (https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/faq?os=app&).
  • Denial grounds (exhaustive in the section): Failure to provide required information/materials; prior revocation; false information; failure to meet other chapter requirements (§ 41-137-23(8)). Caregiver denial adds: not meeting the § 41-137-3 definition, or being under 21 and not the patient's parent/legal guardian (§ 41-137-23(9)). Denial is a final MSDH action subject to judicial review under § 41-137-59 (§ 41-137-23(11)).
  • Designated caregiver definition (§ 41-137-3(s)): Agreed to assist; assists no more than 5 registered qualifying patients, unless each resides in / is admitted to a health-care / residential-care / day-care facility where the caregiver is employed; at least 21 unless the parent/legal guardian of each patient assisted; no disqualifying felony conviction. A caregiver needs a card for each patient (§ 41-137-23(3)(b)); an entity caregiver (health-care/residential/day-care facility) may hold a single card regardless of patient count, with individual cards for employees who may transport (§ 41-137-23(6)).
  • Disqualifying felony (§ 41-137-3(t)): (i) crime of violence as defined in § 97-3-2; (ii) a crime defined as violent where committed and classified as a felony there; or (iii) a state/federal controlled-substances felony, including service of probation/incarceration/supervised release within the previous 5 years without a further similar offence since — except a conviction for conduct for which the chapter would likely have prevented conviction but for occurring before 2 Feb 2022. Establishment employees: no person convicted of a disqualifying felony, and no person under 21, may be employed (§ 41-137-39(2)).

1.4.4 Fees

Statutory fee schedule (§ 41-137-41(xx), quoted in §1.2.1):

Card / item Fee
Qualifying patient application $25
Designated caregiver application $25
Designated caregiver criminal background fee $37
Renewal or replacement of a card $25
Nonresident patient card $75
Qualifying patient application / renewal — Medicaid participant $15
Qualifying patient application — disabled veteran or disabled first responder Waived (proof: practitioner documentation, Social Security Disability documentation, or 100% disabled-veteran determination under 38 CFR § 3.340(a) (2013))

Practitioner registration fees, if any, are [VERIFY] — no practitioner fee was located in § 41-137-41 as opened. Work-permit fee ($25, 5 years) is in § 41-137-39(19) and belongs to Part 4, noted here only for consistency. No insurance/Medicaid reimbursement: "No, Medicaid, nor private insurance, will pay for medical cannabis" (MMCP FAQ, https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/faq?os=app&, citing § 41-137-41 in the FAQ's paraphrase — the reimbursement bar is in § 41-137-13(1)(a)).

1.4.5 Monthly allowable amount — MMCEUs and conversion

Statute (§ 41-137-39(10),(12)–(14), opened directly): - Resident purchase: "A resident cardholder shall not obtain more than a total of twenty-four (24) MMCEUs of allowable medical cannabis in thirty (30) days from a dispensary or a combination of dispensaries." - Resident possession: "a total of twenty-eight (28) MMCEUs." - Nonresident purchase: 6 MMCEUs per week; 12 MMCEUs per consecutive 15 days. - Nonresident possession: 14 MMCEUs. - No possession limit on nonconsumable medical cannabis (suppositories, ointments, soaps, lotions, other topical agents). - Dispensaries must maintain internal confidential records of amounts dispensed and whether dispensed directly or via caregiver, and must verify via the seed-to-sale system that a sale would not push the cardholder over the allowable amount (§ 41-137-39(9),(12); § 41-137-5(6)).

Conversion (current, post-1 July 2025):

Product 1 MMCEU = 24 MMCEUs (30-day resident purchase max) = 28 MMCEUs (resident possession max) =
Flower 3.5 g 84 g (≈2.96 oz) 98 g
Concentrate 1 g total THC 24 g total THC 28 g total THC
Infused product (incl. edibles) 1 g total THC 24 g total THC 28 g total THC

History that must not be confused with current law: Before 1 July 2025, 1 MMCEU for concentrates was 1 g of concentrate itself, and for infused products 100 mg THC — so the old equivalents were 24 g concentrate / 2,400 mg THC per 30 days. Those figures still circulate in secondary guides (including the Bradley 2022 summary and some 2025 guides) and are wrong for current law after SB 2748. Before 1 July 2024 there was also a 6-MMCEU-per-week resident limit; it was removed (SB 2857, secondary reporting) so a resident may now buy the full 30-day amount at once. MSDH's allotment guidance is the operational conversion document: MMCP FAQ, https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/node/161 ("Allotment guidance can be found on our website" — the guidance PDF itself was not opened in this session; [VERIFY] its current URL and contents). Worked example (arithmetic, not medical advice): A resident buying only flower: 24 × 3.5 g = 84 g per 30 days. A resident buying only a 60%-THC concentrate: 24 MMCEUs = 24 g total THC, which at 60% potency is 40 g of concentrate product by weight — the MMCEU counts THC, not product weight, since 1 July 2025. A mixed basket is counted by summing MMCEUs across product types in the seed-to-sale system.

1.4.6 Out-of-state (nonresident) patient registration

  • Eligibility: A nonresident must submit (per § 41-137-41(xviii) rulemaking direction): (1) a practitioner's statement confirming a debilitating medical condition, and (2) documentation demonstrating the nonresident is allowed to possess medical cannabis/cannabis preparations in their home jurisdiction. In practice MSDH requires an active home-state medical card plus a qualifying condition (secondary synthesis — [VERIFY] the current MSDH nonresident application checklist before advising an applicant).
  • Timing: May apply up to 30 days before arriving in Mississippi (§ 41-137-39(14)).
  • Validity: 15 days per card; renewable for another 15-day period; maximum two separate 15-day periods in a 365-day period. The applicant may specify the desired validity period on the application.
  • Limits: 6/week, 12/15 days, 14 possession (see §1.4.5). Fee $75 (§1.4.4).
  • No reciprocity by card alone: A home-state card does not authorise purchase in Mississippi without a Mississippi nonresident card, and a Mississippi card does not authorise purchase in any other state (secondary synthesis consistent with the statute; the Act contains no reciprocity clause — [VERIFY] that no reciprocity amendment has been enacted, as HB 1152's out-of-state provision was vetoed and is not law).

1.4.7 Minors' rules

  • No minimum age to qualify (MSDH toolkit: "There is no minimum age requirement to qualify for medical cannabis in Mississippi. However, patients under the age of 18 must have a parent or legal guardian registered as their caregiver and responsible for administration and dosage.").
  • Certification only by MD/DO (§ 41-137-5(8)); parent/guardian present + signed consent (§ 41-137-5(2)(d)); MSDH may not issue a card under 18 unless the practitioner explained risks/benefits to the custodial parent/legal guardian with health-care-decision responsibility and that person consents in writing to acknowledge harms, allow use, serve as caregiver, and control acquisition/dosage/frequency (§ 41-137-23(5)).
  • Caregiver for a minor must be the custodial parent/legal guardian (MMCP guidance; the statute's under-21 caregiver exception is for a parent/legal guardian of the patient).
  • Entry: an establishment "shall not allow an individual who is younger than twenty-one (21) years old to enter the premises… unless the individual possesses a registry identification card and is accompanied by his or her legal guardian" (§ 41-137-39(17)).
  • Two-practitioner rule at 18–25 (§1.4.2) does not apply to under-18s (different rule) and does not apply if the patient held a card before 18.

1.5 Initiative 65, the Supreme Court ruling, and restoration

1.5.1 What Initiative 65 was

Initiative Measure No. 65 was a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment to create a medical marijuana programme, filed 30 July 2018 by Ashley Durval and certified by then-Secretary of State Delbert Hosemann on 4 September 2019. The Legislature proposed a legislative alternative, Initiative 65A, which was placed on the same ballot. In secondary summaries the contrast was: Initiative 65 — specified conditions, smoking allowed for qualifying patients, start date August 2021, free-market licensing, tax capped at 7%, regulated by MSDH; 65A — no specified conditions, smoking only for terminally ill patients (other forms for others), no specified start date, limited licence cap, Legislature to set the tax rate, agency to be named. Neither 65 nor 65A is law. Do not quote either measure's text as current law; the operative law is SB 2095.

1.5.2 2020 results (3 November 2020)

The ballot asked two questions: first, for/against either measure; second, a preference between 65 and 65A. Reporting differs by denominator, so both presentations are given and the conflict is flagged rather than smoothed over:

  • Contemporaneous / court-record figures (preferred for the "for either" and preference margins): "For Either" 689,840 (68%) to 326,311 (32%) with nearly all precincts reporting on the evening of 5 Nov 2020; Initiative 65 prevailed over 65A by 660,160 (74%) to 233,483 (26%) — as quoted in the Secretary of State's response brief in the litigation (https://live-bscr.pantheonsite.io/sites/default/files/fastcase/additionalPdfs/processed/Michael%20Watson%20-Brief%20-11.06.2020.pdf).
  • Certified-result summary (secondary): 68.52% voted for at least one proposal, of whom 73.7% supported Initiative 65 (https://www.esapllc.com/mssc-init65-2021/).
  • Vote-share-of-all-ballots presentation (secondary, different denominator): For either 61.65%, against both 28.32%, for 65 57.89%, for 65A 20.68% (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Mississippi_elections — secondary, citing the Secretary of State's 2020 General Election page, https://www.sos.ms.gov/Elections-Voting/Pages/2020-General-Election.aspx, which was not opened directly in this session).
  • Final-count note: One secondary source (Northside Sun) reports 65A earned 267,871 votes, or 33.9% of the 787,900 votes cast for either measure — a denominator again different from the 74% preference figure. Official certified totals must be taken from the Secretary of State's 2020 General Election results before republication — [VERIFY]. The one fact on which all sources agree: a large majority voted for medical marijuana, and Initiative 65 beat 65A by roughly three to one among those choosing between them.
  • Campaign-finance colour (secondary, Northside Sun): Mississippians for Compassionate Care raised $4.2M (to 10 Nov 2020), including $1.675M from Rep. Joel Bomgar; opposition (Mississippi Association of Realtors committee) raised $312,296. Dated secondary material only.

1.5.3 The Supreme Court ruling — Butler v. Watson (OPINION, not statute)

  • Case: In re Initiative Measure No. 65; Mary Hawkins Butler, in her individual and official capacities as Mayor of Madison, and the City of Madison v. Michael Watson, Secretary of State, et al., No. 2020-IA-01199-SCT, 338 So.3d 599 (Miss. 14 May 2021), 6–3.
  • Challenge: Filed 26 October 2020, days before the election, by Mayor Butler and the City of Madison, challenging the Secretary of State's certification of Initiative 65's signatures.
  • Constitutional provision: Miss. Const. art. 15, § 273(3) — signatures equal to 12% of votes cast in the last gubernatorial election, with no more than one-fifth (20%) from any one congressional district (older summaries phrase it as an equal-distribution requirement across five districts; the operative text is the one-fifth cap applied to five districts).
  • Reasoning: Mississippi had five congressional districts when § 273 was written, but has had four since the 2000 Census / 2001 reapportionment. It is therefore mathematically impossible to satisfy the five-district distribution requirement. Justice Coleman's opinion (as quoted in secondary summaries): "it is impossible for any petition to meet the requirements and has been impossible since congressional reapportionment in 2001" and "To work in today's reality, it will need amending — something that lies beyond the power of the Supreme Court."
  • Effect: The certification was unconstitutional; the Court voided the certification and any subsequent proceeding, including the November 2020 election results for Initiative 65. The ruling also voided the initiative process itself as currently written — it did not merely strike one measure. Two earlier voter-approved initiatives (Voter ID, eminent-domain limits) were left exposed to the same logic, which is why the Secretary of State urged a legislative fix.
  • No rehearing: Secretary Watson announced the state would not seek rehearing, saying it "would simply delay the inevitable" and urging the Governor to call a special session (https://www.northsidesun.com/politics-state-top-stories/watson-says-state-wont-appeal-initiative-65-ruling).
  • What the ruling did NOT do: It did not hold medical marijuana unconstitutional, did not bar the Legislature from enacting a medical programme by statute (which it did in SB 2095), and did not decide any federal question. The full opinion text was not opened in this session — quotations above are via secondary summaries of the opinion and are [VERIFY against the official opinion] before verbatim republication.

1.5.4 Restoration efforts — current status: NOT restored

Restoration requires a constitutional amendment: two-thirds of each house to place it on the ballot, then a voter majority. No such amendment has passed.

  • 2022–2024: Attempts in each session failed; in 2024 the Senate narrowly passed a measure (26–21, short of the two-thirds needed to place it on the ballot) that would have raised passage to 67% and required 200,000+ signatures across four districts; House–Senate agreement was not reached (https://www.starherald.net/reinstating-ballot-initiative-not-top-mind-lawmakers-they-return-capitol-677c1cb76df19?e_term_id=13016&e_sort_order=).
  • 2025: Sen. Jeremy England's proposal (statutory initiatives only, not constitutional amendments; 10% of active registered voters ≈189,000 signatures, no more than one-third from any one congressional district; Legislature barred from vetoing/changing an adopted initiative for two years except by three-fifths vote in extenuating circumstances) was debated 11 Feb 2025 and did not pass (https://www.mississippifreepress.org/mississippi-voters-still-lack-ballot-initiative-5-years-after-lawmakers-vowed-to-restore-it/).
  • 2026 (most recent, failed): 17 measures filed. 15 died in committee 3 Feb 2026, including three identical Senate resolutions to amend § 273: SC 515 (Sen. Seymour), SC 517 (Sen. Blackmon), SC 519 (Sen. Dupree). Two England measures got past committee: SC 518 (constitutional amendment) was tabled 11 Feb 2026; SB 2919 (bringing forward the initiative code sections) died on the Senate calendar 12 Feb 2026. A separate England bill described in one secondary source would have required referendum signatures from 10% of active registered voters (≈189,000) with no more than one-third from any one district, and died in the Senate 13 Feb 2026 (date differs by one day between secondary sources — [VERIFY] the journal). SB 2921 (DeBar, requiring the Legislature to honour the intent/substance of a citizen initiative when drafting an alternative) died in committee 3 Feb 2026 (https://legiscan.com/MS/text/SB2921). JD Supra's 2026 session recap summarises: "Legislation to restore the state's ballot initiative died before a floor vote in either body." (https://Www.Jdsupra.Com/legalnews/mississippi-2026-legislative-session-2292921/)
  • Public opinion (secondary, polling only): A Speaker's poll reported in October 2026 found 72% support / 7.9% opposition for restoring the process (49.2% strongly support), with Republican support 78–4 and Democratic 66–11, but only 5.6% ranking it their top House-election issue (https://msindy.org/p/speaker-whites-poll-shows-voters). Pollster, sample size, dates and methodology were not stated in the piece as retrieved — [VERIFY] before citing as a poll; do not present it as an official result.
  • Consequence for this commission: As of 25 Oct 2026 there is no citizen-initiative route in Mississippi for adult-use legalisation, decriminalisation, hemp reform, or any other cannabis change. Every change must go through the Legislature (and, for constitutional change, the voters via a legislatively referred amendment).

1.5.5 Choctaw referendum — tribal, not a state initiative

Included here because it is easily confused with a state ballot measure. The Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians' Referendum 2025-01 (10 June 2025) asked tribal members only: "Do you support the Tribe developing legislation to decriminalize and regulate the possession, production, and distribution of marijuana on Tribal lands?" It passed (unofficial 55%–45%; 1,367 to 1,110 in one report; final after absentees 57%–43% in the NORML update — conflict flagged). It authorised a feasibility study (≈$100,000 consultant cost in secondary reporting), not sales. The Tribe is Mississippi's only federally recognised tribe, with 11,000+ members and ~35,000 acres across 10 counties in eastern Mississippi. Current tribal law, per secondary reporting, already removes criminal penalties for Mississippi medical cardholders possessing legal limits on tribal lands — [VERIFY] against tribal law; no tribal code section was located. No tribal cannabis ordinance, regulator, licence, or retail sale was located as of 25 Oct 2026. Full tribal treatment belongs to Part 10, not this file. Sources: https://www.marijuanamoment.net/mississippi-indian-tribe-approves-marijuana-referendum-making-it-first-jurisdiction-in-the-state-poised-to-legalize/ ; https://ganjapreneur.com/mississippi-band-of-choctaw-indians-approve-referendum-allowing-tribe-to-explore-cannabis-legalization/ ; http://norml.org/blog/2025/06/11/mississippi-indian-tribe-approves-referendum-regulating-the-possession-production-and-distribution-of-marijuana-on-tribal-lands/

1.6 Hemp

1.6.1 THC limits and how THC is measured — two different regimes, do not conflate them

Regime Limit Measurement
Hemp (cultivation / plant definition) — §§ 69-25-201 et seq. (Hemp Cultivation Act) + § 41-29-113 exemption 0.3% delta-9 THC on a dry-weight basis THCA x 0.877 plus delta-9 THC, capped at 0.3% on a dry-weight basis, under Mississippi's own hemp definition (Miss. Code sections 69-25-201 et seq.). Pre-harvest field testing under USDA rules for USDA licensees.
Medical cannabis (product potency) — § 41-137-39(11) Flower 30% / concentrates 60% (see §1.3.4) Total THC = THCA × 0.877 + delta-9 THC + all other psychoactive forms/isomers of THC added together. This total-THC formula is a medical-programme potency rule, not the hemp definition — but secondary sources note Mississippi agencies "look at total THC" for hemp products too, which is part of the THCA uncertainty in §1.6.4. Mississippi hemp law DOES use the 0.877 formula in its hemp definition (THCA x 0.877 plus delta-9, capped at 0.3%) — [VERIFY].
Federal hemp definition after 11 Dec 2026 (given baseline) Full total-THC definition + 0.4 mg total THC per container cap Total THC (federal definition, given) — Mississippi has no conforming state definition located (see §1.6.7).

1.6.2 The state hemp programme that does not operate

See §1.2.1, §§ 69-25-201 et seq. In full: SB 2725 (2020) authorised a state plan; no appropriation; MDAC does not issue licences; USDA licenses under the Domestic Hemp Production Program (HeMP platform, FBI criminal-history report, 10-year controlled-substance-felony bar, 3-year licence term unless Mississippi elects to run a state programme). MDAC page opened directly: https://www.mdac.ms.gov/programs/hemp-cultivation-in-ms/ Consequence: There is no Mississippi hemp grower/processor/handler licence type to list in this file's statute table beyond the unimplemented Act, and no MDAC hemp registry to cite. Hemp licence detail belongs to Part 7; the point here is the legal vacuum that makes the § 41-29-113 phrase "hemp or hemp products regulated under Sections 69-25-201 through 69-25-221" ambiguous — if nothing is "regulated under" those sections in practice, does the exemption bite at all? That is the legal question the AG opinion answers one way and hemp sellers answer the other way. It is unresolved by any court holding located in this research — [VERIFY] before advising any seller.

1.6.3 What hemp products are clearly lawful (on the statute text alone)

  • Hemp fibre / industrial products from stalks, processed plant materials for industrial purposes, animal feed with sterilised seeds, and personal-care products with sterilised-seed oil that do not cause THC to enter the body — expressly exempted in § 41-29-113 (see §1.2.1).
  • FDA-approved hemp-derived ingestible products (§ 41-29-113(vi)) — in practice FDA-approved CBD drugs, not over-the-counter CBD.
  • Non-intoxicating CBD/CBG/CBN products are widely sold in Mississippi and are described by secondary sources as permitted — but no Mississippi statute was located that affirmatively legalises retail CBD, and the AG opinion's logic (only FDA-approved ingestibles are exempt) would, read literally, reach non-intoxicating ingestible CBD too. Secondary sources reconcile this by treating the AG opinion as aimed at intoxicating products; the opinion's quoted sentence says "product derived from the hemp plant designed for human ingestion and/or consumption that is not approved by the FDA" without an intoxication qualifier in the sentence as reported. This is the central hemp ambiguity in Mississippi — flag it, do not resolve it by assertion. Enforcement practice (whether CBD retailers are in fact prosecuted) is [VERIFY].

1.6.4 Hemp-derived cannabinoid products — delta-8, delta-9, THCA, HHC, delta-10, THCP/THCB

Position stated plainly: Outside a licensed medical dispensary, intoxicating hemp-derived cannabinoids are treated as prohibited in Mississippi by the Attorney General and by enforcement reporting, but no enacted statute names delta-8, delta-10, HHC, THCP or THCB as banned, and no hemp-product permit/age/testing/labelling statute exists to comply with. A business cannot "comply" with a Mississippi hemp-THC regime because there is none — the only compliant routes are (a) the medical programme, or (b) an FDA-approved product.

Cannabinoid / product Status in Mississippi (this research) Basis
Delta-8 THC (hemp-derived, any form) Prohibited outside the medical programme, on the AG's reading; Schedule I tetrahydrocannabinol under § 41-29-113's broad isomer/derivative language, with only the hemp/FDA exemptions above. Secondary "HB 1547 banned delta-8" claims are wrong as to bill/year — HB 1547 (2019) restated § 41-29-113; it did not enact a delta-8 ban. § 41-29-113 text via https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2019/pdf/HB/1500-1599/HB1547PS.pdf ; AG opinion reporting https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/us-states/mississippi/news/15748808/consumable-hemp-products-illegal-without-fda-approval-mississippi-ag-says
Delta-10 THC Same as delta-8 (isomer/derivative language; AG logic). No separate statutory mention located. Same as above.
THCA (hemp-derived flower, vapes, concentrates) Highest uncertainty. Federally, pre-decarboxylation delta-9 ≤0.3% hemp is the Farm Bill test; Mississippi's medical total-THC formula (THCA×0.877) and the AG consumable-product position both point against hemp THCA, and secondary sources uniformly describe hemp THCA as not permitted outside dispensaries. But no Mississippi court holding or statute naming THCA was located. Mark THCA as prohibited on the AG reading, [VERIFY] for any court test. Inside a dispensary, THCA-containing medical products are lawful within caps (total THC counts THCA). https://www.buddingtrendsblog.com/2025/06/maybe-so-maybe-not-mississippi-ags-office-opines-that-mississippi-law-prohibits-most-consumable-hemp-products-while-recognizing-opinions-limitations/ ; https://hemphop.co/blogs/news/is-thca-legal-in-mississippi-thca-mississippi (secondary, July 2025 AG update framing)
HHC, THCP, THCB and other synthesised/converted cannabinoids Prohibited on the same AG / § 41-29-113 derivative/isomer logic, per secondary sources. No statutory naming located. [VERIFY] for any specific enforcement. https://burningdaily.com/blogs/learn/mississippi-cannabis-hemp-laws (secondary, updated 12 July 2026)
Hemp-derived delta-9 THC (e.g. low-dose edibles/beverages at ≤0.3% dry weight) Not affirmatively legalised by any Mississippi statute located. The 0.3% figure is a plant definition, not a finished-product safe harbour in Mississippi law. The AG opinion reaches any non-FDA-approved ingestible hemp product, which includes delta-9 edibles/beverages. Secondary proposals (HB 1676 as described) would have drawn a line at 0.5 mg total THC/serving or 2.5 mg/package for "intoxicating" products — that proposal did not become law and must not be quoted as a limit. AG opinion reporting, above; HB 1676 description via https://legalclarity.org/are-cannabis-edibles-legal-in-mississippi/ (secondary, [VERIFY] bill number/status)
CBD, CBG, CBN (non-intoxicating) Widely sold; no affirmative retail statute located; AG-opinion scope ambiguity in §1.6.3 applies. Do not state a CBD age limit, testing, or labelling rule for Mississippi — none was located. [UNAVAILABLE — no MS CBD retail statute located]
Hemp flower for smoking (non-intoxicating, ≤0.3% delta-9) Secondary sources say smoking hemp is not itself prohibited but advise against public smoking/driving because hemp is indistinguishable from marijuana by odour/appearance. No Mississippi hemp-smoking ban or permission statute was located. [VERIFY]. https://mississippistatecannabis.org/hemp (secondary)

AG opinion — exact quoted sentence and limits (11 June 2025, Fitch to Rep. Lee Yancey):

"Except for products possessed in strict accordance with the provisions of the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act, the possession – with intent to sell, barter, transfer, manufacture, distribute or dispense – of a product derived from the hemp plant designed for human ingestion and/or consumption that is not approved by the United States FDA is prohibited under Mississippi's Uniform Controlled Substances Law." (as quoted in https://ganjapreneur.com/mississippi-ag-says-intoxicating-hemp-products-are-prohibited-under-state-law/) Limits stated in the opinion itself (via reporting): "Because the cultivation of hemp in Mississippi is legalized, licensed, and controlled by federal law, a complete response to your request is outside the scope of an official opinion" (https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/us-states/mississippi/news/15748808/consumable-hemp-products-illegal-without-fda-approval-mississippi-ag-says). The opinion answered Rep. Yancey's questions after his bill HB 1502 (2025) died on the calendar when the Legislature adjourned 3 April 2025 (per Cannabis Business Times; bill number/status [VERIFY] on billstatus). An AG opinion is advisory to government officials; it is not a statute, not a regulation, and not a court holding. Whether prosecutors/courts follow it for simple possession (as opposed to possession with intent to sell) is [VERIFY] — the quoted sentence is framed around intent to sell/distribute, while other reporting paraphrases it as covering sale and possession generally.

1.6.6 Minimum age, permits, registration, testing, labelling, beverages — hemp-derived products

Answer for each: no Mississippi regime was located.

  • Minimum age: No hemp-THC minimum age statute located. (The only age rules located are medical: 21 to work in / enter an establishment without a card, 21 to buy a non-cardholder topical, 18–25 two-practitioner rule, under-18 caregiver rule.) Do not import another state's 21+ hemp rule.
  • Retail/manufacturer permits: None. MDAC issues no hemp licences; MSDH/MDOR licences are medical only; no hemp-retailer permit list was located.
  • Product registration: None located.
  • Testing/labelling: No hemp-specific testing or labelling statute/regulation located. (USDA licensees are subject to USDA pre-harvest testing for the plant; finished-product testing is not a Mississippi hemp rule located.)
  • THC beverages: No hemp-beverage statute located. Two AG-opinion threads touch beverages: (a) the 2025 consumable-product opinion (any ingestible, including drinks); (b) an earlier AG beverage opinion invoking § 97-31-5 (sale unlawful if the beverage "when drunk to excess, in the form sold, will produce intoxication" and not otherwise legalised; >0.3% THC beverages are marijuana beverages, illegal unless bought under the Medical Cannabis Act) — reported at https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=7ceef611-389a-4fac-bca0-5a8f937bb423, date and official opinion number [VERIFY]. Medical-programme beverages (as edible cannabis products) are lawful within the programme and subject to § 41-137-39(11) demarcation/labelling.
  • Interstate hemp shipments: Federal Farm Bill interstate-transport protection for compliant hemp is a federal question; Mississippi's in-state medical rule (§ 41-137-39(18)) does not govern hemp, and no Mississippi hemp-shipment statute was located. Full interstate treatment belongs to Part 10.

1.6.7 State response to the new federal hemp definition and the 12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026 dates

[UNAVAILABLE] — no response located. Searches on 25 Oct 2026 found no MDAC, MSDH, MDOR, Governor, or Legislature statement, rule, guidance, or bill addressing PL 119-37 §781, PL 119-103 §2019, the total-THC redefinition, or the 0.4 mg per-container cap. Analysis (not a state position): - Because Mississippi already treats intoxicating hemp products as prohibited outside the medical programme (AG reading), the federal change is largely reinforcing rather than disruptive for intoxicating products — the practical Mississippi effect is more likely on (a) any residual non-intoxicating/low-dose hemp ingestibles that sellers currently treat as lawful, (b) USDA-licensed growers whose crop must meet a total-THC (not delta-9-only) test after 11 Dec 2026, and (c) interstate shipments into Mississippi. - The USDA DEA-lab-testing enforcement delay to 31 Dec 2026 (given baseline) matters for Mississippi growers only via their USDA licences, since there is no state testing regime. - The federal medical-marijuana rider through 11 Dec 2026 and Schedule III status do not change Mississippi hemp law; they change the federal treatment of the medical programme (see §1.1). - Follow-up required before publication and in Run 2: re-check MDAC's hemp page (https://www.mdac.ms.gov/programs/hemp-cultivation-in-ms/), MSDH/MMCP, MDOR, and the Legislature's 2026–2027 bill lists for any post-October 2026 hemp-conformity bill. Do not state that Mississippi "has adopted" or "has rejected" the federal definition.

1.7 Packaging, labelling, advertising, delivery, zoning and buffers

1.7.1 Packaging and labelling — medical cannabis

Statute (§ 41-137-39(11)) — see §1.3.4 for the verbatim potency/labelling paragraph: harm notice on every product; edibles demarcated with per-serving and per-package total THC; homogenised edibles; geometric shapes only for molded edibles; no cartoons/toys/animals/children imagery; >30% total THC labelled "extremely potent". Regulation (15 Miss. Admin. Code Part 22, Rule 6.1.4 and MMCP FAQ restatement, §1.2.2): - Not attractive to minors; no toys/cartoon characters/child-enticing colours/images; minimise child appeal; depict no images other than the establishment's business name and logo. - Label must read "Keep out of reach of children". - Child-resistant containers at point of sale/transfer to patient, parent/legal guardian (minor patient), or caregiver. - No candy/candies product names or spellings (kandy, kandies) or candy-look images; no packaging/labelling likely to confuse a patient into thinking the product is a trademarked product or a commercial candy/snack/baked good/beverage. - No health/physical-benefit claims; no Department logo or state/county/municipal seal/flag/crest/insignia suggesting endorsement/manufacture/use by government. - Label contents: product name; batch number; seed-to-sale unique identifier; net quantity/weight + MMCEU equivalency; onset time; ingredients + allergens; nutrition panel (ingested products); total THC and CBD as verified by the testing facility; terpenoid profile if applicable; harm notice; Mississippi standard cannabis symbol for edibles when practicable (required on packaging as of 1 July 2023). - Potency accuracy: edibles labelled with number of THC servings + statement that potency was tested with ±10% allowable variance; potency must test within ±10% of label claim or be repackaged (MMCP FAQ restatement — [VERIFY] rule number). - Hemp-derived products: No Mississippi packaging/labelling regime located (see §1.6.6). Do not apply the medical packaging rules to hemp products by analogy.

1.7.2 Advertising — medical cannabis (near-total ban, upheld)

Rules (MSDH Subpart 3 / MDOR dispensary rules, as summarised in the Cocroft litigation and the 2021 proposed-rule summary — current rule text [VERIFY] against the SOS compilation before quoting rule numbers): - Prohibited: advertising/marketing through any media or mass communication — broadcast, electronic, print, billboards, social media, mass text/email; product display in store windows or public view; inducements such as discounts, coupons or similar sales promotions (2021 proposal summary); paid reviews/endorsements. - Permitted: appropriate signage on dispensary property; a website with general information necessary to serve qualified patients; business-directory listings; sponsorship of advocacy events and non-profit charity events (as summarised in the ABA Cocroft summary). - One-on-one education on risks/benefits was described as permissible in the 2021 proposal summary — current-rule status [VERIFY]. Litigation: Cocroft v. Graham (see §1.2.3) upheld the ban; U.S. Supreme Court declined review May 2025. Open question after Schedule III: The Fifth Circuit's reasoning turns on the activity being federally unlawful. If state-licensed medical activity is Schedule III from 28 April 2026, a new Central Hudson challenge could argue the "lawful activity" prong is now met for medical (not adult-use) advertising. No such post-April 2026 ruling, new lawsuit, or MSDH rule change was located — [VERIFY] before advising any dispensary to advertise. Until a court or MSDH says otherwise, the ban must be presented as current law. Hemp advertising: No hemp-advertising rule located. General consumer-protection / FDA disease-claim rules are federal and outside this file's scope.

1.7.3 Delivery

  • Medical: Prohibited. § 41-137-39(21) (verbatim in §1.3.4 / Part 0): in-store sales only; no drive-through, curbside delivery, or other delivery outside the premises. The Act's rulemaking direction once contemplated "protocol development for the safe delivery of medical cannabis from dispensaries to cardholders" (secondary summary of SB 2095 § 21) — that protocol, if ever adopted, does not override § 41-137-39(21)'s prohibition as written; whether MDOR has adopted any delivery protocol is [VERIFY] and must not be assumed.
  • Transportation between licensees is a separate licensed activity (transportation entity), not patient delivery — Part 4/11 territory.
  • Hemp: No delivery rule located; delivery of a prohibited intoxicating hemp product would be distribution under § 41-29-139 on the AG's reading.

1.8 Seed-to-sale tracking system

  • Statutory system: "Statewide seed-to-sale tracking system certified by the MDOH" (§ 41-137-11, quoted in §1.2.1). It must track from seed/immature plant until purchase by a patient/caregiver or destruction, with daily beginning inventory, harvests, acquisitions, sales, disbursements, remediations, disposals, transfers, ending inventory, and any other inventory-control data. Amounts recorded: dried unprocessed cannabis in ounces/grams; concentrates in grams; infused products in milligrams of THC (§ 41-137-11(2) — note: the recording unit for infused products is mg THC, while the MMCEU unit since July 2025 is 1 g total THC; do not conflate recording units with MMCEU conversion).
  • Vendor: Metrc is identified by multiple secondary sources (Flowhub, Vicente, MSDH-adjacent materials) as Mississippi's seed-to-sale vendor, and dispensaries must verify cardholder status and allotment through it before dispensing. The vendor name does not appear in § 41-137-11 as opened, and no MSDH vendor contract / Metrc Mississippi page was opened in this session — [VERIFY] the vendor against an MSDH page or contract before stating "Mississippi uses Metrc" as an official fact. The safe official statement is: Mississippi uses an MSDH-certified statewide seed-to-sale system under § 41-137-11; secondary sources identify it as Metrc.
  • Dispensary duty: Before dispensing, verify the card, verify the presenter is the cardholder, and determine via the system the maximum amount the cardholder is eligible to receive and what they have received from all dispensaries in the period (§ 41-137-5(6); § 41-137-39(9)).
  • Confidentiality: The system must maintain confidentiality of patient/caregiver data so that only MDOR/MDOH and persons/entities authorised by law access what they are authorised to access (§ 41-137-11(3), partial text opened); MSDH/MDOR "shall not share the name, address or personal data of a registry identification cardholder to any federal government entity" (§ 41-137-39(23)).
  • Hemp tracking: USDA licensees report to USDA (HeMP / USDA reporting), not to the Mississippi medical seed-to-sale system. No Mississippi hemp tracking system exists.

1.9 Employment and drug-testing protections for patients

Short answer: there are no meaningful employment protections, and the statute says so expressly. Do not soften this.

  • § 41-137-13(1)(b)–(f) (verbatim in §1.2.1): no duty to permit/accommodate/modify work; employers may refuse to hire, discharge, discipline, or otherwise adversely act "as a result, in whole or in part, of that individual's medical use of medical cannabis, regardless of the individual's impairment or lack of impairment"; drug-testing policies untouched; no private right of action; federal/DOT restrictions untouched.
  • § 41-137-13(1) also preserves: no reimbursement duty (insurers, employers, workers'-comp); workers'-comp drug-free-workplace premium discount untouched; employer defences to workers'-comp payment on a positive test / refusal to test untouched.
  • § 41-137-13(2) (via SB 2095 summaries, [VERIFY] text): nothing prohibits an employer from disciplining an employee for ingesting in the workplace or working while under the influence.
  • What § 41-137-9 does protect (narrow): A person may not be denied custody/visitation/parenting time solely for cardholder status, and a school/landlord/employer may not be penalised or denied a benefit under state law merely for enrolling/leasing to/employing a cardholder (SB 2095 § 8 summaries). That is a protection against state penalty for associating with a cardholder — it is not a right to keep a job while using medical cannabis, and § 41-137-13 expressly allows the employer to act on the use itself. Presenting § 41-137-9 without § 41-137-13 would be misleading.
  • Drug testing: Employers may test; a positive test for medical cannabis may be acted on even without impairment. Safety-sensitive exclusions are therefore lawful on the statute's face; whether any collective-bargaining, ADA (underlying condition, not cannabis use itself), or FMLA overlay changes an individual case is legal advice territory and is not resolved here. Federal Schedule III status does not create a Mississippi employment protection — no Mississippi employment amendment tied to Schedule III was located ([VERIFY] in Part 2/Run 2 follow-up).
  • Hemp / CBD and drug testing: No Mississippi protection for a hemp-product user who tests positive for THC was located. An employee using a hemp product that causes a positive test is in the same unprotected position on the statute's face, with the added risk that the product itself may be prohibited (see §1.6).

2.2 The 5% medical cannabis excise tax — statute, mechanics, fair market value

Enacting law. Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act, SB 2095, 2022 Regular Session, Laws 2022, ch. 303, §29, effective 2 February 2022 (approved 2 February 2022). The tax provision is codified at Miss. Code Ann. §27-72-1. Source for the session-law history: Justia's §27-72-1 page, which carries the "Added by Laws, 2022, ch. 303, SB 2095, §29, eff. 2/2/2022" note — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-27/chapter-72/section-27-72-1/ (accessed 25 Oct 2026). The enrolled bill text is on the Legislature's site at http://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2022/dt/cr/SB2095CR.pdf (accessed 25 Oct 2026 via search result).

Verbatim operative text — §27-72-1(2) (Justia 2024 Code text, accessed 25 Oct 2026):

"(a) There is hereby imposed, levied and assessed an excise tax on medical cannabis cultivation facilities. A cannabis cultivation facility shall collect and remit an excise tax on forms and in a manner specified by the Commissioner of Revenue."

"(b) The excise tax on cannabis cultivation facilities shall be based on the sales price for which a cannabis cultivation facility first sells cannabis flower or cannabis trim, as the case may be, to a medical cannabis establishment, and the rate of the excise tax shall be five percent (5%) of such sales price. However, if there is common ownership or other interest between the cannabis cultivation facility and the medical cannabis establishment to which the cannabis cultivation facility first sells or transfers the cannabis flower or cannabis trim, as the case may be, the excise tax shall be based on the fair market value of the cannabis flower or cannabis trim, as the case may be, at the time that the cannabis cultivation facility first sells or transfers the cannabis flower or cannabis trim to the medical cannabis establishment, and the rate of the excise tax shall be five percent (5%) of such fair market value. The fair market value of cannabis flower and cannabis trim shall initially be determined by the MDOR not later than November 1, 2022. Beginning January 1, 2023, the MDOR shall recalculate and adjust the fair market value of cannabis flower and cannabis trim twice per calendar year on January 1 and July 1."

"(c) The excise tax imposed by this subsection shall apply regardless of the ownership of the medical cannabis establishment to which the cannabis cultivation facility sells or transfers the cannabis flower or cannabis trim, as the case may be."

"(d) All administrative provisions of the sales tax law and amendments thereto, including those which fix damages, penalties and interest for nonpayment of taxes and for noncompliance with the provision of said sales tax law, and all other requirements and duties imposed upon a taxpayer, shall apply to all persons liable for taxes under the provisions of this subsection. The commissioner shall exercise all power and authority and perform all duties with respect to taxpayers under this subsection as are provided in said sales tax law, except where there is conflict, then the provisions of this subsection shall control."

"(e) All excise taxes collected under the provisions of this subsection shall be deposited into the State General Fund."

What this means, point by point:

  • Taxpayer and trigger. Only the cultivation facility pays. The tax is triggered once, on the first sale or transfer of flower or trim to any medical cannabis establishment — not on every downstream transfer, and not at retail. MDOR's own summary states it the same way: "Medical cannabis cultivators are subject to a 5% excise tax on the first sale/transfer of medical cannabis. Excise tax is due if the cultivator sells to a medical cannabis establishment. Excise tax is due on the transfer of medical cannabis from a cultivator to a related entity." — MDOR, "Medical Cannabis Taxation", https://www.dor.ms.gov/abc/medical-cannabis/medical-cannabis-taxation (accessed 25 Oct 2026).
  • Base — arm's length. 5% of the actual sales price of flower or trim on that first sale.
  • Base — common ownership / other interest. 5% of MDOR's fair market value at the time of first sale/transfer. MDOR's page gives the example of a cultivation facility that has a financial interest in the purchasing establishment "such as having the medical cannabis establishment sell product on a consignment basis" (same MDOR page, accessed 25 Oct 2026). This is an anti-avoidance rule: a vertically integrated group cannot set a nominal transfer price to shrink the tax.
  • What is taxed. Only flower and trim as defined in §27-72-1(1)(a)(ii)–(iii): flower is "the flower, including abnormal and immature flowers, of a plant of the genus cannabis that has been harvested, dried and cured, and prior to any processing whereby the flower material is transformed into a cannabis product" and "does not include the leaves or stem of such plant or hemp"; trim is all other harvested, dried and cured plant parts other than flower, prior to processing, and "does not include hemp" (same Justia page). There is no separate excise rate in §27-72-1 for concentrates, edibles or other finished products as such; the excise attaches to the flower/trim input at first transfer. Whether a processor's later sale of a finished product bears any further excise is therefore no under the text as written — the only excise event is the cultivator's first sale/transfer. [VERIFY against the MDOR excise regulation, Miss. Admin. Code Title 35, Part VIII, ch. 4 (cited on the MDOR page as 35.VIII.4.01), whose full text was not opened in this window.]
  • Administration. Sales-tax-law administrative provisions (damages, penalties, interest, taxpayer duties) apply, with §27-72-1 controlling on conflict. Registration is through MDOR's Taxpayer Access Point (TAP): "You may register for a cannabis excise tax account on TAP" (MDOR taxation page, accessed 25 Oct 2026). Secondary tax guides state monthly electronic filing (including zero-sales months) and a filing date on the 20th of the following month; that filing-date detail was not confirmed on an MDOR page opened in this window and is [VERIFY] — see §2.10.
  • An old, superseded figure to ignore. A pre-enactment summary (September 2021 draft summary, still circulating as a PDF) described a "$15.00 per ounce of flower or trim" excise. That was a draft proposal, not the enacted law. The enacted law is the 5% ad valorem tax above. Do not quote the $15/ounce figure as current law.

Fair market values (MDOR, recalculated 1 January and 1 July each year). From the MDOR taxation page (accessed 25 Oct 2026), complete series as published there:

Period Flower (per lb, common-interest sale) Trim (per lb, common-interest sale)
1 Jul – 31 Dec 2022 $3,200 $640
1 Jan – 30 Jun 2023 $3,200 $640
1 Jul – 31 Dec 2023 $1,610 $230
1 Jan – 30 Jun 2024 $1,428 $164
1 Jul – 31 Dec 2024 $1,281 $88
1 Jan – 30 Jun 2025 $1,607 $69
1 Jul – 31 Dec 2025 $1,965 $81
1 Jan – 30 Jun 2026 $1,673 $57
1 Jul – 31 Dec 2026 $1,505 $62

Worked example (arithmetic, not a tax ruling): a common-ownership transfer of 10 lb of flower in the second half of 2026 bears excise of 5% × (10 × $1,505) = $752.50. At the same period's trim value, 100 lb of trim bears 5% × (100 × $62) = $310. The fall in the flower FMV from $3,200/lb (2022–early 2023) to $1,505/lb (late 2026) is the single largest mechanical driver of falling excise per pound over the programme's life; it is a valuation change, not a rate change — the rate has stayed at 5% throughout.

Regulations. MDOR's taxation page links two regulations hosted on the Secretary of State's site (sos.ms.gov): "Medical Cannabis Excise Tax Regulation" and "Medical Cannabis Establishment Sales Tax Regulation" (Miss. Admin. Code Title 35, Part VIII, ch. 4, rule 4.01 is cited for the FMV rule). The regulation PDFs themselves were not opened in this window — their operative detail (return forms, due dates, recordkeeping, audit) is [VERIFY] against the sos.ms.gov links from https://www.dor.ms.gov/abc/medical-cannabis/medical-cannabis-taxation.

2.3 The 7% sales tax at the dispensary

Verbatim operative text — §27-72-1(3) (Justia, accessed 25 Oct 2026):

"(3) A dispensary, on forms and in a manner specified by the Commissioner of Revenue, shall collect and remit the sales tax levied in Section 27-65-17(1)(a) from the gross proceeds derived from each retail sale of medical cannabis."

The incorporated rate — §27-65-17(1)(a) (FindLaw text of the Code, accessed 25 Oct 2026; MDOR's own sales-tax-rates page confirms the same rate):

"Except as otherwise provided in this section, upon every person engaging or continuing within this state in the business of selling any tangible personal property whatsoever there is hereby levied, assessed and shall be collected a tax equal to seven percent (7%) of the gross proceeds of the retail sales of the business."

MDOR's summary is identical in substance: "Medical cannabis dispensaries will charge the standard 7% sales tax to cardholders at the point of sale" (MDOR taxation page, accessed 25 Oct 2026); and MDOR's sales-tax-rates page lists "Sale of tangible personal property ...... 7%" under §§27-65-17, 27-65-20 and 27-65-25 — https://www.dor.ms.gov/business/sales-use-tax/sales-tax-rates (accessed 25 Oct 2026).

Mechanics:

  • Who bears it economically / who collects. The cardholder pays it at the register; the dispensary collects and remits it. It is not a tax on the dispensary's margin.
  • Base. Gross proceeds of each retail sale of medical cannabis. No reduced rate, exemption, or medical-necessity exemption for medical cannabis was located in §27-65-17 or §27-72-1. A secondary guide's claim that "no sales tax applies to transfers between licensees or to non-cannabis items sold by dispensaries" is not adopted here: transfers between licensees are not "retail sales" under §27-72-1(3) in any event, and non-cannabis items are taxed (or exempt) under the general sales-tax law on their own terms — [VERIFY] for any specific product class.
  • Permit prerequisite. A dispensary applicant must first hold a sales-tax permit: "To complete an application for a dispensary license, you must have FIRST received a sales tax permit ID" and "This process could take up to three weeks" (MDOR taxation page, accessed 25 Oct 2026). MDOR lists the NAICS codes to use on registration: dispensary 455219, cultivator/grower 111419, processor/wholesaler 424590, transporter (local) 484220, transporter (long distance) 484230, testing facility 621511, waste disposal 562211 (same page).
  • No delivery/curbside complication for the tax point. Delivery is outside this report's scope except to note that the tax event is the retail sale; the delivery rules themselves are a Part 1/Part 11 matter.
  • What the patient sees. On a $100 pre-tax purchase outside Jackson and Tupelo, the register total is $107.00 before any local levy (7% × $100). The 5% excise is not itemised at the register: it was paid upstream by the cultivator and is embedded in the wholesale cost. Adding "5% + 7% = 12%" as a consumer-facing rate is therefore misleading — the two taxes have different bases (wholesale flower/trim value vs. retail gross proceeds) and different taxpayers. Secondary sources that quote a "~10%" or "12% combined effective burden" are modelled estimates, not statutory rates, and are not adopted as fact here.

2.4 Local sales-tax levies that stack on top of the 7%

Mississippi has no general local option sales tax of the kind found in neighbouring states. The only general local sales taxes in the state are the two MDOR itself names on its medical-cannabis page: "Dispensaries will also be responsible for special tax levies in the cities of Jackson & Tupelo" (MDOR taxation page, accessed 25 Oct 2026). Both are general levies (they apply to all businesses in the activity class, not to cannabis specifically), and both therefore apply to a dispensary's retail sales in those cities.

A 1% tax is imposed on every person making sales of tangible personal property or services within the municipality. The tax is levied on the gross proceeds of sales or gross income of the business derived from any of the activities taxed at the rate of seven percent (7%) or more under the Mississippi Sales Tax Law, Section 27-65-1 et seq. … Effective March 1, 2014. Repeal date July 1, 2035." — https://www.dor.ms.gov/business/sales-and-use-tax/tourism-and-economic-development-taxes (accessed 25 Oct 2026). MDOR Notice 72-14-2 (25 Apr 2014) confirms the 1% applies to activities taxed at 7% or more and that Jackson businesses "should collect the one percent (1%) Special Infrastructure Tax on all sales of tangible personal property regardless of the point of delivery in Mississippi" (after HB 787). Exemptions (restaurants, hotel/motel rooms, SNAP-eligible food, cable, and sales already exempt from sales tax) do not exempt a dispensary's retail cannabis sale on any reading located.

Tourism / restaurant / hotel levies. Mississippi authorises many narrow local levies (e.g. on restaurants and hotels) under the tourism-and-economic-development statutes. None found in this window is a cannabis-specific tax, and a dispensary is not a restaurant or hotel, so those levies do not attach to dispensary cannabis sales. They are noted here only so they are not mistaken for a cannabis tax. The full MDOR tourism-levy list is at the MDOR page cited for Jackson above.

County taxes. No county-level general sales tax on medical cannabis was located. A county's revenue from the programme, if any, comes through the State General Fund appropriation process (see §2.5), not through a county cannabis tax — [VERIFY] against any individual county's privilege-tax ordinance, which is outside the state-law sources examined.

2.5 Revenue distribution — where the money goes

Current law (in force on 25 Oct 2026).

  • Excise tax: §27-72-1(2)(e) — "All excise taxes collected under the provisions of this subsection shall be deposited into the State General Fund." (Verbatim, §2.2.)
  • Fees and fines under the Medical Cannabis Act: §41-137-61 (2025 Code, Justia, accessed 25 Oct 2026), verbatim in full:

    "All fees and fines collected by the MDOR and MDOH according to the provisions of this chapter shall be deposited into the State General Fund." History note on that page: "Laws, 2022, ch. 303, § 32, eff from and after passage (approved February 2, 2022)." The original SB 2095 §32 text was the same in substance ("All fees and fines collected by the MDOR and MDOH … shall be deposited into the State General Fund").

  • Sales tax: §27-72-1(3) incorporates the general sales-tax levy without creating a cannabis-specific distribution. Dispensary sales-tax collections therefore follow the general sales-tax distribution in §27-65-75 (municipal diversions, etc.) on the same terms as any other retailer's 7% collections. No cannabis-specific share for host cities or counties exists in current law. A reader who assumes "the dispensary's sales tax goes back to its city" is wrong for the state 7% (subject to the general §27-65-75 municipal diversion rules, which were not quantified here because they apply to all retail sales and are not cannabis-specific — [VERIFY] if a host-city revenue estimate is needed).
  • Consequence. Under current law there is no earmark for public health, schools, roads, law enforcement, or the programme's own administration. Programme administration is funded by legislative appropriation from the General Fund, not by a dedicated cannabis fund.

Proposed, not enacted, diversions — do not present as law.

  1. HB 513 (2026 Regular Session, Rep. Creekmore IV, "as passed the House" committee substitute HR43/R1690CS). Would have amended §41-137-61 so that, until 1 July 2030, "Twelve and one-half percent (12-1/2%) of all fees and * * * tax revenues collected by the MDOR and MDOH according to the provisions of this chapter each year up to the amount specified in the next sentence shall be deposited into the Mississippi Public Health Trust Fund created by Section 41-3-24 and the remainder … shall be deposited into the State General Fund", with the annual Trust Fund amount equal to the prior calendar year's fees and tax revenues less the amount appropriated to MDOR and MDOH for programme administration for the upcoming fiscal year; from 1 July 2030, all fees, tax revenues and fines would again go to the General Fund; effective date proposed 1 July 2026. Source: HB 513 committee substitute PDF on the Legislature's site, https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2026/pdf/HB/0500-0599/HB0513PS.pdf (accessed 25 Oct 2026). Status: DIED - passed the House 10 February 2026 (116-0), referred in the Senate 17 February 2026, died in Senate committee 3 March 2026. NOT enacted; §41-137-61 remains General-Fund-only.
  2. SB 2729 (2025 Regular Session, Sen. Bryan). Would have created a Mississippi Public Health Trust Fund fed by the amount by which, in any fiscal year, (a) medical-cannabis dispensary sales-tax revenue and (b) medical-cannabis excise-tax revenue each exceeded $10,000,000, amending §§27-65-75 and 27-72-1 in conformity. Source: SB 2729 as introduced, https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2025/html/SB/2700-2799/SB2729IN.htm (accessed 25 Oct 2026). Status: CORRECTED - the introduced bill's $10,000,000-excess diversion was stripped in committee substitute; the enacted SB 2729 (approved 28 March 2025, eff. 1 July 2025) creates the Public Health Trust Fund from legislative appropriations, donations, gifts/grants and other monies provided by law only, and does not amend §§27-65-75 or 27-72-1. Do not quote the $10,000,000 threshold as a current diversion rule.

2.7 Revenue figures — official data, with conflicts stated, not smoothed over

Warning on the numbers below. Mississippi publishes cannabis revenue in at least three different frames — fiscal-year state revenue reports (Legislative Budget Office / MDOR), calendar-year programme reports (MSDH Medical Cannabis Program annual report), and a combined "Medical Cannabis Excise Tax/Dispensary" line that bundles excise tax with dispensary licence fees. The figures below are not interchangeable, and secondary summaries that add or compare them without stating the frame are unreliable. Where two secondary sources disagree on the same frame, both are shown and the conflict is flagged.

A. Fiscal-year frame — Legislative Budget Office revenue reports (primary state publication, via lbo.ms.gov).

  • FY 2025 year-to-date (July–March) "Medical Cannabis Excise Tax/Dispensary": $6,311,199, vs. $6,444,099 for the same July–March period in FY 2024, a decrease of $132,900 (−2.06%). Source: LBO, "Mississippi Revenue Report", FY2025 March 2025 PDF, https://www.lbo.ms.gov/pdfs/fy25_revrpt_mar_2025.pdf (accessed 25 Oct 2026 via search result). Note: this line, by its label, combines excise tax and dispensary-related collections; it is not a pure excise-tax total and not a sales-tax total.

B. Calendar-year frame — MSDH Medical Cannabis Program annual report, as reported by secondary sources (the annual report PDF itself was NOT opened in this window — [VERIFY] against mmcp.ms.gov).

  • Excise tax collected, 1 January – 15 December 2025: $2,180,141.
  • Sales tax collected on cannabis, 1 January – 15 December 2025: $9,002,941.
  • Licence and registration fees collected, same period: $8,935,649.

C. What is NOT available. No official monthly excise/sales-tax series, no county-by-county tax distribution, and no official hemp-tax revenue series was located in this window.
