2.8 Hemp and hemp-derived products — taxes and fees

Current law: no hemp-specific excise tax, no hemp-specific sales-tax rate.

  • General sales tax applies as for any tangible personal property. A retail sale of a hemp-derived product that is tangible personal property is taxed at 7% under §27-65-17(1)(a) on the same terms as any other retail sale, unless a specific exemption applies. No MDOR guidance page specific to hemp/CBD sales tax was located in this window — [VERIFY] with MDOR's sales-tax guidance before advising a hemp retailer. (Note: the frequently repeated online claim that "CBD is generally not legal recreationally in Mississippi" and the citation of Harper Grace's Law's 0.5% THC / 15% CBD formulation are outdated and misleading as a description of the post-2018 hemp framework; they are not adopted here. Hemp regulation is a Part 1/Part 7 matter.)
  • Hemp cultivation licensing fees (state). Mississippi does not run its own USDA-approved state hemp plan charging a state grower fee; hemp production licences in Mississippi are issued by USDA (federal programme). A secondary hemp overview states: "Mississippi does not charge a fee for a hemp license in the state, as hemp licenses are issued by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA). A USDA-issued hemp production license is valid for three years unless the State of Mississippi opts to commence and administer its own hemp production program within that period." Source: https://mississippistatecannabis.org/hemp (accessed 25 Oct 2026, secondary). [VERIFY] against USDA's hemp licensee list and MDAC's hemp pages in Part 7 work; the "no state fee" point is consistent with the absence of any MDAC hemp-licence fee schedule located here.

As introduced/passed in various forms, it would have imposed a 3% excise tax on consumable hemp products (proceeds to the General Fund), created MSDH (in the introduced version, the Department of Health) licensing for consumable-hemp retailers ($200/year), wholesalers ($250), manufacturers ($500) and processors ($250), with fees to the General Fund, and regulated hemp beverages (12 oz, 5 mg THC per container in the conference discussion).   • Federal hemp changes and Mississippi tax. No Mississippi statute or MDOR notice was located that changes Mississippi hemp taxation in response to PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019 (12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026 dates) or to the federal Schedule III rule. Hemp (as defined federally and under Mississippi's hemp act) is not marijuana, so §280E does not apply to bona fide hemp activity on the federal side in the first place, and Mississippi's §41-137-51 decoupling (below) is written for "medical cannabis establishments", not hemp businesses. Whether Mississippi will enact a hemp excise or a per-container tax to mirror the new federal 0.4 mg cap is [UNAVAILABLE] — no bill text for the 2026 session addressing a hemp tax was located in this window; this is a follow-up for the next legislative session.

2.9 IRS §280E, Mississippi decoupling, and the Schedule III change

The federal rule (given baseline, applied here). IRC §280E disallows deductions and credits for a trade or business trafficking in Schedule I or II controlled substances. Under the given baseline, state-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026, so §280E is generally lifted for that activity; adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I and fully subject to §280E. Non-medical possession in Mississippi remains Schedule I federally. A Mississippi medical licensee's federal position therefore turns on (a) holding a valid state licence and (b) the activity being medical, not adult-use. The federal rule's own text and any IRS/Treasury guidance on transition years, COGS vs. deductions, and inventory accounting are outside this report's Mississippi scope — licensees need tax counsel on the transition, and nothing here is tax advice.

Mississippi decoupling — enacted, and it predates Schedule III. Mississippi decoupled from §280E for state income-tax purposes in the original Medical Cannabis Act itself, four years before the federal Schedule III rule:

Verbatim — §41-137-51 (2025 Code, Justia, accessed 25 Oct 2026), in full:

"Notwithstanding any federal tax law to the contrary, in computing net income for medical cannabis establishments, there shall be allowed as a deduction from income taxes imposed under Section 27-7-5, Mississippi Code of 1972, all the ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on a trade or business as a medical cannabis establishment, including reasonable allowance for salaries or other compensation for personal services actually rendered."

History note on that page: "Laws, 2022, ch. 303, § 26, eff from and after passage (approved February 2, 2022)."

The cross-reference in the general deductions statute confirms the mechanism. §27-7-17(1)(a) (2025 Code, Justia, accessed 25 Oct 2026) allows as business deductions "All the ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business, including a reasonable allowance for salaries or other compensation for personal services actually rendered", and adds: "There shall also be allowed a deduction for expenses as provided in Section 41-137-51." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-27/chapter-7/article-1/section-27-7-17/ (accessed 25 Oct 2026).

What decoupling means in practice, and what it does not mean:

  • State level, before and after Schedule III. Even when marijuana was Schedule I federally, a Mississippi medical cannabis establishment could deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses (rent, salaries, etc.) in computing Mississippi net income, because §41-137-51 says so "notwithstanding any federal tax law to the contrary". The state deduction did not depend on the federal schedule. Secondary compilations that list Mississippi among the states that "in 2022 … permitted 280E deductions" are consistent with §41-137-51 (e.g. Armanino, 6 Feb 2023, listing Mississippi among decoupled states, https://www.armanino.com/articles/cannabis-companies-business-expenses-280e-tax-code/, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — secondary, but the statute itself is primary and dispositive).
  • State level, after Schedule III. The state deduction remains available on the same statutory terms; Schedule III does not repeal §41-137-51, and no 2026 amendment to §41-137-51 was located. The practical change is on the federal return: the federal disallowance that §41-137-51 was working around is, under the given baseline, generally lifted for state-licensed medical activity. The two systems now point the same way for medical licensees, rather than Mississippi pointing one way and federal law the other.
  • Limits of the decoupling. (i) It covers "medical cannabis establishments" only — the defined licensees under Chapter 41-137. It does not create a deduction for unlicensed or adult-use activity, which has no legal existence in Mississippi in any event. (ii) It is a deduction from income taxes imposed under §27-7-5 (the state income tax); it does not reduce the 5% excise tax, the 7% sales tax, withholding tax, or local levies. (iii) It does not address cost-of-goods-sold computation, inventory capitalisation, or entity-level vs. owner-level treatment for pass-throughs — [VERIFY] with MDOR income-tax guidance / a Mississippi tax practitioner for entity-specific application.
  • Mississippi conformity generally. Mississippi's income tax does not simply adopt the Internal Revenue Code wholesale; §27-7-17's "notwithstanding any federal tax law" language for cannabis is the operative decoupling, and no separate Mississippi "conformity date" statute for §280E was located. If a future Mississippi bill were to tie the state deduction to the federal schedule, that would be a change from the current unconditional text — no such bill was located in this window.
  • Tribal question [VERIFY]. If the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians operates a tribal medical programme (Part 10's subject), whether its licensees are "medical cannabis establishments" under Chapter 41-137 or "state-licensed" for federal Schedule III / §280E purposes cannot be answered from the Mississippi tax statutes examined here. The federal rule as given turns on state licensure; a tribal licence is not, without more, a state licence. This is flagged, not resolved, here.
  • Withholding and other taxes. MDOR's taxation page notes: "Applicable Income tax or Withholding tax may be due for any medical cannabis establishments under this program including those licensed by the Mississippi Department of Health" (accessed 25 Oct 2026). No cannabis-specific withholding rule was located; normal withholding rules apply.

2.10 Tax compliance notes and gaps (summary for Part 2)

  • Return forms, due dates, and record-retention periods for the excise and sales taxes are set by the Commissioner of Revenue and the Title 35 regulations linked from MDOR's taxation page; the regulation texts were not opened — [VERIFY].
  • Penalties and interest for non-payment/non-compliance are imported from the sales-tax law by §27-72-1(2)(d); licence suspension/revocation for tax non-compliance is a licensing matter (Parts 4/11), not a tax-rate matter.
  • No cannabis-specific property-tax, franchise-tax, or gross-receipts-tax provision was located. Normal Mississippi business taxes (income, withholding, sales/use on equipment and supplies, property tax on real property) apply to cannabis establishments on the same terms as other businesses, subject only to §41-137-51 for income-tax deductions.
  • No tax credit, exemption, or incentive specific to medical cannabis or hemp was located.

PART 3 — LOCAL RULES

3.1 The opt-out system — statute, deadline, and how county and city decisions interact

Enacting law. SB 2095, §30, codified at Miss. Code Ann. §41-137-57. History note (Justia 2025, accessed 25 Oct 2026): "Laws, 2022, ch. 303, § 30, eff from and after passage (approved February 2, 2022); Laws, 2023, ch. 436, § 16, eff from and after passage (approved March 27, 2023)." The 2023 amendment's content was not separately identified in the sources opened — [VERIFY] what ch. 436 §16 changed in §41-137-57 before relying on the amendment history. The enrolled SB 2095 text is at http://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2022/dt/cr/SB2095CR.pdf.

The deadline — 90 days after 2 February 2022, i.e. 3 May 2022. §41-137-57(1) (Justia, accessed 25 Oct 2026), verbatim in substance:

"The cultivation, processing, sale and distribution of medical cannabis and cannabis products, as performed in accordance to the provisions of this chapter, shall be legal in every county and municipality of this state unless a county or municipality opts out through a vote by the board of supervisors of the county or governing authorities of the municipality, as applicable, within ninety (90) days after February 2, 2022."

The 3 May 2022 deadline is confirmed by contemporaneous reporting: "Mississippi cities and counties have until May 3, 2022, to decide whether they will opt-out" (Northside Sun, reporting Y'all Politics, https://www.northsidesun.com/state-politics-documents/eight-mississippi-cities-opt-out-medical-marijuana-program, accessed 25 Oct 2026); and "May 3 marked the deadline … and 10 counties and 17 cities ultimately opted out, according to the Clarion Ledger" (Cannabis Business Times, https://cannabisbusinesstimes.com/us-states/mississippi/news/15692891/10-counties-17-municipalities-opt-out-of-mississippis-medical-cannabis-program-by-may-3-deadline, accessed 25 Oct 2026). Note the discrepancy between the "10 counties / 17 municipalities" deadline-day count and the longer MDOR list in §3.3 — the MDOR list is a later, cumulative dispensary-opt-out list and is not the same count; see §3.3.

How the vote works — §41-137-57(1)–(2), verbatim key passages (Justia, accessed 25 Oct 2026):

  • Notice: "The governing authorities of the municipality or the board of supervisors of the county, as applicable, shall provide a notice in accordance with the Open Meetings Act (Section 25-41-1 et seq.) of its intent of holding a vote regarding opting out…"
  • Partial opt-out permitted: "The governing authorities of the municipality or the board of supervisors of the county, as applicable, may opt out of allowing one or more of the following: cultivation, processing, sale or distribution of medical cannabis and cannabis products." This is why the lists below distinguish "out for dispensaries only", "out for cultivation/processing only", etc. — a jurisdiction's opt-out is not necessarily all-or-nothing.
  • Who votes, and for what territory: "The governing authorities of a municipality, by a vote entered upon their minutes, may opt out … in the municipality. The board of supervisors of a county, by a vote entered upon its minutes, may opt out … in the unincorporated areas of the county."
  • Default is IN, and the window is one-way: "(2) If the board of supervisors of a county or the governing authorities of a municipality do not opt out … within ninety (90) days after February 2, 2022, then no vote by the board of supervisors or governing authorities, as applicable, may be held to so opt out, and the provisions of this chapter shall remain applicable and operative in the county or municipality, as applicable." A jurisdiction that missed the window cannot later opt out by board vote. (It can still regulate time, place and manner under §41-137-37 — §3.2 — but it cannot ban dispensaries outright; see the "impracticable" limit.)
  • Opting back in by board vote is always available: "If the board of supervisors of a county or governing authorities of a municipality have opted out …, then the board of supervisors or governing authorities of a municipality may later opt in regarding the same through a vote by the board of supervisors or governing authorities, as applicable, entered upon its or their minutes, or an election duly held according to subsection (3) or (4) of this section, as applicable."

How county and city decisions interact — the rule that most summaries get wrong:

  1. A county opt-out covers unincorporated areas only. It does not bind a municipality inside the county, and a municipality's opt-out does not bind the unincorporated county. Meridian / Lauderdale County is the textbook example: the Lauderdale County Board of Supervisors voted 2 May 2022 to opt out (Cannabis Business Times, https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/news/mississippi-lauderdale-county-opts-out-medical-cannabis/, accessed 25 Oct 2026), while "elected officials in Meridian, the county seat, decided to allow medical marijuana to be cultivated, processed and sold within the city limits" (JNM Showcase, https://jnmshowcase.com/citizens-challenge-supervisors-who-banned-marijuana-sales/, accessed 25 Oct 2026). A dispensary in Meridian city limits was therefore lawful despite the county opt-out; a dispensary in unincorporated Lauderdale County was not (subject to the later election in §3.5).
  2. Conversely, a city opt-out does not affect the surrounding unincorporated county. Madison (city, opted out) sits in Madison County, which opted out of dispensaries only in its unincorporated areas but allowed cultivation/processing/distribution there — the two decisions are independent and partial in different ways (see §3.3).
  3. Annexation and contraction are grandfathered — §41-137-57(6):

    "(a) If a municipality that has opted out under this section annexes a geographic area which contains a licensed entity operating under the provisions of this chapter, then the licensed entity may continue its operation in that municipality's newly annexed geographic area." "(b) If a licensed entity operating under the provisions of this chapter is located in a municipality that contracts its corporate boundaries thereby causing the geographic area in which the licensed entity is located to no longer be in the municipality and instead in an unincorporated area of a county that has opted out under this section, then the licensed entity may continue its operation in that area of the county."

  4. Waterway / water-management districts — §41-137-57(7): where real property is owned, leased or otherwise controlled by a waterway or water-management district created in Title 51, the county/municipality opt-out/opt-in decision "shall be binding on all real property in such district" and the county/municipality ordinances under the chapter apply to all real property within its boundaries in the district.
  5. Opt-out does not make possession illegal, and does not block every licensee type — §41-137-57(5):

    "Regardless of whether a county or municipality opts out of allowing the cultivation, processing, sale and/or distribution of medical cannabis and cannabis products, cardholders, cannabis testing facilities, cannabis research facilities, cannabis transportation entities and cannabis disposal entities may possess medical cannabis in the municipality or county if done in accordance with this chapter." In other words, the opt-out bites on cultivation, processing, sale and distribution establishments; it does not criminalise a cardholder possessing medicine in an opt-out town, and it does not exclude testing, research, transport or disposal entities from possessing cannabis there in accordance with the chapter. Whether a testing/research facility may be sited (as opposed to merely possessing) in an opt-out jurisdiction is a separate question — the statute's opt-out list is "cultivation, processing, sale or distribution", and testing/research are not in that list, but MDOR's opt-out map is expressly a dispensary map (see §3.3) — [VERIFY] the siting question for testing/research in an opt-out jurisdiction against MSDH/MDOR guidance before advising a client.

Citizen petition and election to opt back in — §41-137-57(3)–(4), verbatim key mechanics (Justia, accessed 25 Oct 2026):

  • Threshold (county, subsection (3)(a); municipality, subsection (4)(a) — identical): a "proper petition" signed by "at least twenty percent (20%) or fifteen hundred (1500), whichever number is the lesser, of the qualified electors" of the county (for unincorporated areas) or municipality.
  • Duty to call the election: on filing, "it shall be the duty of the board of supervisors" / "governing authorities of the municipality" to call an election.
  • Timing: election "on a date fixed by the order of the board of supervisors" / governing authorities, "which date shall not be more than sixty (60) days from the date of the filing of the petition". Notice by publication "once each week for at least three (3) consecutive weeks" in a newspaper published in (or, if none, having general circulation in) the county/municipality. Election "not earlier than fifteen (15) days from the first publication".
  • Ballot wording (county): "I vote FOR allowing the cultivation, processing, sale and/or distribution of medical cannabis and cannabis products, as applicable, in the unincorporated areas of ________ [Name of County] ( )" / "I vote AGAINST allowing … in the unincorporated areas of ________ [Name of County] ( )". The municipal ballot is the same with the municipality's name and without "unincorporated areas".
  • Effect: majority of participating qualified electors voting FOR makes the chapter "applicable and operative" in that territory; majority AGAINST makes it "illegal to cultivate, process, sell and/or distribute" there as applicable.
  • Cooling-off: "In either case, no further election shall be held in the county [municipality] under the provisions of this section for a period of two (2) years from the date of the prior election and then only upon the filing of a petition" meeting the same threshold.
  • Conduct: county elections "as far as may be possible in the same manner as is provided by law for the holding of general elections" and conducted by the county election commissioners, who canvass, certify to the board, which adopts and spreads an order declaring the results on its minutes; municipal elections likewise under municipal-election law, with municipal election commissioners certifying to the governing authorities.
  • Secretary of State guidance. The Secretary of State published a "County Marijuana Quick Guide_2022 (draft)" reproducing §41-137-57's election mechanics — https://www.sos.ms.gov/sites/default/files/elections/County%20Marijuana%20Quick%20Guide_2022%20%28draft%29.pdf (accessed 25 Oct 2026 via search result). It is a 2022 draft guide, not a current election-results publication.

3.2 What local governments may and may not do — §41-137-37 (local ordinances)

Citation and amendment. Miss. Code Ann. §41-137-37 (SB 2095 §19, Laws 2022, ch. 303, eff. 2 Feb 2022; amended by Laws 2025, ch. 425, §3, eff. 1 July 2025). The 2025 amendment added the sentence in subsection (1) barring a licence applicant from applying to a county/municipality for zoning/permitting action until after receiving the state licence (see below). Source: Justia 2025, https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-37/ (accessed 25 Oct 2026).

Verbatim operative text (Justia, accessed 25 Oct 2026):

"(1) A municipality or county may enact ordinances or regulations not in conflict with this chapter, or with regulations enacted under this chapter, governing the time, place, and manner of medical cannabis establishment operations in the locality. A municipality or county may establish penalties for violation of an ordinance or regulation governing the time, place and manner of a medical cannabis establishment that may operate in the municipality or county. An applicant for a medical cannabis establishment license shall not apply to a county or municipality for any action regarding zoning or permitting of a medical cannabis establishment until after the applicant has received a medical cannabis establishment license from the MDOH or MDOR as applicable."

"(2) No municipality or county may prohibit dispensaries either expressly or through the enactment of ordinances or regulations that make their operation impracticable in the jurisdiction. The main point of entry of a medical cannabis establishment shall not be located within one thousand (1,000) feet of the nearest property boundary line of any school, church or child care facility. A medical cannabis establishment may receive a waiver to this distance restriction by receiving approval from the school, church or child care facility and by applying for a waiver with its respective licensing agency, provided that the main point of entry of the cannabis establishment is not located within five hundred (500) feet of the nearest property boundary line of any school, church or child care facility."

"(3) A dispensary, cannabis research facility or cannabis testing facility may be located in any area in a municipality or county that is zoned as commercial or for which commercial use is otherwise authorized or not prohibited, provided that it being located there does not violate any other provisions of this chapter. A cannabis cultivation facility and/or cannabis processing facility may be located in any area in a municipality or county that is zoned as agricultural or industrial or for which agricultural or industrial use is otherwise authorized or not prohibited, provided that it being there does not violate any other provision of this chapter. A cannabis cultivation facility and/or cannabis processing facility may be located in any area in a municipality or county that is zoned as commercial or for which commercial use is otherwise authorized or not prohibited, provided that the municipality or county has authorized the entity to be located in such area and that it being there does not violate any other provision of this chapter. The municipality or county may authorize this by granting a variance to an existing zoning ordinance or by adopting a change in the zoning ordinance that allows for those entities to be located in specific commercial areas."

"(4) A municipality or county may require a medical cannabis establishment to obtain a local license, permit or registration to operate, and may charge a reasonable fee for the local license, permit or registration, provided that this fee is consistent with fees charged to businesses that are not involved in the cannabis industry."

"(5) No medical cannabis dispensary may be located within a one-thousand-five-hundred-feet radius from the main point of entry of the dispensary to the main point of entry of another medical cannabis dispensary. If the sole basis of denial by the licensing agency in refusing to issue the medical cannabis dispensary a license to operate is that the dispensary fails the distance requirement of this subsection (5), then the licensing agency may refund all or part of the license application fee in Section 41-137-35(5) to the applicant."

What local governments MAY do:

  • Enact time/place/manner ordinances not in conflict with Chapter 41-137 or its regulations, with penalties for violation (§41-137-37(1)).
  • Require a local licence, permit or registration, at a reasonable fee consistent with non-cannabis business fees (§41-137-37(4)).
  • Zone: dispensaries/research/testing in commercial zones (or areas where commercial use is authorised/not prohibited); cultivation/processing in agricultural or industrial zones, or in commercial zones only if the locality authorises it by variance or zoning change for specific commercial areas (§41-137-37(3)).
  • Designate specific commercial zones for dispensaries. The Attorney General's guidance (as summarised in secondary reporting of the AG opinion, https://www.mississippimarijuanacard.com/post/mississippi-a-g-weighs-in-on-cities-ability-to-regulate-cannabis-businesses-if-they-don-t-opt-out, accessed 25 Oct 2026) states: "The City may enact local zoning ordinances that accord with its comprehensive zoning plan designating specific types of commercial zones, such as a medical commercial zone, in which medical cannabis dispensaries may operate", and "Section 19(5) of SB 2095 does not preempt the City's authority to adopt an ordinance or regulation with a minimum distance greater than one-thousand-five-hundred-feet between cannabis dispensaries so long as the ordinance or regulation does not prohibit or make impracticable the operation of dispensaries within the City." The AG opinion text itself was not opened — [VERIFY] against the AG's published opinion before citing it as authority.
  • Impose hours and other time/place/manner conditions, provided they do not cross the "impracticable" line below. Specific local hours rules were not located for the cities in §3.4 (see that table).

What local governments may NOT do (outside a timely opt-out):

  • Prohibit dispensaries, expressly or by ordinances/regulations that make their operation impracticable (§41-137-37(2), first sentence). This is the provision that makes a post-deadline "ban by zoning" unlawful: a city that did not opt out by 3 May 2022 cannot achieve the same result by zoning dispensaries into nowhere.
  • Impose a local licence fee that is a cannabis surcharge in disguise — the fee must be consistent with non-cannabis fees (§41-137-37(4)).
  • Shorten the state buffers by local ordinance in a way that conflicts with the chapter (local ordinances must be "not in conflict"). A locality may, per the AG guidance above, set a larger inter-dispensary distance, but only if it does not make operation impracticable — a fact-specific line, not a fixed number.
  • Act on a zoning/permitting application before the applicant holds the state licence (2025 amendment, §41-137-37(1), last sentence). The practical sequence is therefore: state licence first, local zoning/permitting second. MDOR's dispensary-applicant page reflects the same sequence in substance, requiring "Proof of local license registration if required by city or county" as part of the state application file — the interaction between that MDOR checklist item and the 2025 statutory sequence is [VERIFY] (the MDOR page may predate the 2025 amendment).

State buffers (apply everywhere, including in opt-in jurisdictions):

Buffer Distance Measured from / to Waiver / floor
Establishment to school / church / child care facility 1,000 ft Main point of entry of the establishment to the nearest property boundary line of the school/church/child-care facility Waiver with the facility's approval + licensing-agency waiver application; absolute floor 500 ft — the main point of entry may not be within 500 ft even with a waiver (§41-137-37(2))
Dispensary to dispensary 1,500 ft radius Main point of entry to main point of entry No waiver in the statute; licensing agency may refund all or part of the application fee if distance is the sole basis for denial (§41-137-37(5))

MDOR's dispensary-applicant page states the same two buffers in checklist form and adds the measurement detail that a survey must show the location does not violate the geographic limits, with straight-line point-to-point measurement (MDOR, https://www.dor.ms.gov/abc/medical-cannabis/dispensary-applicants, accessed 25 Oct 2026; MDOR dispensary regulation 35 Miss. Code R. 11-3-100, adopted 1 July 2022, amended 6 Mar 2025, via Cornell LII, https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/mississippi/35-Miss-Code-R-SS-11-3-100, accessed 25 Oct 2026, which clarifies the boundary line is the parcel on which the facility is located, not other parcels the institution may own).

Caps. The Medical Cannabis Act imposes no statewide cap on the number of dispensaries or other establishments (that is a Part 4 point, noted here because local "caps" are sometimes misattributed to state law). Any local cap would have to survive the §41-137-37(2) "impracticable" test; no local numerical cap ordinance was located for the §3.4 cities in this window, and the secondary claim that "Gulfport has adopted zoning requirements that limit the number of dispensaries and cultivation sites" (State Regs Today, https://www.stateregstoday.com/health/marijuana-legalization/local-opt-outs-in-mississippi, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — low-authority secondary) is not adopted without the Gulfport ordinance text — [VERIFY].

Moratoriums. A pre-deadline moratorium is, in effect, a pause pending an opt-out/opt-in decision, not a freestanding power. No current (post-2022) moratorium ordinance for the §3.4 cities was located. The Oxford, MS example in some secondary sources — a city that "implemented a ban … shortly after Initiative 65" and "reversed its decision a few months later" — describes the pre-SB 2095 period and the Initiative 65 era, not a current SB 2095 moratorium, and is not relied on for current Oxford status (see §3.4).

3.3 The official list — what exists, what it covers, and why it must be used with care

The official list that exists: MDOR's Dispensary Opt-Out Map/List.

  • URL tried and opened: https://www.dor.ms.gov/node/137 — "DISPENSARY OPT-OUT MAP | Mississippi Department of Revenue" (accessed 25 Oct 2026). The page text (not just the map image) lists the opt-out jurisdictions. It is the only official, state-published opt-out list located in this window.
  • What it covers: "This Map and List applies to Medical Cannabis Dispensaries." It is not a list of cultivation/processing opt-outs, and it is not a list of jurisdictions that allow each type of business. A jurisdiction absent from the list has not opted out of dispensaries as far as MDOR knows; that does not prove it allows cultivation or processing, and a jurisdiction on the list may still allow cultivation/processing (see the partial opt-outs below).
  • MDOR's own caveat (verbatim, same page): "This map is for informational purposes only. Its accuracy is based on the information known by MDOR at this time and is subject to change. Ultimately, it is the responsibility of each dispensary license applicant to determine the status of any proposed location by contacting local city or county government representatives."
  • Date problem [VERIFY]: the page as opened carries no "last updated" date in its text. Its contents are therefore of unknown currency, and the conflicts in §3.5 (notably Lauderdale County) show it cannot be treated as a live register. Anyone relying on it for a specific address must confirm with the city/county, exactly as MDOR instructs.

The MDOR dispensary opt-out list, transcribed verbatim from the page as opened 25 Oct 2026:

Partial opt-outs (from secondary compilations — [VERIFY] each against the city/county minutes, because MDOR's list does not record partial scope):

  • Madison County: out for dispensaries in unincorporated areas; in for cultivation, processing and distribution (multiple secondary compilations agree on this split).
  • Jones County: in for cultivation; out for processing and dispensaries (secondary; one compilation phrases it as "doesn't allow processing but does allow cultivation").
  • Montgomery County: out for dispensaries; in for processing and cultivation (secondary).
  • North Carrollton: in for dispensaries; out for cultivation (secondary).
  • Winona: in for dispensaries; out for processing and cultivation (secondary).

  • Lauderdale County / Lincoln County: see §3.5 — both appear in the deadline-day opt-out lists, both are reported to have reversed by election, but only Lincoln is absent from the current MDOR list, while Lauderdale is still present. That asymmetry is the clearest evidence the MDOR list's currency must be checked.

What does NOT exist (checked, not found):

  • No MSDH-published "opt-out / opt-in by business type" register was located. MSDH's Business page (https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/node/9, accessed 25 Oct 2026) points only to its Business Search for registered establishments; it does not publish an opt-out list.
  • No Secretary of State publication of §41-137-57 election results was located. The Secretary of State's site hosts the 2022 quick guide (§3.1), not a results database.
  • No single official list of "jurisdictions that allow each type of business" exists: by the statute's design, allowance is the default (any jurisdiction that did not timely opt out for that activity type allows it, subject to zoning/buffers). The MDOR list is therefore best used negatively (if on it, dispensaries are opted out as far as MDOR knows) and not as a positive register of cultivation/processing permission.

3.4 City-by-city check — the required jurisdictions

Method for this table. For each required city/county, the determination is: (1) Is it on the MDOR dispensary opt-out list (§3.3)? (2) Is there a located city/county ordinance or a dated, sourced local action? (3) If neither a specific ordinance nor a contrary action was located, the entry says so — it does not invent a fee, buffer, or hours rule. Presence of operating dispensaries is noted only where a secondary directory reports it, and is labelled secondary, because a directory listing is not proof of current licensure or of local permission. Local fee/buffer/hours detail beyond the state buffers in §3.2 was not located for any city in this table — that absence is itself a finding: either the cities rely on the state buffers and the general business-licence fee, or their cannabis-specific local schedules are not published in a form this research could retrieve. Either way, the 2025 sequence rule (§41-137-37(1)) means a prospective applicant's first step is the state licence, then the city/county.

A hemp/CBD retailer is therefore not barred from an opt-out city by §41-137-57 alone — but (a) general zoning, business-licence and any local tobacco/vape-retailer rules still apply, (b) the 2025 AG opinion on consumable hemp (see §2.8) creates a separate state-law risk for intoxicating hemp products that is not a local rule, and (c) no city smoke/vape-shop ordinance text was located for any §3.4 city — [UNAVAILABLE] as a compiled local hemp-retailer rule set; this is a gap for Part 7/Part 12 follow-up, not a finding that no such local rules exist. In particular, do not assume that because a city opted out of medical cannabis dispensaries it has also banned CBD shops, or vice versa.

3.6 Business concentration — only what official sources say

Constraint applied: this section reports only official-source statements about where licensees are located. It does not rank, estimate, or map clusters from directories, and it does not adopt secondary directory counts (e.g. "Jackson 20, Biloxi 11, Tupelo 11…") as official facts. Those secondary counts are mentioned only to show what was excluded and why.

What official sources say (as located in this window):

  • MSDH's official locator is a search page, not a published county table. MSDH's Business page states: "Lists of registered Mississippi medical cannabis dispensaries, cultivators and other establishments can be found on the Business Search page" (https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/node/9, accessed 25 Oct 2026). The Business Search itself is an interactive search (licence lookup by establishment), not a downloadable county-count dataset — its county-level distribution therefore cannot be stated from MSDH without running the search establishment-by-establishment, which is Part 5's method, not a Part 3 finding. No MSDH or MDOR county-count table, map with counts, or "concentration" statement was located in this window.
  • MDOR's opt-out map is a status map, not a concentration map. It shows where dispensaries are barred (red), not where they are concentrated. The inverse inference — "everywhere not red has dispensaries" — is false: a jurisdiction can be opted in and still have zero dispensaries (for zoning, buffer, market, or timing reasons).
  • Early-programme official-adjacent statement (secondary, dated, not adopted as current): a March 2023 secondary article reported "157 licensed dispensaries … positioned in 32 counties … most dispensaries could be found in Lee, Harrison, and Hinds County" (Compassionate Care Consultants, 24 Mar 2023, https://compcaremd.com/get-your-medical-card-and-visit-a-dispensary-in-mississippi/, accessed 25 Oct 2026). That is a 2023 snapshot from a non-official source and is superseded; it is noted only because it is the closest thing to an early official-era county statement located, and it must not be quoted as the current distribution.
  • Current secondary counts (excluded from findings): Sativa University's directory (accessed 25 Oct 2026) lists 213 dispensaries with city counts headed by Jackson (20), Biloxi (11), Tupelo (11), Hattiesburg (10), Meridian (8), Ocean Springs (8), Oxford (8), Columbus (7), Gulfport (6), Olive Branch (6), Pearl (6), Canton (5); a separate secondary page (Dr. Green Relief, citing "MMCP List, October 8, 2026") claims 11 dispensaries at Jackson city addresses out of 14 in Hinds County, and 361 licensed businesses / 188 dispensaries statewide as of 8 Oct 2026. These figures conflict with each other (Jackson 20 vs. 11; statewide dispensaries 213 vs. 188) and neither is an official MSDH/MDOR publication opened here. No city ranking is therefore stated in this report. The only safe official-adjacent inference is negative: a city on the MDOR opt-out list has no (new) licensed dispensary in that jurisdiction as far as MDOR knows, while a city absent from the list may have dispensaries subject to state licensing, zoning and buffers.
  • What to do for a real concentration answer (Part 5 follow-up): run MSDH's Business Search and MDOR's dispensary list, export or transcribe by county, and date-stamp the run. Until that is done, any statement of the form "dispensaries cluster in X" for Mississippi is [UNAVAILABLE] from official sources in this report.

Run 1 — Parts 4–5: Licence Types and Licence Data Sources

Mississippi Cannabis and Hemp — Run 1, Parts 4 and 5

Scope: Mississippi only. Part 4 (licence types) and Part 5 (licence-data sources) in full detail. Other parts are covered only by brief cross-reference, as instructed. Date accessed for all sources in this file: 25 October 2026, unless a different publication or data date is stated in the row itself. Federal baseline: taken as given in the commission and not re-researched: state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use activity; the federal hemp provisions in PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019 operate on the 12 November / 11 December 2026 dates given; USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026; the federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026; there is no federal cannabis banking law. No contradiction with that baseline was found in the Mississippi licence material reviewed for this file. Whether a future Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians tribal programme would count as "state-licensed" under the federal Schedule III rule is [VERIFY] — see §5.9. Place-name caution applied: all places below are in Mississippi unless stated otherwise (e.g. Jackson, MS, is not Jackson, TN/WY; Philadelphia, MS, next to the Choctaw reservation, is not Philadelphia, PA).

Legal basis in one paragraph. Mississippi is medical-only. The Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act, SB 2095 (2022), codified principally at Miss. Code Ann. §§ 41-137-1 to 41-137-67, created the licensing system below. The Mississippi State Department of Health (MSDH) licenses cultivation, processing, testing, transportation, disposal and research establishments; the Mississippi Department of Revenue (MDOR) licenses dispensaries. Implementing rules are at 15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22. Hemp cultivation in Mississippi is licensed by the USDA, not by the state — see §4.7. There is no state adult-use licence type in force; see §4.8.

How to read the fee tables. "Application fee" = the one-time nonrefundable fee paid when the application is filed. "Annual licence fee" = the nonrefundable fee payable at initial application and at renewal (15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, R. 3.2.2: "nonrefundable fees are required at the time of initial application and renewal"). "First-year state fees" in §4.6 is therefore application fee + annual licence fee, before any local fee, tax permit cost, background-check / fingerprinting fee, or build-out cost. MSDH states that a completed application with all supporting documentation should be allowed 30 days for review and determination, and MDOR likewise determines dispensary applications within 30 days of a completed application (secondary summaries agree; the 30-day MSDH statement is from MSDH's own FAQ).

The binding quantity limits are instead the per-person ownership caps (§4.4), the dispensary-to-dispensary 1,500-foot spacing rule, the 1,000-foot school/church/childcare buffer (waivable to 500 feet), and local opt-outs — those are Part 3 matters and are not repeated here except where they condition a licence.

4.2 MSDH licences — what each allows, size limits, fees

4.2.1 Cultivation: micro-cultivation and cultivation tiers

Canopy definition (operative text). MSDH FAQ, citing 15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, R. 1.2.30, defines canopy as "the total surface area within a cultivation area that is dedicated to the cultivation of flowering cannabis plants. The surface area of the plant canopy shall be calculated in square feet. Measurement shall include all of the area within the boundaries where the cultivation of the flowering cannabis plant occurs. If the surface area of the canopy consists of noncontiguous areas, each component area shall be separated by identifiable boundaries. If a tiered or shelving system is used in the cultivation area, the surface of each tier or shelf shall be included in the calculation." Areas used for immature plants/seedlings before flowering and areas used to support mature plants are excluded from the calculation. Source: https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/faq?category=2 (accessed 25 Oct 2026). There is no plant-count limit stated in the tier rules; the limit is canopy area. Cultivation must be indoors, enclosed and secured (MSDH FAQ, citing 15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, Subpt. 4).

What a cultivation licence allows (15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, R. 3.2.1.A, as reproduced at https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/mississippi/15-Miss-Code-R-SS-22-3-2, accessed 25 Oct 2026): "acquisition and possession of medical cannabis, production of cannabis (e.g., grow, cultivate, harvest, dry, cure, trim) … storage of cannabis and/or raw pre-roll cannabis products; packaging and labeling of cannabis and/or cannabis products; production of raw pre-roll cannabis products, the sale of cannabis and raw pre-roll cannabis products to medical cannabis establishments authorized by this Part or medical cannabis dispensaries licensed by MDOR." Micro-cultivation facilities must additionally meet the ownership requirement in Miss. Code Ann. § 41-137-35(12) (see §4.4).

Code Pt. 22, R. 3.2.2, reproduced at https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/mississippi/15-Miss-Code-R-SS-22-3-2 (Cornell note: "Adopted 1/13/2024"), and MSDH FAQ application-fee list at https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/faq?category=2 — all accessed 25 Oct 2026. The MSDH FAQ lists application fees only; annual fees above are from § 41-137-35 / R. 3.2.2. The two sources agree on every application fee.

Tier 6 note — a genuine conflict to resolve before applying. MSDH's FAQ states Tier VI as "canopy of 100,000 to 150,000 square feet, maximum 2 locations, combined canopy not more than 150,000 square feet" with no upper limit and no location limit. R. 3.2.2 as reproduced by Cornell states Tier VI as "canopy of not less than 100,000 square feet but no more than 150,000 square feet with up to two locations." A 2026 bill text (HB 1753, introduced — not law) reproduces the same 100,000–150,000 sq ft / two-location formulation. Which formulation is in the currently operative rule text must be confirmed against the Secretary of State's current Title 15, Part 22 text before a Tier 6 application is filed [VERIFY — Tier 6 upper limit and two-location rule]. The fee figures ($60,000 / $150,000) are identical in all versions.

Tier-boundary overlaps. The statute/rule as written uses "not less than" lower bounds and "not more than" upper bounds, so adjacent tiers share a boundary figure (e.g. 2,000 sq ft appears in both Micro Tier 2 and Cultivator Tier 1; 5,000 sq ft in both Cultivator Tiers 1 and 2). How MSDH assigns a facility sitting exactly on a boundary figure was not stated on the pages reviewed [VERIFY — boundary assignment].

4.2.2 Processing: micro-processing and standard processing

What a processing licence allows (15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, R. 3.2.1.B): "acquisition of cannabis from licensed cultivation and/or micro-cultivation facilities/entities; possession of cannabis with the intent to manufacture cannabis products; manufacture of cannabis products from unprocessed cannabis and/or a cannabis extract; storage of cannabis and/or cannabis products, packaging and labeling of cannabis and/or cannabis products, the sale of cannabis products to medical cannabis establishments authorized by this Part or medical cannabis dispensaries licensed by MDOR." Micro-processing facilities must additionally meet § 41-137-35(12) (see §4.4). Processing facilities that process edible cannabis products must also comply with MSDH food-manufacture rules and the associated manufactured-food permit (MSDH FAQ, citing 15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, R. 4.1.3: fees and inspection schedules "associated with risk level 4 for the related manufactured food permit"). The manufactured-food permit fee itself was not stated on the pages reviewed [VERIFY — edible-processor food permit fee].

The size measure for processing is annual throughput of dried biomass, not canopy or floor area:

Licence Annual dried-biomass throughput One-time application fee Annual licence fee First-year state fees
Micro-processor Tier 1 Less than 2,000 lb per year $2,000 $3,500 $5,500
Micro-processor Tier 2 Not less than 2,000 lb but less than 3,000 lb per year $2,500 $5,000 $7,500
Processor (standard) Not less than 3,000 lb per year (no upper limit stated) $15,000 $20,000 $35,000

Sources: Miss. Code Ann. § 41-137-35; 15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, R. 3.2.2 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/mississippi/15-Miss-Code-R-SS-22-3-2); MSDH FAQ (https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/faq?category=2) — all accessed 25 Oct 2026. Note the Tier 2 wording in R. 3.2.2 is internally awkward ("not more than but less than three thousand (3,000) pounds"); the operative reading is 2,000–<3,000 lb, with standard processing at ≥3,000 lb. Whether a processor that crosses a throughput threshold mid-year must re-license, and how throughput is audited, was not stated on the pages reviewed [VERIFY].

4.2.3 Transportation (transporter)

What it allows (R. 3.2.1.C): "transportation (e.g., transfer) and storage of cannabis and/or cannabis products to other licensed medical cannabis establishments authorized by this Part and/or medical cannabis dispensaries licensed by MDOR." MSDH FAQ adds: "As a licensed transporter, you must maintain the transportation manifest during transport. See 15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, Subpart 5.9 and 7.1." There is no separate delivery-to-patient licence; sales to cardholders occur only inside a dispensary (see §4.3). Fees: one-time application fee $5,000; annual licence fee $7,500; first-year state fees $12,500. Sources: § 41-137-35; R. 3.2.2; MSDH FAQ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. No vehicle-count, fleet-size or route limit was stated on the pages reviewed [VERIFY].

4.2.4 Waste disposal (disposal entity)

What it allows (R. 3.2.1.D): "disposal or destruction of medical cannabis, cannabis products, and/or cannabis waste." Fees: one-time application fee $5,000; annual licence fee $7,500; first-year state fees $12,500. Sources: § 41-137-35; R. 3.2.2; MSDH FAQ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Whether a cultivator or processor may dispose of its own waste on-site without a separate disposal licence, and the approved destruction methods, are operational rules for Run 2 Part 11 and were not determined here [VERIFY for Run 2].

4.2.5 Testing facility (testing establishment)

What it allows (R. 3.2.1.E): "collection and transportation of medical cannabis test samples, testing of medical cannabis test samples for purposes of analyzing the safety and potency of cannabis and cannabis products." Fees: one-time application fee $10,000; annual licence fee $15,000; first-year state fees $25,000. Sources: § 41-137-35; R. 3.2.2; MSDH FAQ — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Independence constraints (statute, verbatim in substance). Miss. Code Ann. § 41-137-35 provides that an individual or business entity with a direct or indirect ownership or economic interest in a licensed testing facility may also hold such an interest in a licensed transportation entity, and that a testing facility may contract with a licensed transportation entity for transport; but a testing facility "shall not employ an agent or employee who also is employed or has ownership at any other medical cannabis establishment" (SB 2095 text). MSDH "may contract with a private laboratory for the purpose of conducting compliance testing oversight" of licensed testing facilities, and any such oversight laboratory "shall be prohibited from conducting any other commercial medical cannabis testing in this state." The exact subsection numbering of the employment bar was not re-verified against the current Code text in this run [VERIFY — subsection number]. Required tests, accreditation (ISO/IEC 17025) and sampling rules are Run 2 Part 11 matters.

4.2.6 Research facility

What it allows (R. 3.2.1.F): "acquisition of cannabis or cannabis products from licensed cannabis cultivation facilities and licensed cannabis processing facilities in order to research cannabis, develop best practices for specific medical conditions, develop medicines and provide commercial access for medical use." Fees: one-time application fee $10,000; annual licence fee $15,000; first-year state fees $25,000 — except that "A research facility at any university or college in this state shall be exempt from all fees imposed under this section" (Miss. Code Ann. § 41-137-35(8), verbatim). Sources: § 41-137-35; R. 3.2.2; MSDH FAQ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. The University of Mississippi's federal marijuana research history is a Run 2 Part 11 matter and is not developed here.

4.2.7 MSDH fee-payment and completeness rules

  • R. 3.2.3: "All application and license fees shall be paid in a manner set forth by the Department." R. 3.2.4: "The one-time application fee and license fee shall be paid in order for an initial application to be determined complete and move forward in the Department's review." R. 3.2.5: "A fee for a status change from provisional license to regular license is not required." R. 3.2.6: if fees are returned for insufficient funds, MSDH "will cease the application review process," the application "will be denied"; if a licence has already issued, it "will be suspended until the fee payments are remedied," with remediation "within thirty (30) days." Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/mississippi/15-Miss-Code-R-SS-22-3-2 (accessed 25 Oct 2026).
  • All MSDH establishment fees in R. 3.2.2 are stated to be "required at the time of initial application and renewal," i.e. the application fee is one-time per application but the annual fee recurs; whether the "one-time" application fee is charged again on a renewal application was not separately stated [VERIFY — renewal application-fee treatment]. MDOR's dispensary renewal is stated differently (annual fee only) — see §4.3.

4.3 MDOR dispensary licence (the only dispensary licence type)

What it allows. MDOR's page defines the dispensary, tracking the Act, as "an entity licensed and registered with the MDOR that acquires, possesses, stores, transfers, sells supplies, or dispenses medical cannabis, equipment used for medical cannabis, or related supplies and educational materials to cardholders." Source: https://www.dor.ms.gov/abc/medical-cannabis/dispensary-applicants (accessed 25 Oct 2026). Sales are to cardholders inside the dispensary only; drive-through, curbside and delivery outside the premises are prohibited (Act § 41-137-35 framework; the topical-product exception for non-cardholder adults 21+ is a Part 1/Part 12 matter, not a separate licence type). A dispensary "can only be in an area zoned commercial or in an area that is not otherwise prohibited from having commercial businesses" (MDOR page).

Item Amount / rule
One-time nonrefundable application fee $15,000
Annual licence fee $25,000
First year total (MDOR's own presentation) $40,000
Yearly renewal $25,000 (application fee not repeated, per MDOR's "Yearly Renewal: $25,000")

Source: https://www.dor.ms.gov/abc/medical-cannabis/dispensary-applicants (accessed 25 Oct 2026). The same $15,000 / $25,000 figures appear in Miss. Code Ann. § 41-137-35(4).

Requirements stated by MDOR (all from the same page, accessed 25 Oct 2026): legal name and physical address (no P.O. box); proof of Mississippi Secretary of State registration if applicable; Mississippi sales tax permit number (applicants must FIRST obtain a sales-tax permit ID via TAP — Taxpayer Access Point — and MDOR warns "This process could take up to three weeks"); management service agreements if applicable; deed of trust, lease or contingent agreement if applicable; proof the main entrance is not within 1,000 feet of the property boundary line of any school, church or childcare facility (distance waiver form required if within 1,000 feet); no dispensary within a 1,500-foot radius from the main point of entry of another dispensary (measured main-entry to main-entry); proof of local licence registration if required by the city or county; list of all owners, partners, members, officers, board members and anyone with an economic interest; list of all professional licences held by each member and proof of good standing; Acknowledgement of Waiver and Authorization to Release Information for each member; diagram of licensed premises; operations plan; security plan. Forms linked from the page include Licensee Certification and Oath, Waiver and Authorization forms (MSDH and MSDOR versions), Waiver of Minimum Distance Requirements, Affidavit for Background Check, and Statement on Local Licenses and Permits.

Dispensary-specific eligibility (same MDOR page): individuals at least 21 years of age; any owner, board member, officer or person with an economic interest must be at least 21; not currently serving as a member of the Mississippi Senate or House of Representatives or the spouse of such a member "through December 31, 2022" (a spent, date-limited disqualification, reproduced as written on the MDOR page); has not previously held a cannabis-related licence that has been revoked; has no outstanding tax liabilities owed to Mississippi; has never been convicted of a disqualifying felony as defined by the Act; and — stated expressly on the MDOR page — "Applicants are not required to be residents of the State of Mississippi to obtain a dispensary license." This is the key contrast with cultivation/processing/micro licences (§4.4). MDOR also warns that an application filed before an opt-out vote is denied with forfeiture of the $15,000 application fee, and that an application filed after an opt-back-in vote but before MDOR's announced acceptance date/time is rejected without priority (same page).

NAICS codes MDOR directs applicants to use (same page): cultivator/grower 111419; processor/wholesaler 424590; transporter (local freight) 484220; transporter (long distance) 484230; testing facility 621511; dispensary 453998; waste disposal 562211. These are tax-registration codes, not licence types, but they confirm MDOR's taxonomy of the programme.

No tiers, no separate licence types for dispensaries. There is no micro-dispensary, delivery-only, consumption-lounge, wholesale or vertically-integrated licence type in the Act or rules reviewed. Vertical integration is permitted in practice (one person may hold licences across categories subject to the §4.4 caps) but it is not a licence category of its own. A dispensary may hold multiple dispensary licences subject to the

10%-interest cap in §4.4 (five licences).

4.4 Ownership, residency and minimum qualifications (Miss. Code Ann. § 41-137-35)

Minimum qualifications — § 41-137-35(10) (summary of the statutory list; verbatim quotes are short extracts). An individual applicant for a cultivation, processing, dispensary, transportation or disposal licence must be a natural person who: "(i) Is at least twenty-one (21) years of age; (ii) Has not previously held a license … that has been revoked; (iii) Has not been convicted of a disqualifying felony offense; (iv) If possessing a professional or occupational license, that the license is in good standing; (v) Has submitted a sworn statement indicating that he or she is a true and actual owner of the entity … and not … the agent for any other entity; (vi) Has no outstanding tax delinquencies owed to the State of Mississippi; (vii) Is not serving as a member of the Mississippi Senate or Mississippi House of Representatives through December 31, 2022; (viii) Is not the spouse of [such a member] through December 31, 2022." An entity applicant must additionally show the individual applicant is legally authorised to apply for the entity, is the primary point of contact, and that no owner, board member, officer or person with an economic interest fails the individual tests. "Disqualifying felony offense" is defined in the Act / MSDH FAQ as including a crime of violence under Miss. Code Ann. § 97-3-2, a felony violent crime under another jurisdiction's law, and a felony state/federal controlled-substances conviction including service of probation, incarceration or supervised release within the previous five years, subject to the pre-Act-conduct carve-out quoted on the MSDH FAQ page. Source for the (10) text: Miss. Code Ann. § 41-137-35 as reproduced at https://codes.findlaw.com/ms/title-41-public-health/ms-code-sect-41-137-35/ (accessed 25 Oct 2026) — a secondary reproduction; the current official Code text on legislature.ms.gov should be re-checked before a filing [VERIFY — official-text re-check].

Ownership concentration cap — § 41-137-35(9) (verbatim): "No individual or business entity shall have a direct or indirect ownership or economic interest of greater than ten percent (10%) in: (a) More than one (1) cannabis cultivation facility license; (b) More than one (1) cannabis processing facility license; and (c) More than five (5) medical cannabis dispensary licenses." Source: same FindLaw reproduction of § 41-137-35, and SB 2095 as enacted (accessed 25 Oct 2026). Conflict flagged: several secondary summaries state the dispensary cap as four, not five. The statute as reproduced says five; the summaries are wrong on this point unless a later amendment changed it — no such amendment was located in this run [VERIFY — confirm "five" in the current official Code text]. The cap is applied per licence type: a person may simultaneously hold a >10% interest in one cultivation licence, one processing licence and up to five dispensary licences. Whether micro-cultivation and micro-processing licences count within the "one cultivation / one processing" caps, or are treated separately, was not stated on the pages reviewed [VERIFY]. Testing and research licences are not listed in § 41-137-35(9); testing has its own independence rule (§4.2.5).

Residency — the most commonly misstated area. Three distinct regimes:

  1. Standard cultivation and processing — 35% rule, SUNSET 31 December 2022. § 41-137-35(11): applicants for cultivation and processing licences had to show, for a natural person, "proof that the person has been a resident of the State of Mississippi and a citizen of the United States of America for at least three (3) years prior to the application date," or, for a business entity, "proof that at least thirty-five percent (35%) of the equity ownership interests in the entity are held by individuals who have been residents of the State of Mississippi and citizens of the United States of America for at least three (3) consecutive years prior to the application date." The subsection ends: "This subsection (11) shall stand repealed on December 31, 2022." Source: § 41-137-35(11) as reproduced at https://www.casemine.com/act/us/65b0f4d3121ace78b84d7558 (accessed 25 Oct 2026). Consequence: any secondary source that still presents the 35% rule as a live requirement in 2026 is out of date on its face. Whether the repeal was in fact effected and no successor residency rule was enacted is [VERIFY — current Code text].
  2. Micro-cultivation and micro-processing — 100% rule, NO sunset stated in the text reviewed. § 41-137-35(12): a micro-cultivator or micro-processor must show, for a natural person, 3-year Mississippi residency and U.S. citizenship, or, for a business entity, "(i) It was registered as an entity with the Secretary of State in Mississippi; and (ii) One-hundred percent (100%) of the equity ownership interests in the entity are held by individuals who have been residents of the State of Mississippi and citizens of the United States of America for at least three (3) consecutive years prior to the application date." No repeal date is stated for subsection (12) in the reproductions reviewed, and 15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, R. 3.2.1.A–B still states that micro facilities "shall meet the ownership requirement established in Miss. Code § 41-137-35(12)." Consequence: on the texts reviewed, the 100% Mississippi-resident ownership rule for micro licences survives while the 35% rule for standard licences sunset. This must be confirmed against the current official Code before any micro application, because it is the single largest structuring trap in the programme [VERIFY — current status of § 41-137-35(12)].
  3. Dispensaries, transportation, disposal, testing, research — no Mississippi-residency requirement stated. MDOR states expressly that dispensary applicants need not be Mississippi residents (see §4.3). No residency rule for transportation, disposal, testing or research applicants was located in § 41-137-35(10)–(13) as reproduced [VERIFY — absence confirmed only for the text reviewed].

Proving residency — § 41-137-35(13). It is "sufficient to prove Mississippi residency for the individual(s) to submit two (2) of the following source documents: (a) Mississippi Tax Return Form 80-105 or Form 80-205 for each of the three (3) years preceding the application without schedules … redacted to remove all financial information and all but the last four (4) digits of the individual's social security number …; (b) Ownership, lease, or rental documents for place of primary domicile for the three (3) years preceding the application; (c) Billing statements, including utility bills for the three (3) years preceding the application; or (d) Vehicle registration for the three (3) years preceding the application." Source: § 41-137-35(13) as reproduced (accessed 25 Oct 2026).

Other applicant conditions. All owners, officers, board members and persons with an economic interest are background-checked (fingerprint-based Mississippi Central Criminal Database and FBI checks for work-permit applicants — see §4.5; the same disqualifying-felony standard applies to licence applicants). An establishment must notify its licensing agency of ownership changes; secondary summaries state notification within one business day, citing § 41-137-31 — the one-business-day period was not re-verified in this run [VERIFY]. A licence "shall [not] be transferred … to any other person or entity except with the written consent of the applicable licensing agency" (Miss. Code Ann. § 41-137-47(11), as reproduced at https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-47/, accessed 25 Oct 2026). Full transfer/renewal/relocation rules are Run 2 Part 11 matters.

4.5 Work permits for employees and agents

Rule and fee. Every medical cannabis establishment agent and employee must be registered and receive a work permit issued by the licensing agency (MSDH for MSDH-licensed establishments, MDOR for dispensaries) before beginning work. MSDH FAQ states: "Every medical cannabis establishment agent and employee shall be registered and receive a work permit issued by the Department before he/she may work for a licensed medical cannabis entity. This includes any individual with access to the premises … for purposes of providing labor or services on a regular or ongoing basis such as owners, employees, volunteers, and, in some circumstances, contractors. Contractors providing labor or services on an occasional or emergency basis … are excepted from the work permit requirement. See 15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, Subpt. 3." Source: https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/faq?category=2 (accessed 25 Oct 2026). The statutory hook is Miss. Code Ann. § 41-137-39.

Fee (verbatim rule text). 15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, R. 3.11.9 / Subchapter 3 work-permit rules: "Medical Cannabis Establishment Work Permit and registration fee - $25.00," plus "Fingerprinting and Department background records check fee(s) in addition to the work permit registration fee," with all payments "through the Department's electronic payment system(s)." Renewal: "Work Permit fee - $25.00" (R. 4.3.3 in the MSDH work-permit PDF numbering). Sources: https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/sites/default/files/Documents/15.22.4WorkPermits.pdf and https://regulations.justia.com/states/mississippi/title-15/part-22/subpart-3/section-15-22-3-11/ (both accessed 25 Oct 2026). The fingerprint/background fee amount is not stated in the rule text reproduced; secondary sources estimate $40–$100 per person for background checks/fingerprinting generally (non-official, see §4.6) — the MSDH fingerprint fee itself is [VERIFY — amount].

Validity. "The fee for a work permit shall be Twenty-five Dollars ($25.00) and the permit shall be valid for five (5) years. Work permits shall be the property of the employee and shall not be transferable to other employees." Source: Miss. Code Ann. § 41-137-39 framework as reproduced in 2026 bill text (HB 1195, introduced, reproducing the Act) at https://legiscan.com/MS/text/HB1195/2026 (accessed 25 Oct 2026) — the $25 / 5-year figures are corroborated by the MSDH rule text above, which is the authority relied on here.

Eligibility and process. Applicants must be 21 or older (secondary summaries; the MSDH rule text reviewed states the photo, ID, professional- licence, authorisation-for-background-check and attestation requirements but the age rule for work-permit holders was not re-verified in the rule text in this run [VERIFY — work-permit age rule in current rule text]). Required with the application: colour passport-style digital photo taken within six months (plain white/off-white background, full-face, neutral expression, no obscuring head covering except daily religious wear, not digitally enhanced); copy of a current state-issued driver's licence or ID card; copies of all current state-issued professional licences; authorisation for a criminal-history records check; attestation of truth and correctness; and fees. Renewal requires the same package plus, if applicable, a background-check affidavit. An applicant must complete a fingerprint-based check of the Mississippi Central Criminal Database and the FBI Criminal History Database and must not have a disqualifying felony offense (definition in §4.4). MSDH may deny for failure to provide required information, failure to meet requirements, misleading/false/fraudulent information, failure to pay fees, or any other grounds serving the purposes of the Part, with written notice of the reason; failure to complete required continuing education may lead to revocation or suspension (R. 3.11.10–3.11.13). Sources: R. 3.11 as reproduced at https://regulations.justia.com/states/mississippi/title-15/part-22/subpart-3/section-15-22-3-11/ and https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/mississippi/15-Miss-Code-R-SS-22-3-11 (accessed 25 Oct 2026).

Work-permit counts (context, not a licence type). A secondary market report (CannBus, Q3 2026, data as of 29 December 2025) states 5,862 active work permits. This is a secondary figure attributed to official data; no MSDH-published work-permit count was opened in this run [VERIFY — MSDH published count]. It is included here only because work-permit volume is the natural denominator for staffing-cost estimates in §4.6.

Dispensary work permits. MDOR-licensed dispensary employees are covered by the same $25 / 5-year statutory framework, with MDOR as the issuing agency ("with the MDOH and MDOR, as applicable"). Whether MDOR's work-permit application form, portal and fingerprinting channel differ from MSDH's was not determined on the pages reviewed [VERIFY — MDOR work-permit channel].
