4.7 Hemp and hemp-derived product licences/permits (inventory; full detail is Run 2 Part 7)

4.7.1 Hemp cultivation — USDA licence, no state licence

  • Mississippi does not issue hemp licences. MDAC states, verbatim in substance: "The Mississippi Department of Agriculture & Commerce does not issue hemp licenses." and "currently the only legal option for a producer to cultivate hemp in Mississippi now is to obtain a hemp license from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) under the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program." Source: https://www.mdac.ms.gov/programs/hemp-cultivation-in-ms/ (accessed 25 Oct 2026).
  • Why: Senate Bill 2725, the Mississippi Hemp Cultivation Act, signed 29 June 2020, authorised a state plan to be created by the Commissioner of Agriculture and Commerce, but "the necessary funding to implement the program was not appropriated by the Mississippi Legislature" (MDAC, same page).
  • USDA licence terms (as stated by MDAC): apply via the USDA Hemp eManagement Platform (HeMP) with a copy of an FBI criminal-history report; no USDA licence if convicted of a felony related to a controlled substance in the last 10 years; licences "are active for three years unless the State of Mississippi elects to administer a State hemp production program." USDA's approved-plan list (updated 17 February 2026) lists Mississippi as "USDA Hemp Producer License" — i.e. no approved state plan. Source: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review (accessed 25 Oct 2026). Fee: no USDA application or licence fee was found in the USDA pages checked by a secondary guide, and MDAC states Mississippi charges no fee because it issues no licence; the USDA fee position should be confirmed in 7 CFR Part 990 before advising an applicant [VERIFY — USDA fee in current rule text]. Secondary reporting (hempcbdbusinessplans.com, accessed 25 Oct 2026) states there is no renewal application fee under the USDA programme and, as of May 2026, 118 active hemp licensees in Mississippi per the USDA public search tool — both secondary figures, [VERIFY against the USDA search tool itself].
  • No Mississippi hemp processor/handler licence exists as a state licence type on the evidence reviewed; processing is within the USDA producer framework and general state law. Whether Mississippi requires any separate state registration for hemp processing/handling is [VERIFY — Run 2 Part 7 must confirm or rule out a processor registration].

4.7.2 Hemp-derived (consumable hemp) products — no licence in force

  • As of 25 October 2026, no Mississippi licence or permit for makers or retailers of consumable hemp products (delta-8, delta-9, THCA and similar hemp-derived products) was located on MSDH, MDOR or MDAC pages. Retail sale of such products in Mississippi is therefore not governed by a state hemp-product licensing regime in force; the operative constraints (THC limits, age, labelling, testing) are Part 1/Part 7 matters for Run 2, and any claim that a "hemp licence" authorises retail sale of intoxicating hemp products in Mississippi should be treated as [UNAVAILABLE / not evidenced] unless Run 2 locates a current authority.
  • General business registrations still apply (Secretary of State entity registration, sales-tax permit, local privilege licence where required) but those are not hemp-specific licences.

4.7.3 PROPOSED ONLY — HB 1502 (2025) consumable-hemp licences (NOT LAW)

HB 1502 (2025 Regular Session, Rep. Yancey) would have renamed the Mississippi Hemp Cultivation Act as the Mississippi Hemp Act, transferred administration from MDAC to the State Department of Health, and created a licensing regime for consumable hemp products. It did not become law and must not be quoted as current law. Its proposed (never operative) annual fees, from the introduced bill text, were: consumable hemp retailer $200; wholesaler $250; manufacturer $500; processor $250, with licences to begin 1 July 2025 under the bill's timetable, plus a proposed 3% excise tax and a proposed MDOR public directory of certified manufacturers/products from 1 October 2025. Sources: introduced text at https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2025/pdf/HB/1500-1599/HB1502IN.pdf (accessed 25 Oct 2026); fee passage as reproduced in search results from the same text. Status conflict flagged: BillTrack50 records HB 1502 as "Died On Calendar (on 04/03/2025)" (https://www.billtrack50.com/billdetail/1796956, accessed 25 Oct 2026), while a secondary industry blog (May 2025) states the bill passed the House but "failed to move through the Senate by one single vote." The procedural endpoint is therefore [VERIFY — House/Senate history on billstatus.ls.state.ms.us]; what is certain is that HB 1502 is not law and its licences, directory and tax do not exist. A conference report (HB1502CR) exists in the Legislature's document system, which shows the bill progressed further than a simple House death — another reason to verify the history rather than repeat either summary. Run 2 Part 7 must re-confirm whether any successor hemp-product bill was enacted in 2026.

4.7.4 Hemp beverages

No separate Mississippi hemp-beverage licence type in force was located. HB 1502 would have folded hemp beverages (proposed: ≤5 mg THC per 12-ounce container, 21+, within the light-beer/wine regulatory framework) into the alcoholic-beverage regime; because HB 1502 did not pass, that beverage licensing route does not exist. Any current hemp-beverage authorisation under general alcohol or food law is [VERIFY — Run 2 Part 7].

4.8 Adult-use licence types — PROPOSED ONLY (none in force)

There is no adult-use (recreational) licence type in Mississippi state law. No adult-use bill or ballot measure was found in the sources reviewed for 2026 (secondary market report, Q3 2026, states "Adult-use legalization: no bill or ballot measure found in the sources reviewed" — CannBus, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/ms_cannmir.html, accessed 25 Oct 2026). Accordingly, no adult-use licence type can be listed here even as a well-defined proposal, and the following must not be mistaken for one:

  • 2026 medical-expansion bills, vetoed, not adult-use: HB 895 (would have removed the 60% potency cap on concentrates, ended mandatory six-month follow-ups, lengthened caregiver cards) and HB 1152 (Right to Try Medical Cannabis Act — wider conditions, nonresident access) both passed the Legislature and were vetoed by Governor Tate Reeves on 26–27 March 2026 (veto date reported as both 26 and 27 March in secondary sources — [VERIFY — veto date]); no override was reported. They would have amended medical licences, not created adult-use licences. Sources: secondary reports at https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/ms_cannmir.html and https://blog.mpp.org/blog/mississippi-legislature-convened-lets-make-cannabis-policy-a-priority/ (accessed 25 Oct 2026). Final bill status must be confirmed on billstatus.ls.state.ms.us before Run 2 cites them.
  • Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians referendum (tribal, not state): On 10 June 2025 the Tribe approved Referendum No. 2025-01 (55% in favour; reported 1,367 to 1,110) asking whether members support the Tribe developing legislation to decriminalise and regulate possession, production and distribution of marijuana on tribal lands, followed by a feasibility study. The referendum question itself, as reported, was "Do you support the Tribe developing legislation to decriminalize and regulate possession, production, and distribution of marijuana on Tribal lands?" — it did not itself create tribal licences, and Tribal Council action would still be required. Sources (secondary): https://blog.mpp.org/blog/mississippi-native-tribe-votes-to-legalize-cannabis/ and https://www.marijuanamoment.net/mississippi-indian-tribe-approves-marijuana-referendum-making-it-first-jurisdiction-in-the-state-poised-to-legalize/ (both accessed 25 Oct 2026). Whether any tribal licence type now exists, and whether it would count as "state-licensed" for federal Schedule III purposes, is [VERIFY — official tribal source required; Run 2 Part 10]. No tribal licence type is listed as a Mississippi licence in this file.

4.9 Social equity, minority and small-business provisions

Finding: there is no social-equity licensing programme in the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act as enacted. No priority licensing, fee waiver or reduction, licence reservation, incubator, or expungement-linked licensing preference for any equity category was located in Miss. Code Ann. § 41-137-35, in 15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, R. 3.2, or on MSDH/MDOR licensing pages reviewed. A 2026 secondary policy brief agrees: "Mississippi's Medical Cannabis Act does not include a notable social-equity licensing carve-out comparable to programs in other states" (drugpolicywatch.info, accessed 25 Oct 2026).

What exists instead — and it cuts the other way:

  1. Micro tiers as the small-business mechanism. The micro-cultivator ($1,500–$2,500 application; $2,000–$3,500 annual) and micro-processor ($2,000–$2,500 application; $3,500–$5,000 annual) tiers are the Act's low-capital entry points. They are, however, coupled to the 100% Mississippi-resident ownership rule in § 41-137-35(12) (see §4.4) — a residency gate, not an equity preference — and that rule's current status must be verified.
  2. Express exclusion from minority-business and economic-development programmes. SB 2095 as enacted amended a series of economic- development statutes to exclude medical cannabis establishments from the definitions of "eligible company," "private company," "qualified business or industry," "minority business enterprise" and "minority business enterprise supplier," and from certain income-tax credits and bond-financing eligibility. Source: SB 2095 conference report summary, https://index.ls.state.ms.us/isysnative/UzpcRG9jdW1lbnRzXDIwMjJccGRmXGNyXHNiMjA5NWNyLnBkZg==/sb2095cr.pdf (accessed 25 Oct 2026); see also the enacted text's exclusion language ("The term 'minority business enterprise' does not include any medical cannabis establishment as defined in the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act"). The precise current Code sections carrying these exclusions were not re-verified in this run [VERIFY — current Code sections].
  3. No fee relief for any applicant category was located in the fee rules, except the university/college research-facility exemption (§4.2.6). In particular, no veteran, minority-owned, women-owned, disabled-owned or formerly-incarcerated applicant fee waiver exists in R. 3.2.2 [VERIFY — absence confirmed only for the texts reviewed].
  4. Ownership caps as an anti-concentration device, not an equity device. The § 41-137-35(9) caps (one cultivation, one processing, five dispensaries at >10% interest) limit single-operator dominance but do not reserve licences for any group.

Any claim that Mississippi offers social-equity licences, equity fee discounts or equity priority scoring should be treated as [UNAVAILABLE — not evidenced] unless Run 2 locates a post-2022 amendment creating one.

PART 5 — LICENCE DATA SOURCES

Headline finding. Mississippi has no published downloadable licence-holder dataset (no CSV, XLSX or PDF licensee list) from MSDH or MDOR that was located in this run. The authoritative sources are interactive search tools with no download option observed (MSDH Business Search; USDA public hemp search), plus a static map/list page for dispensary opt-outs (MDOR), plus general business-entity search (Secretary of State) and ad-hoc enforcement reporting (no dashboard). Every source below states its format, access route, update frequency as stated (or "not stated"), latest data date, fields, and limitations. Where a direct download link exists, it is given exactly; where none exists, that is stated rather than papered over.

A note on the seed-to-sale system (cross-reference). Mississippi's designated seed-to-sale system is Metrc (Marijuana Enforcement, Tracking, Reporting & Compliance). Secondary sources agree on this (e.g. https://www.flowhub.com/mississippi-cannabis-laws, accessed 25 Oct 2026: "Metrc serves as the seed-to-sale tracking system for the State of Mississippi cannabis program"; MSDH's own FAQ requires the "Unique identifier number created by the seed to sale system" on every product label, citing 15 Miss. Admin. Code Subpart 6). Metrc is a licensee compliance system, not a public licence-holder directory: no public Metrc licensee list for Mississippi was located, and Metrc data is not downloadable by the public [VERIFY — no public Metrc directory located]. Do not cite Metrc as a Part 5 public data source.

  11. Tribal: check Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians official publications for any cannabis code, regulator or licences; resolve the federal "state-licensed" question for any tribal programme.

Run 1 — Part 6: Market Data

MISSISSIPPI — RUN 1, PART 6: MARKET DATA

Scope: Mississippi only. Medical cannabis only — Mississippi has no adult-use programme. This part covers market data only; law, licence-type rules, local rules and licence-data inventories are covered in Parts 1, 3, 4 and 5 respectively and are cross-referenced here only where a market figure depends on them.

Date accessed for all sources in this file: 25 October 2026, unless a source's own publication date is given.

How to read this file — read this first, because Mississippi publishes the same market on two different calendars:

  1. Calendar-year (CY) figures come from the Mississippi State Department of Health (MSDH) / Mississippi Medical Cannabis Program (MMCP) Annual Report. The CY2025 edition is explicitly a 1 January–15 December 2025 (charts labelled to 29 December 2025) window, not a full calendar year — see §6.1. The CY2024 edition's patient figure is read on 30 December 2024 and the CY2025 figure on 15 December 2025, so the year-on-year step is not a clean 12 months.
  2. State fiscal-year (FY) figures come from the Mississippi Department of Revenue (MDOR) quarterly retail-sales reports. Mississippi's fiscal year runs July–June. MDOR states its figures are "Amounts reported at each quarter end (not revised)" and are derived from the Metrc Mississippi Official Tracking and Compliance system, cover medical cannabis products only (not paraphernalia), and that "Sales activity began January 2023."
  3. CY and FY totals must never be compared with each other as if they were the same period, and must never be averaged together. Where a secondary source conflates them (see §6.9, PotCulture Magazine), that is flagged as a conflict, not adopted.
  4. Official vs secondary labelling is strict in this file. A figure is labelled Official only where it is reported as coming from an MSDH/MMCP Annual Report or an MDOR quarterly report / MDOR taxation page. Where I read that figure only through a secondary write-up of the official report (because the MMCP Annual Report PDF itself could not be opened as readable text in this research window — see §6.10), the figure is labelled Official-via-secondary and the secondary carrier is named. Figures from trade press, analyst sites or operator blogs are labelled Secondary and dated. My own arithmetic on official inputs is labelled Calculated.
  5. No monthly series is reproduced in full in this file, for a stated reason, not by omission: MSDH publishes a monthly "Retail Sales by Month" chart inside its Annual Report, but in this research window that chart could not be recovered as readable monthly values (the CY2024 edition is an image-only PDF; the CY2025 monthly values were not published as a text table in any source opened). The partial monthly points that are published in text are given in §6.2.4. Inventing the missing months would violate the sourcing rules. See §6.10 for the exact gap and the recommended follow-up (direct request for the MMCP Annual Report data tables / MDOR monthly Metrc extract).

Federal baseline (given, fixed, not re-researched): state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; IRS 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use; there is no federal cannabis banking law. Nothing found in this Part 6 research contradicts that baseline. Its market relevance is noted only in §6.8 (banking) — no Mississippi-specific 280E revenue effect has been quantified in any source opened, and none is estimated here.

  • The Dec 2024 type rows sum exactly to 387 (200+61+62+18+16+20+6+4). The Dec 2025 rows sum to 341, plus 1 research = 342, matching CannBus's "342 (CannBus sum)". The Dec 2024 research count, if any, is not stated in the secondary summary — [VERIFY] whether Dec 2024 research licences were zero or omitted from the summary.

Secondary commentary (CannBus, DankReports, Cannabusinessplans) uniformly reads this as consolidation / weaker operators exiting as revenue per store rose — see §6.6. That interpretation is Secondary, not an MSDH finding, though MSDH's report is said to "suggest… consolidation" (Cannabusinessplans paraphrase — [VERIFY] wording against the report itself).
  • Licensed vs active dispensaries — conflict, [VERIFY]: the Dec 2025 Annual Report figure is 171 dispensaries. A January 2026 press report cited by CannBus states "about 175 of about 190 licensed dispensaries were active in January 2026", and cannabismississippi.org gives "~175 active dispensaries" (Feb 2026). These cannot all describe the same stock on the same date: 171 (Dec 2025, Annual Report) is adopted as the official year-end stock; ~175 active / ~190 licensed (Jan 2026, press) is listed as a secondary, differently-dated, differently-defined (licensed vs active) figure. Do not present 190 as the December 2025 count.
  • Testing-lab consolidation (Secondary, dated): seven testing labs launched in 2023; two remained at Dec 2025 (Steep Hill Mississippi and Alchemy Analytics); on 7 Aug 2026 those two announced a merger into Southern Precision Analytics, which would leave a single testing company in the state — Magnolia Tribune, 7 Aug 2026, via CannBus — https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/ms_cannmir.html — accessed 25 Oct 2026. [VERIFY] completion of the merger and the post-merger licence count; this is after the Dec 2025 snapshot.
  • Work permits (people, not licences — do not add to licence totals): 491 provisional (Oct 2022); "just over 3,000" (Dec 2023); 5,862 active at 29 Dec 2025 (Official-via-secondary: MSDH CY2025 Annual Report, via CannBus). Work-permit fee $25, valid five years (statute; see Part 4). Work permits are not jobs: no official Mississippi cannabis-jobs count was found — [UNAVAILABLE] (CannBus §14 likewise reports "No state job count in the sources reviewed"). National benchmarks sometimes quoted alongside Mississippi (e.g. 412,500 US legal cannabis jobs, early 2026) are not Mississippi data and are excluded from this file's totals.
  • No licence cap: Mississippi imposes no numerical cap on business licences (statute; see Part 4). The dispensary decline is therefore a market exit, not a cap effect.

6.5 Official price data

Mississippi does not price in grams at retail in its official reporting. It prices in Mississippi Medical Cannabis Equivalency Units (MMCEUs). The official price table is headed "Average Cost Per MMCEU" by product category. Any per-gram figure is a conversion, and the basket matters — see the warning below.

6.5.1 Average cost per MMCEU (MSDH CY2025 Annual Report, via secondary)

Product category (as named in the report) Average cost per MMCEU Per-gram equivalent Status
Bud / Flower / Shake / Trim $22.50 per MMCEU $6.43/g (22.50 ÷ 3.5 g) — Calculated using the regulatory definition that 1 MMCEU of flower = 3.5 g Official-via-secondary: MSDH CY2025 Annual Report, via DankReports ("derived directly from MMCP's CY 2025 annual report ($22.50 average per 3.5g unit)") — https://www.dankreports.com/mississippi-cannabis-market-analysis/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026; conversion factor confirmed by DistrictCannaMetrics' citation of MMCP Revised Administrative Regulations §1.2.97 (1 MMCEU = 3.5 g flower / 1 g concentrate / 100 mg infused product) — https://www.districtcannametrics.com/mississippi.html — accessed 25 Oct 2026
Other categories (concentrates, infused edibles, pre-rolls, etc.) Dollar values per MMCEU not recovered in text form — [UNAVAILABLE] in this window. DankReports and CannBus both note the $22.50 figure could not be confirmed in the report text they read, and no other category's dollar average was published in text in any opened source. Do not quote category prices other than the $22.50 flower-basket figure.
Price changes, 2024 → 2025 Concentrates +21%; infused edibles +48% (average price per product unit) — Secondary summary of the Annual Report: Cannabusinessplans — https://cannabusinessplans.com/mississippi-cannabis-market/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Direction and magnitude are as reported by that carrier; the underlying per-unit dollar values were not recovered — [VERIFY] against the Annual Report price table.

Basket warning (must travel with the $6.43/g figure wherever it is quoted): the $22.50 category is named "Bud/Flower/Shake/Trim" — it blends whole bud with shake and trim. It is therefore not a whole-bud-only price and is not like-for-like with other states' whole-bud per-gram prices. DistrictCannaMetrics excludes Mississippi from its cross-state whole-bud price chart on exactly this ground. DankReports' cross-state table ($6.43/g for Mississippi vs $2.96/g Michigan, $8.10/g Arkansas, etc.) is reproduced in secondary literature but inherits this basket problem; it is not adopted here as a like-for-like comparison. The $6.43/g figure is valid only as "the MMCEU flower-basket price converted at the regulatory 3.5 g factor."

6.6 Market saturation (only where officially reported or transparently calculated)

No official saturation metric is published by MSDH or MDOR. MSDH does not publish "licences per patient", "sales per capita" or a saturation assessment in any source opened. Every ratio in this section is therefore Calculated from adopted official inputs, with the formula shown, so it can be checked rather than trusted. Do not attribute any ratio below to MSDH or MDOR.

Ratio 2024 (where calculable) 2025 Formula
Patients per dispensary 248 (49,626 ÷ 200) 386 (66,041 ÷ 171) Active patients ÷ dispensary stock
Dispensaries per 1,000 patients 4.03 2.59 Dispensaries ÷ patients × 1,000
Total licences per 1,000 patients 7.80 (387 ÷ 49,626 × 1,000) 5.18 (342 ÷ 66,041 × 1,000) Total licences ÷ patients × 1,000
Cultivation licences per 1,000 patients 2.48 (123 ÷ 49,626 × 1,000) 1.67 (110 ÷ 66,041 × 1,000) Cultivation licences ÷ patients × 1,000
Retail sales per dispensary $483K (96.55M ÷ 200) $812K (138.86M ÷ 171) CY retail sales ÷ dispensary stock
Retail sales per patient per year $1,946 (96.55M ÷ 49,626) $2,103 (138.86M ÷ 66,041) CY retail sales ÷ active patients
Retail sales per patient per month $162 $175 Annual per-patient figure ÷ 12
Patients as share of state population ~1.7% (49,626 ÷ ~2.95M) ~2.2% (66,041 ÷ 2,954,160) Patients ÷ Census population estimate (Jul 2025: 2,954,160, via CannBus citing Census QuickFacts)
Dispensaries per 100,000 adults 21+ — 8.1 (DankReports denominator ~2.1M) or 7.4 (CannBus denominator 2,954,160 × 77.7%) Dispensaries ÷ adults 21+ × 100,000 — denominator-dependent; see §6.4.2

Interpretation (Secondary, not official — DankReports/CannBus consensus, stated here as their reading, not as fact): the store base contracted (−14.5%) while sales per store rose ~68% ($483K → $812K) and patients per store rose ~56% (248 → 386). Both secondary analysts read this as the early licence-issuance excess working itself out: marginal operators exiting, surviving stores consolidating volume toward a sustainable level given a $25,000 annual dispensary licence fee. Whether $812K per store is in fact sustainable is not established by any official source and is not asserted here.

Modelled "legal capture" — Secondary model, explicitly not official: DankReports models ~378,000 regular Mississippi cannabis consumers (18% of ~2.1M adults 21+, at 1.0 g/day) and a ~$887M total addressable market at $6.43/g, implying ~16% legal capture for the $138.86M CY2025 market and noting 66,041 cardholders are ~17.5% of the modelled consumer base — https://www.dankreports.com/mississippi-cannabis-market-analysis/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. The 18% participation and 1.0 g/day inputs are framework assumptions, not Mississippi data. The 16% figure is included only as a labelled model, because it is the only published capture estimate found; it must not be quoted as an observed market share.

Geographic concentration — Official position: [UNAVAILABLE]. No official county-by-county patient, sales or licence breakdown was found in any opened MSDH or MDOR source. A secondary analysis (Silent Majority 420, undated 2025 analysis) claims Harrison County (Gulf Coast) has the highest patient count, followed by Rankin County and Jackson County — https://www.silentmajority420.com/mississippi-cannabis-market-analysis-the-magnolia-states-medical-foundation-and-the-adult-use-question/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. That claim is Secondary and unverified against official data and is not adopted. Per the task rules, no cluster ranking is estimated here. County distribution is a Part 3 / Part 5 follow-up (MSDH or MDOR county map/counts, if published).

6.7 Hemp acreage, grower counts and hemp-derived product market

6.7.1 The structural fact that governs all hemp numbers in Mississippi

The Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce (MDAC) does not issue hemp licences. This is stated verbatim on MDAC's own page, directly opened:

"Senate Bill 2725, also known as the Mississippi Hemp Cultivation Act, was signed into law on June 29, 2020. This act legalized the cultivation of hemp under a state plan to be created and implemented by the Commissioner of Agriculture and Commerce. Although the act allowed for a state hemp cultivation program, the necessary funding to implement the program was not appropriated by the Mississippi Legislature. As a result, currently the only legal option for a producer to cultivate hemp in Mississippi now is to obtain a hemp license from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) under the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program… The Mississippi Department of Agriculture & Commerce does not issue hemp licenses."

Source: MDAC, "Hemp Cultivation in Mississippi" — https://www.mdac.ms.gov/programs/hemp-cultivation-in-ms/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Corroborated by USDA AMS, "List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans" (updated 17 Feb 2026): Mississippi = "USDA Hemp Producer License" (no approved state plan) — https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Full licence-type detail is Part 7; the market consequence is stated here: there is no MDAC hemp licence series to report, by design.

6.7.2 Hemp acreage and grower counts by year — [UNAVAILABLE] as a Mississippi-specific series

Item Finding
MDAC hemp grower / acreage series Does not exist — MDAC issues no licences and publishes no grower or acreage count (see §6.7.1).
USDA hemp licence count for Mississippi, by year [UNAVAILABLE] — USDA publishes the plan status (above) but no Mississippi-specific licensee count or acreage total was found in any opened USDA source in this window. USDA hemp licences are issued through the Hemp eManagement Platform (HeMP) and are valid for three years; the licensee list is not published as a Mississippi state total in the sources opened. Do not substitute a national USDA total.
USDA NASS hemp acreage for Mississippi [UNAVAILABLE] — the USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service Mississippi crop releases checked (Acreage 2024; Crop Production Monthly Aug/Oct/Dec 2024) report corn, cotton, hay, peanuts, rice, soybeans and wheat, with no hemp row for Mississippi — https://www.nass.usda.gov/Statistics_by_State/Mississippi/Publications/Crop_Releases/Acreage/2024/msacreage24.pdf and https://data.nass.usda.gov/Statistics_by_State/Mississippi/Publications/Crop_Releases/Crop_Production_Monthly/2024/mscropaug24.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Absence from these releases is consistent with hemp acreage being too small to meet NASS publication thresholds or not separately estimated for Mississippi, but that inference is not asserted as fact — the finding is simply that no NASS Mississippi hemp figure was located.
USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) hemp acreage reporting FSA confirms a Mississippi hemp acreage-reporting deadline of 31 July 2025 (vs 15 July 2025 for all other crops) — USDA FSA, "USDA Reminds Mississippi Producers to File Crop Acreage Reports", 9 Jun 2025 — https://www.fsa.usda.gov/news-events/news/06-09-2025/usda-reminds-mississippi-producers-file-crop-acreage-reports — accessed 25 Oct 2026. FSA publishes the deadline, not a Mississippi hemp acreage total, in that notice. County-level FSA acreage data, if it exists, would require a county-office / FSA data request — recommended follow-up in §6.10.
Hemp acreage / grower counts by year (table) No table can be honestly completed. Any year-by-year hemp table for Mississippi built from the sources above would be empty for every year. That emptiness is itself the finding, and it is stated rather than filled with national proxies or neighbouring-state figures.

Warning on a misleading secondary source: at least one secondary "how to grow hemp in Mississippi" page describes an MDAC application process with site GPS coordinates, background checks and fees. That description contradicts MDAC's own page (which says MDAC does not issue licences) and is rejected here. Do not use it for any hemp count or process claim. (Carrier: foodhandlersguide.com hemp page — accessed 25 Oct 2026 — not relied on.)

6.7.3 Hemp-derived product market figures — no official figure; secondary position is a ban, not a market

Item Finding
Official Mississippi hemp-derived product sales, tax or shop-count figure [UNAVAILABLE] — no MDAC, MSDH or MDOR hemp-derived product market series was found. There is no state hemp-derived product permit registry to count from (see Part 5 follow-up).
Legal status context (why there is no legal market to size) Secondary sources uniformly report intoxicating hemp-derived cannabinoids (delta-8, delta-10, HHC, THCP) as prohibited in Mississippi, and report Attorney General Lynn Fitch's opinion of 11 June 2025 as effectively prohibiting the sale of most hemp consumable products without FDA approval — see, e.g., Exhale Well, "Is Delta-8 Legal?" (updated 2025) — https://www.exhalewell.com/is-delta-8-legal/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026, and Cannabis Business Times, "Moving the Goalposts" (2024) — https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/business-issues-benchmarks/hemp-regulations-in-us/news/15686531/moving-the-goalposts-state-regulation-of-hempderived-cannabinoids — accessed 25 Oct 2026. The law itself is Part 1; this section records only the market consequence: a prohibited product has no legal market series, and any illicit/grey-market sales figure would be an estimate. None is estimated here.
Evidence of continued grey-market availability (Secondary, dated) Cannabis Business Times (2024) cites a study finding retailers in ban states including Mississippi still self-reported selling delta-8 THC. That is evidence that prohibition ≠ absence, but it is not a sales figure and is not quantified here.
CBD / non-intoxicating hemp product market figure for Mississippi [UNAVAILABLE] — no Mississippi-specific CBD sales figure (official or credible secondary) was found. National CBD market figures were not substituted, as they would not be Mississippi data.
Federal hemp-definition dates (context for any future hemp market) Given baseline, not re-researched: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 Nov 2026 but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 Dec 2026; after 11 Dec 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA DEA-lab testing enforcement delayed to 31 Dec 2026. No Mississippi-specific response figure (e.g. expected licence or acreage change) was found — [UNAVAILABLE]. Mississippi's hemp position at the access date is USDA-licence-only cultivation (§6.7.1) plus the June 2025 AG opinion environment above; how the December 2026 federal change affects Mississippi growers is a Part 1 / Part 7 follow-up, not a market figure.

6.8 Cannabis-friendly banks and credit unions

Federal context (given baseline): there is no federal cannabis banking law. Any bank serving Mississippi cannabis businesses therefore does so under its own BSA/AML compliance programme, not under a federal safe harbour. No Mississippi bank or credit union is named in any official MSDH/MDOR publication opened — official banking data is [UNAVAILABLE]; the institutions below are all Secondary (their own announcements / trade coverage), and inclusion here means "publicly markets cannabis/hemp banking to Mississippi businesses", not "verified as currently banking any named Mississippi licensee" (client lists are not published).

The following Run 1 headlines are adopted unchanged in Parts 7–8:

  • Mississippi is medical only, under the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act, SB 2095 (signed 2 February 2022), Miss. Code §§ 41-137-1 et seq. First medical sales 25 January 2023.
  • Purchase limit 24 MMCEUs per 30 days; from 1 July 2025 (SB 2748) 1 MMCEU = 3.5 g flower or 1 g total THC.

Federal baseline (given, fixed — not re-researched; contradictions flagged only)

  • Split scheduling: state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). Adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I.
  • IRS § 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to § 280E.
  • Hemp: PL 119-37 § 781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 § 2019 limits it until 11 December 2026. After 11 December 2026, the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply.
  • USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026.
  • The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026.
  • There is no federal cannabis banking law.
  • Mississippi's medical programme is state-licensed; tribal "state-licensed" status is [VERIFY] and is not asserted in this report.

PART 7 — HEMP LICENCES

7.0 Answer in one paragraph

Mississippi has one operative hemp cultivation licence and it is federal, not state: the USDA Hemp Producer License issued by the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS) under 7 CFR Part 990, Subpart C. Mississippi has no USDA-approved state hemp plan, MDAC issues no hemp licences, and the state grower-licence / processor-registration system written into the Mississippi Hemp Cultivation Act (SB 2725, 2020) was never put into operation because the funding condition was not met. There is no Mississippi licence or permit in force for makers or retailers of consumable hemp products (delta-8, delta-9, THCA and similar), and no separate Mississippi hemp beverage licence in force. Every licence of that kind that appears below is a proposed bill that did not become law, and is labelled as such. A USDA producer licence authorises production of hemp plants; it does not authorise production of medical or recreational marijuana, and it does not by itself make a finished consumable product lawful — product legality is governed separately by state controlled-substance and food/drug law and, after 11 December 2026, by the federal total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap (see § 7.8).

Secondary guides consistently say no application/renewal fee. Positive primary USDA "licence is free" statement not located — see § 7.4.4 [VERIFY] 7 CFR Part 990; AMS FAQ; AMS plan list

7.2 Does Mississippi run its own USDA-approved state plan, or use the USDA programme?

Mississippi uses the USDA programme. It does not run its own USDA-approved state plan.

7.2.1 MDAC's own statement (opened directly, 25 October 2026)

Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce, "Hemp Cultivation in MS":

  • https://www.mdac.ms.gov/programs/hemp-cultivation-in-ms/

Verbatim in substance (paraphrase is marked; the operative sentences are quoted):

"SB 2725, the Mississippi Hemp Cultivation Act, was signed by Governor Tate Reeves on June 29, 2020, legalizing the cultivation of hemp in Mississippi under a state plan to be created by the Commissioner of Agriculture and Commerce."

"The necessary funding to implement the program was not appropriated by the Mississippi Legislature."

"Currently the only legal option for a producer to cultivate hemp in Mississippi now is to obtain a hemp license from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) under the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program."

"The Mississippi Department of Agriculture & Commerce does not issue hemp licenses."

That page is the primary basis for the "unfunded, inoperative state programme" finding in this report. MDAC's role in Mississippi hemp today is therefore informational only: it points producers to USDA. It does not accept applications, issue licences, register processors, or publish a state licensee list.

7.2.2 USDA AMS plan list (opened directly, 25 October 2026; list updated 17 February 2026)

USDA AMS, "State and Tribal Plan Review":

  • https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review

The list records Mississippi as "USDA Hemp Producer License" — i.e. producers in Mississippi are licensed directly by USDA, not under a state plan. The same list records the Mississippi Band of Choctaw as "USDA Hemp Producer License". That is a hemp-plan status only. It is not evidence of a tribal cannabis programme (that is Part 10 work), and it does not resolve the tribal "state-licensed" Schedule III question, which remains [VERIFY].

7.2.3 SB 2725 (2020) — what the state law says on paper

The Mississippi Hemp Cultivation Act, SB 2725 (2020), is codified at Miss. Code §§ 69-25-201 et seq. The Act on paper creates a state system. The system was never funded into operation. The paper provisions below must not be presented as licences a person can apply for today.

Exclusivity / local preemption on paper — § 69-25-201. As shown in SB 2725 bill text via search results (full as-sent text not opened directly in this run — see § 7.10, gap 1; do not re-attempt that failed open), regulation of hemp cultivation and processing is governed exclusively by the Act, and a municipality, county or other political subdivision "shall not enact, adopt or enforce a rule, ordinance, order, resolution or other regulation that allows, prohibits or penalizes the cultivation, production or processing of hemp in this state." This is a paper-law point for an inoperative state programme. Whether it has any operative effect on a USDA licensee's local land-use obligations is [VERIFY] — a USDA licence does not by itself override local building, water, or environmental requirements (see § 8.2).

Definitions — § 69-25-203 (Justia reproduction of the 2024 Code — [VERIFY against official Code]):

  • https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-69/chapter-25/article-4/section-69-25-203/

"Hemp" means Cannabis sativa L. and any part of that plant, including the seeds thereof and all derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts, and salts of isomers, whether growing or not, with a delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol concentration of not more than 0.3% on a dry weight basis that is grown or processed under the provisions of this article.

"Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol" means the percentage of tetrahydrocannabinolic acid by weight multiplied by 0.877, plus the percentage of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol by weight.

"Grower" means a person, business entity, joint venture or cooperative that cultivates, grows or harvests hemp.

"Processor" means a person, business entity, joint venture or cooperative that receives hemp for processing into commodities, products or hemp seed, and includes an entity that brokers and/or stores hemp.

"Legal description of land" means global positioning system coordinates and also metes and bounds including township, range and section.

"State plan" means the plan contemplated by 7 CFR Part 990, Subpart B.

Note the state-law definition is a delta-9-THC definition (0.3% delta-9 on a dry weight basis, with the 0.877 THCA conversion). It is not the post-11 December 2026 federal total-THC definition with a 0.4 mg per container cap. Do not conflate the two; see § 7.8.

Licensing and registration on paper — § 69-25-207. As reproduced in the HB 1502, SB 2706 and SB 2540 bill texts that bring the section forward (see § 7.7), the section provides in substance:

  • Cultivation and processing are authorised, subject to department regulation, and may only be performed by persons or business entities holding a valid licence or registration under the article.
  • The Commissioner shall create a State Plan for USDA submission and approval.
  • The department is authorised to accept applications and issue licences/registrations for all hemp growers and hemp processors.
  • All hemp growers must be licensed by the department; all hemp processors must register with the department.
  • Licence holders and registered processors must keep crop/processing records subject to inspection.

Operative distinction (state this plainly): § 69-25-207 describes a state grower-licence / processor-registration system that has never been put into operation, because the funding condition was not met and no USDA-approved state plan exists. It must not be presented as a licence a person can apply for today. No separate Mississippi hemp processor/handler licence in force was located.

Funding condition. SB 2725 House Committee Amendment No. 1, marked "Adopted" in search results:

  • https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2020/html/ham/SB2725_H_Cmte_Amend_01.htm

provided in substance that the provisions giving the Commissioner/MDAC authority to administer the Act "shall be subject to legislative appropriation or receipt of necessary funding from any private or public entity for purposes of implementation," with Mississippi State University programmes remaining exempt. The full amendment document was not opened directly in this run, so the verbatim appropriation wording is [VERIFY against the opened amendment document]. The MDAC funding statement itself (§ 7.2.1) was opened directly and is the primary basis for the "unfunded" finding.

Special fund on paper — § 69-25-205. The section would establish a State Treasury special fund for administering the State Plan, from appropriations, gifts, grants, federal funds, application fees, registration fees and other funds, administered by the department, with unexpended monies not lapsing into the State General Fund. This is paper law for a programme that was not funded into operation. Do not present it as an active fund with a balance — no balance was located and none is asserted.

7.3 The USDA Hemp Producer License — what it allows, who issues it, how to apply

Sources opened directly on 25 October 2026: 7 CFR § 990.21, § 990.24, § 990.71 via Cornell eCFR reproductions; USDA AMS Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ); USDA AMS plan list (§ 7.2.2). Via search results only (labelled): 7 CFR § 990.22, § 990.25, § 990.27, § 990.32, § 990.1, USDA AMS HeMP page.

  • USDA AMS FAQ: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/frequently-asked-questions-faq
  • 7 CFR § 990.21: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/7/990.21
  • 7 CFR § 990.24: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/7/990.24
  • 7 CFR § 990.71: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/7/990.71

7.3.1 What it allows — and what it does not

  • It authorises production of hemp (Cannabis sativa L. at or below the acceptable hemp THC level) under the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program, 7 CFR Part 990, Subpart C (USDA plan).
  • AMS FAQ, verbatim in substance: "You cannot produce medical or recreational marijuana with a hemp license." A USDA hemp licence is not a Mississippi medical cannabis licence, does not authorise medical cannabis cultivation under §§ 41-137-1 et seq., and does not authorise adult-use production (adult-use remains Schedule I and has no Mississippi licensing pathway).
  • It does not authorise a finished consumable product as such. Product legality is a separate question (see § 7.8).

7.3.2 Who issues it

USDA Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS) — not MDAC, not MSDH, not MDOR. This follows directly from Mississippi's "USDA Hemp Producer License" plan status (§ 7.2.2).

7.3.3 Application route

Hemp eManagement Platform (HeMP). AMS FAQ (opened directly): create a HeMP account and submit a USDA Hemp Application. Applications are accepted on a rolling basis throughout the year. HeMP producer functions include applying, renewing, amending and printing the licence, submitting disposal/remediation reports (AMS-27) and annual reports (AMS-28), and viewing lab results and registered FSA lots. The AMS HeMP page itself was reached via search results only in this run:

  • https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/hemp-emanagement-platform-hemp

so any HeMP screen detail beyond the FAQ description is [VERIFY on the live HeMP page].

7.3.4 Application contents — 7 CFR § 990.21(a)(3) (opened directly)

An application must include:

  • Contact information. Individual: full name, residential address, telephone, email. Business entity: full business name, principal business location address, full name and title of key participants, email if available, EIN.
  • A current criminal history report for the individual, or for all key participants if a business entity, dated within 60 days of the application submission date. An application without all required criminal history reports is not complete. Incomplete applications are returned and may be resubmitted.

7.3.5 Key participants — 7 CFR § 990.1 (via search results)

A key participant is a sole proprietor, a partner in a partnership, or a person with executive managerial control in a corporation (e.g. CEO, COO, CFO). It does not include non-executive managers such as farm, field or shift managers, nor a tribal government leader acting in that capacity unless that member exercises executive managerial control over hemp production.

7.3.6 Felony bar — 7 CFR § 990.22(a)(2) (via search results) and AMS FAQ (opened directly)

No licence unless criminal history reports confirm all key participants have not been convicted of a felony, under state or federal law, relating to a controlled substance within the past 10 years, unless the exception in § 990.20(b) applies. AMS FAQ states the same 10-year bar in plain terms. The content of the § 990.20(b) exception was not opened in this run and is not described here — [VERIFY in § 990.20 text before advising any applicant with a prior conviction].

7.3.7 Other approval conditions — § 990.22(a) (via search results)

In addition to the felony bar, USDA approval requires: a complete and accurate application; prior/current licensee submission of all required reports; no materially false statements; licence not currently suspended; applicant is not a stand-in for a suspended/revoked/ineligible person; the state/tribe where hemp is produced does not have a USDA-approved plan and has not submitted a plan awaiting decision; and the state/tribe does not prohibit hemp production. USDA gives written notice of approval or denial. Mississippi satisfies the last two conditions: it has no USDA-approved plan (and no plan awaiting decision was located) and it does not prohibit hemp production — the Hemp Cultivation Act legalised cultivation, even though the state programme was never funded.

7.4 Term, renewal, modification, fees

7.4.1 Term — 7 CFR § 990.21(a)(6), § 990.22(b), § 990.71(a)

A USDA hemp producer licence is valid until 31 December of the year three years after the year in which the licence was issued. MDAC summarises this as "active for three years unless the State of Mississippi elects to administer a State hemp production program." The regulation text controls over the summary: the expiry is a fixed 31 December date in the third following year, not a rolling three-year anniversary. Example for illustration only (arithmetic from the rule, not a USDA example): a licence issued in 2026 is valid until 31 December 2029.

7.4.2 Renewal is not automatic

Renewal applications are subject to the same terms, information and approval criteria as initial applications unless the regulation or law has since been amended. A renewal is therefore a fresh application with fresh criminal history reports (within 60 days of submission), not a rubber stamp.

7.4.3 Modification

A licence modification is required for any change to application information, including sale of a business, production in a new location, or change in key participants. A buyer of a hemp operation cannot simply inherit the seller's licence — the licence is tied to the licensee, locations, and key participants on the application. (Licence-transfer rules for medical cannabis establishments are Part 11 work and are not addressed here; do not import them into hemp.)

7.4.4 Fees — partially resolved, still flagged

  • No fee is prescribed in § 990.21 or § 990.22 as opened, and the AMS FAQ as opened does not list a licence fee.
  • Multiple secondary guides consistently state there is no USDA application or renewal fee.
  • Adopted position (narrows Run 1's [VERIFY] but does not close it): "No fee stated in the primary rule text as opened; secondary guides consistently say no fee." A positive USDA statement that the licence is free was not located in a primary USDA page in this run, so a [VERIFY] note remains for any applicant advice.
  • The FBI Identity History Summary itself has its own FBI charge; the amount was not verified in this run and must not be stated as $18 (that figure appeared only in a Wisconsin secondary guide and is not adopted).
  • Sampling and testing costs are not a USDA licence fee. The rule as opened does not state a USDA sampling fee; in practice sampling and testing are arranged by/for the licensee (see § 7.6.1). The exact amount depends on the sampler/lab and was not established for Mississippi — [VERIFY] before quoting any figure to an applicant.

7.5 Is there a separate USDA handler / processor licence?

No separate USDA handler licence type was located in Part 990 as reviewed. Part 990 creates a producer licence. Handling, transport and storage by a licensed producer are part of production/handling under the producer framework, while manufacture of finished consumable products is governed by other state/federal food, drug and controlled-substance law, not by a USDA hemp-product licence. The state processor registration on paper (§ 69-25-207(5), § 7.2.3) is inoperative, as above. Whether a non-producer transporter or storer in Mississippi needs any licence at all under Part 990 is [VERIFY in the full Part 990 text] — do not assert that transport by a third party is covered by the producer's licence, and do not assert that it is prohibited. Interstate transport is Part 10 work; § 990.63 in older search summaries states states may not prohibit transportation of hemp lawfully produced under an approved state plan or under the USDA plan, but that point is not developed here.

7.6 Pre-harvest sampling, testing, harvest, disposal and reporting for USDA licensees in Mississippi

7.6.1 Lot and sampling — § 990.24 (opened directly)

  • Lot: A lot is a contiguous area in a field, greenhouse or indoor growing structure planted with the same variety/strain. Different varieties/strains or noncontiguous areas require separate lots, each sampled and tested separately. The licensee may not collect its own compliance samples.
  • Timing: No more than 30 days prior to anticipated harvest, a sampling agent must collect samples for total delta-9-THC testing.
  • What is cut: Samples are cut from flowering tops: top 5 to 8 inches from the "main stem" (including leaves and flowers), "terminal bud" (end of a stem), or "central cola" (cut stem that could develop into a bud).
  • Method standard: Sufficient at 95% confidence that no more than 1% of plants in the lot would exceed the acceptable hemp THC level, and must produce a representative, homogeneous sample.
  • Access: An authorised representative of the licensee should be present if possible. Sampling agents must be given complete, unrestricted access during business hours to all hemp/cannabis plants, production and storage areas, land, buildings and structures used for cultivation, handling and storage, and all locations listed on the licence.
  • No early harvest: The crop must not be harvested before samples are taken. Post-harvest samples are only for remediated biomass.

7.6.2 Testing standard — § 990.25 (via search results)

Post-decarboxylation or other similarly reliable methods; total THC reflects THC + THCA conversion; laboratory quality assurance, method validation, sensitivity, disposal procedure for non-compliant samples, and measurement of uncertainty (MU) estimated and reported with results.

Acceptable hemp THC level — § 990.1 (via search results): when MU is applied to the reported total delta-9-THC on a dry weight basis, the resulting distribution/range includes 0.3% or less. The rule's example: 0.35% ± 0.06% gives 0.29%–0.41%, which includes 0.3% and is therefore within the acceptable level for plan compliance. This MU rule affects plan compliance; it does not change the statutory hemp definition or the CSA definition of marihuana, and it does not change the post-11 December 2026 federal total-THC / 0.4 mg per container product definition.

7.6.3 DEA-registered lab point — FLAG THE CONFLICT, do not resolve it by assertion

  • Given federal baseline (adopted for federal dates): USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026.
  • AMS FAQ as opened 25 October 2026: hemp testing laboratories must be registered with DEA to test hemp for compliance by 31 December 2025, and on 14 November 2024 USDA, with DEA, extended the deadline (previously 1 January 2025) to 31 December 2025.
  • Treatment in this report: Both are presented. The given baseline is adopted for federal dates. The FAQ date is flagged [VERIFY against a current USDA notice], because the FAQ text may predate the 2026 delay or may describe a different enforcement scope. Do not present the FAQ date as the current deadline.

7.6.4 After testing — § 990.26 (via search results)

  • Harvest no later than 30 days after sample collection; if harvest is not completed within 30 days, a second pre-harvest sample is required.
  • Harvested lots must not be commingled with other lots or material.
  • Lots meeting the acceptable level may enter commerce. Lots not meeting it are subject to § 990.27.
  • A producer may request additional pre-harvest testing if the original result is believed to be in error, by the same or another laboratory.

7.6.5 Non-compliant plants — § 990.27 (via search results)

Cannabis exceeding the acceptable hemp THC level constitutes marijuana, a Schedule I controlled substance under the CSA, and producers must either use a DEA-registered reverse distributor or law enforcement to dispose of non-compliant plants, or ensure disposal on site at the farm/production facility. Producers must notify USDA of intent to dispose of or remediate and verify disposal/remediation with required documentation. Remediation requires additional sampling and testing of the post-remediated crop.

7.6.6 FSA reporting — AMS FAQ (opened directly)

  • FSA (Farm Service Agency) is the USDA agency that issues lot numbers for tracking hemp from production to harvest.
  • All licensed producers must set up a Farm Profile with FSA and report hemp within 30 days from the date hemp was planted.
  • The deadline for reporting to FSA is 15 July annually.
  • Producers must visit their nearest FSA field office. All production locations must be reported to FSA, with acreage or greenhouse/indoor square footage and licence number, per Part 990 reporting provisions in search results.

7.6.7 USDA reporting — § 990.71 (opened directly)

  • Disposal/remediation report on the appropriate form no later than 30 days after completion, containing producer name/address, USDA licence number, geospatial location or other valid land descriptor for the production area, completion date, and signature of licensee/authorised representative.
  • Annual report by 15 December each year, containing licence number, licensee name/address, and for each lot: location type, geospatial location, total planted acreage, total acreage disposed and remediated, and total harvested acreage.
  • The testing laboratory must report test results for all samples tested to USDA (licence number, licensee name, business address, lot ID, lab name, test/report dates, pre-harvest or post-harvest retest identification, test result). Informal in-season monitoring tests do not need to be reported.

7.6.8 Recordkeeping and inspection — § 990.32 (via search results)

Maintain records of all hemp plants acquired, produced, handled, disposed of or remediated, sufficient to substantiate required reports, for at least 3 years, available for USDA inspection during reasonable business hours, including acquisition, production/handling, storage, and disposal/remediation of non-compliant plants. USDA inspectors/auditors must have access to premises where hemp may be held during reasonable business hours.

7.6.9 Research production — § 990.21(d) (opened directly)

Producers producing hemp for research must obtain a USDA licence, but hemp for research that does not enter commerce is not subject to §§ 990.24 and 990.26 sampling if the producer adopts a USDA-approved alternative sampling method with 95% confidence that the crop will not test above the acceptable hemp THC level. Non-compliant plants must still be disposed of under § 990.27. Only DEA-registered research institutions may keep hemp testing over 0.3% until the end of a study. Reporting under § 990.71, including disposal, still applies.

7.7 Hemp-derived product maker / retailer licences — none in force; every proposal failed

Finding, consistent with Run 1: No Mississippi licence or permit in force for makers or retailers of consumable hemp products (delta-8, delta-9, THCA and similar), and no separate hemp beverage licence in force, was located. Re-checking 2025–2026 bills in this run found no successor that created a licence (see table). General business registrations are not hemp licences (see § 7.9).

7.7.2 The 11 June 2025 Attorney General opinion — what it is and is not

  • Request: Rep. Lee Yancey, after HB 1502 died.
  • Issuer: Attorney General Lynn Fitch, 11 June 2025.
  • Secondary reporting (Cannabis Business Times, Budding Trends blog, both dated June 2025, via search results) states the opinion concluded that sale is prohibited except through a duly licensed medical cannabis dispensary in strict accordance with the Medical Cannabis Act, and possession is prohibited only as possession with intent to sell, barter, transfer, manufacture, distribute or dispense, except possession in strict accordance with the Medical Cannabis Act. Simple possession is NOT answered in the opinion, which states a complete response is outside the scope of an official opinion (section 7-5-25 federal-law limit).
  • The opinion itself, as quoted in secondary reporting, says: "Because the cultivation of hemp in Mississippi is legalized, licensed, and controlled by federal law, a complete response to your request is outside the scope of an official opinion," and "Mississippi law does not specifically address the possession or sale of products derived from the hemp plant designed for human ingestion and/or consumption."
  • Treatment: The full AG opinion text was not opened directly in this run — flag as [VERIFY — open AG opinion text directly] before quoting it verbatim in any later compilation. An AG opinion is not a statute, its scope is contested, and no court test was located in Run 1. It does not create a licence, and it does not by itself create a permit requirement.

7.7.3 Beverage-specific AG analysis — secondary only

Secondary analysis of the same opinion (JD Supra / Lexology analysis, via search results) states:

  • Neither the Hemp Cultivation Act nor any other state law specifically addresses the sale of hemp beverages.
  • The opinion pivots to Miss. Code § 97-31-5, which makes it unlawful to sell/barter/give away/keep for such purposes any preparation which, when drunk to excess in the form sold, will produce intoxication, except for medicinal, household, cooking/baking, or disease-treatment purposes.
  • The opinion notes whether a hemp beverage when consumed in excess would produce intoxication is a factual determination outside the opinion.
  • If a beverage has THC over 0.3% it would be classified as a marijuana beverage, illegal unless purchased under the Medical Cannabis Act through a licensed dispensary (per the secondary analysis).

Present this as secondary analysis of an opinion, not as a beverage ban statute. Enforcement letters reported in secondary press (Poplarville Police Department and Pearl River County Sheriff, 2025, demanding removal within 48 hours / by the next day, citing the AG opinion) are enforcement practice, not law, and must be labelled as secondary.

7.7.4 What a hemp-product business therefore faces today

In the absence of a state product licence: a maker or retailer of consumable hemp products in Mississippi operates without a hemp-specific state licence, under general business law, general food/drug law, the Uniform Controlled Substances Law as interpreted (contested — see § 7.7.2), the § 97-31-5 intoxication-preparation provision as analysed (secondary — see § 7.7.3), and, after 11 December 2026, the federal total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap (see § 7.8). That is a statement of the absence of a licensing regime, not a statement that any particular product is lawful. Product-specific legality is [VERIFY] case by case and is not determined in this report.

7.8 Federal cliff note — what changes after 11 December 2026 for hemp

Under the given federal baseline, after 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. Consequences for Part 7:

  • A USDA producer licence authorises plant production; it does not grandfather a finished product that exceeds 0.4 mg total THC per container under the federal definition.
  • A product lawful under Mississippi law as it stands in October 2026 may still fall outside the federal hemp definition after 11 December 2026.
  • Secondary illustration only (LegalClarity): a typical delta-8 gummy contains 25–50 mg THC per piece, orders of magnitude above 0.4 mg per container. Use that only as a secondary illustration, not as an official Mississippi figure.
  • No Mississippi response to PL 119-37 / PL 119-103 dates was located in Run 1, and none was located in this run either — still [UNAVAILABLE]. Re-check MDAC, MSDH, MDOR and Legislature sources after the 12 November / 11 December 2026 dates.

7.9 General business registrations — not hemp licences

Secretary of State entity registration, a sales-tax permit, and a local privilege licence where required may apply to a business generally, but they are not hemp-specific licences and must not be described as such. Whether a general food-manufacturing or food-facility registration applies to a particular hemp-product maker under general law is [VERIFY] case by case; no such general registration is inventoried here as a hemp licence, because the task is hemp licence types, and general registrations would mislead if listed alongside them.

8.1 Zoning and buffer framework for suitability — Run 1 § 41-137-37, carried forward unchanged

  • A dispensary, cannabis research facility or cannabis testing facility may be located in any area zoned as commercial, or for which commercial use is otherwise authorised or not prohibited, provided it does not violate other provisions of the chapter.
  • A cannabis cultivation and/or processing facility may be located in any area zoned as agricultural or industrial, or for which agricultural/industrial use is otherwise authorised or not prohibited.
  • The main point of entry of a medical cannabis establishment shall not be located within 1,000 feet of the nearest property boundary line of any school, church or childcare facility. A waiver is possible with approval from the school/church/childcare facility and application to the licensing agency, provided the main entry is not within 500 feet of the nearest property boundary line.
  • No medical cannabis dispensary may be located within a 1,500-foot radius from the main point of entry of one dispensary to the main point of entry of another dispensary.
  • A municipality/county may enact time, place and manner ordinances not in conflict with the chapter, may require a local licence/permit/registration at a reasonable fee consistent with non-cannabis businesses, and may not prohibit dispensaries expressly or through ordinances that make their operation impracticable.
  • 2025 amendment in § 41-137-37(1) (Justia reproduction — [VERIFY against official Code]): an applicant for a medical cannabis establishment licence shall not apply to a county/municipality for any zoning or permitting action until after the applicant has received a medical cannabis establishment licence from MSDH or MDOR as applicable. This sequencing matters for every "potential dispensary site" listing: commercial zoning alone does not make a site licensable.
  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-37/

8.2 Medical-cannabis-suitable vs. hemp-suitable land — the distinction that decides every row below

Suitability type What it requires What a listing alone does NOT prove
Medical-cannabis-suitable (dispensary) Commercial zoning (confirmed in municipal code) + 1,000 ft / 500 ft school/church/childcare rule + 1,500 ft dispensary-to-dispensary rule + jurisdiction not opted out for dispensaries (re-check a dated MDOR source — the Run 1 MDOR list is dispensaries-only, undated and informational-only) + state licence before any zoning/permit application (§ 8.1 sequencing) + local time/place/manner compliance A broker's "commercial zoning" claim; a "potential dispensary site" headline; proximity to a highway
Medical-cannabis-suitable (cultivation / processing) Agricultural or industrial zoning (confirmed in code) + enclosed, secured indoor facility compliance per Run 1 (15 Miss. Admin. Code Pt. 22, Subpt. 4, via MSDH FAQ) + state cultivation/processing licence (separate licences — a cultivation licence does not include processing) A building's size, lights, or "turn-key" claim; a seller's licence claim without a licence number and expiry verified with MSDH
Hemp-suitable land USDA producer licence + FSA lot registration + pre-harvest sampling and compliant testing (§ 7.6) + water, access, and local land-use/building/environmental compliance A farmland listing; a "hemp farm" marketing tag; the state-law local-ban bar in § 69-25-201, which is paper law for an inoperative state programme (§ 7.2.3) and whose effect on a USDA licensee's local obligations is [VERIFY], not asserted preemption
Neither, by default Outdoor "hemp-suitable" farmland is not automatically "medical-cultivation-suitable," because medical cultivation must be indoors, enclosed and secured. Conversely, an industrial warehouse is not automatically hemp-suitable, because hemp production still requires a USDA licence, an FSA lot, and compliant sampling/testing for that lot. —

Consistency statement — adopted Run 1 headlines

The following Run 1 headlines are adopted unchanged in this file, and are not re-litigated except where a new conflict is flagged in §9.4 / §10.4 and in the "Conflicts with Run 1" list at the end:

  • Medical only. Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act, SB 2095, §§ 41-137-1 et seq., signed 2 February 2022. First medical sales 25 January 2023.
  • 66,041 patients / 259 practitioners at 15 December 2025; 342 licences at December 2025, including 171 dispensaries.
  • Initiative 65 struck down in Butler v. Watson, 338 So.3d 599 (14 May 2021); all 17 initiative-process restoration measures in 2026 died or were tabled.
  • Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians Referendum 2025-01 authorised a feasibility study / developing legislation only — not sales, licences or legalisation on its own.
  • Local opt-out deadline 3 May 2022; MDOR dispensary opt-out list as transcribed in Run 1 Part 3: 80 municipalities + 17 counties, dispensaries only, undated, "informational only".
  • MDAC issues NO hemp licences; Mississippi hemp production is under USDA licences only (unfunded state plan).
  • Nonresident (out-of-state patient) limits in Run 1: 6 MMCEUs per week, 12 per 15 days, 14 MMCEUs possession, 15-day card, maximum two 15-day periods per 365 days.

Federal baseline applied in this file (given, fixed — not re-researched)

  • Split scheduling: state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). Adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I.
  • IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to §280E.
  • Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026. After 11 December 2026, the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply.
  • USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026.
  • The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026.
  • There is no federal cannabis banking law.
  • Tribal "state-licensed" question — [VERIFY], do not assert: whether a future Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians programme would count as "state-licensed" under the federal Schedule III rule is unverified in this file, exactly as in Run 1. No authority was located that answers it either way. A tribal programme is, on the face of the words, tribal-licensed, not state-licensed; DEA has not, in 91 FR 22714, treated a tribal licence as equivalent; the rule defines the qualifying licence by state (District of Columbia / territorial) issuer only.

9.1.2 What is NOT a Mississippi cannabis regulator

  • The Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians is a sovereign tribal government, not a Mississippi state agency. It has no state-issued cannabis licence to grant, and no tribal cannabis regulator was located (see Part 10). Do not list it in the state-regulator table.
  • USDA, DEA and FDA are federal, not Mississippi, regulators. USDA is the hemp-licensing authority for Mississippi producers (see §9.2 and §10.2). DEA/FDA are relevant only through the given federal baseline (Schedule III rule, FDA-approved products). No federal agency licenses Mississippi medical cannabis businesses.
  • Metrc is the seed-to-sale software vendor / system, not a regulator. Run 1 Part 1 (§1.8) identified Metrc only via secondary sources and flagged it; that flag is carried here — the MSDH-certified statewide seed-to-sale system is required by § 41-137-11, but the vendor name is not asserted as official in this file.
  • The Mississippi Board of Pharmacy, Board of Medical Licensure, Board of Nursing and similar professional boards regulate the underlying professional licences of practitioners and pharmacists; they do not license cannabis establishments and no cannabis-specific rule from them was located for this part. They are noted here only to prevent over-claiming: practitioner registration for the medical programme runs through MSDH/MMCP, not through a separate cannabis board.

9.1.3 Medical Cannabis Advisory Committee — § 41-137-63 (the one advisory body in the Act)

Statute (reproduction — [VERIFY against the official Code]): Miss. Code § 41-137-63, Laws 2022, ch. 303, § 33 (approved 2 February 2022), as amended Laws 2023, ch. 436, § 9 (approved 27 March 2023). Text as reproduced at https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-63/ (opened 25 Oct 2026):

"(1)(a) There is established a Medical Cannabis Advisory Committee, which shall be the committee that is required to advise the Legislature about medical cannabis and cannabis product, patient care, services and industry."

Composition — nine members, verbatim in substance (same source):

  • Governor appoints three: (1) one representative from MDOH/MSDH; (2) one registered qualifying patient; (3) one physician with experience in medical cannabis issues.
  • Lieutenant Governor appoints three: (1) one owner or agent of a medical cannabis cultivation facility; (2) one representative from MDOH/MSDH; (3) one qualified certified nurse practitioner, physician assistant or optometrist.
  • Speaker of the House appoints three: (1) one owner or agent of a medical cannabis processing facility; (2) one owner or agent of a medical cannabis dispensary; (3) one representative from MDOR.

Duties (same source, § 41-137-63(1)(c)): meet at least twice per year to evaluate and make recommendations to the Legislature, MSDH and MDOR on: (i) timely patient access to high-quality medical cannabis statewide; (ii) effectiveness of establishments in serving patients, including dispensary education/support, price reasonableness, security, and sufficiency of dispensary numbers; (iii) effectiveness and sufficiency of testing facilities; (iv) sufficiency of regulatory and security safeguards ensuring access only to cardholders; (v) recommended additions/revisions to MSDH/MDOR rules or the chapter, including security, handling, labelling, nomenclature and whether additional licence types should be made available; (vi) research studies on health effects. The committee must accept public comment in writing and in person at least once per year, give members at least ten days' written notice of meetings, elect its chairman annually (no more than two consecutive years), and serve without compensation (expenses reimbursed as authorised by law). Terms are concurrent with legislative terms; reappointment is permitted.

Repeal date — read this before citing the committee as current: the same reproduction heads the section "[Repealed effective December 31, 2026]" and provides, at § 41-137-63(2): "This section shall stand repealed on December 31, 2026." A 2026 bill to extend that repealer, HB 1773 (Shanks), was introduced — "AN ACT TO AMEND SECTION 41-137-63 … TO EXTEND THE DATE OF THE REPEALER ON THE MEDICAL CANNABIS ADVISORY COMMITTEE" (https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2026/dt/HB/1700-1799/HB1773IN.pdf, accessed via search 25 Oct 2026) — but HB 1773 was referred to Public Health and Human Services on 19 January 2026 and no enactment was located; the committee therefore stands repealed on 31 December 2026 unless another extension is produced [VERIFY on billstatus before stating the committee survives past 31 December 2026]. As of the research date (25 October 2026) the committee exists on the statute book; after 31 December 2026 it does not, unless an extension was enacted. Do not describe the committee as permanent.

Early membership (secondary, dated): secondary reporting (Enterprise-Journal, 2023, via search) named an early chair from the dispensary sector and members including a cultivator chief operating officer, a health-department physician and a patient advocate. Membership at any later date is [VERIFY] — no current roster was located on an official MSDH page in this session, and names from 2023 reporting are not carried forward as the current committee.

No other cannabis advisory board was located. In particular, no separate hemp advisory board, no MDAC hemp task force with ongoing regulatory authority, and no MDOR dispensary advisory board was found. The 2019 Hemp Cultivation Task Force (see §9.2) was a study body, not a regulator, and its report is not a rule.

9.1.4 How the regulators divide enforcement (summary, consistent with Run 1)

  • MSDH enforces licence, testing, packaging/labelling, tracking and cardholder rules for everything except dispensaries.
  • MDOR/ABC enforces dispensary licensing, in-dispensary purchase/sale/distribution rules and cannabis tax collection.
  • MBN / DPS and local law enforcement enforce the Uniform Controlled Substances Law against unlicensed possession, cultivation, sale and trafficking, including on the hemp side where a violation is referred for investigation.
  • The Attorney General prosecutes hemp-chapter criminal actions on behalf of the state (hemp bill text, §10.2) and issues advisory opinions; it does not license.
  • MSDH and MDOR both maintain work-permit registries for their respective licensees' employees (work permits $25, five years — Run 1 Part 4, adopted).

9.2 Key dates — chronology with sources and conflicts resolved explicitly

All dates below are Mississippi dates unless a federal date is stated. Where Run 1 and a new source conflict, the conflict is stated and the adopted date is named.
