1977 or 1978 — [VERIFY year] First-offence small-possession fine-only regime (≤30 g, $100–$250, summons-enforceable) — commonly called Mississippi's "decriminalisation" of first-offence small possession. It is not legalisation and not a civil offence: a first offence remains under § 41-29-139, and second/third offences within two years carry jail exposure (see Run 1 §1.3.1). MPP, "State Laws With Alternatives to Incarceration for Marijuana Possession" (https://www.mpp.org/issues/decriminalization/state-laws-with-alternatives-to-incarceration-for-marijuana-possession/) lists Mississippi as "1977". The commission brief for this part dates it 1978, and most secondary summaries say 1978. Conflict adopted as unresolved: this file does not choose 1977 over 1978. The session law enacting the fine-only tier was not opened in Run 1 or in this session. Do not quote a single year as settled until the 1977/1978 session law is opened. The operative current penalty text is § 41-29-139(c) (Run 1 §1.3.1), not the 1970s history.
2014 Harper Grace's Law — HB 1231, § 41-29-136. CBD oil defined (2014 text) as processed cannabis plant extract, oil or resin containing more than 15% cannabidiol (or a dilution with at least 50 mg CBD per ml) and not more than 0.5% THC. Obtainable only on a Mississippi-licensed physician's order, obtained from or tested by the National Center for Natural Products Research at the University of Mississippi and dispensed by the Department of Pharmacy Services at the University of Mississippi Medical Center. Affirmative and complete defence to prosecution for a patient (or parent/guardian/custodian) with a debilitating epileptic condition or related illness, plus a hold-harmless agreement and a bar on child-removal proceedings based solely on authorised CBD-oil possession/use. HB 1231 as sent to Governor, https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2014/dt/HB/1200-1299/HB1231SG.pdf (via search); 2014 § 41-29-136 reproduction, https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/2014/title-41/chapter-29/article-3/section-41-29-136/ (via search). Repeal-date conflict carried from Run 1, unresolved: the 2014 text says repealed from and after 1 July 2017; later extension bills moved the repealer (2017 HB 459 to 2020; 2017 SB 2610 text to 2021; 2021 HB 119 to 2024); a current FindLaw print heads § 41-29-136 "Section is repealed by its own terms on July 1, 2027" (https://codes.findlaw.com/ms/title-41-public-health/ms-code-sect-41-29-136/, via search). Do not state Harper Grace's Law's current repeal status as settled until the current official Code is opened. 9.2.1 Tax changes — what actually changed, and what did not

No medical cannabis tax rate change was located between SB 2095 (2022) and the research date. The rates adopted from Run 1 Part 2 stand: 5% excise at cultivation's first sale/transfer, 7% sales tax at the dispensary, all excise/fees/fines to the State General Fund (§§ 27-72-1, 41-137-61). What changed over time is the fair market value used where the excise is charged on common-ownership transfers (flower falling from $3,200/lb in 2022–early 2023 to $1,505/lb for July–December 2026, trim $62/lb in that period — Run 1 Part 2, adopted; the FMV series is a valuation schedule, not a rate change). Proposed diversions — HB 513 (2026, House-passed, 12.5% to Public Health Trust Fund until 2030) and SB 2729 (2025, $10m-threshold diversion) — are proposed, not enacted (Run 1 Part 2). No enacted hemp excise or hemp-specific sales tax was located (Run 1 Part 2).

9.2.2 Hemp-derived product law changes — summary (full law in Run 1 Part 1)

There is no enacted Mississippi hemp-derived cannabinoid product statute to date in this file: no minimum age, permit, registration, testing, labelling or beverage statute was located (Run 1 §1.6.6). The only dated "changes" are non-enactments and an opinion: HB 1502 (2025) died; SB 2314 (2025, Schedule I listing of certain hemp products) not enacted; HB 1676 (2024, 5% intoxicating-hemp excise) not enacted; AG opinion 11 June 2025 (opinion, not statute). Any claim that Mississippi "banned delta-8" by HB 1547 is wrong — HB 1547 is a 2019 restatement of § 41-29-113 (Run 1 §1.6.5). No Mississippi response to PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019 was located — [UNAVAILABLE].

9.3.2 The Supreme Court ruling — In re Initiative Measure No. 65; Butler v. Watson, 338 So.3d 599 (Miss. 2021) [OPINION, not statute]

Citation and posture. No. 2020-IA-01199-SCT, decided en banc 14 May 2021, 6–3, opinion by Justice Josiah Coleman. Petitioners: Mayor Mary Hawkins Butler (individually and as Mayor of Madison) and the City of Madison. Respondent: Michael Watson, Secretary of State. Opinion text (Justia reproduction, opened 25 Oct 2026): https://law.justia.com/cases/mississippi/supreme-court/2021/2020-ia-01199-sct-0.html.

Operative reasoning, verbatim (opinion ¶¶1–7, Justia reproduction):

"In article 15, section 273(3), of our State's Constitution of 1890, 'The people reserve unto themselves the power to propose and enact constitutional amendments by initiative.'"

"An initiative sponsor must collect a number of signatures equal to twelve percent of all votes cast for Governor in the preceding gubernatorial election. … At issue today is the additional requirement that the 'signatures of the qualified electors from any congressional district shall not exceed one-fifth (1/5) of the total number of signatures required to qualify an initiative petition for placement upon the ballot.'"

"Petitioners point out that Mississippi now has four, not five, congressional districts. They further point out that four (the number of districts) multiplied by twenty (the maximum percentage of signatures that may come from any one congressional district) equals only eighty. Therefore, Petitioners assert, it would have been impossible for the petition seeking to place Initiative 65 on the ballot to be properly certified as meeting the section 273 prerequisites by the Secretary of State."

"…the loss of congressional representation did, indeed, break section 273 so that, absent amendment, it no longer functions."

What the Court did and did not decide (opinion ¶¶10–11, important precision):

  • The Court held it had original and exclusive jurisdiction under § 273(9) over review of the Secretary of State's approval of the petition — and only over that decision.
  • Quote (¶11): "The Court does not have jurisdiction to review, affirm, or overturn the 'will of the people' as evidenced by the results on November 3, 2020. The November 2020 results are not before us. The only matter subject to the Court's review today is the decision of the Secretary of State finding that the Initiative 65 petition was sufficient to be placed on the ballot."
  • The disposition was therefore: certification reversed, and "any subsequent proceedings on it were void" (Justia summary, same page). In practical effect the certification, the ballot placement and the election result for Initiative 65 were voided — but the Court's legal holding is about the certification, not a referendum on medical marijuana.
  • The Court also held it cannot amend the Constitution itself: "Nowhere therein does the Constitution allow amendment by the Supreme Court" (¶4, citing McNeal v. State). Only a constitutional amendment — proposed by the Legislature and voted on by the electors, or by a repaired citizen-initiative process — can restore the process.

Consequences carried into this file:

  1. Initiative 65 never became law, despite winning the vote.
  2. The entire citizen-initiative process under § 273 is unworkable as written — not just for cannabis. No citizen initiative (medical, adult-use, Medicaid, or any other subject) can currently qualify for the ballot in Mississippi until § 273 is amended.
  3. Two earlier voter-approved initiatives (voter ID, eminent-domain limits) were left exposed to the same logic in commentary at the time (Run 1 §1.5.3) — that exposure is noted as commentary, not as a holding of Butler.
  4. The Legislature's response was statutory, not constitutional: SB 2095 (2022) created a medical programme by statute. A statute can be amended or repealed by the Legislature; it does not restore the initiative process.

9.3.3 Status of the initiative process — NOT restored (as of 25 October 2026)

Current position: Mississippi voters have no working citizen-initiative process. Restoration requires a constitutional amendment: a resolution passed by the Legislature (two-thirds in each house for a constitutional amendment proposal, then a vote of the qualified electors) — a statute alone cannot repair § 273, because § 273 is constitutional text.

2026 restoration measures — all dead or tabled (Run 1 §1.10.3, adopted; no 2026 measure was found alive in this session):

Measure Content (as summarised in Run 1) Status (Run 1, adopted)
SC 515 / SC 517 / SC 519 (2026) Constitutional amendments to amend § 273 and reinstate the initiative process (identical resolutions, different sponsors) Died in committee 3 Feb 2026
SC 518 (2026, England) Constitutional amendment to reinstate the initiative process (10% of active registered voters, no more than one-third per district; two-year legislative hands-off rule) Tabled in the Senate 11 Feb 2026
SB 2919 (2026, England) Bring-forward initiative code sections (companion to SC 518) Died on the Senate calendar 12 Feb 2026
SB 2921 (2026, DeBar) Require the Legislature to honour the intent/substance of a citizen initiative when drafting an alternative Failed / died in committee 3 Feb 2026

Run 1 counted 17 restoration measures filed in 2026 (15 died in committee 3 Feb 2026, SC 518 tabled, SB 2919 died on the calendar). The four measures above are the named vehicles; the remaining filed measures are not individually named in Run 1 or this part — their individual bill numbers are [VERIFY] on billstatus if a complete 2026 filing list is needed. No restoration measure passed. A Speaker's poll reporting 72% support for restoration (secondary, October 2026, cited in Run 1 §0 — https://msindy.org/p/speaker-whites-poll-shows-voters, via Run 1) is polling, not law, and its sample/method were not located in this session [VERIFY].

2025 note (secondary, carried with flag): a 2025 bill to restore a statute-only initiative died on the Senate calendar (CannBus Q3 2026 summary, https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/ms_cannmir.html, via search: "A 2025 bill to restore a statute-only initiative died on the Senate calendar"). A statute-only initiative would in any case not repair the constitutional § 273 defect for constitutional amendments. Bill number [VERIFY].

What restoration would unlock for cannabis: only with a repaired process could citizens again place a medical-expansion, adult-use or decriminalisation measure directly on the ballot. Until then, cannabis change in Mississippi can come only from the Legislature (statute or constitutional amendment proposal) or, for tribal lands, from the Tribal Council (Part 10) — not from a citizen petition.

9.3.4 Local opt-in elections — cross-reference to Run 1 Part 3, with the Lauderdale conflict preserved

Run 1 Part 3 is the controlling local-rules source; this section adds only the election detail Part 9 requires and does not contradict Run 1 Part 3. The statutory mechanism (Run 1 §3.1, §41-137-57) is: a governing board may opt back in at any time by vote; or citizens may petition (20% of electors or 1,500 electors, whichever is less) triggering an election within 60 days, with three weeks' newspaper notice; a two-year cooling-off period follows any election (Run 1 Part 3). County opt-outs cover unincorporated areas only; city decisions are independent.

PART 10 — TRIBAL AND INTERSTATE

10.1 Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians

10.1.1 Who the Tribe is (official tribal source)

The Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians is, in the Tribe's own words on its official home page (https://choctaw.org/, opened directly in this session):

"The Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians are the descendants of those who refused to leave their homeland during the Trail of Tears. The Tribe is the only federally recognized Native American tribe in the State. It is a sovereign nation with more than 11,000 Tribal members, and more than 35,000 acres of fee and trust lands in Mississippi and Tennessee."

That status — only federally recognised tribe in Mississippi, sovereign nation, ~35,000 acres across ten counties in eastern Mississippi (plus the Henning, Tennessee satellite community, counted with Bogue Chitto) — is adopted from the official tribal home page and from consistent secondary reporting. It matters for everything below: tribal law on tribal trust land is made by the Tribal Council, not by the Mississippi Legislature, and Mississippi state cannabis law does not automatically govern tribal trust land. Conversely, tribal law does not govern land outside tribal jurisdiction.

Tribal communities (secondary, consistent across referendum reporting): Bogue Chitto (including the Henning, Tennessee satellite community, represented by Bogue Chitto council members), Bogue Homa, Conehatta, Crystal Ridge, Pearl River, Red Water, Standing Pine and Tucker — eight Mississippi communities plus the Henning satellite. Referendum reporting counts "seven of nine jurisdictions" in favour in one secondary account (Ganjapreneur, counting Henning separately) and "only two [communities] voted to reject" (Standing Pine, Leake County; Conehatta, Newton County) in another (Mississippi Free Press) — the difference is whether Henning is counted separately. The community-level split is therefore reported as: in favour — Bogue Chitto (including Henning), Bogue Homa, Crystal Ridge, Pearl River, Red Water, Tucker; against — Conehatta, Standing Pine. Red Water voted in favour at the highest percentage (72%, Mississippi Free Press); Henning passed narrowly, 24–22 (same source).

Tribal government (secondary, with official-structure caveat): Tribal Council as the legislative body (17 members — the Free Press reports Resolution CHO 25-044 passed with 14 members voting for it and three absent, implying a 17-member council; the council's exact current composition is [VERIFY] against the Tribe's official government pages, which were not opened beyond the home page in this session); Tribal Chief Cyrus Ben as chief executive (named in referendum reporting as the chief who cautioned voters — see §10.1.2); Tribal Election Committee as the election administrator (it convened 11 June 2025 to count absentees and certify — see §10.1.2). No tribal cannabis regulator, tribal cannabis code section, or tribal licensing office was located (see §10.1.4).

10.1.2 Referendum 2025-01 — scope, question, vote, and what it did NOT do

Authorising resolution. At a special-call meeting on 27 March 2025, the Tribal Council passed Resolution CHO 25-044, calling a referendum "to determine the will of the Choctaw people" — 14 members voted for it, three absent (Mississippi Free Press, "Mississippi Choctaws to Vote on Decriminalizing Marijuana", 9 June 2025, updated 11 Sept 2025, http://www.mississippifreepress.org/mississippi-choctaws-to-vote-on-decriminalizing-marijuana-on-tuesday/, via search). Information sessions were held in May 2025 in the Choctaw communities.

Ballot question — verbatim (as reported consistently across tribal, press and advocacy sources):

"Do you support the Tribe developing legislation to decriminalize and regulate possession, production, and distribution of marijuana on Tribal lands?"

Note the verb: "developing legislation". The question does not itself decriminalise, regulate, license or legalise anything. It asks whether the Tribe should develop legislation to do so.

Vote — 10 June 2025, certified 11 June 2025, with a percentage conflict resolved here in favour of raw counts:

Count For Against Total Source
Unofficial, evening of 10 June 2025 (Tribe's Facebook post, via secondary reporting) 1,367 1,110 2,477 Ganjapreneur, https://ganjapreneur.com/mississippi-band-of-choctaw-indians-approve-referendum-allowing-tribe-to-explore-cannabis-legalization/ (via search); Marijuana Moment, https://www.marijuanamoment.net/mississippi-indian-tribe-approves-marijuana-referendum-making-it-first-jurisdiction-in-the-state-poised-to-legalize/ (via search). 1,367 / 2,477 = 55.2% — consistent with the "55%–45%" unofficial reporting.
Certified, 11 June 2025 (Tribal Election Committee, after absentee count) 1,415 1,164 2,579 Mississippi Free Press, "Choctaw Voters Elect Tribal Council, Pass Marijuana Referendum", http://www.mississippifreepress.org/choctaw-voters-approve-marijuana-referendum-elect-council-members/ (via search): "After the Tribal Election Committee convened at 1:00 PM to count absentee ballots and certify the election on June 11, the measure passed by a vote of 1,415 to 1,164".
Percentages as printed in secondary sources "55%–45%" (unofficial); "57%–43%" (NORML update after absentees); "57% to 47%" (Free Press certified report) — — Conflict — resolved in favour of raw counts: 1,415 / 2,579 = 54.9% for, 45.1% against. The "57%–43%" and "57% to 47%" percentages do not match the certified raw counts (57 + 47 = 104, an arithmetic impossibility in the Free Press report). This file therefore adopts the certified raw counts (1,415–1,164) and the computed 54.9%–45.1% split, and flags all three printed percentages as unreliable secondary arithmetic. The Tribe's official final count document itself was not located — [VERIFY] the Tribal Election Committee's certified tally before republication of any percentage. Run 1's "55%–45% unofficial vs 57%–43% final" conflict is thus superseded by this raw-count analysis, not by choosing one printed percentage over another.

What tribal leadership said the vote meant — verbatim (secondary reporting of public hearings, not tribal ordinance text):

  • Chief Cyrus Ben, at a community meeting (Mississippi Free Press, May 2025): "This vote does not automatically authorize or legalize marijuana on Choctaw tribal trust land."
  • Chief Ben, same meeting: "This does not mean that dime bags will start selling on our streets the next day" — "All this means is that [the Tribal Council] will conduct a study of feasibility to determine the best use of marijuana on our lands. That is the next step after this vote."
  • Chief Ben's stated consequence of a "no" vote: "nothing more will be done" (Free Press, June 2025 pre-vote report).

Sample-ballot possibilities (secondary, not law): the sample ballot provided before the vote stated that, if the referendum passed, the Tribe may proceed with allowing retail sales; allowing marijuana to be grown, processed, tested and distributed for retail sales on tribal lands; and/or changing current law to remove criminal penalties for adults 21+ possessing small amounts for personal use (Free Press certified report, via search). The word "may" is doing all the work: these are options for future legislation, not enacted rules. The referendum's own feasibility-study framing (next paragraph) is the operative next step.

Next step authorised — feasibility study only. Upon passage, the Tribal Council was "poised to engage consultants to conduct a feasibility study of legalization, along with research on potential regulations" (Marijuana Moment, via search) and to "perform a comprehensive study to evaluate the marijuana market (medical and/or recreational) and analyze the potential economic benefits, including any potential risks to the tribe" (Free Press certified report). Secondary reporting put the consultant cost at about $100,000 (Ganjapreneur, via search). No feasibility-study report, consultant report, or study conclusion was located in this session — [UNAVAILABLE]. Whether the study has been commissioned, completed or published is not established here.

10.1.3 Tribal council legislation since the referendum — none located

Finding: no tribal cannabis ordinance, tribal cannabis regulation, tribal licensing rule or tribal council cannabis legislation enacted after Referendum 2025-01 was located in this session. Searches for Choctaw tribal council cannabis legislation, a 2026 tribal cannabis ordinance, and a tribal cannabis programme returned only the June 2025 referendum reporting and commentary about the possibility of future legislation (including a risk-manager commentary piece that itself states the Tribe "has not indicated a move toward legalizing recreational cannabis on their lands" and quotes the Tribe's director of public information, Misty Brescia, to the effect that tribal code still says marijuana is illegal on tribal lands until the Tribal Council changes it — secondary, via search at https://cannabisriskmanager.com/wp-content/themes/cannabis/generate-pdf.php?post_id=23247).

Because no tribal ordinance text was located, no verbatim tribal operative text can be quoted in this part — and none is invented. In particular:

  • No tribal definition of "marijuana", "medical cannabis" or "adult-use cannabis" was located.
  • No tribal possession limit, purchase limit, age limit, product-form rule or potency cap was located.
  • No tribal licence type, fee, application or regulator was located.
  • No tribal tax, revenue-sharing or compact provision was located.

Any source that describes a Choctaw cannabis ordinance, licence or sale as existing is, on the evidence located for this file, describing the referendum's contemplated future, not an enacted tribal law. The often-repeated secondary headline that the referendum "legalized" cannabis on tribal lands (e.g. Marijuana Herald, June 2025: "has officially approved a proposal to legalize recreational marijuana") is wrong as a statement of current law and is expressly not adopted: the referendum authorised developing legislation and a feasibility study, and Chief Ben's own pre-vote statements contradict a "legalized" reading.

Current tribal law position — secondary only, [VERIFY] against the tribal code: secondary reporting (Ganjapreneur, via search) states: "Under current tribal law, criminal penalties are removed for Mississippi medical cannabis cardholders who possess legal limits on tribal lands." The same reporting, and the Brescia commentary above, state that tribal code otherwise still says marijuana is illegal on tribal lands. Both propositions rest on secondary reporting; no tribal code section was located in Run 1 or this session to confirm either one. Do not quote a tribal code section number for either proposition. The safe statement is: on the evidence located, a Mississippi medical cardholder is the only category of person for whom any secondary source claims a tribal-law carve-out, and that carve-out itself is unverified against tribal law.

10.1.4 Tribal regulator, who may buy, and operations — all negative findings

Question Answer on the evidence located (25 Oct 2026)
Is there a tribal cannabis regulator? No regulator located. No tribal cannabis commission, department, office or licensing authority was found on the Tribe's official site (home page opened; government pages beyond it were not returned in this session — the guessed government URL returned 404 and is not cited) or in secondary reporting. [UNAVAILABLE / none located — do not name a regulator.]
Is there a tribal medical programme? No. No tribal medical cannabis programme, tribal patient registry, tribal practitioner certification or tribal medical card was located.
Is there a tribal adult-use programme? No. No tribal adult-use sale, licence or retail operation was located. The referendum contemplated both medical and adult-use reforms in the feasibility study; it enacted neither.
Is there a tribal dispensary or cultivation operation on trust land? No operation located. No tribal dispensary, tribal cultivation facility, tribal processing facility or tribal testing facility was found in any source opened for this part. Secondary commentary comparing the Choctaw position to the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians (North Carolina) — which did open tribal sales — is a comparison, not evidence of a Choctaw operation. Do not transfer the Cherokee timeline to the Choctaw.
Who may buy under tribal law today? Nobody, under a tribal programme — because there is none. A Mississippi medical cardholder buying at a Mississippi-licensed (state) dispensary off tribal land is buying under state law, not tribal law. A person on tribal land today is, on the secondary position above (unverified), subject to tribal code that still treats marijuana as illegal except for the claimed Mississippi-cardholder carve-out. Non-members have no tribal purchase right located.
What would have to happen before tribal sales could occur? (1) Feasibility study (authorised, outcome [UNAVAILABLE]); (2) Tribal Council enactment of tribal cannabis legislation amending the tribal code; (3) creation of a tribal regulator and licensing system (or adoption of another framework); (4) resolution of the federal questions in §10.1.5. None of steps (2)–(4) was located as done.

10.1.5 Legal framework with the state, and the Schedule III "state-licensed" question

State–tribal framework as it stands:

  • There is no Mississippi–Choctaw cannabis compact, agreement or memorandum located in Run 1 or this session — [UNAVAILABLE]. Do not assert that a compact exists, is being negotiated, or has been rejected; none of those propositions was located.
  • Mississippi state medical cannabis law (§§ 41-137-1 et seq.) licenses establishments and cardholders under state law. It contains no tribal-programme provision located in Run 1 or this session, and no provision authorising a tribal licence to substitute for a state licence (or vice versa).
  • The Tribe's sovereignty means the Tribal Council — not the Mississippi Legislature — would make tribal cannabis law for tribal trust land. That is a statement about jurisdiction, not about federal legality: tribal legislation would still operate under federal law, including the Controlled Substances Act as amended by the given Schedule III rule.
  • Federal enforcement discretion (the former Cole Memorandum approach, and the referendum's own note that "federal enforcement of cannabis laws 'has been limited'" — Ganjapreneur, via search) is policy, not law, and is not relied on here as a legal basis for any tribal programme.

Schedule III — [VERIFY], with the reasoning stated, not just the flag:

The given federal rule (91 FR 22714, effective 28 April 2026) moves state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III. A future Choctaw programme, if enacted by the Tribal Council, would be tribal-licensed. On the rule text, only one reading is available: "State medical marijuana license" (21 CFR 1300.01) means a licence issued by a state entity (or a District of Columbia or federal territorial entity). A tribal licence is not listed, so tribal marijuana is not Schedule III under 91 FR 22714. A different outcome would require new DEA guidance, a rule amendment, or a court ruling [VERIFY - none located]. Readings considered:

  1. Textual reading: "state-licensed" means licensed by a state; a tribal licence is not a state licence, so tribal medical marijuana would remain Schedule I federally even if the Tribe legalised it. This is the literal-text argument.
  2. Functional-equivalence reading: a federally recognised tribe exercising sovereign regulatory authority over its own territory might be treated as analogous to a state for Schedule III purposes, if DEA guidance or a court so held. No such guidance or holding was located.
  3. USDA-hemp analogy (not a marijuana answer): for hemp (not marijuana), USDA expressly lists the Mississippi Band of Choctaw under "USDA Hemp Producer License" (see §10.1.6) — i.e. the federal hemp system already contemplates tribal producers under a federal licence where there is no approved tribal plan. That analogy does not answer the marijuana Schedule III question, because hemp and marijuana are different federal categories and the hemp system is a USDA licensing system, not a DEA scheduling rule.

Bottom line for Schedule III: do not describe any future Choctaw programme as Schedule III, as state-licensed, or as §280E-relieved. On the rule text it is none of the three; only future DEA guidance or a court ruling could change that [VERIFY] and must be answered from the rule text, any DEA guidance, and any tribal–federal arrangement that may emerge — none of which was located.

§280E consequence of the open question: because a tribal programme is not treated as state-licensed under 91 FR 22714 as written, its operators would remain fully subject to federal §280E (adult-use treatment) even for medical activity, regardless of Mississippi's state decoupling (§ 41-137-51, which covers Mississippi medical establishments — Run 1 Part 2). If it were treated as state-licensed medical activity, the given Schedule III §280E relief would generally apply. Both branches are stated here so the file does not silently assume either.

10.1.6 Tribal hemp — the one federal hemp fact that IS established

USDA list, opened directly (updated 17 February 2026): https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review

  • Mississippi (state): "USDA Hemp Producer License" — USDA will issue the producer licence (no approved state plan).
  • Mississippi Band of Choctaw (tribe): "USDA Hemp Producer License" — USDA will issue the producer licence (no approved tribal plan).

The USDA page defines the descriptor: "USDA Hemp Producer License: USDA will issue the producer license." It distinguishes that status from "Approved Plan (pdf)" and *"Approved Plan (pdf) " (approved under the final rule effective 22 March 2021).

What this does and does not mean:

  • It does mean a Choctaw tribal producer can hold a USDA hemp production licence, on the same federal footing as a Mississippi state producer — i.e. there is a federal hemp route for tribal land, and it is a USDA licence, not a tribal-plan licence.
  • It does not mean the Tribe has a tribal hemp programme, a tribal hemp regulator, or a tribal hemp plan. The USDA listing is the opposite of an approved tribal plan: it records that USDA, not the Tribe, issues the licence.
  • It does not create any marijuana right. Hemp (federal definition, as amended by the given baseline after 11 December 2026) and marijuana are distinct. A USDA hemp licence authorises hemp production within the federal hemp definition; it does not authorise marijuana cultivation, processing or sale.
  • Neighbouring hemp-plan status for comparison (same USDA page, updated 17 February 2026): Alabama — Approved Plan; Arkansas — Approved Plan; Louisiana — Approved Plan; Tennessee — Approved Plan. Mississippi and the Choctaw are the outliers among the five jurisdictions in this part in having no approved plan and relying on USDA licences.

Tribal hemp operations: no specific Choctaw hemp producer, acreage or operation was located in this session — [UNAVAILABLE]. The USDA list records the licensing route, not a list of licensees (the USDA HeMP producer search is the licensee-level source — see Run 1 Part 5, where its URL/fields were flagged [VERIFY]).

10.2 Interstate issues — hemp, medical cannabis, and what may be brought into Mississippi

10.2.1 The governing distinction: hemp vs marijuana, and in-state vs interstate

Product Federal category (given baseline) Mississippi treatment Interstate movement
Hemp meeting the federal definition at the time of movement Not a controlled substance (2018 Farm Bill removal from Schedule I); after 11 Dec 2026, only if it meets the full total-THC definition and the 0.4 mg per container cap Lawful to cultivate only under a USDA licence (MDAC issues none); hemp-derived product rules are the Run 1 vacuum (no permit/age/testing/labelling statute located; AG opinion 11 June 2025 only) Interstate transport of lawfully produced hemp is protected against state prohibition under the USDA Office of General Counsel opinion (see §10.2.2), subject to the post-11 Dec 2026 definition change
Marijuana / medical cannabis (Mississippi-licensed) State-licensed medical → Schedule III (28 Apr 2026); adult-use → Schedule I; non-medical possession → Schedule I Lawful only for MSDH/MDOR cardholders and licensees, within MMCEU limits, in-state only (§ 41-137-39(18), §10.2.3) No lawful interstate commerce in Mississippi medical cannabis was located. Establishments may not transport it out of state; patients have no Mississippi-law right to import it; no interstate medical-cannabis agreement was located
Marijuana bought lawfully in another state Depends on that state's law and federal scheduling (medical vs adult-use) Not lawful in Mississippi by virtue of the other state's law. Mississippi law governs possession in Mississippi (see §10.2.3) Bringing it into Mississippi is the act Mississippi law regulates — see §10.2.5

10.2.2 Hemp shipments — into, out of, and through Mississippi

Mississippi hemp transport statute (enacted text — [VERIFY against the current official Code], from SB 2725 / § 69-25-209 as brought forward in later bills, including SB 2540 (2026) introduced text via search):

"Hemp growers must keep a copy of their hemp grower's license in all vehicles used to transport hemp under normal cultivation activities. Any person transporting or delivering hemp for commerce purposes shall have a dated invoice, bill of lading, or manifest in his or her possession during the entire time he or she is transporting or delivering hemp. The invoice, bill of lading, or manifest shall include the following information: (a) The seller's and the purchaser's license and/or registration number, name and address; (b) The specific origin and destination of the hemp being transported; (c) The quantity of hemp being transported; and (d) Any additional information and/or documentation required by the department."

Sources: SB 2725 committee substitute, https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2020/dt/SB/2700-2799/SB2725CS.pdf (via search); HB 1208 committee substitute (same transport section), https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2020/pdf/HB/1200-1299/HB1208CS.pdf (via search). Caution: this section was written for a state licensing system that was never funded. How its "license number" requirement applies in practice to a USDA licensee (whose licence number is a USDA number, not an MDAC number) is [VERIFY] against MDAC/USDA guidance — no MDAC transport guidance for USDA licensees was located. The prudent reading, stated here as guidance rather than as settled law, is: carry the USDA licence copy plus a dated invoice / bill of lading / manifest with seller and purchaser licence/registration numbers, names and addresses, specific origin and destination, and quantity. Do not travel with hemp and no paperwork.

Enforcement referral (same hemp chapter, via HB 1502 (2025) introduced text restating the chapter, https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2025/pdf/HB/1500-1599/HB1502IN.pdf, via search): where a hemp violation involves a THC concentration exceeding 0.3% on a dry-weight basis (or USDA tolerance) with a culpable mental state greater than negligence, the State Health Officer reports the violation and the grower to the U.S. Attorney General, the Mississippi Attorney General and the Mississippi Public Safety Commissioner, and the violation is referred to the Mississippi Bureau of Narcotics for investigation; MBN "may detain, seize and/or destroy the crop and may initiate a criminal case" under the hemp article or the Uniform Controlled Substances Law; the Attorney General prosecutes hemp criminal actions on behalf of the state. This is the chapter's enforcement spine — it is quoted here from a bill text that restates the chapter, not from a standalone official Code print, so subsection numbers are [VERIFY].

Federal interstate hemp protection (USDA Office of General Counsel opinion, 28 May 2019 — summary, [VERIFY] official opinion text): USDA OGC concluded that (a) hemp is no longer a controlled substance; (b) states and tribes may not prohibit the interstate transportation or shipment of hemp lawfully produced under a state or tribal plan or under a USDA licence (and likewise for hemp lawfully produced under the 2014 Farm Bill); (c) states may prohibit cultivation within their borders, but not transit of lawfully produced hemp. Secondary summary: Ward and Smith, "Hemp News: Updates on Interstate Travel, Interstate Commerce, and Crop Insurance", https://www.wardandsmith.com/article/hemp-news-updates-on-interstate-travel-interstate-commerce-and-crop-insurance (via search). The OGC opinion itself was not opened in this session — cite the opinion, not this summary, for any legal reliance.

Through-shipments: on the OGC position, hemp lawfully produced in, say, Tennessee (approved plan) or Louisiana (approved plan) and shipped through Mississippi to another state may not be prohibited by Mississippi merely because it transits Mississippi — provided it is lawfully produced hemp at the time of movement and the shipment carries the documentation in §10.2.2. Through-shipment is not the same as sale into Mississippi: a through-shipment that is offloaded and sold in Mississippi becomes a Mississippi sale, governed by Mississippi hemp / controlled-substances law (including the AG-opinion position on intoxicating hemp — Run 1 §1.6.4).

Into Mississippi (sale or delivery in Mississippi): hemp shipped into Mississippi for sale or processing in Mississippi must still satisfy Mississippi law at the destination. Because Mississippi has no hemp-derived product permit/testing/labelling statute (Run 1), there is no Mississippi "hemp import permit" to obtain — but that absence is not a clearance: a product that is marijuana under Mississippi law (exceeding the applicable THC definition, or an intoxicating hemp product within the AG opinion's scope) is not made lawful by having been lawfully produced elsewhere. See §10.2.5.

Out of Mississippi: hemp lawfully produced in Mississippi under a USDA licence may be shipped out of Mississippi on the same federal footing, subject to the destination state's law. Mississippi medical cannabis may not be shipped out (see §10.2.3) — the two products must not be conflated in any shipment documentation.

10.2.3 Medical cannabis — no interstate commerce, in-state only (verbatim statute)

§ 41-137-39(18) (reproduction — [VERIFY against the official Code]; text as restated in 2023 and 2026 bill texts, e.g. HB 1158 committee substitute, https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2023/dt/HB/1100-1199/HB1158CS.pdf, and HB 1195 (2026) introduced text, https://legiscan.com/MS/text/HB1195/2026, via search):

"A medical cannabis establishment shall only purchase, grow, cultivate, and use cannabis that is grown and cultivated in this state. Any medical cannabis that is grown and cultivated in this state shall not be transported outside of this state."

That single subsection answers most interstate medical-cannabis questions:

  • A Mississippi licensee may not source cannabis from another state.
  • A Mississippi licensee may not ship Mississippi-grown medical cannabis to another state, even to a state where medical cannabis is legal.
  • There is no Mississippi "export licence", "interstate transfer" or "wholesale to another state" category in Run 1 Part 4, and none was located here.

Patient movement: the Act gives a cardholder no right to import medical cannabis into Mississippi or to export Mississippi medical cannabis out of Mississippi. A Mississippi cardholder who travels to another state and buys medical cannabis there is governed, while in that state, by that state's law (see §10.2.4); on return to Mississippi, possession is governed by Mississippi law (see §10.2.5). The Act's in-state-only rule binds establishments; for patients, the practical rule is the same — Mississippi law does not recognise an out-of-state purchase as a Mississippi purchase, and no Mississippi rule deems imported medical cannabis to be Mississippi medical cannabis.

Federal overlay (given baseline, not a Mississippi rule): even state-licensed medical marijuana, now Schedule III, has no federal interstate-commerce authorisation in the material given for this file. The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider (through 11 December 2026) limits certain federal enforcement spending; it is not an interstate-commerce licence. Do not advise that Schedule III "allows" interstate medical-cannabis shipments — no such authorisation was located.

Interstate laws or agreements — none located: no Mississippi interstate medical-cannabis compact, reciprocity agreement, mutual-recognition agreement or border-state agreement was located in Run 1 or this session — [UNAVAILABLE]. The only interstate mechanisms that exist are the unilateral visiting-patient rules of individual states (§10.2.4), which are not agreements with Mississippi. If a compact is ever claimed, it should be produced as a signed document with parties and effective date before it is cited.

10.2.4 Out-of-state patients buying in Mississippi, and Mississippi residents buying in neighbouring states

10.2.4.1 Into Mississippi — nonresident registration (Run 1 figures confirmed)

Adopted from Run 1 §§1.4.6 and 0, and confirmed against the MSDH programme overview (MMCP Toolkit, August 2026, https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/sites/default/files/2026/MMCP%20Tool%20Kit%20-%20August%202026/MSDH_Medical_Cannabis_Program%20Overview.pdf, via search):

  • No reciprocity by card alone. A home-state medical card does not authorise purchase at a Mississippi dispensary. The visitor must obtain a Mississippi nonresident card.
  • Eligibility (Run 1 §1.4.6): diagnosed with a debilitating medical condition by a practitioner in the home state; not a Mississippi resident, or resident for fewer than 45 days; holds an active home-state medical cannabis registration/card. The MSDH overview states the same in substance: "Out-of-state visitors may apply for a temporary Mississippi medical cannabis card if they meet the medical eligibility requirements and hold an active medical cannabis card from their home state. Applications may be submitted up to 30 days before arriving in Mississippi."
  • Fee: $75 (Run 1 §1.4.4, § 41-137-41 — adopted).
  • Validity: maximum two 15-day periods in a 365-day year from issuance (MSDH overview, same paragraph). Run 1 states this as "15-day card, max two 15-day periods per 365 days" — identical.
  • Limits (Run 1, adopted): 6 MMCEUs per week; 12 MMCEUs per consecutive 15 days; 14 MMCEUs possession. (Resident limits for contrast: 24 MMCEUs per 30 days; 28 possession.)
  • What the nonresident card does not do: it does not authorise home cultivation, delivery, drive-through/curbside purchase, public or in-vehicle smoking/vaping, or purchase above the nonresident limits — the same programme restrictions as for residents (Run 1 §§1.3, 1.4).
  • Vetoed expansion — not law: HB 1152 (2026, "Right to Try") would have allowed out-of-state residents to participate under a petition procedure; it was vetoed 26 March 2026 (adopted date, §9.2) and is not law. Do not describe HB 1152's out-of-state provision as current law.

10.2.4.2 Out of Mississippi — what each neighbouring state actually allows a Mississippi resident to buy

Method note: neighbouring-state rules below are stated for the Mississippi resident travelling — i.e. whether that state will sell to them, and on what credential. Each neighbour's rule is that state's law, not Mississippi law, and each visiting-patient detail that rests only on secondary summaries is flagged [VERIFY] against that state's official programme page. The return leg — whether the purchase can legally be brought back into Mississippi — is in §10.2.5 and is uniformly negative for marijuana.

Neighbour Can a Mississippi resident buy medical cannabis there? On what basis? Return to Mississippi? Source (accessed 25 Oct 2026)
Louisiana (south-west border; closest pharmacy markets: e.g. Shreveport, New Orleans, Baton Rouge) Yes — as a visiting qualifying patient, at a Louisiana marijuana pharmacy (retail permit holder). Louisiana does not have card "reciprocity" in the sense of honouring a Mississippi card as a Louisiana card — it has a visiting-patient statute. Secondary claims that "Louisiana does not accept out-of-state cards" and secondary claims that "Louisiana accepts out-of-state cards" are both imprecise: the statute allows a visiting patient to obtain marijuana on production of a valid home-state card, subject to the form and pharmacy checks below. La. R.S. § 40:1046.1 (official Louisiana law, via legis.la.gov and Justia reproduction): a "visiting qualifying patient" is a patient with a debilitating medical condition who is not a Louisiana resident (or resident <30 days) and is in actual possession of a valid medical marijuana registry card (or equivalent) issued under another state's laws. Quote (§ 40:1046.1(B)): "A visiting qualifying patient may obtain medical marijuana from a marijuana pharmacy upon producing evidence of his valid medical marijuana registry identification card, or its equivalent, which has been issued under the medical marijuana laws of another state, district, territory, commonwealth, or insular possession of the United States." Pharmacy must require the patient to certify on a board/department-approved form that they have been diagnosed with a debilitating condition and will not divert the product; retain copies of the home-state card, photo ID and signed form; review prescription-monitoring-program records before dispensing; and report the dispensing to the prescription monitoring program. Full text: https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?d=1295726 and https://law.justia.com/codes/louisiana/2022/revised-statutes/title-40/rs-40-1046-1/ (via search). Louisiana programme note: Louisiana patients do not hold a state "card" in the Mississippi sense — they hold a clinician recommendation transmitted to a pharmacy — so a Mississippi cardholder should expect the pharmacy to apply the visiting-patient form process, not to "swipe" a Mississippi card. No — see §10.2.5. Louisiana-purchased marijuana may not lawfully be transported into Mississippi as Mississippi medical cannabis. Louisiana statute (above) for the purchase; §10.2.5 for the return leg. Louisiana's own medical programme (clinician-discretion qualification, 10 base pharmacies + satellites, flower limits — Run 1 Louisiana context in the parent programme) is not restated here beyond the visiting-patient rule.
Arkansas (north-west border) Yes — as a visiting patient, on an Arkansas visiting-patient card, not on the Mississippi card itself. Arkansas does not honour out-of-state cards at the dispensary counter. Arkansas Department of Health (ADH) visiting-patient programme (secondary summaries of ADH FAQs, consistent across sources): visitor holds a valid home-state card/recommendation; the home-state approved condition must also be an Arkansas qualifying condition; $50 non-refundable fee; card valid 90 days per application; processing up to 14 days; apply via the ADH registry (mmj.adh.arkansas.gov). Sources via search: https://legalclarity.org/arkansas-medical-marijuana-laws-what-patients-need-to-know/; http://altwellclinic.com/arkansas/faqs (ADH portal link). No — see §10.2.5. ADH official FAQs / portal were not opened directly in this session — visiting-patient fee, 90-day validity and condition-match requirement are flagged [VERIFY against ADH] before a patient relies on them. Arkansas purchase limits for visiting patients (2.5 oz / 14 days, the resident limit) are likewise [VERIFY] for visitors specifically.
Alabama (east border) No. Alabama does not offer reciprocity and does not sell to out-of-state residents. A Mississippi resident cannot buy at an Alabama dispensary on a Mississippi card, and cannot obtain an Alabama card as a visitor. Alabama programme (Run 1 Alabama, adopted): patient must be an Alabama resident, certified in person in Alabama by an AMCC-registered physician, and enrolled in the AMCC patient registry. Secondary summaries are unanimous: "Alabama does not issue medical cannabis cards to non-residents, even visitors who hold another state's card" (Dr Green Relief, via search, https://www.drgreenrelief.com/alabama-medical-marijuana-card/); AMCC dispensary rules: "Not sell or deliver medical marijuana to residents from other states" (via search, https://alabamacannabis.org/laws). First Alabama legal sale: 4 June 2026, Callie's Apothecary, Montgomery (Run 1 Alabama, adopted). No — and there is nothing to bring back, because there is no lawful Alabama purchase for a Mississippi resident in the first place. Alabama hemp products are a separate question (Alabama consumable-hemp law, Title 28 Ch. 12 — Run 1 Alabama) and do not create a marijuana purchase right. Run 1 Alabama (adopted) for residency and first-sale date. Conflict flagged: one secondary source dates the first Alabama sale 4 May 2026 (https://alabamacannabis.org/laws, via search). This file adopts Run 1 Alabama's 4 June 2026 date (Callie's Apothecary, Montgomery; Talladega 28 Aug 2026; Athens 14 Sep 2026) and treats 4 May as [VERIFY] / likely a licence-authorisation date misreported as a sale date.
Tennessee (north border) No medical cannabis purchase at all — for anyone, including Tennessee residents. Tennessee has no medical marijuana programme, no state-issued medical cards and no licensed medical dispensaries. Tennessee law (Run 1 Tennessee, adopted): marijuana is Schedule VI under Tennessee law; possession of any amount is an offence (Tenn. Code § 39-17-418, secondary summaries); the only medical-related provision is a narrow low-THC cannabis-oil exclusion (<0.9% THC, §§ 39-17-402 / 68-7-101, with documentation requirements) — a defence / exclusion, not a purchase programme, and not a route for a Mississippi resident to buy marijuana in Tennessee. Secondary summaries are unanimous that Tennessee does not honour out-of-state cards (e.g. https://www.thecassellfirm.com/drug-crime/is-marijuana-legal-in-tennessee-what-you-must-know/, via search). No. See §10.2.5. Tennessee hemp-derived cannabinoid products (TABC-licensed, 21+, face-to-face, from 1 July 2026 under Title 57 Ch. 7 — Run 1 Tennessee) are a different product category from marijuana and are governed on return by §10.2.5's hemp analysis, not by any medical-cannabis rule. Run 1 Tennessee (adopted) for the no-programme position. Tennessee hemp detail is Run 1 Tennessee, not restated in full here.

Summary for a Mississippi resident travelling: of the four neighbours, two (Louisiana, Arkansas) will sell medical cannabis to a properly documented Mississippi visitor while the visitor is in that state, one (Alabama) will not sell to a non-resident at all, and one (Tennessee) has nothing medical to sell to anyone. None of those purchases creates a right to possess the product in Mississippi on return.

10.2.5 What can legally be brought into Mississippi — the return-leg rules

1. Mississippi medical cannabis bought in Mississippi, possessed in Mississippi — lawful (within limits). A Mississippi cardholder (resident or nonresident, within their respective MMCEU limits and possession cap) may possess Mississippi-dispensary medical cannabis in Mississippi. This is the only marijuana possession route in this section that is lawful on both legs.

2. Marijuana bought in another state, brought into Mississippi — not lawful as Mississippi medical cannabis. Reasons, stated cumulatively:

  • Mississippi law does not recognise an out-of-state purchase as a Mississippi purchase. The nonresident-card system (§10.2.4.1) is the only Mississippi route for an out-of-state patient to buy in Mississippi — it does not retroactively authorise a purchase made elsewhere.
  • Mississippi establishments may only use in-state-grown cannabis (§ 41-137-39(18)), and the programme has no import category. A product's lawful status in Louisiana or Arkansas does not travel with it across the Mississippi line.
  • A Mississippi cardholder who brings Louisiana- or Arkansas-purchased marijuana into Mississippi and possesses it in Mississippi is possessing marijuana that was not obtained through the Mississippi programme. Whether a particular possession would in practice be charged as simple possession (≤30 g, fine-only first offence — Run 1 §1.3.1) or as a higher-tier offence depends on amount, intent and the charging decision; this file states the lawfulness position (not lawful as medical cannabis), not a prediction about charging. Amounts above the Mississippi possession cap (28 MMCEUs resident / 14 nonresident) would in any event exceed the programme's possession limit even if the product had been bought in Mississippi.
  • No "personal import" exception, "medical necessity" import defence, or border-county exception was located in the Medical Cannabis Act or the Uniform Controlled Substances Law for this file — [UNAVAILABLE if such a defence is claimed; do not assert one without a statute or case citation].
  • Federal law compounds the problem: interstate transport of marijuana (even state-licensed medical marijuana) has no federal authorisation in the material given, and adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I federally. This file does not advise evasion of either state or federal law.

3. Lawfully produced hemp brought into Mississippi — lawful only as hemp, and only while it remains hemp. A hemp shipment that (a) was lawfully produced under a state plan, tribal plan or USDA licence, (b) meets the federal hemp definition at the time of movement (after 11 December 2026: full total-THC definition + 0.4 mg per container cap, given baseline), and (c) travels with the § 69-25-209 documentation (§10.2.2), may be transported into and through Mississippi on the USDA OGC position. It ceases to be protected as hemp if:

  • it exceeds the applicable federal hemp THC definition at the time of movement (in particular, a product that was "hemp" under a pre-December 2026 definition but exceeds 0.4 mg total THC per container after 11 December 2026 is not federal hemp after that date — see §10.2.4's federal-cliff note);
  • it is an intoxicating hemp product within the scope of Mississippi's AG-opinion position (Run 1 §1.6.4) when sold / possessed in Mississippi outside the medical programme — the federal hemp-transport protection does not answer the Mississippi sale/possession question for intoxicating products, which is governed by Mississippi law and the AG opinion, not by the OGC transit opinion;
  • it is in fact marijuana (THC content, product form or labelling that takes it outside the hemp definition), in which case it is governed by §10.2.5(2), not by the hemp rules, regardless of what the seller called it.

4. Hemp-derived products bought in a neighbouring state and brought into Mississippi — same hemp analysis, plus the neighbour's own limits. Example: a Tennessee hemp-derived cannabinoid product lawfully sold in Tennessee (TABC-licensed, 21+, face-to-face) is not automatically lawful in Mississippi: Mississippi has no hemp-derived product permit system to "recognise" it, and if the product is intoxicating hemp within the AG opinion's scope, Mississippi's position (outside dispensaries) is prohibitory on that opinion. A non-intoxicating CBD product that meets the federal hemp definition and travels with proper documentation stands on the hemp footing in (3). Product-by-product analysis is required; no blanket "neighbouring-state hemp products are lawful in Mississippi" rule was located.

5. FDA-approved cannabis-derived medicines (e.g. Epidiolex, Marinol/dronabinol as prescription drugs) are prescription medicines under federal and state pharmacy law, not Mississippi medical-cannabis programme products. They are mentioned here only to prevent confusion: a prescription for an FDA-approved product is not a Mississippi medical cannabis card, and a Mississippi medical cannabis card is not a prescription for an FDA-approved product. No interstate issue specific to those medicines was located for this part.

6. Tribal-land movement (special case, [VERIFY] in full): movement between Mississippi state land and Choctaw tribal trust land is not addressed by any state–tribal agreement located (see §10.1.5). A Mississippi cardholder travelling onto tribal land, and a tribal member travelling off tribal land with any cannabis product, are in a jurisdiction-switching position for which no agreement, tribal ordinance or state guidance was located. Do not advise that state-law possession protection automatically follows a cardholder onto tribal trust land, or that any tribal-law protection follows a person off tribal land — both propositions are [VERIFY] against tribal law and any future tribal legislation.

10.2.6 Interstate checklist (for the parent file's Run 2 synthesis — not legal advice)

  • Hemp shipment: USDA/state/tribal-plan licence + dated invoice/bill of lading/manifest (licence numbers, names/addresses, origin, destination, quantity) + federal hemp definition met at time of movement (post-11 Dec 2026: total-THC + 0.4 mg/container).
  • Mississippi medical cannabis: in-state only, establishment-to-establishment via licensed transporters with seed-to-sale manifests (Run 1 Part 1 §1.8 / Part 11 territory), dispensary sale in-store only to cardholders.
  • Visitor into Mississippi: home-state card + Mississippi nonresident card ($75, 15 days × 2 / 365 days, 6/12/14 MMCEU limits) — home card alone is insufficient.
  • Mississippi resident in Louisiana: home (Mississippi) card + photo ID + Louisiana visiting-patient form + pharmacy PMP check — purchase lawful in Louisiana only.
  • Mississippi resident in Arkansas: Arkansas visiting-patient card ($50, 90 days, condition must match Arkansas list) — [VERIFY against ADH].
  • Mississippi resident in Alabama: no purchase route.
  • Mississippi resident in Tennessee: no medical purchase route; hemp-derived products only, under Tennessee hemp law, with Mississippi return-leg analysis in §10.2.5(4).
  • Return to Mississippi with marijuana bought elsewhere: not lawful as Mississippi medical cannabis (see §10.2.5(2)).

Federal baseline — given, not re-researched

  • Split scheduling: state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). Adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I.
