Hearings are transcribed by a court reporter, are "confidential and are not open to the public", and the licensee may be represented at its own expense or self-represent; the burden is on the licensee/aggrieved party to prove the Department's decision was (a) arbitrary or capricious, (b) unsupported by substantial evidence, (c) beyond the Department's power, or (d) in violation of statute or rule (the rendered text cuts off at "(d) violated a statutory or" — the full fourth ground is [VERIFY]). An informal review may be granted but is not required before appeal and does not toll the 20-day limit — Rule 11.1.6(E)–(G) as rendered.
  • MDOR dispensary appeals are in Title 35 Part XI, Ch. 29 ("Appeal Process for Medical Cannabis Dispensaries", as indexed in S-2). The full text of Ch. 29 was not read line-by-line for this file [VERIFY]; do not assume the MSDH 20-day / Hearing Officer procedure applies to dispensaries. MDOR Ch. 04 ¶105 confirms only that "[a]n applicant may appeal a renewal denial as provided by law."

Variance as a safety valve (MSDH Subpart 10): the Department may waive Part 22 provisions on its own initiative or on a licensee's written request, granted or denied by the State Health Officer with specific reasons for denial; a variance "shall not" be considered for "provisions that are purely statutory", "will not be approved to circumvent any relevant rule, regulation or standards", and the licensee "should continue to meet Department-published rules … while the [request] is under consideration" — Rules 10.1.1–10.1.4. A variance is not a licence transfer, renewal or surrender mechanism and does not extend a licence term.

11.2.6 Medical — relocation: new address, zoning re-check, buffer re-check

MSDH licensees — no standalone relocation chapter was located in the text read. The MSDH provisions that bear on a move are:

  • The licence is premises-specific: the facility is "a permanent structure in a fixed location where a medical cannabis establishment operates" (Rule 1.2.24); the application, site plan, premises diagram and seed-to-sale location mapping (Rule 4.11.5: locations "must [shall] be designed … in accordance with the licensee's approved site plan") all tie the licence to an approved premises.
  • Renewal requires an "updated and/or revised diagram of the licensee's premises" where applicable (Rule 3.8.3(A)(1)(d)) and written communication of "all material changes to the required plans and/or standard operating procedures" (Rule 3.8.4).
  • Zoning: MSDH establishments may be located in agricultural/industrial-zoned areas (Rule 4.3.1) or in commercial areas only where the municipality/county has authorised the entity there (by variance or zoning change) (Rule 4.3.2); a municipality/county may require a local licence/permit/registration (Rule 4.3.3); no individual may reside at the same address / on the same property as an establishment, and an establishment must have its own separate, independent address (Rule 4.3.4).
  • Consequence stated as [VERIFY], not as a rule: because no MSDH relocation rule was located, whether an MSDH licensee may relocate on a mere plan update, must file a new application, or must obtain prior written approval — and whether buffers are re-measured on a move — cannot be stated from the MSDH text read. The safe operating assumption, and the only one consistent with the premises-specific licence and the MDOR relocation rule below, is to seek prior MSDH approval in writing before any move. That assumption is flagged, not presented as a rule.

MDOR dispensaries — Title 35 Part XI, Ch. 07 (the operative relocation rule for dispensaries, revised eff. 1 Dec 2025):

"A licensee must submit an update to its license to the Department for approval prior to any relocation of a dispensary even if the move is entirely within a premises in control of the licensee. This includes but is not limited to, expansions, changes in physical address, or changes to the co-location of multiple establishment types. A licensee may request to transfer its location within the city it is currently located within or to a different city or county location." — Ch. 07 ¶100.

Required update contents — Ch. 07 ¶101: (1) "[d]ocumentation from the local government confirming that the proposed relocation would comply with all local zoning restrictions"; (2) "[u]pdated facility plan, security plan, operating plan, and proof of compliance with permitting requirements"; (3) "[u]pdated survey showing that all distance requirements are met and/or a distance waiver has been attained, as applicable"; (4) "[a] new sales tax permit for the location … if the move is to a new address."

"A request for relocation to the Department would be subject to all distance restrictions applicable to dispensary applicants." — Ch. 07 ¶102. "A transfer shall not occur prior to approval by the Department." — Ch. 07 ¶103.

Buffer re-check on relocation is therefore express for dispensaries: the updated survey must show all distance requirements are met (1,000 ft from schools/churches/childcare, 1,500 ft from another dispensary, measured from main point of entry — MDOR Ch. 03 and the dispensary-applicants page, S-3) or a distance waiver attained. For MSDH licensees, buffer re-check on relocation is not separately stated and is [VERIFY] (see above).

11.2.7 Medical — required insurance or bonding minimums

Stated explicitly: no insurance or bonding minimum amount (dollar figure, policy limit, or bond amount) was located in any official text read for this file. No figure is invented here.

What was located:

  • MSDH renewal: the renewal application must include, as applicable, a "Copy of licensee's current insurance policy" — Rule 3.8.3(A)(1)(e). The rule requires production of a policy; it states no minimum coverage amount, no required policy type, and no bond. Whether MSDH applies an unwritten minimum in practice, or requires a particular type (e.g. general liability, product liability, property) is [VERIFY with MSDH].
  • MDOR dispensaries: a full-text search of the Title 35 Part XI PDF (S-2) for "insurance" returned no hits. The MDOR renewal, transfer, relocation and security chapters state no insurance or bond requirement at all. The absence is reported, not filled.
  • Transport vehicles (the only insurance quantum rule located): "Vehicles used to transport cannabis and/or cannabis products must [shall] be insured at or above the legal requirements in Mississippi" — MSDH Rule 7.2.2; and a transport entity must submit "the license plate numbers, proof of insurance, and vehicle identification numbers for each vehicle being used to transport cannabis or cannabis-infused products" before use — Rule 7.2.1. "At or above the legal requirements in Mississippi" means the generally applicable Mississippi motor-vehicle insurance minimums, not a cannabis-specific minimum; the cannabis rules do not state a higher figure.
  • No surety bond, letter of credit, escrow, or capital-reserve requirement for any medical licence type was located in the MSDH or MDOR texts read. The Act's rulemaking list (via S-10, § 41-137-41) does include "[r]easonable requirements to ensure the applicant has sufficient property or capital to operate", but no implementing capital/bond figure was located in §§11.1–11.4's sources [VERIFY if a capital-adequacy rule exists in the initial-application rules, which are outside §§11.1–11.4's core but may impose one].

Bottom line for §11.2.7: a Mississippi medical licensee must be able to produce a current insurance policy at MSDH renewal and must insure transport vehicles to at least Mississippi's legal minimums. There is no located cannabis-specific insurance minimum and no located bonding minimum to quote.

11.2.8 Hemp — USDA licence transfer / renewal / term; and the absence of any Mississippi hemp licence transfer regime

There is no Mississippi hemp licence transfer regime, because there is no Mississippi hemp licence to transfer. MDAC's own page (S-7) states the position in terms, opened and read for this file:

"Senate Bill 2725, also known as the Mississippi Hemp Cultivation Act, was signed into law on June 29, 2020. This act legalized the cultivation of hemp under a state plan to be created and implemented by the Commissioner of Agriculture and Commerce. Although the act allowed for a state hemp cultivation program, the necessary funding to implement the program was not appropriated by the Mississippi Legislature."

"As a result, currently the only legal option for a producer to cultivate hemp in Mississippi now is to obtain a hemp license from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) under the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program."

"The Mississippi Department of Agriculture & Commerce does not issue hemp licenses."

USDA's plan list confirms the same allocation: Mississippi is listed as "USDA Hemp Producer License" (USDA AMS, state-and-tribal plan review page, via search result; the MDAC page is the authority cited here). Consequently: no MDAC transfer form, transfer fee, transfer approval, relocation approval, or renewal exists to describe. Any "transfer" of a Mississippi hemp operation is a matter of USDA licence modification (below) and of general Mississippi business/property law (sale of the entity, lease assignment, etc.), not of a state hemp licence regime.

USDA licence term, renewal and modification — 7 CFR § 990.21 and § 990.71(a):

  • Term: "USDA-issued hemp producer licenses shall be valid until December 31 of the year three years after the year in which license was issued" — § 990.21(a) (as rendered in the Part 990 text); repeated at § 990.71(a): "Licenses will be valid until December 31 of the year three years after the license is issued." MDAC (S-7) states the same in plain terms: "Once issued, USDA hemp production licenses are active for three years unless the State of Mississippi elects to administer a State hemp production program." Example: a licence issued in 2026 expires 31 December 2029.
  • Renewal — no automatic renewal: "USDA hemp producer licenses must be renewed prior to license expiration. Licenses are not automatically renewed. Applications for renewal shall be subject to the same terms, information collection requirements, and approval criteria as provided in this subpart for initial applications unless there has been an amendment to the regulations in this part or the law since approval of the initial or last application" — § 990.21(b). USDA accepts applications "on a rolling basis" and "[t]he license application will be used for both new and renewal applicants" — § 990.71(a). The application must include contact information (individual: full name, business EIN, business address, telephone, email if available; entity: full entity name, principal business location, and full name/title/email if available of each key participant) and a current FBI Identity History Summary for the applicant / each key participant, "dated within 60 days of submission of the application submittal"; incomplete applications are returned and may be resubmitted; all applicants consent to comply with Part 990 by submitting — § 990.71(a)(1)–(3) and § 990.21 application provisions. A felony related to a controlled substance in the last 10 years bars issuance (MDAC, S-7, summarising the USDA criterion).
  • Transfer — the rule does not use the word "transfer" for USDA licences; it uses "modification": "A license modification is required if there is any change to the information submitted in the application including, but not limited to, sale of a business, the production of hemp in a new location, or a change in the key participants under a license" — § 990.21(c). In other words: a sale of the licensed business, a move to a new production location, or a change in key participants does not automatically carry the licence to a new person; it triggers a modification requirement. The regulation text read does not spell out the modification procedure, form, fee (if any), timing, or approval standard — secondary commentary notes the same silence. Modification procedure is therefore [VERIFY] with USDA/HeMP before structuring a hemp-business sale in Mississippi. Do not describe a USDA hemp licence as "freely transferable" or as "non-transferable" without that qualification: the accurate statement on the regulation text is that the licence is tied to the application information, and a sale / new location / key-participant change requires a licence modification.
  • Key participant (for modification and renewal): § 990.1 defines "key participant" in substance as a sole proprietor, a partner in a partnership, or a person with executive managerial control in a corporation (e.g. CEO/COO/CFO-level); farm/field/shift managers are not key participants. A change in key participants is therefore a modification trigger even if the licensed entity itself does not change.
  • Research licences: producers producing hemp for research must obtain a USDA licence; research hemp not entering commerce is exempt from §§ 990.24 and 990.26 sampling if the producer adopts a USDA-approved alternative sampling method capable of ensuring, at 95% confidence, that no more than 1% of plants exceed the acceptable hemp THC level; disposal of non-compliant research plants follows § 990.27 (only DEA-registered research institutions may keep over-limit hemp until study end); reporting follows § 990.71 including disposal — § 990.21(d).
  • No Mississippi hemp licence fee, renewal fee, or transfer fee exists to quote, because MDAC issues no licence. USDA application/licence fees under Part 990: none located in the sections read [VERIFY — HeMP application materials should be checked for any fee before filing; the absence of a fee in §§ 990.21/990.71 is not proof that HeMP charges nothing].
  • Hemp-derived product businesses (processors, retailers, brands): no Mississippi licence, transfer, or renewal regime for hemp-derived product businesses was located (Run 1: no hemp-derived product permit statute; nothing in this run changes that). A hemp-derived product business in Mississippi therefore has no state hemp licence to transfer or renew; its regulatory exposure is instead (i) the producer-level USDA regime for any cultivation it does, (ii) general Mississippi business, food, and consumer-protection law, and (iii) the AG-opinion theory noted in Run 1 (intoxicating hemp products outside the medical programme treated as prohibited — opinion, not statute), plus, after 11 December 2026, the federal total-THC / 0.4 mg per container regime in the given baseline. Each of those is flagged, not expanded, because §§11.1–11.4 do not include a hemp-product-permit section.

11.3 CULTIVATION RULES

11.3.1 Medical — canopy by tier (Run 1 tiers reproduced), plant counts, indoor/outdoor/greenhouse, enclosed/locked facility

Canopy definition — MSDH Rule 1.2.30:

"Canopy means the total surface area within a cultivation area that is dedicated to the cultivation of flowering cannabis plants. The surface area of the plant canopy must [shall] be calculated in square feet. Measurement must [shall] include all of the area within the boundaries where the cultivation of the flowering cannabis plant occurs. If the surface area of the canopy consists of noncontiguous areas, each component area must [shall] be separated by identifiable boundaries. If a tiered or shelving system is used in the cultivation area, the surface of each tier or shelf must [shall] be included in the calculation. Calculation of the area of the plant canopy should not include: A. The areas within the cultivation area that are used to cultivate immature cannabis plants and seedlings prior to flowering; and, B. The areas within the cultivation area that are used to support mature cannabis plants."

The MSDH FAQ (S-6) states the same definition and adds: "Cultivators' growing capacity is determined based on the tier of the license and its associated canopy space."

Tier table — MSDH FAQ (S-6), current as opened 25 October 2026, matching Run 1:

Licence class Tier Canopy
Micro-cultivator Tier 1 1,000 square feet or less
Micro-cultivator Tier II (Tier 2) More than 1,000 square feet but not more than 2,000 square feet
Cultivator Tier I (Tier 1) Not less than 2,000 square feet but not more than 5,000 square feet
Cultivator Tier II (Tier 2) Not less than 5,000 square feet but not more than 15,000 square feet
Cultivator Tier III (Tier 3) Not less than 15,000 square feet but not more than 30,000 square feet
Cultivator Tier IV (Tier 4) Not less than 30,000 square feet but not more than 60,000 square feet
Cultivator Tier V (Tier 5) Not less than 60,000 square feet but not more than 100,000 square feet
Cultivator Tier VI (Tier 6) 100,000 to 150,000 square feet, maximum 2 locations, combined canopy not more than 150,000 square feet

Conflict C-1 (preserved, see §0): Run 1 recorded a rule version giving Tier 6 as "100,000–150,000" square feet. The current FAQ says "100,000 to 150,000 square feet, maximum 2 locations, combined canopy not more than 150,000 square feet" with no upper limit. This file adopts the FAQ wording and flags the conflict. Do not advise a Tier 6 applicant that 150,000 sq ft is a ceiling, or that there is no ceiling, until § 41-137-35 and current Rule 3.2.2 are checked [VERIFY]. Note also the tier-boundary drafting: micro Tier 2 ends at 2,000 sq ft and standard Tier 1 begins at "not less than 2,000" sq ft, so a canopy of exactly 2,000 sq ft falls in both wordings as rendered — a boundary applicant should confirm the intended class with MSDH [VERIFY].

Plant counts — stated explicitly: there is no plant-count limit in the rules read. Capacity is canopy-only. The MSDH FAQ (S-6) answers "How many plants is a licensed cultivator allowed to grow?" by pointing to canopy tier, not to a plant number, and no plant-count cap (per tier, per licence, or per patient) appears in the MSDH Subpart 4 or Subpart 5 text read. This confirms Run 1 ("no plant-count limit, canopy only"). What is limited is batch size for testing (25 lbs per harvest batch package — Rule 5.2.1), not plant numbers.

Indoor / outdoor / greenhouse — Rule 4.4.1 (verbatim, operative sentences):

"All cultivation commercial cannabis activities must [shall] take place in indoor, enclosed, locked and secure facilities with controls over environmental conditions such as humidity, temperature, and light and that preclude unfiltered air exchange with the outdoors. Condition changes outside of the facility should not significantly alter or affect environmental conditions inside the facility[.] Outdoor cultivation … of cannabis and processing of cannabis products are prohibited. 'Home grow' of cannabis is prohibited."

Consequence: outdoor cultivation is prohibited; greenhouse cultivation as an outdoor or semi-outdoor method is prohibited on the face of Rule 4.4.1 (a greenhouse that is a fully indoor, enclosed, locked, secure structure with sealed environmental control and no unfiltered air exchange would need to be assessed against Rule 4.4.2's building tests — see below — but no rule was located that authorises "greenhouse" as a distinct cultivation class, and no greenhouse tier or standard was located). A cultivator should not assume a greenhouse qualifies; the building tests below are the test.

Enclosed / locked facility — Rule 4.4.2 (building tests, all must be met):

All cultivation business operations and activities must take place "within a building or secure structure that meets all state and local electrical, fire, plumbing and building codes and specification(s)" and:

  • (A) "Has a complete roof enclosure supported by connecting permanent walls, constructed of solid materials extending from the ground to the roof", providing (1) a sealed environment preventing unfiltered air exchange with the outdoors, (2) control over temperature, humidity, light, carbon-dioxide levels, etc., and (3) protection from all external elements;
  • (B) "Is secure against unauthorized entry";
  • (C) "Has a foundation, slab, or equivalent base to which the floor is securely attached";
  • (D) "Has commercial grade door locks on all external doors that are locked at all times";
  • (E) "Restricts access to only authorized personnel to locked and secure areas identified with signage and daily records of entry and exit";
  • (F) plumbing adequate to supply water and convey sewage/waste without cross-contamination of potable water;
  • (G) water supplies sufficient for cultivation activities;
  • (H) toxic cleaning compounds, sanitising agents, solvents and pesticides "identified and stored in a manner that is in accordance with applicable local, state or federal law, rule, or regulation";
  • (I) a pest-control and management plan implemented on the premises;
  • (J) biosecurity measures "implemented and adhered to at all times."

The cultivation-facility definition is to the same effect (Rule 1.2.22): a cultivation entity "acquires, grows, cultivates, and harvests medical cannabis in an indoor, enclosed, locked, and secure area."

Facility construction / design — Rule 4.4.3 (selected): floors, walls and ceilings adequately cleanable, kept clean and in good repair; prevention of drip/condensate contamination; aisles/working spaces unobstructed and of adequate width; adequate lighting in hand-washing, dressing/locker, toilet rooms and all areas where cannabis is examined, produced, packed or stored and where equipment/utensils are cleaned; shatter-resistant light bulbs/fixtures/skylights/glass suspended over exposed cannabis, or other breakage protection; adequate ventilation/control to minimise dust, odours and vapours (including steam and noxious fumes) where they may contaminate.

Zoning and siting — Rules 4.3.1–4.3.4: cultivation establishments may be in agricultural- or industrial-zoned areas (or areas where such use is authorised/not prohibited); in commercial areas only where the municipality/county has authorised the entity there (variance or zoning change); a local licence/permit/registration may be required at a reasonable, non-discriminatory fee; no individual may reside at the same address or on the same property as an establishment, and the establishment must have its own separate, independent address (an adjoining residence requires a separate address, e.g. "123 County Road" vs "123 A County Road").

Other cultivation-facility operational rules located in Subpart 4 (for completeness, since §§11.3–11.4 overlap here):

  • Separation of functions (Rule 4.4.6): if one establishment is licensed as both cultivation and processing in the same physical space, "there must [shall] be physical separation between the two by connecting permanent walls, constructed of solid materials extending from the ground to the roof with separate means of entrance and exit."
  • Plant access / inspection (Rule 4.4.5): cultivation licensees "shall maintain physical access to their stock of cannabis plant(s) for safe and easy observation and inventory of each plant group. Aisles must [shall] be open and accessible so as to allow inspection of the plants by the Department and must [shall] provide a safe means for access and viewing of plants if plants are located/placed on an upper rack that requires scaffolding or a ladder for viewing."
  • Consumption ban on premises (Rule 4.2.14): licensees "shall not permit the consumption of cannabis and/or cannabis products on its licensed premises or by employees during working hours."
  • Personnel training (Rule 4.2.12, cultivation facilities, as rendered): employees trained in at least (A) the cultivation-facility rules in Part 22, (B) security measures/controls for prevention of diversion/inversion/theft/loss, (C) proper use of the statewide seed-to-sale system, (D) emergency response (severe weather, fire, natural disasters, unauthorised intrusions), and (E) facility safety/sanitation procedures — "for a minimum of eight (8) hours of initial training and five (5) hours of annual training" (the rendered text attaches the hour figures to the training list; the exact paragraph structure is [VERIFY] against the clean rule, but the 8-hour initial / 5-hour annual figures are as rendered).
  • Provisional licences (Rule 1.2.115): a provisional licence may issue "when a temporary condition of non-compliance … exists" if MSDH is satisfied preparations are being made to qualify for a regular licence and health/safety will not be endangered; "[b]usiness activities and operations can be limited by the Department for this licensure category." A provisional licence is not a cultivation tier and does not change canopy limits.

11.3.2 Medical — plant-growth-regulator (PGR) ban: what the law actually says

The located rule is a processing ban, stated in a definition — not a freestanding cultivation-use ban in the passages read:

"Plant Growth Regulator Cannabis — The term 'plant growth regulator cannabis' shall mean a cannabis plant whose growth and structure has been modified using plant growth hormones. A cannabis processing facility shall not process and/or manufacture plant growth regulator cannabis." — Rule 1.2.108.

What this does and does not establish:

  • Established: a processing facility may not process or manufacture PGR cannabis. PGR cannabis that reaches a processor must therefore be refused/segregated (and, by the general rules, cannot be turned into a compliant product by processing).
  • Not established in the passages read: an express prohibition on a cultivator applying plant growth hormones / regulators during cultivation, or a testing requirement for PGR residues, or a destruction duty specific to PGR plants. The definition's operative sentence binds processors, not cultivators, in its terms.
  • Adjacent rules that may bear on PGR use but do not name it: the pesticide/chemical storage rule (Rule 4.4.2(H) — toxic compounds, sanitising agents, solvents and pesticides stored per applicable law); the general adulteration ban (Rule 5.1.3 — licensees "shall not treat or otherwise adulterate a cannabinoid product, concentrate, cannabinoid extract, or extract with any non-cannabinoid additive that would increase potency, toxicity or addictive potential, or that would create an unsafe combination, with caffeine or other chemical that may increase carcinogenicity or cardiac effects"); and the pesticide testing regime (Rule 5.4.3, Appendix A). Whether any of these, or a separate MSDH pesticide/PGR list, prohibits cultivation use of specific PGRs is [VERIFY] — do not advise a cultivator that PGR use is either permitted or prohibited on the basis of Rule 1.2.108 alone. The commission's question ("plant-growth-regulator ban if in law") is therefore answered as: a processing ban is in law; a cultivation-use ban was not located in the text read.

11.3.3 Medical — tracking from seed (seed-to-sale)

Statutory system — § 41-137-11 (via S-10): the seed-to-sale tracking system used by cultivation facilities, dispensaries, processing facilities, testing facilities, research facilities, transportation entities and disposal entities must be capable of (a) letting facilities interface with the statewide system to enter/access information; (b) giving MDOR and MDOH access to all information in the system's database; (c) maintaining confidentiality of patient/caregiver data so that only MDOR/MDOH and persons/entities authorised by law access what they are authorised to access; (d) producing analytical reports to MDOR/MDOH on total quantity of daily/monthly/yearly sales per product type, average prices, and total inventory/sales-record adjustments; and (e) determining, in real time by patient registration number, the amount a patient/caregiver has purchased that day. Banks/financial institutions may be given limited financial (not medical/personal) information needed for federal compliance (§ 41-137-11(4), via S-10). Verify against the official Code [VERIFY] — this paragraph is taken from a reproduction.

MSDH tracking rules — Rule 4.11 and definitions:

  • System definition (Rule 1.2.129): "Seed-to-Sale System means the specialized inventory management system utilized throughout the medical cannabis program that allows for the tracking of cannabis from early life cycle until final sale to a qualified patient or caregiver or disposal/destruction by a cannabis disposal entity."
  • Use: "Cannabis cultivation [l]icensees must [shall] use the Department designated seed-to-sale system directly for inventory tracking or may use an approved third-party integrator for interface into the Department designated seed-to-sale system" — Rule 4.11.1. Licensees must identify "an employee with primary responsibility for seed-to-sale tracking (e.g., seed-to-sale system administrator)" — Rule 4.11.2; and "ensure that all reporting into the Department approved statewide seed-to-sale system is clear, accurate, and transparent" — Rule 4.11.3. The vendor is not named in these rules (see §0 / §11.3.6 on Metrc).
  • Tagging (Rule 4.11.4): inventories must be "properly tagged and labeled in any manner which is compatible with the state seed-to-sale tracking program", with tags that "may include bar codes, RFID tags, NFC tags, or other equivalent system for assigning unique numbers to cannabis plants, products, and packages"; tags must contain the legal name and correct licence number of the establishment; a tag may be fastened to the stalk or other Department-approved position before a plant can support a tag's weight (8 inches in height), and "shall remain affixed for the entire life of the plant until disposal"; cannabis must be "continuously and properly tagged (individually or as packages) at all stages of production, including all cultivation phases and/or production steps"; mother plants "must [shall] be tagged before any cuttings or clones are generated therefrom" and cuttings/clones "shall be recorded in the state seed-to-sale program as being derived from that mother plant's tag"; a destroyed/stolen/fallen-off tag must be replaced and the change reflected in the system; tags already affixed "shall not" be reused; each wholesale package must have a tag during storage and transfer and "may only contain one batch"; immature plant batches must be package-tagged before transfer if not previously tagged; inventory must be tagged during storage and transfer either as individual units, or as a single wholesale package under one tag only if all units are from the same production batch; if units are removed from a wholesale package, each unit or new package must be separately tagged.
  • Locations (Rule 4.11.5): "All locations related to [the] commercial production of cannabis and cannabis products must [shall] be easily distinguishable in the statewide seed-to-sale system. Locations identified in the system must [shall] be designed to easily and labeled in accordance with the licensee's approved site plan and in a manner that identifies [the] location position of inventory within the facility at all times."
  • Plant-batch logging (Rule 1.2.107): a plant batch is "logged into the seed-to-sale system as a group on the date received as clones or planted, whichever is earliest, and prior to maturing to the vegetative phase of growth."
  • Unique identifier (Rule 1.2.136): "a unique number generated by the seed-to-sale system and assigned to all usable medical cannabis for the purpose of tracking cannabis from early life cycle until final sale to a qualified patient or caregiver or disposal/destruction by a cannabis disposal entity."
  • Costs: "All associated costs for [seed-to-sale participation] are the financial responsibility of the medical cannabis establishments" (Rule 4.10 area, as rendered in S-1 at the seed-to-sale discussion).
  • Enforcement linkage: failure to log and/or tag in the seed-to-sale system is an express ground for seizure, destruction, confiscation or administrative hold — Rule 11.1.3(A). Test samples, test results, COAs, manifests and waste must all be entered/recorded in the system at the points stated in §§11.1.4–11.1.5 and in Subpart 8 (waste weighed/recorded in the system on-site and at final destination).

What "from seed" means in practice under these rules: tracking begins at the plant-batch stage (clones received / seeds planted, logged as a group before vegetative phase), follows the plant by tag for its entire life, follows mother-plant → cutting/clone lineage, follows harvest batches (≤25 lbs) and production batches through testing (quarantine until passing results are in the system), transfer (manifest from the system), and ends at sale to a patient/caregiver or disposal/destruction by a disposal entity. There is no separate "seed" registration step located in the rules read; the earliest system event is the plant-batch log.

11.3.4 Medical — cultivation and the other Part 11 topics that touch cultivation

For cross-reference (not full treatment, which belongs in other Parts): cultivation waste must be rendered unusable/unrecognisable under video surveillance (Rule 1.2, "Plant Waste" definition; Subpart 8); cultivation products may not be transferred to a dispensary except in compliant packaging/labelling (Subpart 6); cultivation-to-processing and cultivation-to-dispensary transfers move only via licensed transport entities with system manifests (Subpart 7); and cultivation premises are subject to unannounced MSDH inspection (Rule 4.6.1(B) sanitation/inspection context; Act inspection during business hours, via S-10).

11.3.5 Hemp — plot / field registration and reporting to USDA (lot, GPS, acreage)

No Mississippi plot/field registration exists — there is no state hemp plan, no MDAC registration form, and no Mississippi lot register. Registration and reporting are to USDA (licence application + FSA) and, for annual/test/disposal reporting, to USDA under § 990.71. The elements are:

Licence-application location information (7 CFR § 990.71(a) / § 990.21 application provisions): the application must include the producer's contact information and, for an entity, the principal business location and key participants (see §11.2.8). The licence application provisions read do not themselves list "lot, GPS, acreage" as application fields — those fields enter through FSA reporting and the annual report below. Any HeMP application screen that asks for geospatial coordinates at application stage should be treated as application-system detail [VERIFY in HeMP], not as a § 990.71(a) application element.

FSA reporting (the "plot/field registration" in practice): USDA's programme requires producers to report hemp production locations to the Farm Service Agency (FSA). The Part 990 text as rendered states: "All locations where hemp is produced must be reported to FSA", together with "(b) Acreage dedicated to the production of hemp, or greenhouse or indoor square footage dedicated to the production of hemp" and "(c) The hemp license number" (Part 990, § 990.70-area text via S-8 search rendering). USDA's FAQ (S-9) states: "The deadline for reporting to FSA is July 15 annually" and "[l]icensed producers are required to visit their nearest FSA field office." The full § 990.70 text (FSA reporting contents, deadlines, and any pre-planting vs post-planting timing) was not opened line-by-line for this file [VERIFY — 7 CFR § 990.70]. The July 15 date is taken from the USDA FAQ as rendered in search results; confirm it in the FAQ page itself before advising a producer on a deadline.

Annual report to USDA — § 990.71(c) (verbatim fields): "Each USDA licensee shall submit an annual report to USDA. The report form shall be submitted by December 15 of each year and contain": "(1) USDA licensee's license number. (2) USDA licensee's name. (3) USDA licensee's address. (4) Lot, location type, geospatial location, total planted acreage, total acreage disposed and remediated, and total harvested acreage."

So the lot / GPS / acreage triad the commission asks for is reported annually by: lot (lot identification), location type + geospatial location (the GPS / land-descriptor element), and planted / disposed-and-remediated / harvested acreage. "Location type" distinguishes, for example, field vs greenhouse/indoor production; the regulation text read does not define the location-type taxonomy [VERIFY in HeMP / USDA guidance if a producer needs the code list].

Test-results reporting — § 990.71(d): the licensee "must ensure that the laboratory that conducts the test of the sample(s) from its lots reports the test results for all samples tested to USDA. Informal testing conducted throughout the growing season for purposes of monitoring THC concentration do not need to be reported to USDA." The report must contain: licence number; licensee name; business address; lot identification number for the sample; name of testing laboratory; date of test and report; identification of a pre-harvest or post-harvest retest; and test result.

Disposal / remediation reporting — § 990.71(b): on any disposal or remediation activity, the licensee must report on the appropriate form to USDA "no later than 30 days after the date of completion of disposal or remediation activity", containing: producer name/address; USDA licence number; geospatial location or other valid land descriptor for the production area subject to disposal/remediation; date of completion; and signature of the licensee or authorised representative.

"Lot" for hemp (working definition, from Part 990 usage): a lot is the contiguous production unit that is sampled and tested as one unit — the sampling method must ensure, at 95% confidence, that no more than 1% of plants in the lot exceed the acceptable hemp THC level and that the sample represents a homogeneous composition of the lot (§ 990.24(b)). The formal § 990.1 definition of "lot" (contiguous area, same variety, etc.) was not opened verbatim for this file [VERIFY — 7 CFR § 990.1]; do not quote a lot definition beyond the functional description above.

No Mississippi acreage cap, plant-count cap, or setback/buffer rule for hemp cultivation was located. Hemp cultivation in Mississippi is not subject to the medical programme's 1,000 ft / 1,500 ft buffers, canopy tiers, or indoor-only rule. Any local restriction is governed by the general principle in SB 2725 (as summarised in secondary sources, not re-proved here) that localities may not prohibit hemp cultivation — that summary is not adopted as a verified holding in this file [VERIFY if a locality dispute arises].

11.3.6 Hemp — pre-harvest sampling window, harvest reporting, non-compliant crop rules (cultivation side)

Sampling window: "No more than 30 days prior to the anticipated harvest" — § 990.24(a). This is a maximum window (sample no earlier than 30 days before anticipated harvest), not a minimum; the sample must be taken before any harvest of that lot (§ 990.24(e)).

Harvest window and harvest reporting (cultivation side):

  • Harvest must be completed "no later than thirty (30) days after the date of sample collection"; failure to complete harvest within 30 days requires "a second pre-harvest sample of the lot … to be submitted for testing" — § 990.26(a)–(b).
  • Harvested lots "shall not be commingled with other harvested lots or other material" — § 990.26(c). Compliant lots "may enter the stream of commerce" — § 990.26(d).
  • Harvest reporting itself is through the annual report (total harvested acreage by lot, § 990.71(c)(4)) and, where applicable, the disposal/remediation report (§ 990.71(b)). No separate "harvest report" form or deadline (e.g. within X days of harvest) was located in Part 990 as read [VERIFY in HeMP guidance]. A producer should not assume harvest-day reporting is unnecessary: the annual-report and test-report duties are the located duties, and any HeMP harvest-notification feature is system detail, not a located regulation.

Non-compliant crop rules (cultivation side; waste/disposal mechanics belong to the waste section but are stated here as the commission directs):

  • A lot that does not meet the acceptable hemp THC level is subject to § 990.27 (see §11.1.7 for the full text): over-limit plants "constitute marijuana" under § 990.27(a)'s wording; the producer must use a DEA-registered reverse distributor or law enforcement, or ensure on-site disposal at the farm/production facility; must notify USDA of intent to dispose or remediate and verify disposal/remediation with documentation; and if remediating, must have the post-remediated crop re-sampled and re-tested for THC.
  • Remediation methods (e.g. blending, replanting, stripping flower) are not specified in § 990.27 as read; the regulation requires only re-sampling/re-testing after remediation. Any USDA remediation guidance listing approved methods is [VERIFY].
  • Negligent-violation consequences (Part 990, §§ 990.28–990.29 area, as rendered in secondary/Part 990 summaries — [VERIFY against §§ 990.28–990.29 text, which was not opened verbatim for this file]): the programme's compliance provisions treat a producer who makes reasonable efforts to grow compliant hemp and whose hemp does not exceed 1% total THC on a dry-weight basis as not committing a negligent violation for that lot; negligent violations are corrected by a corrective action plan; three negligent violations in five years make a producer ineligible to produce hemp for five years from the third violation; culpable violations (greater than negligence) are reported to the U.S. Attorney General and the chief state law-enforcement officer. These consequences are flagged [VERIFY] because §§ 990.28–990.29 were not opened verbatim; they are not quoted as verified law in this file. Do not advise on negligent-violation exposure without checking §§ 990.28–990.29.
  • Interaction with the post-11 December 2026 baseline: a crop that is compliant at 0.3% total THC under Part 990 today may still need to be assessed against the federal total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap after 11 December 2026 for finished products; the pre-harvest lot-compliance test and the finished-product container cap are different tests at different points in the chain. No Mississippi rule bridging the two was located [UNAVAILABLE].

11.3.7 A note on "seed-to-sale" for hemp

There is no hemp seed-to-sale system in Mississippi or under USDA Part 990 as read. Hemp tracking is by licence + FSA location reporting + lot-based sampling/testing + annual/test/disposal reporting (§ 990.71), not by plant/package tags in a state system. Do not describe hemp as "tracked in Metrc" or in any state seed-to-sale system: that would conflate the medical system (§11.3.3) with the hemp system. The vendor question for medical (Metrc, secondary-only) is addressed in §11.3.6's companion note below.

11.3.8 Seed-to-sale vendor — Metrc: status in this file (applies to §§11.1–11.4 generally)

Metrc is not confirmed as the MSDH-certified vendor by any official source opened for this file. The MSDH rules say only "Department designated" / "Department approved statewide" system (Rules 4.11.1, 4.11.3). MDOR's definition says only "the seed-to-sale system administered by the Department of Health" (Title 35 Part XI, Ch. 01 ¶110). Secondary sources (software vendors, law-firm summaries) name Metrc, and Run 1 recorded Metrc as secondary-only. This file preserves that status: Metrc = secondary-only, [VERIFY] before naming it as the vendor in any filing, contract, or client advice. The same caution applies to any claim that dispensaries "verify cardholder status through Metrc" — the statutory duty is to verify through "the statewide seed-to-sale tracking system under Section 41-137-11" (§ 41-137-5(6), via S-10); the vendor name is not part of the located statutory text.

11.4 SECURITY

11.4.1 Medical — MSDH security framework (Subpart 4, Rules 4.4–4.5) and who it binds

Subpart 4's security rules are written for "cannabis cultivation licensees" in their original drafting but were broadened in the consolidated text to "licensees" / "medical cannabis establishments" in several paragraphs (visible blackline: "Cannabis cultivation facilities Licensees"). The provisions below are stated with their rendered scope; where the rendered scope is ambiguous between "cultivation only" and "all MSDH licensees", that ambiguity is flagged rather than resolved.

Security manager — Rule 4.5.1:

"Cannabis cultivation facilities Licensees must [shall] designate a security manager with responsibility for overall facility security to include, but not limited to: adherence to security requirements; conducting semiannual audits of security measures to identify areas of needed improvements/corrective actions; employee training on security measures and controls; and, prevention of diversion/theft of cannabis and/or cannabis products."

So: a named security manager; semiannual security audits; security training; diversion/theft prevention. The rule does not state the manager's qualifications, work-permit status beyond the general work-permit rules, or whether the manager must be on-site — [VERIFY] if a job description depends on it.

Perimeter — Rule 4.4.4: the perimeter of all licensed establishments "shall be designed and maintained to discourage theft and diversion". In addition to local zoning, all cultivation licensees must: (A) "[m]aintain adequate lighting to facilitate video surveillance at all times (24 hours per day/7 days per week)"; (B) have landscaping that "prevents the concealment of any person(s) from sight or video surveillance"; (C) have fencing "that ensures secure perimeter access and points of entry onto the premises including but not limited to around the grounds and that all stages of commercial cannabis activities are inaccessible to and hidden from view of the public" (licensed testing entities are exempt from this fencing requirement); (D) post at each entrance, conspicuously, "PERSONS UNDER 21 YEARS OF AGE NOT PERMITTED ON THESE PREMISES"; and (E) post at each entrance, conspicuously, "THESE PREMISES ARE UNDER CONSTANT VIDEO SURVEILLANCE".

Locks and access — Rule 4.4.2(D)–(E) (see §11.3.1): commercial-grade door locks on all external doors, "locked at all times"; access restricted "to only authorized personnel to locked and secure areas identified with signage and daily records of entry and exit."

Alarms — Rule 4.5.2 (cultivation licensees/locations, as rendered): alarm systems must:

  • (A) "Upon attempted unauthorized entry, … transmit a signal directly to a central protection company or a law enforcement agency that has a legal authority to respond. A designated employee of the cannabis cultivation facility licensee must [shall] also be notified";
  • (B) "Provide continuous, uninterrupted coverage (24 hours/7 days) for all points of ingress and egress to the facility, including without limitation doorways, windows, loading areas";
  • (C) "Provide continuous, uninterrupted coverage (24 hours/7 days) of any room with an exterior wall, any room containing cannabis (of any type or stage of growth) and any room used for cannabis cultivation production operations and activities of any type";
  • (D) "Be equipped with failure notification systems to notify the cannabis cultivation facility licensee and law enforcement of any failure in the alarm system"; and
  • (E) "Have the ability to remain operational during a power outage."

Video surveillance — Rule 4.5.3 (cultivation licensees/locations, as rendered): video surveillance must:

  • (A) "Provide continuous, uninterrupted coverage (24 hours/7 days) for all points of ingress and egress to the facility, including without limitation doorways, windows, loading areas, and parking areas";
  • (B) "Provide continuous, uninterrupted coverage (24 hours/7 days) of any room with an exterior wall, any room containing cannabis (of any type or stage of growth), and any room used for cannabis cultivation production operations and activities of any type";
  • (C) "Digital archiving capabilities for a minimum of (120) days";
  • (D) "On-site and off-site monitoring capabilities";
  • (E) "At least one on-site display monitor, of at least twelve inches, connected to the system at all times must [shall] be available";
  • (F) "Have the date and time embedded on all surveillance recordings without significantly obscuring the picture";
  • (G) "Use cameras that are capable of recording in both high and low lighting conditions";
  • (H) "Destruction of all plant waste … must take place under direct video surveillance at all times";
  • (I) "Have the ability to remain operational during a power outage";
  • (J)–(K) ("should", not "shall"): licensees "should undertake a vulnerability assessment of their standby power systems" (components, hazards, what is/is not on backup, what must not go down); and "should have a backup power system/generator for backup power supply for up to a minimum of forty-eight (48) hours for portions of the facility that should be supplied with standby power during a power interruption" and "should have a safe and secure location for a digital back-up archiving system in the facility located in a locked and secure area to prevent any unauthorized access or theft of video/recording system monitors or video footage." The 48-hour generator and vulnerability-assessment items are recommendations in the rendered text, not mandates — do not cite them as requirements.

Retention period — 120 days (Rule 4.5.3(C) for MSDH cultivation; MDOR dispensaries also 120 days, see §11.4.2). Exceptions to 120 days within the MSDH rules: sampling video retained 90 calendar days (Rule 5.3.3(E)); no separate retention stated for alarm logs in the passages read [VERIFY].

Access to security information by the Department — Rule 4.5.4: "Upon request, a medical cannabis establishment must [licensees shall] make all information related to security alarm systems and video surveillance, monitoring, and recordings available to the Department within the timeframe requested." The transport-storage parallel is Rule 7.3.6 (same duty for transport establishments).

Theft / breach notification — Rule 4.5.5 (as rendered, with blackline tension):

"Cannabis testing facilities Licensed medical cannabis establishments shall notify local law enforcement and the Department of any theft, robbery, break-in, or security breach that occurs on the laboratory's premises, no later than 10 calendar days twenty-four hours after the facilities licensee first becomes aware of the event. The [notice] to the Department shall include at minimum a description of any property that was stolen or destroyed, and the quantity of any usable cannabis that was stolen."

The rendered text shows "10 calendar days" struck in favour of "twenty-four hours". Adopted deadline: 24 hours (the operative, non-struck figure), with the blackline tension flagged here. The rule's subject ("testing facilities" vs "licensed establishments", "laboratory's premises") is ambiguous as rendered; the safe reading is that any MSDH licensee suffering theft/robbery/break-in/security breach notifies local law enforcement and MSDH within 24 hours with property and cannabis-quantity details. MDOR dispensaries have their own 24-hour theft/loss duty (see §11.4.2).

Visitor / contractor access controls — Rule 4.2.15 (see also §11.4.3): contractors/visitors who will not handle cannabis/plants/products (electricians, plumbers, engineers, alarm technicians, etc.) do not require an establishment-issued individual identification card; a contractor may enter a limited-access area only wearing a visitor identification badge, signed in on a visitor entry log, and prevented from accessing cannabis/plants/products; if working where immediate access to cannabis is possible, the contractor must be supervised by a licensee/employee at all times; if locked doors/compartments/physical measures prevent access, the licensee/employee must take reasonable precautions to keep the contractor in those areas; the badge must be displayed conspicuously and carry an identifying mark (letter/number/symbol/combination), on a sticker, lanyard card, pinned card, or other effective means; the visitor log must include entry date/time, departure date/time, visitor full name, state/federal ID identifying number, badge identifying mark, accompanying person's ID-card number if required, and purpose; any contractor/visitor noncompliance in a limited-access area must be reported in writing to the Department within 24 hours with all log information.

Employee access controls (general): only authorised personnel in locked/secure areas (Rule 4.4.2(E)); daily records of entry/exit for those areas; work permits required before working/volunteering/≥10% ownership (Rule 3.11.1); transport employees carry a valid unrestricted Mississippi driver's licence, valid work permit, and a picture identification badge, all in their possession while transporting (Rule 7.1.2); disposal-entity employees carry the same three items (Rule 8.1.2). Employee training on security measures/controls is part of the cultivation training list (Rule 4.2.12(B)) and the security manager's duties (Rule 4.5.1).

Storage (MSDH, general) — what the rules do and do not say about vaults:

  • No rule was located that requires a "vault" by that name, a safe rating (e.g. TL-15/TL-30), or a vault construction standard for MSDH licensees. The word "safe" appears in the transport-storage alarm/video rules as a room descriptor ("any room containing a safe" — Rules 7.3.5(5)(c), 7.3.5(6)(b)), not as a vault mandate.
  • What is required: locked and secure areas with signage and daily entry/exit records (Rule 4.4.2(E)); commercial-grade locks on external doors locked at all times (Rule 4.4.2(D)); cannabis/products tagged during storage and transfer (Rule 4.11.4(G), (I)); wholesale packages containing only one batch during storage/transfer (Rule 4.11.4(G)); quarantined product segregated from other product pending passing results (Rule 5.3.10(L)); administrative-hold product "completely and physically segregate[d]" in a limited-access area and safeguarded (Rule 11.1.4(C)); reserve samples "securely store[d]" against degradation/contamination/tampering in a controlled-access area (Rules 5.8.2, 5.3.11(A)); and transport-storage locations meeting the Rule 7.3.5 tests (see §11.4.4).
  • Dispensary storage is stricter and is stated separately (MDOR Ch. 09, see §11.4.2: locked, secured location/enclosure, not visible from outside, when closed). Do not import the dispensary storage rule into MSDH cultivation/processing storage, or vice versa.

11.4.2 Medical — MDOR dispensary security (Title 35 Part XI, Chs. 08–11, 15, 17, 23)

Security plan — Ch. 08:

"An applicant must have a security plan that is included in its operation plan that is approved by the Department as part of the initial application process. This security plan will list the measures that will be taken by the dispensary to ensure that medical cannabis products are properly secured and safe. It shall include information relating to surveillance systems, camera placement, door security, alarm systems, and measures taken to secure manners of egress and ingress onto the premises. At a minimum, the security plan must meet all requirements set forth in these regulations." — Ch. 08 ¶100.

Changes require prior written approval: "A licensee must notify the Department in writing of any proposed changes to a security plan and must have approval prior to implementing any change. The Department will notify a licensee in writing whether the change is approved" — Ch. 08 ¶101. Withdrawal: "The Department may withdraw approval of the security plan at any time if there have been one or more documented instances of theft or loss of cannabis products on the licensed premises within the past year. If the Department withdraws its approval … the licensee will be given thirty (30) days to modify the plan in a manner that satisfactorily safeguards against future theft or loss … Failure to modify in a satisfactory manner within the prescribed time may result in suspension or revocation" — Ch. 08 ¶102. Non-compliance with an approved plan "will result in disciplinary action" — Ch. 08 ¶103.

Securing product / locks — Ch. 09:

"A licensee is responsible for the security of all cannabis products on the licensed premises, providing adequate safeguards against theft or diversion of cannabis products, and records that are required to be kept." — Ch. 09 ¶100.

"The licensee must ensure that commercial grade, non-residential door locks are installed on every external door, and gate if applicable, of a licensed premises where cannabis products are present." — Ch. 09 ¶101.

"During all hours when the licensee is not operating, a licensee must ensure that: 1. All points of ingress and egress from a licensed premises are securely locked and any keys or key codes to the enclosed area remain in the possession of the licensee, licensee representative, or authorized personnel; and 2. All cannabis products on a dispensary's premises are kept in a locked, secured location or enclosure within any area such that cannabis products are not visible from any area outside the licensed premises." — Ch. 09 ¶102.

Note: Ch. 09 requires a "locked, secured location or enclosure" for closed-hours storage. It does not use the word "vault" and states no safe/vault rating. The closed-hours rule is the dispensary storage rule; the open-hours rule is access control (Ch. 15 / Ch. 17, below).

Alarms — Ch. 10 (revised eff. 4 Mar 2025):

"A dispensary must have a fully operational security alarm system, activated at all times when the dispensary is closed for business." — Ch. 10 ¶100.

The system must "(1) Be able to detect unauthorized entry onto the licensed premises and unauthorized activity within any limited access area where cannabis and/or cannabis products are present; and (2) Be programmed to notify the licensee, licensee representative, or authorized personnel and, unless properly deactivated by the user, local law enforcement in the event of an unauthorized entry." — Ch. 10 ¶101.

Exception: "A dispensary that has at least one authorized representative physically present on the licensed premises at all times when it is closed for business is not required to comply with Paragraphs 100 and 101 of this Chapter" — Ch. 10 ¶102. On request, the dispensary "shall make all information related to security alarm systems, monitoring, and alarm activity available to the Department" — Ch. 10 ¶103. No MDOR alarm failure-notification time (contrast MSDH Rule 4.5.2(D)) and no MDOR alarm power-outage capability sentence were located in Ch. 10 [VERIFY if a power-outage alarm standard exists elsewhere in Part XI].

Video surveillance — Ch. 11 (revised eff. 4 Mar 2025):

  • System: "A licensed premises must have a fully operational video surveillance recording system" — Ch. 11 ¶100. Minimum equipment: digital video recorders; video monitors; digital archiving devices; "a minimum of one (1) monitor on-premises capable of viewing video"; and interface devices if required — Ch. 11 ¶101(1). The system must be able to produce/print a still photograph from any camera image — ¶101(2); must have "a failure notification system that provides, within one (1) hour, notification to an authorized representative of surveillance interruption or failure for more than thirty (30) minutes" — ¶101(3); and must have "sufficient battery backup to support a minimum of one hour of recording time in the event of a power outage" — ¶101(4). Contrast MSDH: MSDH requires operation during a power outage without a stated battery-hour figure (Rule 4.5.3(I)) plus a "should" 48-hour generator recommendation (Rule 4.5.3(K)); MDOR requires a 1-hour battery minimum. Both are correct for their own licensees; do not conflate them.
  • Coverage (continuous recording, 24 hours/day) — Ch. 11 ¶102: (1) all areas where cannabis products may be present, including point-of-sale areas; (2) all points of ingress/egress to/from areas where products may be present and any entrance/exit door; (3) all areas where the dispensary provides parking for cardholders; (4) all areas where the dispensary receives products from a third party or loads products for transport to a third party.
  • Quality and retention — Ch. 11 ¶¶103–104 (as rendered): cameras in required-coverage areas must record "at a minimum resolution of HD 1080p and record at least twenty (20) fps"; must be "capable of recording in both high and low lighting conditions"; recordings must be kept "for a minimum of one hundred and twenty (120) calendar days"; maintained "in a format that can be easily accessed for viewing and easily reproduced"; kept longer on Department request; date/time embedded "without significantly obscuring the picture"; made available "immediately upon request to the Department in a format specified by the Department"; Department notified "within forty-eight (48) hours of any equipment failure or system outage lasting thirty (30) minutes or more"; and recordings "back[ed] up … off-site and in real-time for the surveillance room or surveillance area."
  • Stopping recording — Ch. 11 ¶¶105–106 (as rendered): a dispensary may stop recording/backing up a surveillance area only if all other cameras are shut down under the section or for individual-camera maintenance (during which the formerly surveilled area "must be monitored at all times by an employee"); recording must resume by the date/time in the notice; no licensed privileges may be exercised in an area where recording was stopped; and recording may be stopped in areas where products are not present due to seasonal closure or prolonged inactivity of at least 30 days, on at least 24 hours' prior written notice to the Department including a plot plan/diagram showing deactivated cameras and their count/description, stop date/time, reason, and resume date/time. A dispensary "may not engage in any privileges of the license in an area that does not have camera coverage as required by law or in an area where camera coverage has been stopped, including but not limited to possessing, storing, transferring, or receiving cannabis products" — ¶106.

Access control — Ch. 15 and Ch. 17:

  • Ch. 15 ¶100: the dispensary "shall maintain control of areas of the premises designated for sales to ensure that only authorized individuals are able to enter", by either (1) stationing an employee at the entry door during all hours of public operation to check valid identification and control entry, or (2) keeping entry doors locked with a buzzer/other alert means, with an employee checking valid identification before allowing entry.
  • Ch. 15 ¶101: individuals are prohibited from entering unless over 21, or under 21, accompanied by a guardian, and holding a valid patient card.
  • Ch. 15 ¶102: cannabis products "may only be displayed in such a way that prevents access to persons who are not employees."
  • Ch. 15 ¶103: a dispensary may share a building with another business but "cannot share a premises"; the licensed premises "cannot share common entries or exits with other businesses" and there cannot be an interior entrance/exit connecting it to another business.
  • Ch. 17 ¶100: except topical products, the dispensary "must keep all permitted cannabis products in limited access areas where access is restricted to licensees and employees." Ch. 17 ¶101: except topicals, a non-licensee/non-employee may not handle products in the point-of-sale area unless supervised by a licensee/employee at all times. Ch. 17 ¶102: except topicals, a patient may handle products without supervision only after the sale is complete and the items are no longer within the premises or an area the licensee controls.
  • Ch. 18 ¶101: during operating hours / hours of apparent activity, there must be "an on-site employee authorized to cooperate with the Department during inspections … and requests to review business records or surveillance videos."

Dispensary theft/loss reporting — Ch. 27 (as indexed; full text partially rendered in search results): each dispensary employee must notify the Department "within twenty-four (24) hours upon discovery of the theft or loss of any cannabis product in transit that was either shipped from or to the dispensary", and cannabis-product thefts/unexplained losses must be reported to the Department (the balance of Ch. 27 ¶102 was not fully rendered for this file — the full Ch. 27 text, including any on-premises theft deadline beyond the in-transit sentence, is [VERIFY]). Each employee is also responsible for monitoring for unusual usage or questionable disposition and notifying the Department immediately on discovery of fraudulent/unlawful recommendation, unusual usage, or questionable disposition — Ch. 27 ¶100 (as rendered in search results).

Dispensary storage and sale — Ch. 23 (indexed; full text not read line-by-line for this file): Ch. 23 is titled "Storage and Sale of Cannabis Products" (S-2 index). Its operative storage sentences beyond Ch. 09 ¶102 were not verified for this file [VERIFY — Ch. 23]. Do not quote Ch. 23 storage standards beyond the Ch. 09 rule above.

11.4.3 Medical — visitor / employee access controls (consolidated)

Control MSDH (all MSDH licensees unless noted) MDOR dispensaries
Who may enter cannabis areas Only authorised personnel in locked/secure areas, with signage and daily entry/exit records (Rule 4.4.2(E)); establishment agents must hold work permits (Rule 3.11.1) Only licensees/employees in limited-access areas (Ch. 17 ¶100); entry controlled by staffed door or locked door + buzzer + ID check (Ch. 15 ¶100); entrants must be 21+ or under-21 guardian-accompanied cardholders (Ch. 15 ¶101)
Visitors / contractors Badge + log + supervision rules (Rule 4.2.15, see §11.4.1); noncompliance reported in writing within 24 hours Licensee responsible for conduct of employees, customers, contractors and visitors on the premises at all times (Ch. 18 ¶101); no separate MDOR visitor-log rule was located [VERIFY]
Badges Transport/disposal employees: picture ID badge + driver's licence + work permit in possession while transporting (Rules 7.1.2, 8.1.2); contractor visitor badge with identifying mark (Rule 4.2.15(C)) No dispensary employee-badge rule was located in the chapters read [VERIFY — Ch. 20 (Employees) may contain one; its full text was not read line-by-line]
Keys / codes (closed hours) External doors locked at all times, commercial-grade locks (Rule 4.4.2(D)) Keys/key codes remain in possession of licensee/representative/authorised personnel when closed (Ch. 09 ¶102(1))
Signage "PERSONS UNDER 21…" and "THESE PREMISES ARE UNDER CONSTANT VIDEO SURVEILLANCE" at each entrance (Rule 4.4.4(D)–(E)) Exterior sign identifying owning entity + licence number, conspicuously placed (Ch. 14 ¶100); licence displayed conspicuously in point-of-sale area (Ch. 14 ¶101)

11.4.4 Medical — transport security (vehicles, manifests, GPS)

Transport window and responsibility — Subpart 7:

  • Transport entities must comply with all Mississippi motor-vehicle laws (Rule 7.1.1); employees must hold a valid unrestricted Mississippi driver's licence and valid work permit, plus a picture ID badge, all in possession while transporting (Rule 7.1.2); the entity "shall be responsible for any and all cannabis and/or cannabis products within its custody, control, or possession" (Rule 7.1.3).
  • Transport to establishments only "during the hours of 5:00 a.m. until 9:00 p.m." (Rule 7.1.4); if the entity possesses product outside approved hours, it "must [shall] immediately go to its nearest facility and store the cannabis and/or cannabis products in accordance with the rules in this Part" (Rule 7.1.8).
  • Trip plan (Rule 7.1.5): before transport, a trip plan must be created for each transportation event, including at minimum: transporting employees' names; their work permits; date and start time; originating establishment's physical location; receiving establishment's physical location; description of product (quantities by weight/unit per type, with seed-to-sale unique identifying numbers per item); anticipated stops with locations and arrival/departure times; anticipated route; any storage at the transporter's facilities; estimated arrival date/time; and vehicle make/model/colour/licence plate. A copy goes to the originator and is maintained by the transporter; a copy "must [shall] be kept in the vehicle during transport" (Rule 7.1.6). "Reasonable deviations" from the anticipated route are permitted (e.g. mandatory detours for construction, accidents) but "[a]ll deviations must [shall] be reflected in the transportation entity's vehicle GPS system at all times" (Rule 7.1.7).
  • Manifest (Rules 7.1.10–7.1.12): before transport, the originator must provide the transporter a copy of the inventory/transportation manifest "generated from the seed-to-sale system", including at minimum: originator licence number, name and contact; receiver licence number, name and contact; receiver physical delivery address; quantities by weight/unit per type with seed-to-sale unique numbers per item; transport date with departure time and approximate arrival time; names and work-permit numbers of accompanying individuals; and vehicle make/model/colour/licence plate. A manifest "must [shall] be included with each transport" and "shall not be altered after departing the originating [establishment]" and must be made available to law enforcement if requested. (Sample manifests have their own, more detailed contents at Rule 5.9.5–5.9.6 — see §11.1.4.)
  • Occupancy: "There must [shall] not be any passenger or operator in a vehicle transporting cannabis and/or cannabis products that is not employed by the cannabis transportation entity while cannabis and/or cannabis products are present" (Rule 7.1.13).
  • Dispensary delivery timing (Rule 7.1.14): only product that has undergone and passed regulatory compliance testing with an accompanying COA may be transferred to dispensaries via a licensed transport entity; product "that has not been transported to a licensed dispensary for retail sale within twelve (12) months of the date on the COA shall be destroyed or retested by the licensee in possession thereof", and retesting is permitted "only … if the cannabis has not been modified in any way."
  • Transporter independence / prohibitions (Rule 7.1.9): transport entities may not grow/cultivate, manufacture/process, retail-sell, resell, transport/store/deliver to non-licensed entities, or provide product directly to patients/caregivers.

Vehicles — Rule 7.2:

  • Before use, the entity must submit "the license plate numbers, proof of insurance, and vehicle identification numbers for each vehicle" (Rule 7.2.1); vehicles "must [shall] be insured at or above the legal requirements in Mississippi" (Rule 7.2.2) — see §11.2.7.
  • Equipment (Rule 7.2.3): "(1) An alarm system; (2) A global positioning system (GPS) to monitor location, routes, etc. at all times with the ability to grant the Department and/or state and local law enforcement access to the system; and, (3) Locked storage container as defined in Rule [1.2.73]." GPS is therefore expressly required for medical transport vehicles, with Department/law-enforcement access capability. GPS route-deviation reflection is separately required by Rule 7.1.7.
  • Staffing or video alternative (Rule 7.2.4, except test samples): every transport vehicle must meet one of: "(1) Staffed with a minimum of two (2) employees when a vehicle contains cannabis and/or cannabis products. At least one (1) employee shall remain with the vehicle any time it contains cannabis and/or cannabis products; or (2) Utilize video surveillance of the vehicle (meeting video surveillance requirements in Rule [7.3.5]) to include: a. Installation of video cameras in the interior of vehicles transporting cannabis and/or cannabis products; and, b. Video surveillance of the interior of the vehicle, particularly the locked storage areas where cannabis and/or cannabis products are located."
  • Sanitation: vehicles "shall be maintained in a sanitary condition" (Rule 7.2.5). Markings: a transport vehicle "must [shall] not bear any markings to indicate the vehicle contains cannabis or bear the name or logo of the medical cannabis establishment" (Rule 7.2.6). Test-sample vehicles carry the parallel no-markings rule at Rule 5.3.10(F).

Storage during/outside transport — Rule 7.3:

  • No transport unless first "packed in a cannabis container by the originating medical cannabis establishment" (Rule 7.3.1). A transport cannabis container must be "(1) Sealable and sealed during transport; (2) Locked during transport; (3) Clearly labeled as medical cannabis and/or medical cannabis-product; (4) Maintained in a locked and secure storage compartment that is part of the vehicle or a locked storage container with a separate key or combination lock" (Rule 7.3.2). Only the originator, the intended recipient, local/state/federal law enforcement, or MSDH/MDOR employees may open a sealed container (Rule 7.3.3). Product "shall be transported so it is not visible or recognizable from outside the vehicle" (Rule 7.3.4).
  • Transporter storage locations (Rule 7.3.5) must: be at a location approved/licensed as part of the transporter's licence; be secure, enclosed with permanent walls, with temperature/relative-humidity controls preventing adulteration; be locked at all times; be accessible only to specifically identified transporter employees; have an alarm system meeting the Rule 7.3.5(5) tests (direct transmission to central protection company or law enforcement on attempted unauthorised entry, designated-employee notification, 24/7 coverage of ingress/egress points, 24/7 coverage of any room with an exterior wall / containing a safe / used to store product, failure notification to transporter and law enforcement, operation during power outage); and have continuous 24/7 video surveillance meeting the Rule 7.3.5(6) tests (ingress/egress including parking, exterior-wall/safe/storage rooms, 120-day digital archiving, on-site and off-site monitoring, embedded date/time, high- and low-light cameras). Disposal-entity storage (Rule 8.1.5) mirrors Rule 7.3.5 in substance (licensed location, secure permanent walls, locked at all times, specifically identified employees only, same alarm and 120-day video tests), with disposal under video surveillance (Rule 8.1.8).
  • MDOR dispensary transport: "A dispensary shall adhere to all applicable Department of Health transportation requirements when receiving or shipping medical cannabis" — Title 35 Part XI, Ch. 26 ¶100 (revised eff. 1 Dec 2025). Dispensaries therefore do not have a separate transport-vehicle/GPS regime; they use MSDH-licensed transporters under Subpart 7.

11.4.5 Hemp — security requirements, or their absence

Stated explicitly: no USDA or Mississippi hemp-specific security regime (cameras, alarms, locks, vaults, visitor controls, transport GPS/manifests) was located for hemp in this run.

What does apply to a Mississippi USDA hemp licensee, and is the full extent of the located security-adjacent duties:

  • Sampling access: the licensee must give sampling agents "complete and unrestricted access during business hours to all hemp and other cannabis plants, (whether growing or harvested), all hemp production and storage areas, all land, buildings, and other structures used for the cultivation, handling, and storage of all hemp and other cannabis plants, and all locations listed in the producer license" — § 990.24(d); and have an authorised representative present at sampling "if possible" — § 990.24(c).
  • Lot integrity: harvested lots must not be commingled with other lots or material — § 990.26(c); non-compliant lots must be disposed of or remediated with USDA notification and verified documentation — § 990.27(b).
  • Reporting integrity: FSA location reporting, annual lot/acreage reporting, test-results reporting, and disposal/remediation reporting (§ 990.71) — see §§11.3.5–11.3.6.
  • General law: ordinary Mississippi criminal law (theft, burglary, trespass), general business-premises duties, and any lease, lender, insurer, or buyer security requirements a hemp business voluntarily assumes. No hemp-specific camera-retention period, alarm standard, lock standard, vault/safe standard, visitor-log rule, employee-badge rule, or transport-security rule (vehicle alarm/GPS/manifest) was located in 7 CFR Part 990 or in any Mississippi hemp source opened. A hemp business that also holds a medical licence is bound by §§11.4.1–11.4.4 for its medical operations only; those rules do not extend to its hemp operations by their terms.
  • Hemp-derived product businesses: likewise, no located Mississippi security rule for hemp retail, storage, or transport (see §11.2.8). Interstate transport of compliant hemp is protected at the federal level (no state/tribe may prohibit interstate transportation/shipment of hemp produced in compliance with Part 990 / an approved plan / the 2014 Farm Bill framework), but that is a transport permission, not a transport security standard, and it is noted here only to prevent confusion with the medical manifest/GPS regime.
