0. Fixed baselines adopted for this file

0.1 Run 1 consistency baseline (adopted exactly, per commission)

Item Adopted position
Programme Medical only, under SB 2095, Miss. Code §§ 41-137-1 et seq.
Patient quantity 24 Mississippi Medical Cannabis Equivalency Units (MMCEUs) per 30 days; 28 MMCEUs possession. From 1 July 2025, 1 MMCEU = 3.5 g flower or 1 g total THC (concentrate or infused product).
Potency caps Flower/trim: 30% total THC. Concentrates/tinctures: 60% total THC.
Prohibited conduct No home grow; no delivery / drive-through / curbside; no public or in-vehicle smoking/vaping.
Seed-to-sale The MSDH-certified statewide system under § 41-137-11. The vendor name "Metrc" was identified only via secondary sources in Run 1. It is not presented as officially confirmed in this file, for the reason in §0.2, item 3.
Patient employment No employment protection (§ 41-137-13); employers may drug-test and act on medical use regardless of impairment. See §11.8.5 for the distinction from licence-holder/staff rules.
Licence types / fees (Run 1 Part 4) MSDH: cultivation (micro + Tiers 1–6), processing (micro + standard), testing, transportation, disposal, research. MDOR: dispensary. Work permits $25, 5-year. No social equity programme. Fees re-verified in §§11.5 and 11.9 below.
Hemp licensing MDAC issues NO hemp licences; USDA only, under an unfunded state plan position. No hemp-derived product permit statute was located in Run 1.
Attorney General opinion, 11 June 2025 Treats intoxicating hemp products outside the medical programme as prohibited. This is an opinion, not a statute, and is not upgraded to law in this file.

0.2 Federal baseline (given, fixed, not re-researched)

Split scheduling: state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). Adult-use remains Schedule I. IRS § 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical; adult-use remains fully subject. Hemp: PL 119-37 § 781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 § 2019 limits it until 11 December 2026. After 11 December 2026, the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026. The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026. No federal cannabis banking law exists.

Where a Mississippi or federal text opened for this file still uses pre-28 April 2026 Schedule I language (notably 7 CFR § 990.27, which calls non-compliant cannabis "a schedule I controlled substance"), that is flagged as a text-versus-baseline tension and is not silently rewritten. See §11.5.6.

0.3 Conflicts found in this run — what is adopted and why

# Conflict Adopted position and reason
C-1 MMCEU infused-product value. The MSDH rule text opened for this file (Board-adopted 11 October 2023) defines 1 MMCEU at Rule 1.2.97 as "One hundred (100) milligrams of THC in an infused product." The Run 1 / commission baseline, and the MDOR rule text showing revisions effective 1 December 2025 (35.XI.01, ¶ 114), both give 1 g of total THC in an infused product. Adopt Run 1 / MDOR: 1 g total THC. The MSDH PDF opened is a 2023 version; the later MDOR text and the 1 July 2025 change in the commission baseline are the more current statement. The MSDH 100 mg figure is treated as superseded for this purpose and is not relied on anywhere else in this file. A check of any MSDH post-2023 amendment to Rule 1.2.97 remains [VERIFY] — see §11.10, G-1.
C-2 Inducements: prohibited vs permitted. Older MSDH drafts and many secondary summaries quote former Rule 3.4.1: "Licensed Entities are prohibited from using inducements…" with a list including discount cards, coupons, punch cards, BOGO, daily/weekly/monthly deals, giveaways and sampling. The current MSDH text opened for this file, Subpart 9, Rule 9.3.1, says the opposite: licensees may utilise inducements, with the same examples (minus giveaways/sampling — see §11.7). MDOR Title 35, Part XI, Chapter 13, ¶ 100 likewise says dispensaries may utilise inducements. Adopt the current rules: inducements are permitted within the stated limit. The prohibition summaries are treated as describing a superseded draft/earlier rule, not current law. Any reader relying on a secondary summary that still says "prohibited" should be directed to MSDH Rule 9.3.1 and MDOR Chapter 13. 0.4 How to read the flags in this file

  • [VERIFY] = a fact, figure or current status that could not be confirmed from an official source opened in this run, or that conflicts between sources, and must be re-checked before reliance.
  • [UNAVAILABLE] = no source (official or secondary) locating the item was found in this run; it is not asserted to be non-existent in law, only that no rule, list or programme was located.
  • "No rule located" = a search of the MSDH Part 22 text, the MDOR Part XI text and the sources cited found no provision on that point. It is a statement about the search, not a legal opinion that the conduct is unregulated by other law (e.g. general criminal, tax or local law).
  • Verbatim quotations are reproduced exactly as they appear in the opened source, including obvious typographical errors in the source PDF (e.g. "must shall" in the MSDH blackline text). Where a quotation is from a blackline/adopted text, that is noted.

11.5 WASTE DISPOSAL

11.5.1 Medical — what counts as "cannabis waste"

MSDH Title 15, Part 22, Rule 1.2.29 (2023 adopted text) defines "Cannabis Waste" as:

"A. Unused, surplus, returned or out-of-date cannabis; recalled cannabis; unused cannabis; plant debris of the plant of the genus cannabis, including dead plants and all unused plant parts, except the term shall not include seeds, roots, stems, and stalks and fan leaves; B. All product which is deemed to fail laboratory testing and cannot be remediated or decontaminated; C. All products and inventory from medical cannabis establishments that have gone out of business and/or are unable to legally transfer or sell cannabis and/or cannabis products and inventory to another medical cannabis establishment; or D. Products and inventory from medical cannabis establishments that may be destroyed and/or rendered unrecognizable and unusable through disposal as a result of Department corrective and/or administrative actions."

And, in the same rule:

"E. All cannabis waste must be disposed of by licensed disposal entity."

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rule 1.2.29 — https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/sites/default/files/Documents/RevisedAdminRegulationsMMCPBOHADOPTED10.11.2023.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Two related definitions must be read with it, because they carve material out of the licensed-disposal route:

  • "Non-cannabis Waste" (Rule 1.2.100): "The term 'non-cannabis waste' means the seeds, roots, stems, and stalks of a plant of the genus cannabis."
  • "Plant Waste" (Rule 1.2.108, unnumbered in the PDF as printed): "The term 'plant waste' includes the seeds, roots, stems, stalks and fan leaves (not containing trichomes), that do not contain THC that shall be rendered unrecognizable via composting and disposal of by the cultivation licensees while under direct video surveillance."

Practical consequence, stated carefully: Seeds, roots, stems, stalks and (non-trichome) fan leaves are excluded from the Rule 1.2.29 "cannabis waste" definition and are dealt with as plant waste / non-cannabis waste, rendered unrecognisable by the cultivation licensee itself under direct video surveillance (see also Rule 4.5.3(H) below). Everything else in Rule 1.2.29(A)–(D) — including failed-test product that cannot be remediated, recalled product, out-of-date/returned product, and inventory of a defunct or non-transferring establishment — must go through a licensed disposal entity. Whether a particular borderline item (e.g. a fan leaf bearing trichomes) falls inside or outside the exclusion is not resolved in the text opened and is [VERIFY] on a case-by-case basis with MSDH; the rule turns on trichome presence and THC content for fan leaves, not on the leaf alone.

11.5.2 Medical — the disposal licence: scope, fees, and what a disposal entity may and may not do

Licence category. MSDH Rule 3.2.1(D):

"Cannabis Disposal License. Establishments licensed as cannabis disposal entities may engage in the following commercial cannabis activities: disposal or destruction of medical cannabis, cannabis products, and/or cannabis waste."

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rule 3.2.1(D) — link as above — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Fees — verified against the Run 1 figure. MSDH Rule 3.2.2(F):

"Waste Disposal Entity. One-time application fee of $5,000.00. Annual license fee of $7,500.00."

This confirms the Run 1 Part 4 figure ($5,000 application / $7,500 annual). It is corroborated by the MSDH FAQ application-fee list, which lists under "Waste Disposal — Waste Disposal: $5,000.00" (application fee; the FAQ list is a one-time application-fee list and does not restate annual fees). MSDH FAQ: https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/faq?category=2 — accessed 25 Oct 2026. No conflict was found on the disposal fee. The annual $7,500 figure rests on Rule 3.2.2(F) in the 2023 adopted text; a post-2023 MSDH fee amendment, if any, is [VERIFY] per §0.3, C-4, but no contrary figure was located.

Scope limits — disposal entities are not general licensees. MSDH Rule 8.1.4:

"Unless specifically licensed by the Department to do so, cannabis disposal entities are prohibited from the following activities related to the medical cannabis program: 1. Growing/cultivating cannabis; 2. Manufacturing/processing cannabis and/or cannabis products; 3. Retail sales of cannabis and/or cannabis products; 4. The resale of cannabis and/or cannabis products to other entities and medical cannabis establishments; 5. Transportation, storage, and delivery of cannabis and/or cannabis products (outside of the purposes of disposal and/or destruction of cannabis waste); and, 6. Provision of cannabis and/or cannabis products directly to qualifying patients and/or caregivers as defined in this Part."

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rule 8.1.4 — link as above — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Transport overlay. Rule 8.1.1: disposal entities "must shall also comply with all applicable rules and regulations in this Part to include, but not limited to, licensure and registration as a cannabis transportation entity (see 15 Miss. Admin Code Pt. 22, Subpart 7 for transportation requirements) if the cannabis disposal entity transports cannabis and/or cannabis products." In other words, a disposal entity that moves waste itself needs the transportation overlay; a disposal entity that does not transport does not thereby acquire a general transport right. The disposal entity is responsible for all cannabis/products "within its custody, control, or possession" (Rule 8.1.3).

Dispensary-side duty. MDOR Title 35, Part XI, Chapter 18, ¶ 110:

"A licensee must utilize a permitted Medical Cannabis Waste Disposal Entity, as described in the Department of Health regulations, in order to dispose of any Medical Cannabis products."

Source: MDOR Title 35 Pt. XI, Ch. 18, ¶ 110 (revised effective 1 Dec 2025) — http://sos.ms.gov/adminsearch/ACCode/00000758c.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026. This is the dispensary's counterpart to MSDH Rule 1.2.29(E): a dispensary may not self-dispose of medical cannabis products outside the permitted-entity route, except for the plant-waste carve-out discussed in §11.5.1, which by its terms applies to cultivation licensees.

Testing-facility overlay. A testing entity's application must include either "a copy of an approved waste disposal license issued under this Chapter or an executed contract with an approved waste disposal licensee issued under this Chapter" (MSDH Rule 3.1.3(A)(18), renewal at Rule 3.1.3(B)(10), as opened). Testing samples have their own post-testing rule at §11.5.5 below.

11.5.3 Medical — rendering unusable and unrecognisable: the 50% rule and the two mixing routes

The core destruction standard is MSDH Rule 8.1.7:

"Cannabis waste shall be disposed through of either via a process which renders the waste unusable and unrecognizable through physical destruction or a recycling process that the waste disposal facility is authorized to conduct pursuant to by Mississippi law to carry out."

The operative grinding/mixing rule is Rule 8.1.9:

"Medical cannabis and/or cannabis products shall be rendered unusable by grinding and incorporating the cannabis plant waste with other ground materials, so the resulting mixture is at least fifty percent 50% non-cannabis waste by volume. This includes compostable mixed waste and non-compostable mixed waste meeting the requirements below."

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rules 8.1.7, 8.1.9 — link as above — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Route A — compostable / organic method (Rule 8.1.10). Cannabis waste to be disposed of as compost or by another organic waste method may be ground and incorporated with:

  1. Food waste; 2. Yard waste; 3. Vegetable based grease oils; 4. Agricultural Materials; 5. Biodegradable products and paper; 6. Clean wood; 7. Fruits and vegetables; or 8. Plant matter; 9. Bokashi or other compost activators; or, 10. Other materials or methods approved by the Department that will render the cannabis waste unusable and unrecognizable.

Route B — non-compostable / landfill / incineration method (Rule 8.1.11). Cannabis waste to be disposed of in a landfill or by another disposal method, such as incineration, may be ground and incorporated with:

  1. Paper waste; 2. Cardboard waste; 3. Plastic waste; 4. Soil; 5. Nonrecyclable plastic; 6. Broken glass; 7. Sawdust; or 8. Other materials or methods approved by the Department that will render the cannabis waste unusable and unrecognizable.

In both routes the 50% non-cannabis waste by volume floor in Rule 8.1.9 applies to the resulting mixture. The text opened does not prescribe a specific grinder, particle size, or composting time/temperature; any such specification, if it exists in MSDH guidance or a disposal entity's approved SOP, was not located in the rule text and is [VERIFY].

What "recycling process" means in Rule 8.1.7 is not further defined in Subpart 8 as opened. It is limited by its own terms to a process "that the waste disposal facility is authorized to conduct pursuant to Mississippi law." No list of authorised recycling processes for cannabis waste was located in the rule text. [VERIFY] before relying on any recycling route other than the two grinding/mixing routes above.

11.5.4 Medical — on-site vs licensed disposal: who destroys what, where

Waste stream Who destroys it Where / under what control
Cannabis waste as defined in Rule 1.2.29(A)–(D) (unused/surplus/returned/out-of-date/recalled product; failed-test product that cannot be remediated; defunct-establishment inventory; Department-ordered destruction) Licensed disposal entity only (Rule 1.2.29(E)) At the originating establishment and again at the final destination — both weighings recorded in seed-to-sale (Rule 8.1.6, §11.5.5); destruction under the disposal entity's video surveillance (Rule 8.1.8); disposal-entity storage, if any, only at a Department-licensed location meeting Rule 8.1.5 (secure, enclosed, permanent walls, locked at all times, limited-access, alarm + 24/7 video, 120-day digital archiving)
Plant waste / non-cannabis waste (seeds, roots, stems, stalks, non-trichome fan leaves not containing THC) Cultivation licensee itself, by composting/disposal rendering it unrecognisable "while under direct video surveillance" (Rule 1.2.108 definition; Rule 4.5.3(H): "Destruction of all plant waste (as defined in this Chapter Part) must take place under direct video surveillance at all times")
Testing reserve samples and sample-preparation residues Testing entity, after the retention period, or returned under chain of custody See §11.5.5
Failed-test batches that can be remediated Not destroyed at first failure; remediation/sterilisation route under Subpart 5, §11.5.5 Only destroyed if remediation/retesting fails (see §11.5.5)
Inventory on licence non-renewal / termination Licensee, as instructed/approved by the Department Rule 3.8.3(C): a licensee whose licence is not renewed "shall cease all operations immediately upon expiration…, schedule a close out inspection with the Department, and destroy all cannabis and cannabis products in the licensee's possession in a manner approved by the Department." Rule 3.9.1(C): on permanent abandonment/cessation, "Destroy all cannabis plants, cannabis and cannabis products in its possession as instructed by the Department."
Department-ordered destruction / seizure Department, under Subpart 11 Rule 11.1.1(G): the Department may "Order destruction of cannabis plants, cannabis and/or cannabis products"; Rule 11.1.3: the Department may seize, destroy, confiscate or place an administrative hold on plants/products for, among other reasons, failure to log/tag in seed-to-sale, non-compliant alteration, packaging/labelling failure, non-compliant cultivation/harvest/manufacture/transfer, or improper handling/storage/transport/possession

No on-site destruction right for ordinary licensees beyond plant waste. No provision was located in Subpart 8 permitting a cultivation, processing or dispensary licensee to destroy Rule 1.2.29 cannabis waste on its own premises without a licensed disposal entity, other than the plant-waste carve-out and the Department-instructed destruction on termination/non-renewal above. A licensee that claims an on-site destruction right for other waste should be asked to cite the provision; on the text opened, it does not exist. [VERIFY] if a variance under Subpart 10 has been granted in an individual case — variances are individual, are not in the rule text, and cannot be generalised.

MDEQ / local permitting overlay. MSDH Rule 8.1.12:

"Licensure and/or permitting may also be required through the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality for cannabis disposal entities as well as local permitting, may also be required dependent upon the location of the cannabis disposal entity."

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rule 8.1.12 — link as above — accessed 25 Oct 2026. The rule does not name the MDEQ permit type. Whether a given disposal method (landfill, incineration, composting) triggers a specific MDEQ solid-waste, air or water permit is a facility-specific question under general MDEQ law, not a cannabis-specific rule located in this run. See also §11.6.1.

11.5.5 Medical — record-keeping in seed-to-sale, and failed-test destruction

Weighing and recording — two points minimum. MSDH Rule 8.1.6:

"All medical cannabis waste set designated for disposal shall be properly weighed and recorded in the state's seed-to-sale system. Waste set for disposal must be weighed and recorded, at the following points at a minimum: 1. On-site at the medical cannabis establishment for which the cannabis disposal entity is providing services; and, 2. At the final destination where disposal/destruction occurs."

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rule 8.1.6 — link as above — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

General recordkeeping that covers disposal. MSDH Rule 4.9.2 requires establishments to maintain, for a minimum of five (5) years: books/records fully accounting for each business transaction; copies of transportation manifests; employment records; records of all pesticide/chemical applications; and records of theft, loss or other unaccountability. Rule 4.9.5 adds:

"All cannabis plants, cannabis and cannabis products must shall be physically inventoried on a weekly basis and records maintained for a minimum of five (5) years. Any removal, including but not limited to disposal or destruction, of cannabis plants, cannabis or cannabis products must shall be recorded."

Rule 4.9.4: all records must be maintained on-site or electronically (virtually) and available for Department review at the licensee's address. Testing-facility manifests must be retained at least three (3) years from receipt (Rule 5.9.8) — a shorter, sample-specific period that does not shorten the general five-year rule for the establishment's own records.

Seed-to-sale mechanics. MSDH Rule 4.11.1: licensees must use the Department-designated seed-to-sale system directly or via an approved third-party integrator. Rule 4.11.4: tags must remain affixed for the entire life of the plant "until disposal"; inventory must be continuously tagged at all stages. Rule 4.9.1: participation in and use of the system is mandatory, and all associated costs are the establishments' financial responsibility. Vendor name: not stated in the rule text opened — see §0.3, C-3. Do not cite Metrc as the system on the basis of this file.

Video retention for disposal. Disposal-entity video surveillance must have digital archiving for a minimum of 120 days (Rule 8.1.5(6)(c), applying the same standard as Rule 4.5.3(C) for cultivation locations). Sampling video (testing) is retained 90 calendar days (Rule 5.3.3(E)) — a different period, for a different activity, and not a disposal-video period.

Failed-test destruction — the remediation fork. Not every failed batch is waste on first failure. MSDH Subpart 5, Rules 5.5.x, as opened:

Failure type Consequence on first failure
Pesticides (Rule 5.5.7) No remediation. Must be destroyed. "If a sample from a batch fails pesticide testing, the batch may not be remediated and must shall be destroyed in a manner permitted under this Part and/or approved by the Department and identified on the Department's website."
Solvents (Rule 5.5.5) May be remediated using procedures reducing solvent concentration below the action level, then resampled/retested (including for solvents and pesticides if not otherwise required). If not remediated, or if remediation fails, "must shall be destroyed in a manner specified by the Department."
Water activity / moisture (Rule 5.5.6) May be used to make concentrate/extract, or continue to dry/cure, then resampled/retested.
Potency (Rule 5.5.8) Usable cannabis failing potency "may be repackaged in a manner that enables the item to meet the standard," then resampled/retested.
Any failure after remediation/sterilisation (Rule 5.5.9) "must shall be destroyed in a manner approved by the Department." A batch may only be remediated twice; if it fails after a second remediation attempt and second retesting, "the entire batch shall be destroyed in a manner approved by the Department." The cultivator/processor must inform the testing facility before sampling that the batch previously failed and is being retested after remediation/sterilisation, and must document all sampling, testing, sterilisation, remediation and destruction resulting from a failing test (Rule 5.5.9(C)–(D)). Within one (1) business day of completing analyses of a remediated batch's representative sample, the testing entity must upload the COA into seed-to-sale (Rule 5.5.9(E)).

Testing samples themselves. MSDH Rule 5.8.1: the testing entity must retain the reserve sample (any portion not used in testing) for a minimum of 45 business days after the analyses, "after which time it may be destroyed and denatured to the point the material is rendered unrecognizable and unusable." Rule 5.8.2: secure storage prohibiting degradation, contamination and tampering. Rule 5.8.3: the reserve sample must be provided to the Department on request. Rule 5.3 (sample handling, as opened in the 2023 text): any portion of a test sample not destroyed during analysis must be returned to the licensed producer under chain of custody or destroyed in accordance with the wastage requirements of the rule. Testing entities must also have SOPs for disposal of samples, digestates, leachates, extracts and other sample-preparation products (Rule 3.1.3(A)(17)).

11.5.6 Medical — inspections of disposal

General inspection authority covers disposal. MSDH Rule 3.5.1: the physical location, all general business records (inclusive of employee records), all financial records, and vehicles used to transport cannabis/products are "subject to reasonable inspection by the Department." Rule 3.5.2: "The Department shall conduct at least one on-site inspection of all medical cannabis establishments. Inspections by the Department may be scheduled or unannounced but generally shall occur during the reported hours of operation included in the licensee's operating plan." Rule 3.5.4: licensees must cooperate with inspections, complaint-resolution requests and information/data requests. Rule 3.5.5: if the Department reasonably believes it has discovered criminal activity or other violations of Mississippi law during an inspection, it may refer the matter to appropriate state or local law enforcement or regulatory authorities.

Disposal-specific inspection hooks, in addition to the general rule:

  • Commencement: a licensee may not commence cultivating/producing/dispensing until it receives written notice authorising commencement following the Department's initial inspection to determine compliance (Rule 3.4, as opened).
  • Renewal: an annual inspection within sixty (60) days prior to expiration "may be required at the Department's discretion for renewal" (Rule 3.8.5); renewal may be denied or the licence suspended/revoked/not renewed for, among other reasons, outstanding fines, an owner convicted of a disqualifying felony, or regulatory non-compliance (Rule 3.8.6).
  • Close-out inspection on non-renewal (Rule 3.8.3(C), §11.5.4 above).
  • Disciplinary schedule (Appendix B): "Failure to accurately track inventory and/or destruction of product" — $10,000 and/or one-week suspension, per untagged plant/package/batch at the time of the Department's finding; "Disposal/Destruction activities during a license suspension period" — revocation. General penalty for a violation not specifically listed: $5,000 per instance/finding.

No disposal-specific inspection frequency (e.g. quarterly disposal audits) was located in Subpart 8. The "at least one on-site inspection" in Rule 3.5.2 is the only frequency floor stated for establishments generally; whether MSDH in practice inspects disposal entities more often is [VERIFY] and is not asserted here.

11.5.7 Hemp — destruction of non-compliant hemp (pre-harvest, over 0.3% THC)

Governing framework for Mississippi hemp producers. Mississippi has no USDA-approved state hemp plan (Run 1 baseline; MDAC issues no licences). A Mississippi producer therefore operates under the USDA hemp production plan, 7 CFR Part 990, Subpart C. The operative destruction provision is 7 CFR § 990.27. Its text, as opened (eCFR / Cornell LII), is:

"(a) Cannabis plants exceeding the acceptable hemp THC level constitute marijuana, a schedule I controlled substance under the Controlled Substances Act (CSA), 21 U.S.C. 801 et seq., and producers must either use a DEA-registered reverse distributor or law enforcement to dispose of non-compliant plants or ensure the disposal of such cannabis plant on site at the farm or hemp production facility. (b) Producers must notify USDA of their intent to dispose of or remediate non-conforming plants and verify disposal or remediation by submitting required documentation. (c) If a producer elects to perform remediation activities, an additional sampling and testing of the post-remediated crop must occur to determine THC concentration levels."

Source: 7 CFR § 990.27 — https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/7/990.27 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Who orders destruction. On the text of § 990.27, destruction is producer-executed after a non-compliant test result, not ordered lot-by-lot by USDA in the first instance: the producer must dispose or remediate, must notify USDA of intent, and must verify by documentation. USDA's role is notification, verification and compliance (see § 990.28, referenced in § 990.26(e): lots not meeting the acceptable hemp THC level "are subject to § 990.27"). There is no Mississippi state agency in this chain, because there is no state plan and MDAC issues no hemp licence. A Mississippi-specific "control order" or state-supervised destruction procedure of the kind found in some state plans (e.g. Pennsylvania's plan, where the department issues a control order) was not located for Mississippi and must not be imported. Whether USDA in practice requires a state or federal official to be present for a given Mississippi destruction is [VERIFY] — § 990.27 itself does not state a presence requirement, while USDA's 2021 Remediation and Disposal Guidelines note that a state/tribal plan may require officials to be present, which does not apply to a USDA-plan producer in the same way.

Pre-harvest mechanics that trigger § 990.27. Under 7 CFR § 990.26, as opened: the producer must harvest no later than thirty (30) days after sample collection; if harvest is not completed in 30 days, a second pre-harvest sample is required; harvested lots must not be commingled with other lots or material; lots meeting the acceptable hemp THC level may enter commerce; lots not meeting it are subject to § 990.27; a producer may request additional pre-harvest testing if the original result is believed to be in error, by the original or another laboratory. Source: 7 CFR § 990.26 — https://www.ecfr.gov/api/renderer/v1/content/enhanced/2024-04-23/title-7?subtitle=B&chapter=IX&part=990 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

"Acceptable hemp THC level" — measurement of uncertainty. Under the USDA framework as described in the 2021 final rule and USDA guidance, a sample is within the acceptable hemp THC level if 0.3% falls within the laboratory's measurement of uncertainty around the reported result. This file does not restate the full sampling/testing procedure (that is Run 1 / Part 7 territory), but the point matters for destruction: a result numerically above 0.3% does not automatically trigger destruction if 0.3% is within the measurement of uncertainty. The lot is non-compliant only when the result, with its uncertainty, exceeds the acceptable level. Any Mississippi producer or adviser who treats a bare 0.31% result as automatically destructive without checking the uncertainty range is misreading the USDA rule. The precise uncertainty application to a given lab report is [VERIFY] against that report and the lab's accreditation.

Methods — what USDA guidance allows. 7 CFR § 990.27 itself does not list physical methods (ploughing, burning, etc.); it specifies who may dispose (DEA-registered reverse distributor, law enforcement, or on-site disposal at the farm/production facility) and that disposal/remediation must be notified and verified. USDA's Hemp Remediation and Disposal Guidelines (15 January 2021) fill in the on-farm methods for state/tribal/USDA plans generally:

  • Remediation, option 1: separate and remove all flowers from stalks, leaves and seeds of the lot, retaining the non-flower parts.
  • Remediation, option 2: shred the entire lot into homogeneous "biomass" (all flowers, buds, trichomes, leaves, stalks, seed and plant parts chopped/shredded into a uniform blend, lots kept separate, not combined), then resample and retest; if the biomass still exceeds the acceptable level, it must be destroyed.
  • Disposal (destruction) methods described in state-plan guidance collected by USDA and in the Guidelines include ploughing under, mulching/composting, disking, bush mowing, deep burial, and burning — performed on-farm, with the lot held and not entering commerce.

Source: USDA Hemp Remediation and Disposal Guidelines (15 Jan 2021) — https://ams-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/media/HempRemediationandDisposalGuidelines.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Caveat: the Guidelines are guidance, not the regulation, and the state-plan examples (Connecticut, South Carolina plans) are not Mississippi law. They are included here only to show the methods USDA contemplates; a Mississippi USDA-plan producer should confirm the intended method with USDA before acting, because § 990.27 does not itself enumerate methods. The method, the decision (destroy vs remediate), and the verification documentation must be notified to USDA under § 990.27(b).

Reporting to USDA. § 990.27(b) (above): notify USDA of intent to dispose or remediate, and verify disposal/remediation by submitting required documentation. Under § 990.28 compliance provisions (referenced in the USDA plan), disposal/remediation records must be made available for inspection by USDA inspectors/auditors during reasonable business hours. No Mississippi state reporting form or MDAC reporting duty for hemp destruction was located, consistent with MDAC issuing no hemp licences. [UNAVAILABLE] as a Mississippi-specific form: there is none to cite.

Negligent vs culpable violations — why destruction is not the only consequence. Under 7 CFR 990.29 (USDA-plan violations; 990.28 is audit/compliance, 990.30 is suspension): a negligent violation (e.g. a hot lot grown with reasonable efforts, where the THC level does not exceed 1.0% on a dry-weight basis (7 CFR 990.29(a)(3), USDA plan)) requires a corrective action plan and periodic compliance reporting for at least two years, with no criminal enforcement for the negligent violation itself; three negligent violations in five years make the producer ineligible for five years from the third violation; a culpable violation (mental state greater than negligence) must be reported to the U.S. Attorney General and the chief state law-enforcement officer. The 0.5% negligent-violation threshold in § 990.6 is a violation-classification threshold, not a second THC limit for hemp: a lot above 0.3% (outside measurement of uncertainty) is still non-compliant and subject to § 990.27 even if the violation is classified as negligent. Do not conflate the two numbers.

11.5.8 Hemp — post-11 December 2026 federal definition issues

Given baseline applied (not re-researched). After 11 December 2026, the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply (PL 119-37 § 781 as limited by PL 119-103 § 2019). The consequences for destruction, stated as implications of that baseline and flagged where they require a USDA update, are:

  1. More material becomes "non-compliant." Hemp and hemp-derived products that satisfied the pre-December 2026 delta-9-only 0.3% dry-weight test may fail a total-THC test (delta-9 + THCA × 0.877, the USDA post-decarboxylation method) or, for products, the 0.4 mg per container cap. A lot or product that was compliant on 10 December 2026 is not grandfathered by anything in the baseline given for this file. Whether any transition, sell-through or enforcement-discretion provision applies to Mississippi USDA-plan producers after 11 December 2026 is [VERIFY] — no Mississippi or USDA transition rule for this date was located in this run.
  2. The disposal route in § 990.27 does not change on its face, but its premise does. § 990.27(a) as opened still calls non-compliant plants "a schedule I controlled substance." After the given federal baseline (Schedule III for state-licensed medical marijuana; adult-use Schedule I), a non-compliant hemp lot is not state-licensed medical marijuana, so the Schedule III move does not reclassify it as medical. Whether USDA/DEA will amend § 990.27's Schedule I label, or treat post-December 2026 non-compliant hemp under a different disposal authority, is [VERIFY]. Until USDA amends the rule or issues guidance, a producer should not assume the reverse-distributor / law-enforcement / on-site options in § 990.27(a) have changed — but should also not assume the Schedule I label in the current CFR text is the final post-December 2026 position.
  3. Container-cap failures are a product problem, not a crop problem. § 990.27 governs "cannabis plants" and lots. It does not, on its face, govern a finished hemp-derived product that exceeds 0.4 mg total THC per container after 11 December 2026. No Mississippi rule and no USDA-plan provision located in this run prescribes destruction, recall or remediation for such a finished product. That gap is stated plainly in §11.5.9.
  4. DEA-registered lab testing delay. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026 (given baseline). That delay concerns who may test, not whether a hot lot must be destroyed. It does not suspend § 990.27.

11.5.9 Hemp — disposal of hemp-derived product waste

No Mississippi rule located. No Mississippi statute, MDAC rule, MSDH rule or MDOR rule located in this run prescribes how a hemp business must dispose of hemp-derived product waste (e.g. expired CBD products, manufacturing trim/waste from hemp processing, unsold intoxicating-hemp products). The MSDH waste-disposal regime in Subpart 8 applies to medical cannabis waste and to licensed medical cannabis establishments; it does not, on its face, extend to hemp businesses, which are not medical cannabis establishments. The MDOR waste-disposal duty (Chapter 18, ¶ 110) applies to dispensary licensees, not hemp retailers.

What does apply, by other law (stated at a general level only):

  • A hemp crop that is non-compliant is governed by § 990.27 (§11.5.7 above).
  • A hemp-derived product that is also a controlled substance under federal law after the December 2026 changes would be subject to federal controlled-substance disposal law (DEA reverse distributor / law enforcement), but no Mississippi-specific procedure for that product category was located. [VERIFY] with DEA/USDA before destroying or transferring such product.
  • Ordinary commercial waste (packaging, non-cannabis manufacturing waste) is subject to general Mississippi solid-waste and local law, not to a cannabis-specific rule located here.
  • The 11 June 2025 Attorney General opinion (intoxicating hemp products outside the medical programme treated as prohibited) does not itself prescribe a waste-disposal method, and is an opinion, not a statute (Run 1 baseline). It must not be cited as a disposal rule.

Bottom line for hemp product waste: [UNAVAILABLE] as a Mississippi cannabis/hemp-specific rule. A hemp business that needs to destroy product should document the product, quantity, reason, method and any USDA/DEA notification, retain that record, and seek USDA/DEA direction if the product may be a controlled substance — but this file does not invent a Mississippi procedure that was not located.

11.5.10 Waste — summary table

Licensed disposal entity required? Yes, for Rule 1.2.29 cannabis waste (MSDH Rule 1.2.29(E)); dispensaries must use a permitted entity (MDOR Ch. 18, ¶ 110) No Mississippi licensed disposal entity for hemp; crop destruction under USDA § 990.27; product waste: no rule located
Destruction standard Unusable + unrecognisable; grinding + ≥50% non-cannabis waste by volume (Rules 8.1.7, 8.1.9) § 990.27: DEA reverse distributor / law enforcement / on-site at farm or facility; remediation by flower separation or whole-lot shredding to biomass, then retest (USDA Guidelines)

11.6 ENVIRONMENTAL RULES

Reading note. Mississippi has no cannabis-specific environmental code in the sources opened for this file. The medical programme's environmental provisions are scattered through MSDH operational, sanitation and testing rules, plus general state law (MDEQ water, air, waste) that applies to any facility or farm, not only to cannabis. This section therefore does two things for each topic: (1) states the cannabis-specific rule if one exists, with a verbatim quote; and (2) states explicitly where the state level is silent and only general law applies. Local odour ordinances are excluded per the commission (Run 1 Part 3).

11.6.1 Medical — water use and withdrawal

No cannabis-specific water-use, water-withdrawal, irrigation-volume or water-efficiency rule was located in MSDH Title 15, Part 22 or MDOR Title 35, Part XI. The MSDH text requires running water for hand-washing/sanitation (Rule 4.6.2(B): hand-washing areas "shall include running water at a suitable temperature"), requires plumbing to be kept in good repair and to prevent drip/condensate contamination (Rule 4.4.3, as opened), and requires facilities to be kept clean and sanitary — but it does not set a water budget, a withdrawal cap, a metering duty, or a recycling duty for cultivation.

General Mississippi water law that therefore governs, at a general level: Under Miss. Code §§ 51-3-1 et seq. (Mississippi Water Laws) and MDEQ Office of Land and Water Resources rules, a person may not initiate drilling of a groundwater well or placement of a surface-water intake until an appropriate groundwater or surface-water use permit has been issued by the Permit Board or its designee, subject to exempted diversions/withdrawals. MDEQ's forms page states: "Effective 7/1/2026, there are no permit fees associated with groundwater or surface water withdrawal permits." Source: MDEQ, Office of Land and Water Resources, forms page — https://www.mdeq.ms.gov/permits/water-availability-and-use/forms/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026; MDEQ Administrative Procedures Act Rules (Title 11, Part 7, Ch. 1), Rule 1.2 (basic requirements) — https://www.mdeq.ms.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/11-Miss.-Admin.-Code-Pt.-7-Ch.-1-FINAL.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Application to medical cannabis: Because MSDH requires cultivation to take place "in an indoor, enclosed, locked, and secure area" (Rule 1.2.22, cultivation facility definition) and defines "indoor cannabis cultivation" as production "in a completely enclosed and secure facility with a sealed, controlled environment" (Rule 1.2.62), a Mississippi medical cultivator is ordinarily a municipal-water or permitted-well indoor user, not an open-field irrigator. But the absence of a cannabis-specific water rule means:

  • No MSDH water-use report, water-per-unit-of-cannabis metric, or drought restriction specific to cannabis was located. [UNAVAILABLE] as a cannabis-specific rule.
  • A cultivator that drills its own well or diverts surface water must still obtain the MDEQ permit described above, on the same terms as any other user. Whether a municipal-water user needs any MDEQ permit is a general-law question, not a cannabis question, and is [VERIFY] with MDEQ for the specific source.
  • No rule was located requiring a cultivator to disclose its water source in its MSDH application. If MSDH application forms (not opened in this run) ask for it, that is a form requirement, not a rule in Part 22 as opened. [VERIFY] against the current MSDH application forms.

11.6.2 Medical — wastewater

No cannabis-specific wastewater discharge, effluent-limit, sewer-discharge or nutrient-runoff rule was located in MSDH Part 22 or MDOR Part XI. The MSDH sanitation rules require rubbish/waste to be conveyed, stored and disposed of so as to minimise odour, pest attraction/harborage and contamination (Rule 4.6, as opened), and require toxic materials (cleaning compounds, sanitising agents, pesticide chemicals) to be identified and stored so as to protect against contamination of cannabis, products, contact surfaces or packaging (Rule 4.6.3(C)). Those are product-protection rules, not discharge permits.

General law that therefore governs: Wastewater discharge to waters of the state or to a publicly owned treatment works is governed by general Mississippi law (MDEQ National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System / state operating permits, and local sewer-use ordinances), not by a cannabis rule. No cannabis-specific effluent limit (e.g. for fertiliser salts, pesticides in wash water, or extraction solvents in wastewater) was located. A processing facility using solvents must also comply with general hazardous-waste and sewer rules for those solvents; MSDH's solvent rules (Subpart 5, Appendix A, Table 2) set product residual-solvent action levels (e.g. benzene 2 ppm, chloroform 60 ppm, ethanol 5,000 ppm), not wastewater limits. Conflating product action levels with discharge limits would be an error.

Bottom line: state-level cannabis wastewater rule — silent. [UNAVAILABLE] as a cannabis-specific rule; general MDEQ/local sewer law applies.

11.6.3 Medical — pesticides: allowed, prohibited, and tested

This is the one environmental topic where Mississippi does have a detailed cannabis-specific regime — but it is a testing regime, not an allowed-use list. The distinction matters and is the most common source of error in secondary summaries.

(a) No MSDH "allowed pesticides" list was located. The MSDH rule text opened contains no schedule of pesticides that may be applied to medical cannabis, and no schedule of pesticides that are prohibited from application, as a use list. What it contains is:

  • A definition (Rule 1.2.105): "'Pesticide' means any substance or mixture of substances (organic or conventional) intended for preventing, destroying, repelling, or mitigating any pest, or any substance or mixture of substances intended for use as a plant regulator, defoliant or desiccant. 'Pesticide' shall not include any article that is a 'new animal drug' as designated by the [FDA]."
  • A use precaution (Rule 4.6.3(D), as opened, pest control): "The use of pesticides to control pests in the production center is permitted only under precautions and restrictions that will protect against the contamination of cannabis, cannabis products, components, contact surfaces, or packaging materials." And Rule 4.6.3(C): toxic cleaning compounds, sanitising agents and pesticide chemicals must be identified and stored so as to protect against contamination.
  • A recordkeeping duty (Rules 4.9.2(D), 4.9.3): records of all pesticide and chemical applications, including (A) date of application, (B) name of the individual making the application, (C) product applied, (D) section, including square footage, receiving the application, (E) amount applied, and (F) a copy of the label of the product applied. Retained at least five years (Rule 4.9.2).
  • A biosecurity / pest-exclusion duty (Rule 4.6.3(D) and Rule 4.4, as opened): pests must not be allowed in any area of a production centre; adequate screening or other protection against pests must be provided; fans/air-blowing equipment must be located/operated to minimise contamination.

(b) The testing regime — Appendix A, Table 1(D) action levels, with "Destroy" as the required action. MSDH Rule 5.4.3:

"A. Usable Medical cannabis and medical cannabis products required to be tested for pesticides shall be tested by a Mississippi licensed, and registered cannabis testing facility entity approved for the analytes listed in Appendix A, Table 1. B. The cannabis testing facility entity shall report whether any Residual Pesticides are detected above the limit of detection (LOD) and shall report the result of the testing in ppms on the Certificate of Analysis. The cannabis testing facility shall indicate 'pass' or 'fail' on the Certificate of Analysis. C. A batch fails pesticide testing if a cannabis testing facility entity detects the presence of a pesticide above the action levels listed in Appendix A, Table 1 in a sample: 1. During an initial test where no reanalysis is requested; or 2. Upon reanalysis as described in Rule 5.5.1 of this Part."

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rule 5.4.3 — link as above — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Appendix A, Table 1(D), "Pesticides, Fungicides, Growth Regulators," lists approximately 60 analytes with CAS numbers, maximum allowable concentrations, and the required action "Destroy" (the table as opened shows "Destroy" as the action for the pesticide group). Examples (maximum allowable concentration, ppm):

The full table (including etoxazole, fenpyroximate, fludioxonil, hexythiazox, imazalil, kresoxim-methyl, metalaxyl, methiocarb, methomyl, methyl parathion, naled, oxamyl, phosmet, prallethrin, propiconazole, propoxur, pyridaben, spiromesifen, spirotetramat, spiroxamine, tebuconazole, thiacloprid, and others) is in Appendix A of the MSDH PDF as opened. These are action levels for product testing, not permissions to apply. A pesticide being listed with an action level does not mean MSDH authorises its application; it means that if residue above that level is detected, the batch fails and must be destroyed (Rule 5.5.7, §11.5.5). Conversely, a pesticide not listed in Appendix A is not thereby authorised either — Rule 5.4.3(B) requires reporting of any residual pesticide detected above the LOD, and the absence of an action level for an unlisted compound is [VERIFY] with MSDH (whether it is treated as fail-on-detection, or by another standard).

No remediation for pesticide failure. See §11.5.5, Rule 5.5.7: a batch failing pesticide testing "may not be remediated and must shall be destroyed."

(c) EPA / FIFRA position — why there is no federal list to import. Under the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), a pesticide must be registered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for a specific use site, and its label directions (including the crop/site list) must be followed. EPA has not registered pesticides for use on marijuana/cannabis as a crop site, because marijuana was a Schedule I controlled substance with no accepted medical use under federal law at the time of the relevant EPA decisions, and EPA cannot set tolerances for a crop it cannot assess for inhalation/ingestion/dermal exposure in that framework. EPA has set a tolerance for hemp in one narrow case (ethalfluralin, for hemp seed, April 2023 — secondary reporting, not relied on for a Mississippi rule), but that does not create a federal cannabis pesticide list.

Consequences for Mississippi, stated plainly:

  • A Mississippi medical cultivator cannot point to a federal EPA label listing "cannabis" or "marijuana" as an approved use site, because no such label exists. [VERIFY] against the specific product label before any application — the label is the federal legal control.
  • A Mississippi cultivator also cannot point to an MSDH "allowed list," because none was located in Part 22. The operative Mississippi controls are (i) the precaution/storage/recordkeeping duties above, (ii) the label law (apply only as the label directs; a label that lists only a different crop does not authorise cannabis use), and (iii) the product testing action levels that will destroy a batch if residues exceed them.
  • Whether Schedule III for state-licensed medical marijuana (given baseline, effective 28 April 2026) will lead EPA to register pesticides for medical cannabis or set tolerances is [VERIFY]. No EPA medical-cannabis pesticide registration or tolerance was located in this run, and none is asserted. The Beyond Pesticides / University of Washington commentary (April 2026, secondary) suggesting rescheduling "would open" EPA rulemaking is speculation, not a rule, and is not relied on.
  • Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce (MDAC) pesticide role: MDAC is Mississippi's state pesticide regulatory agency under general pesticide law (Miss. Code §§ 69-23-1 et seq.), but no MDAC cannabis-specific pesticide list, guidance or registration for medical cannabis was located in this run. [UNAVAILABLE] as a cannabis-specific MDAC list. General MDAC pesticide applicator licensing and label-enforcement law applies to applicators as it does to any pesticide user; it is not restated here because it is not cannabis-specific.

11.6.4 Medical — fertiliser and soil

No cannabis-specific fertiliser, nutrient, soil-amendment, growing-medium or soil-testing rule was located in MSDH Part 22 or MDOR Part XI. The MSDH text requires:

  • Sanitary conditions, clean/repaired floors/walls/ceilings, and pest protection (Rule 4.6.2);
  • That toxic materials be stored to protect against contamination (Rule 4.6.3(C));
  • Product testing for heavy metals (Appendix A, Table 1(B) — e.g. action levels for arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury, chromium, nickel, copper, with product-type variations), for foreign material (Rule 5.4.10: fail if, among other thresholds, more than one-fourth of the sample area is covered by sand, soil, cinders or dirt; or 1 insect fragment / 1 hair / 1 mammalian excreta per 3.0 g), and for microbiological contaminants and mycotoxins.

Those testing rules indirectly constrain fertiliser/soil practice (a fertiliser or soil that introduces heavy metals, pathogens or foreign material will fail product testing), but they do not prescribe fertiliser types, application rates, soil testing, or organic/conventional distinctions for cannabis. General Mississippi fertiliser law (MDAC fertiliser registration, Miss. Code §§ 69-25-1 et seq. framework) applies to fertiliser products as commercial products, not as a cannabis cultivation rule. State-level cannabis fertiliser/soil rule: silent. [UNAVAILABLE] as a cannabis-specific rule.

11.6.5 Medical — energy use and efficiency

No cannabis-specific energy-use, energy-efficiency, lighting, HVAC, carbon, or renewable-energy rule was located in MSDH Part 22 or MDOR Part XI. The only energy-adjacent provisions in the MSDH text opened are:

  • Alarm and video-surveillance systems must "have the ability to remain operational during a power outage" (Rules 4.5.2(E), 4.5.3(I), 8.1.5(5)(e));
  • Licensees "should" undertake a vulnerability assessment of standby power systems and "should have a backup power system/generator for backup power supply for up to a minimum of forty-eight (48) hours for portions of the facility that should be supplied with standby power" (Rule 4.5.3(J)–(K)) — note "should," not "must shall," in the text as opened;
  • Indoor cultivation is defined as a "sealed, controlled environment that prevents unfiltered air exchange with the outdoors, provides control of environmental conditions such as humidity, temperature, light, and carbon dioxide levels" (Rule 1.2.62) — a containment definition, not an efficiency standard;
  • Adequate lighting in hand-washing, dressing/locker, toilet and production areas (Rule 4.4.3(D)), and shatter-resistant bulbs/fixtures over exposed cannabis (Rule 4.4.3(E)).

There is no kWh-per-gram limit, no lighting-efficiency standard, no HVAC efficiency standard, no carbon reporting duty, and no renewable-energy requirement specific to medical cannabis in the text opened. General Mississippi building/electrical codes and utility rules apply as they do to any indoor facility. State-level cannabis energy rule: silent.

11.6.6 Medical — odour (state level only)

No state-level ambient odour standard, odour-setback, odour-mitigation-plan or odour-complaint procedure specific to medical cannabis was located in MSDH Part 22 or MDOR Part XI. The only odour provisions in the MSDH text opened are indoor product-protection provisions, not ambient standards:

  • Rule 4.4.3(F): facilities must "Provide adequate ventilation or control equipment to minimize dust, odors, and vapors (including steam and noxious fumes) in areas where they may cause allergen cross contact or contaminate cannabis, cannabis products, or components."
  • Rule 4.6.2 / 4.6.3 (sanitation): rubbish "shall be so conveyed, stored, and disposed of as to minimize the development of odor, minimize the potential for the waste becoming an attractant and harborage or breeding place for pests, and protect against contamination."

Neither provision sets an odour concentration limit at the property line, requires carbon filtration or other specific odour-control technology, or creates a state odour-complaint process for cannabis. Local odour ordinances (zoning, nuisance) are Run 1 Part 3 and are expressly not repeated here. Whether MDEQ air regulations (general nuisance / air-pollution rules) have been applied to a cannabis facility in Mississippi is [VERIFY] — no such application was located in this run.

11.6.7 Hemp — environmental rules (separately)

Topic Hemp position (Mississippi, USDA-plan producer)
Water use / withdrawal No hemp-specific water rule located. The same general MDEQ water-permit law described in §11.6.1 applies: a groundwater well or surface-water intake requires a Permit Board permit (subject to exemptions), with no permit fees effective 1 July 2026 (MDEQ forms page). USDA's hemp plan does not set a water budget. An outdoor hemp farm is more likely than an indoor medical cultivator to need a withdrawal permit, but the permit is a general agricultural-water permit, not a hemp permit.
Wastewater No hemp-specific wastewater rule located. General MDEQ/local sewer law applies, as in §11.6.2. Field runoff of fertiliser/pesticide is governed by general agricultural and water-quality law, not by a hemp rule located here.
Pesticides No Mississippi hemp pesticide list located, and no federal hemp pesticide list (with the narrow ethalfluralin hemp-seed tolerance exception noted in §11.6.3(c), secondary) to import. The FIFRA label problem is the same as for medical cannabis, but with one difference: hemp is a lawful agricultural commodity under the 2018 Farm Bill, so EPA can in principle assess hemp tolerances (and did so for ethalfluralin seed), whereas it has not done so for marijuana. That does not create a usable list for Mississippi hemp flower, fibre or grain: a pesticide label must still list hemp (or a sufficiently general site) to be lawfully applied, and most labels do not. MDAC, as the state pesticide agency, has published no hemp pesticide list located in this run. [UNAVAILABLE] as a Mississippi hemp list. A hemp producer must check each product label and, if in doubt, MDAC/EPA guidance for that product. USDA's hemp plan does not itself authorise any pesticide.
Fertiliser / soil No hemp-specific fertiliser/soil rule located. General MDAC fertiliser law and USDA hemp-plan agronomy (variety, acreage reporting, sampling) apply. MSU Extension general agronomy guidance (soil testing, lime/P/K by soil test) is general agricultural guidance, not a hemp rule. The MSU "sunn hemp" variety trials (§11.9.4) concern Crotalaria juncea, a different species from industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa), and must not be cited as industrial-hemp fertiliser guidance.
Energy No hemp-specific energy rule located. Outdoor hemp production has no indoor lighting/HVAC load comparable to indoor medical cultivation; processing/drying energy is governed by general law only.
Odour (state level) No state-level hemp odour rule located. Hemp, like any crop, may be subject to general nuisance law and local ordinances (Run 1 Part 3 territory for local rules), but no state hemp odour standard was located. The MSDH ventilation/odour-minimisation rules in §11.6.6 apply to medical cannabis establishments, not to hemp farms.

11.7 SAMPLING, GIVEAWAYS, DISCOUNTS AND PROMOTIONS

11.7.1 Medical — the current inducement rule (and why older summaries are wrong)

MSDH Rule 9.3.1 (current text opened):

"Medical Cannabis Establishments Licensees may utilize inducements to assist qualified patients. Inducements must shall not persuade or influence the use of medical cannabis outside of practitioner recommendations and/or limitations or the amounts allowed by the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act. Examples of inducements include, but are not limited to: 1. The use of discount cards; 2. The use of coupons; 3. The use of 'punch cards' to offer discounts/free products; 4. Promotion of sales/discounts on medical cannabis of any type; 5. The use of 'buy one, get one' discount approaches; and, 6. The use of any type of 'daily deal', 'weekly deal', 'monthly deal', etc."

MSDH Rule 9.3.2:

"Any and all medical cannabis and/or medical cannabis products that are part of an inducement program as defined in Rule 3.4.1 9.3.1, remain subject to seed-tosale tracking requirements, any practitioner limitation included on the qualified patient's written certification, and MS Medical Cannabis Equivalency Unit MMCEU allotment limitations of set forth in the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act."

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rules 9.3.1–9.3.2 — https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/sites/default/files/Documents/RevisedAdminRegulationsMMCPBOHADOPTED10.11.2023.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026. (The "Rule 3.4.1" cross-reference inside Rule 9.3.2 is a renumbering remnant; the substance is Rule 9.3.1.)

MDOR Rule, Chapter 13, ¶ 100 (dispensaries):

"Dispensaries may utilize inducements to assist qualified patients. Inducements must not persuade or influence the use of medical cannabis outside of practitioner recommendations and/or limitations or the amounts allowed by the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act. Examples of authorized inducements include: 1. The use of discount cards; 2. The use of coupons; 3. The use of 'punch cards' to offer discounts/free products; 4. Promotion of sales/discounts on medical cannabis, including 'buy one, get one' discounts, and daily/weekly/monthly deal discounts; and 5. The giving away of educational materials, including but not limited to, branded merchandise."

Source: MDOR Title 35 Pt. XI, Ch. 13, ¶ 100 (revised effective 1 July 2022, as reproduced in the PDF showing revisions to 1 Dec 2025) — http://sos.ms.gov/adminsearch/ACCode/00000758c.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

The conflict, stated once and clearly (see §0.3, C-2): Secondary summaries that say "discount cards, coupons, samples, and giveaways are prohibited" in Mississippi are describing the superseded former Rule 3.4.1 prohibition (which listed, as prohibited inducements, discount cards, coupons, punch cards, sales/discount promotions, BOGO, daily/weekly/monthly deals, giveaways of any type, and sampling of any type). That prohibition is not the current rule. Under the current MSDH and MDOR rules, discount cards, coupons, punch cards (including for free products), sales/discount promotions, BOGO and daily/weekly/monthly deals are authorised inducements, subject to the single stated limit in §11.7.2. A compliance programme built on the old prohibition would wrongly forbid lawful discounts; a programme built on the current rule must still respect the giveaway/sampling gap in §11.7.3.

11.7.2 Medical — discounts and loyalty programmes: what limits exist?

Question Answer on current rules
Are discounts permitted? Yes. Discount cards, coupons, sales/discount promotions of any type, BOGO, daily/weekly/monthly deals — MSDH Rule 9.3.1(1), (2), (4), (5), (6); MDOR Ch. 13, ¶ 100(1), (2), (4).
Is there a percentage or dollar cap on a discount? No cap was located. No rule in MSDH Subpart 9 or MDOR Chapter 13 states a maximum discount percentage, a minimum price, a "no below-cost" rule, or a per-transaction discount limit. The only stated limit is the purpose limit in §11.7.2, next row. [VERIFY] against any MSDH/MDOR guidance or tax rule that might treat a discount as affecting taxable gross proceeds — the discount rules themselves do not address tax.
What is the single stated limit? Inducements "must shall not persuade or influence the use of medical cannabis outside of practitioner recommendations and/or limitations or the amounts allowed by the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act" (MSDH Rule 9.3.1; MDOR Ch. 13, ¶ 100). In practice: an inducement may not be used to push a patient past their practitioner limitation or past their MMCEU allotment (24 MMCEUs / 30 days; 28 possession; see §0.1).
Do discounted/free products still count against MMCEU and practitioner limits? Yes. Rule 9.3.2: inducement products "remain subject to seed-tosale tracking requirements, any practitioner limitation included on the qualified patient's written certification, and [MMCEU] allotment limitations." A "free" product obtained via a punch card is not extra allotment; it is tracked and counted like a sale. A dispensary that gave free product outside the tracking/allotment system would violate Rule 9.3.2 even if the discount itself was authorised.
Are loyalty programmes permitted? Yes, in the form stated: "punch cards to offer discounts/free products" (MSDH Rule 9.3.1(3); MDOR Ch. 13, ¶ 100(3)). No separate "loyalty programme" rule, points-cap, expiry rule, or tier rule was located. A punch-card programme is a loyalty programme for these purposes; any other loyalty mechanic (points, tiers, referral bonuses) is not separately addressed and is [VERIFY] — it would need to fit within the Rule 9.3.1 examples ("include, but are not limited to") and the practitioner/MMCEU limit, and must not become a vehicle for giveaways/sampling outside §11.7.3.
Must a discount be advertised in a particular way? No discount-specific advertising format was located. Discount promotion is itself an authorised inducement (Rule 9.3.1(4)), but promotion remains subject to the advertising ban and content rules in §11.7.5: a discount may be promoted through permitted branding channels (website/social presence with general information, business directories, logos, charity sponsorships — Rule 9.2.2), but not through prohibited media (broadcast/electronic/print/mass text/mass email/public-space advertising — Rule 9.1.1). The interaction is: the discount is lawful; the medium used to tell patients about it may still be prohibited.
Do discounts affect sales-tax / excise-tax computation? No rule in Subpart 9 or MDOR Chapter 13 addresses this. MDOR tax rules are outside the chapters opened for this section. [VERIFY] with MDOR tax guidance before assuming a discounted price is the taxable gross proceeds figure. This file does not state a tax treatment for discounted or free product.

11.7.3 Medical — giveaways and sampling: the gap in the current list

Giveaways of cannabis product. The current MSDH list (Rule 9.3.1) does not include a general "giveaways" category. It includes "punch cards to offer discounts/free products" — i.e. free product earned through a punch-card programme — but not a standalone free-product giveaway (e.g. "free gram with any visit," "free product for new patients," prize-draw product). The current MDOR list (Chapter 13, ¶ 100) likewise does not include free cannabis product as a standalone category; its fifth category is "The giving away of educational materials, including but not limited to, branded merchandise" — i.e. non-cannabis giveaways (merchandise, educational materials).

Adopted reading, with the uncertainty flagged: On the current text, (a) free cannabis product via a punch card is authorised (expressly); (b) branded merchandise / educational materials given away are authorised for dispensaries (MDOR, expressly); (c) a standalone giveaway of cannabis product outside a punch-card programme is not expressly authorised in either current list, and the former rule expressly prohibited "Giveaways of any type." Whether the current "include, but are not limited to" language in Rule 9.3.1 is intended to carry forward standalone giveaways, or whether their omission is deliberate, is [VERIFY] with MSDH. This file does not treat standalone cannabis giveaways as authorised, and does not treat them as prohibited either — it treats them as not expressly authorised, which is the only position the current text supports. A licensee planning a standalone giveaway should seek MSDH/MDOR guidance in writing before running it.

Sampling — to patients, to staff, and trade samples. No rule was located in MSDH Subpart 9, MDOR Part XI, or MSDH Subpart 5 that authorises:

  • Sampling to patients (e.g. free trial doses, "try before you buy" at a dispensary);
  • Sampling to staff (e.g. employee free product for familiarity/training);
  • Trade samples between licensees (e.g. a cultivator providing free product to a dispensary for evaluation, outside a tracked sale/transfer).

The only "sampling" in the MSDH text opened is laboratory sampling for compliance testing (Subpart 5, Rule 5.3: samples collected on-site by testing-entity personnel, video-recorded, minimum increments, reserve-sample retention — §11.5.5), plus R&D testing (Rule 1.2.120: "optional testing performed before final compliance testing"). Neither is patient/staff/trade sampling.

Why sampling cannot be assumed from the inducement rule: (i) The former Rule 3.4.1 expressly listed "Sampling of any type" among prohibited inducements; the current Rule 9.3.1 omits it, just as it omits standalone giveaways — omission from a "but are not limited to" list is ambiguous, not an authorisation. (ii) Any free product, however labelled, remains subject to seed-to-sale tracking and MMCEU/practitioner limits (Rule 9.3.2), so a "sample" that bypassed tracking would violate Rule 9.3.2. (iii) Consumption on dispensary premises is prohibited (MDOR Chapter 18, ¶ 101(5): a licensee/employee may not "Engage in or permit any other person to engage in the consumption of any type of cannabis product on the premises"; MSDH Appendix B penalises "On-site use of cannabis by employee(s)" at $5,000 per employee found using cannabis on the premises). An in-store tasting/sample-consumption model would therefore conflict with the consumption ban even if the product transfer itself were tracked. (iv) Staff "sampling" as consumption on premises would likewise conflict with the on-premises use prohibition and with MDOR Chapter 18, ¶ 101(1) (licensee/employee may not "Use or be under the influence of alcoholic beverages, cannabis, or controlled substances on the licensed premises").

Bottom line on sampling: [VERIFY] as a distinct authorisation; no patient, staff or trade sampling rule was located. If a licensee wishes to provide product for evaluation, the only clearly authorised routes on the current text are a tracked sale/transfer within MMCEU/practitioner limits, or a punch-card free product within those same limits — both of which are sales-programme mechanics, not "sampling" as a separate category. Any claim that Mississippi authorises sampling should be required to cite a current rule; none was located in this run.

11.7.4 Medical — what a dispensary may sell, and why it matters for promotions

MDOR Chapter 16 (items authorised for sale) limits dispensary sales to medical cannabis, equipment used for medical cannabis, related supplies and educational materials; except for topical products, only to cardholders. Prohibited from sale on the premises: clothing, food not containing cannabis, beverages not containing cannabis, propane/butane, and vaping products not containing cannabis (Chapter 16, ¶ 105). Topical products may be sold to a non-cardholder aged 21+ (Chapter 16, ¶ 106); no other product may be sold to a non-cardholder regardless of age (¶ 106).

Promotional consequence: A promotion that offers a non-authorised item (e.g. branded clothing as a purchase incentive) would conflict with Chapter 16 even if the inducement rule were read broadly. The MDOR-authorised non-cannabis giveaway in Chapter 13, ¶ 100(5) is "educational materials, including but not limited to, branded merchandise" — the tension between Chapter 13(5) (giving away branded merchandise is authorised) and Chapter 16(105) (selling clothing, etc., is prohibited) is resolved by the sale/giveaway distinction: giving away merchandise is not selling it. Whether a "free merchandise with purchase" mechanic is a giveaway (Chapter 13) or a sale of a prohibited item (Chapter 16) is [VERIFY] — the rules do not address bundled purchase incentives expressly.

11.7.5 Medical — advertising and promotion limits as they affect discounts (including Cocroft v. Graham)

The advertising ban (MSDH Subpart 9, Rule 9.1.1). MSDH-licensed establishments and entities acting on their behalf "are prohibited from advertising and marketing in any media, including but not limited to":

  • Broadcast or electronic media: radio; television; unsolicited internet pop-up advertising; social media;
  • Print media: newspaper;
  • Other forms: mass text/messaging communications; mass email communications; display of medical cannabis/products in windows or public view; advertisement in any manner viewable or perceived as a public space (including adopt-a-highway signs and electronic interstate signs); solicited/paid patient/caregiver reviews/testimonies/endorsements; solicited/paid practitioner reviews/testimonies/endorsements.

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rule 9.1.1 — link as above — accessed 25 Oct 2026. MDOR Chapter 12, ¶ 100 incorporates this by reference: "Dispensaries shall comply with all restrictions on advertising and marketing set forth in Department of Health regulations."

Content prohibitions (Rule 9.1.2). No MSDH licensee "shall engage in advertising that contains any statement or illustration that: (A) Depicts the actual consumption of cannabis or cannabis products; (B) Promotes the overconsumption of cannabis or cannabis products; (C) Makes any health, medicinal, or therapeutic claims about cannabis or cannabis products; (D) Makes safety claims of any type; (E) Includes the image of a cannabis leaf or bud; or (F) Includes any image designed or likely to appeal to minors, including cartoons, toys, animals, or children or any other likeness, images, characters, or phrases that are designed in any manner to be appealing to children and/or youth."

Permitted branding (Rule 9.2.2) — the only promotion channels stated: (1) establishment of a website and/or social media presence providing general information on contact information, retail dispensing locations, and a list of products available; (2) listings in business directories (inclusive of phone books, cannabis-related or medical publications); (3) display of cannabis in company logos and other branding activities; (4) sponsorships of health or not-for-profit charity or advocacy events. Rule 9.2.3: branding must not target minors, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, or promote non-medical use. Rule 9.2.4: business signage is subject to local zoning/permitting. Rule 9.2.1: the Department will make business name, location(s) and contact information available through a public website.

The tension inside Rule 9.1.1 / 9.2.2, noted, not resolved: Rule 9.1.1 prohibits advertising on "social media," while Rule 9.2.2(1) permits "a website and/or social media presence that provides general information." The reconciliation on the face of the rules is that a general-information presence (contact, locations, product list) is branding, while advertising/marketing on social media (promotional messaging, discount advertising, endorsements) is prohibited. Whether a social-media post announcing a discount is "general information" or "advertising" is not resolved in the text and is [VERIFY] — a licensee that posts discount promotions on social media risks falling on the Rule 9.1.1 side of the line. The same caution applies to mass text/email: Rule 9.1.1 prohibits mass text/email advertising, but does not address one-to-one patient communications; that distinction is also [VERIFY] and is not stated as a safe harbour in this file.

Patient education is not advertising (Rule 9.4). Education on risks/benefits between a practitioner and/or establishment and a qualified patient, caregiver, parent or legal guardian is permissible and "is not considered advertising or marketing" (Rule 9.4.1); it may include branded written/video materials (Rule 9.4.2) and instruction on safe use (Rule 9.4.3); pictures/images of cannabis/products must be limited to patient education materials (Rule 9.4.4); materials must include risks/side effects (including poisoning risk and the closest poison control centre number), strain/form/route information, tolerance/dependence/withdrawal information, substance-abuse signs/referral information, and other safe-use warnings (Rule 9.4.5). Education therefore cannot be used as a vehicle for discount promotion that would otherwise be prohibited media advertising — education content is defined by risk/benefit and safe-use content, not by price promotion.

Cocroft v. Graham — summary only as it bears on promotions. Cocroft v. Graham, No. 24-60086 (5th Cir. 22 Nov 2024), affirming the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi's dismissal: Clarence Cocroft and Tru Source Medical Cannabis, LLC challenged Mississippi's medical-cannabis advertising restrictions on First Amendment grounds. The Fifth Circuit applied the Central Hudson commercial-speech test and held that, because federal law criminalises marijuana, the proposed advertising did not concern "lawful activity" within the meaning of Central Hudson, so "the First Amendment poses no obstacle to a ban on such speech" and the restrictions were upheld. The U.S. Supreme Court denied certiorari on 5 May 2025, No. 24-1024, leaving the Fifth Circuit's ruling in place. Sources (secondary, for case history only): Network for Public Health Law case summary — https://www.networkforphl.org/resources/cocroft-v-graham/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026; Institute for Justice case page ("The Supreme Court declined in May 2025") — https://ij.org/case/mississippi-advertising/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Does Schedule III change Cocroft? [VERIFY] — no conclusion is stated in this file. The reasoning in Cocroft turned on federal illegality under the Controlled Substances Act: marijuana was Schedule I, so state-licensed dispensing was not "lawful activity" for Central Hudson purposes. Under the given federal baseline, state-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026, while adult-use remains Schedule I. Whether that move makes state-licensed medical dispensing "lawful activity" for First Amendment purposes, and whether a new challenge (or a motion to revisit the Mississippi rules) would succeed, depends on at least three questions no source opened in this run answers: (1) whether Schedule III medical marijuana, still subject to CSA registration, prescription and dispensing controls that state dispensaries do not satisfy, counts as "lawful" under Central Hudson step one; (2) whether Mississippi has amended or will amend its advertising rules in response to rescheduling (no such amendment was located); and (3) whether a court would treat the 2024 Cocroft judgment as binding on a post-rescheduling challenge. No Mississippi advertising rule amendment in response to Schedule III was located, and no post-April 2026 court decision revisiting Cocroft was located. Until such an amendment or decision exists, the operative position for a licensee is: the MSDH/MDOR advertising rules in §§11.7.5 above remain in force, and Cocroft remains the last appellate word on their constitutionality. A licensee should not treat Schedule III as having repealed the advertising ban.

Practical promotion checklist (current rules, for a medical licensee):

  1. Discount/loyalty mechanic itself: permitted if it fits Rule 9.3.1 / MDOR Chapter 13 and does not push past practitioner/MMCEU limits (Rule 9.3.2).
  2. Medium: permitted branding channels only (Rule 9.2.2); no broadcast, social-media advertising, newspaper, mass text/email, window/public display, public-space, or paid testimonial/endorsement advertising (Rule 9.1.1).
  3. Content: no consumption depiction, overconsumption promotion, health/medicinal/therapeutic claims, safety claims, leaf/bud imagery (in advertising; education materials are the exception in Rule 9.4.4), or minor-appealing imagery (Rule 9.1.2).
  4. Product: no free cannabis product outside a punch-card programme without written MSDH/MDOR guidance (§11.7.3); no sampling model without a cited current rule (§11.7.3); no on-premises consumption (§11.7.3).
  5. Tracking: every inducement product tracked in seed-to-sale and counted against MMCEU/practitioner limits (Rule 9.3.2).

11.7.6 Hemp — sampling, giveaways, discounts and promotions

No Mississippi hemp-specific sampling, giveaway, discount or promotion rule was located. There is no hemp analogue to MSDH Subpart 9 or MDOR Chapter 13 in the sources opened. Consequences, by category:

  • Discounts / loyalty: No hemp discount cap, loyalty rule, or discount prohibition was located.
