A hemp business's discounts are governed by general commercial law (including, for intoxicating hemp products, the overlay of the 11 June 2025 AG opinion and the post-December 2026 federal container cap — neither of which is a discount rule). A discount that pushes a product over the 0.4 mg per container cap after 11 December 2026 does not become lawful because it is discounted; the cap is a product rule, not a price rule.
  • Giveaways / sampling of hemp-derived products: No hemp sampling or giveaway rule was located. In particular, no Mississippi rule authorises or prohibits free samples of CBD or other hemp-derived products as a category. General law (age restrictions if any apply to the specific product category, local law, and federal law for the product) would govern, but no hemp-specific sampling rule is cited here because none was located. [UNAVAILABLE] as a hemp-specific rule.
  • Advertising of hemp products: No Mississippi hemp advertising ban analogous to the medical ban was located. Hemp product advertising is subject to general advertising law (including FTC substantiation for health claims, and FDA law for drug/disease claims), not to MSDH Subpart 9. A hemp business must not assume the medical advertising ban applies to it, and must not assume the medical branding permissions apply to it either — the two regimes are separate, and the hemp regime, for sampling/promotion purposes, is the general law.
  • Interaction with the medical programme: A hemp business that also holds a medical licence is subject to Subpart 9 / Chapter 13 for its medical activity. It cannot use a hemp promotion to circumvent the medical advertising ban for medical product (e.g. advertising medical discounts on a hemp storefront's social media as "hemp" promotion). No rule expressly addresses this cross-promotion scenario; it is flagged as [VERIFY] rather than resolved by analogy.

11.8 DRUG TESTING, BACKGROUND CHECKS AND WORK PERMITS

Scope distinction, stated at the outset. This section covers licence-holder and staff rules: who must hold a work permit, background checks, disqualifying offences, age minimums, drug testing of licence holders/staff, and work-permit renewal/revocation. It does not cover patient employment protections, which are in §11.8.5 only as a contrast — Run 1 established there is no patient employment protection under § 41-137-13, and that position is not re-litigated here. A person can therefore be in two different positions at once: as a patient, they have no protection against an employer acting on their medical use; as a licensee employee, they must pass a criminal background check and hold a work permit, but the medical programme does not impose a drug test on them as a condition of that permit (see §11.8.4).

11.8.1 Who must hold a work permit

Statute. Miss. Code § 41-137-39(1)(a)–(b) (Justia 2025 republication):

"(1)(a) Medical cannabis establishments shall conduct a background check into the criminal history of every person seeking to become a principal officer, board member, agent, volunteer, or employee before the person begins working at or for the medical cannabis establishment. (b) Every person seeking to become a principal officer, board member, agent, volunteer, or employee shall apply for or authorize the division to obtain state and national criminal background checks to be conducted by the Mississippi Justice Information Center of the Department of Public Safety and the Federal Bureau of Investigation."

Source: Miss. Code § 41-137-39 — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-39/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. (The "division" language in the republication reflects the statute's drafting history; the operating agency for work permits in the current rules is MSDH, "the Department" in Part 22.)

Rule — MSDH Rule 3.11.1:

"A medical cannabis establishment representative as defined in this Part employee shall be registered for and (receive) obtain a work permit license issued by the Department before the individual may work for, volunteer at, or maintain his/her ownership interest of ten percent (10%) or greater, whether direct or indirect, in, a medical cannabis establishment licensed and registered by the Department or MDOR as applicable."

Rule — definition of "representative" (Rule 1.2.90):

"'Medical Cannabis Establishment Representative' means an owner holding a 10% or greater economic interest, director, officer, board member, manager, employee, volunteer or agent of a medical cannabis establishment. This term also includes independent contractors who perform services for a medical cannabis establishment if the establishment controls what will be done and how it will be done. … All medical cannabis establishment agents representatives must possess a work permit."

And Rule 1.2.142 (work permit definition, as opened): a work permit is "the official document issued by the Department that authorizes a person to function as a Medical Cannabis Establishment Representative Employee of a Medical Cannabis Establishment regulated by the Department. All medical cannabis establishment agents must also possess a work permit."

Who is therefore covered — exhaustive on the text:

Person Work permit required? Basis
Employee (any role, if the establishment controls what/how work is done, including independent contractors meeting the control test) Yes, before beginning work Rules 3.11.1, 1.2.90; Rule 4.2.1: "An individual will not be able to shall not begin work at a medical cannabis establishment until after he or she receives obtains a work permit license issued by the Department."
Volunteer Yes, before volunteering Rule 3.11.1 ("work for, volunteer at")
Owner holding ≥10% economic interest (direct or indirect) Yes, before maintaining that interest Rule 3.11.1; Rule 1.2.90
Director, officer, board member, manager, agent Yes Rule 1.2.90 (all are "representatives")
Principal officer / board member / owner at licensing stage (not just employment stage) Yes — fingerprinting/background checks required for anyone proposed as owner, officer, director, board member or anyone with ≥10% economic interest (Rule 3.3.1) Rule 3.3.1; see §11.8.3
Dispensary employee (MDOR licensee) Yes — MDOR, not only MSDH, licensees are covered Rule 3.11.1 ("licensed … by the Department or MDOR as applicable"); MDOR Chapter 20, ¶ 100: "A dispensary may not employ any individual who does not have a valid work permit."
Caregiver (patient's designated caregiver) No — different regime. Caregivers are not establishment representatives. They have their own background-check process (MSDH caregiver background-check directions: $37.00 processing fee per caregiver in addition to the $25 caregiver application fee, fingerprint card, "Reason Fingerprinted" code MC4200015 — MSDH caregiver directions document, via search result). Caregiver checks are not work permits and must not be conflated with them. The $37 caregiver fingerprint fee is not the work-permit fingerprint fee (which is stated only as "fee(s) in addition to" the $25 permit fee — see §11.8.2). MSDH caregiver background-check directions — https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/sites/default/files/Documents/Directions%20for%20Medical%20Cannabis%20Caregiver%20(1)%20(2)-1.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026 (secondary procedural document, not a rule)
Practitioner (certifying physician/NP/PA/optometrist) No work permit — practitioners are licensed by their own boards and registered with MSDH as practitioners, not as establishment representatives No work-permit provision for practitioners was located in Subpart 3
Visitor / delivery driver not employed/controlled by the establishment No work permit on the text opened, unless the person meets the "representative"/control test (e.g. a transporter employee is covered, because transportation-entity employees must hold work permits and carry them during transport — Rules 8.1.2, 7.x; see §11.8.1, transport note) Rules 1.2.90 (control test), 8.1.2

Transport note. Disposal-entity employees transporting cannabis must possess a valid Mississippi driver's licence and a valid work permit, and the entity must issue each employee a picture identification badge; all documents must be in the employee's possession when in a vehicle transporting cannabis/products (Rule 8.1.2). Transportation manifests must list work-permit numbers of individuals accompanying the transport (Rule 7.x, as opened). Employees must also "maintain a copy of the Department issued work permit on their person while present at a medical cannabis establishment" (Rule 4.2, as opened).

Permit is personal and non-transferable. Rule 3.11.5: "A medical cannabis work permit shall be the property of the licensed permitted individual and shall not be transferable to others non-transferrable." Rule 3.11.6: a holder must notify the Department in writing within ten (10) business days of a name change and complete a new application as specified in Subchapter 3.

Seed-to-sale entry. Rule 4.2.4: all employees must be entered into the state's seed-to-sale system within seven (7) calendar days of their start dates.

11.8.2 Work-permit fee, term, and application contents

Fee — verified against Run 1. MSDH Rule 3.11.9:

"Application and Permit Fees: Initial and Renewal. The following nonrefundable fees are due and payable at the time of initial registration for a work permit and at the time of renewal of such permit: A. Medical Cannabis Establishment Work Permit and registration fee of $25.00. B. Fingerprinting and Department background records check fee(s) in addition to the work permit registration fee. C. All payments must shall be made through the Department's electronic payment system(s) found on the Department's website."

The renewal fee is restated identically in the same rule: "Renewal Application and Permit Fees: 1. Work Permit fee - $25.00, and 2. Fingerprinting and Department background records check fee(s) in addition to the work permit registration fee."

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rule 3.11.9 — link as above — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

This confirms the Run 1 figure: $25, plus fingerprint/background fees in addition. The fingerprint/background fee amount is not stated in Rule 3.11.9; it is stated only as "fee(s) in addition to" the $25. Do not quote a work-permit fingerprint fee amount from the caregiver $37 figure — that is a different process (see §11.8.1). The work-permit fingerprint/background fee amount is [VERIFY] against the current MSDH portal/fee schedule. All fees are nonrefundable and payable through the Department's electronic payment system.

Term — verified against Run 1: five years. Rule 3.11.4: "A work permit license shall be valid for five (5) years from the date of issuance by the Department." Rule 4.2.1 (same): "An individual is required to renew his or her permit every five (5) years." MDOR Chapter 20, ¶ 101 (same): "An individual is required to renew his or her permit every five (5) years." No conflict was found on the five-year term.

Application contents (Rule 3.11.8). An initial or renewal application must be accompanied by:

  • A. Current digital photograph meeting detailed requirements: clear colour head-and-shoulders headshot; passport-style; .jpg/.png/.gif; taken within the last six (6) months; plain white/off-white background; full-face view directly facing camera at eye level, nothing obscuring the face; neutral expression, both eyes open; no hat/head covering obscuring hair/hairline unless worn daily for a religious purpose (full face visible, no shadows); not digitally enhanced (no "filters"); other Department photo requirements as specified;
  • B. Copy of a current driver's licence or state-issued ID card issued by the state department of motor vehicles;
  • C. Copies of all current state-issued professional licences;
  • D. Authorisation for the Department to perform a criminal history records check;
  • E. Attestation that the information provided to apply for the work permit/registration is true and correct;
  • F. Fees as required by the Department.

And Rule 3.11.7: the applicant must complete the Department's application, include all documentation, pay the nonrefundable application and fingerprinting/background fees, and be registered/approved as a valid work-permit holder prior to beginning work at/for an MSDH- or MDOR-licensed establishment.

Continuing education — a condition of holding the permit, not just obtaining it. MDOR Chapter 20, ¶ 101: "An individual will not be able to work at a dispensary until after he or she receives a work permit and completes eight (8) hours of continuing education relating to medical cannabis. Thereafter, it is the individual's responsibility to annually complete five (5) hours of continuing education relating to medical cannabis to maintain such certification." MSDH Rule 3.11.13 (same structure): "If an individual does not complete the annual continuing education requirements by this Part, the Department may revoke the individual's work permit or suspend the work permit until such time as the education requirements are completed." (The MSDH text as opened says "annual continuing education requirements" without restating the 8-hour initial / 5-hour annual figures in Rule 3.11.13 itself; the figures are in MDOR Chapter 20, ¶ 101 and in the MSDH work-permit subpart as a whole. Whether the 8/5-hour figures apply identically to MSDH-licensed (non-dispensary) employees, or only via MDOR Chapter 20 for dispensary employees, is [VERIFY] — the MSDH text opened does not restate the hour figures in Rule 3.11.13, and this file does not assume they are identical for both regulators.)

11.8.3 Background checks: fingerprinting, databases, disqualifying felonies, lookback, and owner/principal checks

Databases and method. MSDH Rule 3.11.3:

"An applicant for an initial work permit or renewal of a work permit must shall complete a fingerprint-based background check of the Mississippi Central Criminal Database and the Federal Bureau of Investigation Criminal History Database and must shall not have a disqualifying felony offense."

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rule 3.11.3 — link as above — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Statutory counterpart, § 41-137-39(1)(c)–(e): checks "shall conform to the applicable federal standards, and shall include the taking of fingerprints"; the applicant authorises release to MDOH/MSDH and "shall be responsible for the payment of any fee associated with the criminal background checks"; on completion, the Mississippi Justice Information Center of the Department of Public Safety forwards all information obtained to MDOH/MSDH. MSDH does not conduct name-based background searches for caregivers (MSDH caregiver directions: "Please submit a physical fingerprint card to complete the Mississippi background check") — that statement is for caregivers, but it illustrates the fingerprint-card mechanics of the MSDH criminal-history unit generally; whether work-permit applicants use the same card process or an electronic Livescan process is [VERIFY] against the current MSDH work-permit instructions, which were not opened as a standalone document in this run.

Establishment's own duty. Rule 4.2.2: "Medical cannabis establishments must shall complete a criminal history background check on each employee to verify that the employee does not have a disqualifying felony." This is in addition to the Department's check: the establishment must itself verify, and Rule 3.11.10 provides: "Medical cannabis establishments shall not employ [any person] who has been convicted of a disqualifying felony offense as defined in this Part." (The 2023 blackline text reads "Cannabis testing facilities Medical cannabis establishments shall not employ a medical cannabis establishment agent, any person who has been convicted…" — the operative prohibition is clear despite the blackline artefacts.)

Disqualifying felony offense — verbatim definition (Rule 1.2.48):

"A. A conviction for a crime of violence, as defined in Section 97-3-2 Mississippi Code of 1972, as amended, or B. A conviction for a crime that was defined as a violent crime in the law of the jurisdiction in which the offense was committed, and that was classified as a felony in the jurisdiction where the person was convicted; or C. A conviction for a violation of a state or federal controlled substances law that was classified as a felony in the jurisdiction where the person was convicted, including the service of any term of probation, incarceration or supervised release within the previous five (5) years and the offender has not committed another similar offense since the conviction. A disqualifying felony offense shall not include a conviction that consisted of conduct for which the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act would likely have prevented the conviction but for the fact that the conduct occurred before the effective date of the Medical Cannabis Act."

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rule 1.2.48 — link as above — accessed 25 Oct 2026. The MDOR definition (Chapter 1, ¶ 107) is substantively identical, with the same three limbs and the same pre-Act-conduct carve-out.

Lookback — read the definition precisely, because it is not a single lookback period:

Limb Lookback / time element
(A) Mississippi crime of violence (§ 97-3-2) No time limit stated. A conviction for a § 97-3-2 crime of violence is disqualifying whenever it occurred, on the text opened.
(B) Out-of-state violent crime classified as a felony where convicted No time limit stated. Same structure as (A), for the law of the convicting jurisdiction.
(C) State/federal controlled-substances felony Five-year service element + no-similar-offence condition. The text, as printed, is grammatically compressed: "including the service of any term of probation, incarceration or supervised release within the previous five (5) years and the offender has not committed another similar offense since the conviction." The natural reading — and the reading in the MDOR text — is that a controlled-substances felony is disqualifying if the person served probation/incarceration/supervised release within the previous five years (and has not committed another similar offence since). Whether a controlled-substances felony whose sentence was fully served more than five years ago, with no similar offence since, is therefore not disqualifying is the implication of the five-year language, but the rule does not state the converse in terms ("a felony older than five years is not disqualifying"). That converse is [VERIFY] with MSDH/MDOR — do not advise an applicant that an old drug felony is automatically non-disqualifying on the basis of this file alone.
Pre-Act conduct carve-out (all limbs) A conviction is not disqualifying if it "consisted of conduct for which the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act would likely have prevented the conviction but for the fact that the conduct occurred before the effective date of the Medical Cannabis Act." This is the Act's amelioration for pre-legalisation medical-cannabis conduct. Its application to a specific conviction (e.g. pre-2022 possession that would now be lawful medical possession) is fact-specific and [VERIFY] with MSDH on the specific record.

What is NOT disqualifying on the text opened: Non-violent, non-controlled-substances felonies are not listed in Rule 1.2.48. Misdemeanours are not listed. Arrests without conviction are not listed. The rule turns on conviction for the listed categories. An establishment that applies a broader bar (e.g. "any felony") would be applying a policy stricter than the rule; whether such a stricter employer policy is lawful is a general employment-law question, not a programme rule, and is not addressed here.

Owner / principal background checks at licensing (distinct from work permits, but overlapping). MSDH Rule 3.3.1:

"Fingerprinting and criminal history record checks are required for anyone proposed as an owner, officer, director, board member or anyone with an economic interest of ten percent (10%) or more of a medical cannabis establishment [and for] each applicant applying to obtain a medical cannabis work permit."

Licence applications must also include, for each owner, attestations (signed/dated) that the owner has not been convicted of an excluded/disqualifying felony, has no prohibited familial/financial relationship/interest, and pledges not to divert cannabis (Rule 3.10.4(E), for testing-facility ownership changes, stating the general pattern; the cultivation/processing/dispensary application provisions in Subpart 3 impose the same background-check-affidavit pattern — see Rule 3.1, as opened). At renewal, the Department "may conduct additional background checks to determine that the licensee continues to meet the requirements" (Rule 3.8.3(B)), and a licence "may be suspended, revoked, or [not] renewed" if "An owner has been convicted of a disqualifying felony" (Rule 3.8.6(B)). At ownership transfer, the transferee must submit the same fingerprinting/background-check information as a new applicant, and the Department may revoke/suspend on discovery of an unapproved transfer (Rules 3.10.1–3.10.3).

Minimum qualifications for licence applicants (statute, for context). § 41-137-35(10) (as enacted by SB 2095, via HB 1158 republication): an individual applicant for a cultivation, processing, dispensary, transportation or disposal licence must be a natural person who is at least 21, has not previously held a licence of those types that was revoked, has not been convicted of a disqualifying felony, holds any professional/occupational licence in good standing, has submitted a sworn statement of true/actual ownership and intent to carry on the business for themselves/entity (not as agent for another entity), has no outstanding Mississippi tax delinquencies, and (as originally enacted, time-limited) was not a member of the Mississippi Legislature or spouse thereof through 31 December 2022. The legislature/spouse limb was time-limited to 2022 and is not a current bar on its face; it is noted here only to prevent a reader of the original SB 2095 text from treating it as current. [VERIFY] the current codified § 41-137-35(10) against the official Code before advising on applicant qualifications — the republication opened for this file is a bill text, not the current official Code section.

11.8.4 Drug testing of licence holders and staff — required by MSDH/MDOR, or employer discretion?

No MSDH or MDOR rule was located requiring drug testing of medical cannabis licence holders, owners, or staff as a condition of licensure or of a work permit. The work-permit regime requires a criminal background check (fingerprint-based, Mississippi Central Criminal Database + FBI), not a drug screen. The application contents in Rule 3.11.8 contain no drug-test result, no drug-screen consent, and no drug-test panel. The denial grounds in Rule 3.11.11 (failure to provide required information; failure to meet Part requirements; misleading/incorrect/false/fraudulent information; failure to pay fees; any other grounds serving the purposes of the Part) contain no drug-test failure ground. The revocation/suspension grounds in Rule 3.11.14 (violation of the Chapter/Part or any disqualifying felony offence) and the continuing-education ground in Rule 3.11.13 likewise contain no drug-test ground.

What the rules DO prohibit on premises (not a drug-testing regime, but a conduct regime):

  • MDOR Chapter 18, ¶ 101(1): a licensee/employee may not "Use or be under the influence of alcoholic beverages, cannabis, or controlled substances on the licensed premises."
  • MDOR Chapter 18, ¶ 101(5): a licensee/employee may not engage in or permit consumption of any type of cannabis product on the premises.
  • MSDH Appendix B: "On-site use of cannabis by employee(s)" — $5,000 per employee found using cannabis on the premises of the establishment.

These are observed-conduct prohibitions (use / being under the influence / consumption on premises), enforceable by inspection and discipline. They are not a testing protocol: no rule states who tests, what panel, what cutoff, what confirmation, what Medical Review Officer process, or what consequence follows a positive test off premises. An employer that wishes to drug-test its own medical-cannabis employees must therefore look to general Mississippi employment/drug-testing law (including the Mississippi drug-free workplace / workers' compensation premium-discount framework, Miss. Code §§ 71-7-1 et seq., and any applicable federal DOT or federal-contract testing duties), not to MSDH/MDOR programme rules. Whether an employer may test, and what it may do with a result, is governed by that general law and by § 41-137-13 for patients (see §11.8.5) — but § 41-137-13 is about patients' medical use, not about whether a cannabis licensee as an employer may test its own staff.

Bottom line: drug testing of licence holders/staff is employer discretion under general law, not an MSDH/MDOR programme requirement, on the text opened. [VERIFY] against any MSDH/MDOR guidance or licence condition that might impose testing on a specific licensee — no such general requirement was located, but an individual licence condition or variance could differ, and this file does not rule that out.

A related trap to avoid: Do not infer a drug-testing requirement from the fact that the programme tests product for pesticides, solvents, heavy metals, etc. Product testing (Subpart 5) is not people testing. The two regimes share the word "testing" and nothing else.

11.8.5 The patient-employment contrast (§ 41-137-13) — stated only to prevent conflation

Miss. Code § 41-137-13(1) (Justia 2025 republication) provides, in relevant part, that the chapter "shall not be construed to":

"(b) Require any employer to permit, accommodate, or allow the medical use of medical cannabis, or to modify any job or working conditions of any employee who engages in the medical use of medical cannabis or who for any reason seeks to engage in the medical use of medical cannabis; (c) Prohibit any employer from refusing to hire, discharging, disciplining, or otherwise taking an adverse employment action against an individual with respect to hiring, discharging, tenure, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment as a result, in whole or in part, of that individual's medical use of medical cannabis, regardless of the individual's impairment or lack of impairment resulting from the medical use of medical cannabis; (d) Prohibit or limit the ability of any employer from establishing or enforcing a drug-testing policy; … (f) Permit, authorize, or establish any individual's right to commence or undertake any legal action against an employer for refusing to hire, discharging, disciplining or otherwise taking an adverse employment action against an individual with respect to hiring, discharging, tenure, terms, conditions or privileges of employment due to the individual's medical use of medical cannabis;"

Source: Miss. Code § 41-137-13 — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-13/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. It also preserves federal employment/contracting restrictions, including U.S. Department of Transportation regulations in Title 49 CFR (§ 41-137-13(1)(e)), and preserves the workers' compensation drug-free workplace premium discount and related defences (as described in secondary employer guidance; the statutory text for those limbs should be checked against the official Code — [VERIFY] for the full § 41-137-13(1)(g)–(h) text, which was not fully reproduced in the source opened).

This is the Run 1 position, unchanged: no patient employment protection; employers may drug-test and act on medical use regardless of impairment. It has no bearing on whether a licensee employee must pass a drug test to obtain a work permit (they must not, on the programme rules — §11.8.4), and it does not create a work-permit drug-test requirement by implication.

11.8.6 Renewal, denial, suspension and revocation of work permits

Action Rule Grounds / procedure
Renewal Rules 3.11.4, 3.11.9, 4.2.1; MDOR Ch. 20, ¶ 101 Every 5 years; $25 + fingerprint/background fee(s) (nonrefundable, electronic payment); new fingerprint-based Mississippi + FBI check; must not have a disqualifying felony (Rule 3.11.3, applying to renewal as well as initial).
Denial (initial or renewal) Rule 3.11.11 (A) Failure to provide required information; (B) Failure to meet Part requirements; (C) Misleading/incorrect/false/fraudulent information; (D) Failure to pay all applicable fees; (E) Any other grounds serving the purposes of the Part.
Notice of denial Rule 3.11.12 Department must notify the applicant in writing, including the reason for denial.
Suspension / revocation for education failure Rule 3.11.13; MDOR Ch. 20, ¶ 102 If annual continuing education is not completed, the Department may revoke or suspend the permit until education is completed (MSDH); MDOR: permit "may be revoked or suspended until such time as the education requirements are completed."
Fine / suspension / revocation generally Rule 3.11.14 Department may fine, suspend or revoke a work permit for a violation of the Chapter or any rules/regulations in the Part, or any disqualifying felony offence.
Appeal Rule 3.11.15–3.11.16 Aggrieved applicant/permit-holder may file an administrative appeal in writing with the Department within twenty (20) days of receipt of the initial notice; failure to appeal in 20 days makes the decision final. The hearing decision on denial/revocation/suspension is a final Department decision, subject to judicial review as provided in Miss. Code § 41-137-59 (cited in Rule 3.11.16 as Section 31 of the Act).
Disciplinary amounts for the establishment (not the individual permit) MSDH Appendix B Failure of an employee to possess an active work permit: $5,000 per employee found without one. Employment of a person under 21: $5,000 per employee found under 21. These are establishment penalties; the individual's permit consequences are in Rules 3.11.11–3.11.14 above.

Age minimum — verified. § 41-137-39(2)(b): "A medical cannabis establishment may not employ any person who: (a) Was convicted of a disqualifying felony offense; or (b) Is under twenty-one (21) years of age." MSDH Rule 3.11.2: "To be eligible to obtain a work permit, an individual shall must be at least twenty-one (21) years of age." MDOR Chapter 20, ¶ 100 (same): a dispensary "may not employ anyone who has been convicted of a disqualifying felony offense or is under the age of twenty-one (21)." MDOR Chapter 15, ¶ 101 (premises access, for context): individuals are prohibited from entering unless over 21 or under 21, accompanied by a guardian, and holding a valid patient card — the patient access rule is different from the employment rule, and a minor patient cardholder is not thereby employable. No conflict was found on the under-21 employment ban; it is adopted exactly as in Run 1.

11.8.7 Hemp — USDA licence background/eligibility and any Mississippi hemp-employee rule

Federal hemp felony ban — 10-year lookback. 7 CFR § 990.20(b) (USDA plan, applicable to Mississippi producers):

"Convicted felon ban. A person with a State or Federal felony conviction relating to a controlled substance is subject to a 10-year ineligibility restriction on participating in and producing hemp under the USDA plan from the date of the conviction. An exception applies to a person who was lawfully growing hemp under section 7606 of the Agricultural Act of 2014 (7 U.S.C. 5940) before December 20, 2018, and whose conviction also occurred before that date."

Source: 7 CFR § 990.20(b) — https://www.customsmobile.com/regulations/title7_chapterIX_part990_subpartC_section990.20 (eCFR text via CustomsMobile) and https://www.ecfr.gov/api/renderer/v1/content/enhanced/2024-04-23/title-7?subtitle=B&chapter=IX&part=990 — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

The state/tribal-plan counterpart, 7 CFR § 990.6(e), is substantively identical (10 years from conviction; same 2014 Farm Bill pilot exception; plus a further exemption for producers lawfully growing under a § 7606 pilot before 31 October 2019). Material falsification of an application makes the person ineligible under the USDA plan (§ 990.20(c)).

Key differences from the medical disqualifying-felony rule — do not conflate them:

Feature Medical work permit (§ 41-137-39 / Rule 1.2.48) USDA hemp licence (§ 990.20(b))
Offence scope (A) § 97-3-2 crimes of violence (no time limit stated); (B) out-of-state violent felonies (no time limit stated); (C) controlled-substances felonies (5-year service element) Only state/federal felony convictions "relating to a controlled substance"
Lookback No single period; 5-year element only for limb (C) 10 years from the date of conviction, flat
Who is checked Every representative: owner ≥10%, director, officer, board member, manager, employee, volunteer, agent/contractor meeting the control test "Key participants" of the applicant entity (see below); the plan must define who is "participating" and obtain a criminal history report for at least one individual per licence/authorisation (§ 990.6(e)(2)–(3) pattern; USDA-plan application requires key-participant information)
Method Fingerprint-based Mississippi Central Criminal Database + FBI check Criminal history report (USDA-plan application; FBI/state check mechanics via USDA — specific fingerprint process [VERIFY] against the current USDA application instructions)
Pre-Act / pilot exception Pre-Act medical-cannabis conduct carve-out (Rule 1.2.48, final sentence) 2014 Farm Bill § 7606 pilot exception (lawfully growing before 20 Dec 2018 + conviction before that date)
Effect of a disqualifying record No work permit; establishment must not employ the person; owner conviction can block licence renewal (Rule 3.8.6(B)) 10-year ineligibility from participating in and producing hemp under the USDA plan

USDA licence application — key participants. 7 CFR § 990.21(a)(3) (as opened): the applicant must provide, among other information, contact information (full name, residential address, telephone, email); if a business entity, the full business name, principal business location, full name and title of the key participants, title, email (if available), and EIN. The USDA plan's definition of "key participant" (persons with a direct or indirect financial interest, or in executive/leadership positions — the full § 990.1 definition was not reproduced in the passages opened) determines who is subject to the felony check for an entity applicant. Do not assume every hemp farm employee is checked: on the USDA structure, the check attaches to key participants / persons defined as participating, not to every field worker. The precise USDA-plan key-participant definition and whether Mississippi USDA-plan applicants must submit fingerprints for each key participant are [VERIFY] against the current USDA hemp licence application and 7 CFR § 990.1.

Age minimum for hemp — none located. No age minimum (21 or otherwise) for hemp producers, key participants or hemp employees was located in 7 CFR Part 990 as opened, and no Mississippi hemp-employee age rule was located. This is not a statement that minors may work on a hemp farm — general Mississippi child-labour law, agricultural-labour law, and any USDA-plan condition would govern, and none of those was the subject of this section. The point for this file is narrow: there is no hemp analogue to the medical under-21 employment ban in § 41-137-39(2)(b) located in this run. Do not import the medical 21+ rule into hemp.

Drug testing for hemp licensees/employees — none located. No USDA hemp-plan provision located requires drug testing of a hemp producer, key participant or employee as a condition of a hemp licence. General employer drug-testing law (and DOT/federal-contract duties where applicable) would govern an employer's own testing decision, as in §11.8.4. [UNAVAILABLE] as a hemp-licence drug-testing rule.

Mississippi hemp-employee rule — none located. Consistent with MDAC issuing no hemp licences and having no state hemp plan, no Mississippi rule governing hemp employees (work permits, background checks, age, training, or drug testing for hemp workers) was located in this run. A hemp business in Mississippi is therefore governed, for employment purposes, by (a) the USDA felony eligibility rule for key participants (§ 990.20(b)), (b) general Mississippi and federal employment law, and (c) any condition USDA imposes on the specific licence. It is not governed by MSDH work permits: a hemp farm worker does not need an MSDH medical cannabis work permit, and an MSDH work permit does not authorise hemp production. Conflating the two regimes would be an error.

Hemp business vs medical licensee — if the same person does both. A person who holds a USDA hemp licence and works for a medical cannabis establishment needs an MSDH work permit for the medical work (and must pass the medical disqualifying-felony test), even if they satisfy the USDA 10-year hemp test, and vice versa. The two eligibility tests are independent: passing one does not satisfy the other, because the offence scopes and lookbacks differ (see table above). In particular, a violent-felony conviction with no time limit under the medical rule could bar medical employment while not barring hemp participation (if it is not a controlled-substances felony), and a controlled-substances felony within 10 years bars hemp participation even if its sentence was served more than five years ago and it might therefore fall outside the medical limb (C) five-year element — subject to the [VERIFY] in §11.8.3 on the converse of limb (C).

11.9 RESEARCH AND UNIVERSITY WORK

11.9.1 University of Mississippi — federal marijuana research history (official university / DEA / NIDA sources only for history)

Institutional home. The programme sits in the University of Mississippi (Ole Miss) School of Pharmacy, Research Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences (RIPS), National Center for Natural Products Research (NCNPR). The timeline below is taken only from the University's own published history page and from NIDA/DEA sources, as commissioned. Secondary commentary is identified as such and is not used for dates.

Timeline — University of Mississippi School of Pharmacy history page (official university source):

Year Event (as stated on the University history page)
1908 University of Mississippi School of Pharmacy founded by pharmacist Henry Minor Faser, first dean.
1964 Research Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences (RIPS) established as the research arm of the School of Pharmacy, "with a mission to discover and develop new drugs from natural sources." Chemical structures of THC and CBD determined by Prof. Raphael Mechoulam (Hebrew University of Jerusalem), spurring worldwide cannabinoid research.
1968 "Program committee of National Institute on Mental Health (NIMH) offered a contract to provide standardized marijuana for researchers. Dr. Norman Doorenbos, chair of UM Department of Pharmacognosy, applied for and was awarded the contract." Dr. Coy Waller joined UM as associate director of RIPS. "First experimental plot of marijuana was grown at the UM site, using seeds from Mexico, Panama, Southeast Asia, Korea, India, Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan and Lebanon."
1969 "A secured garden was constructed for the first substantial crop grown at the UM site. An additional plot was planted in southern Mississippi on UM forest lands."
1970 Dr. Carlton E. Turner joined as postdoctoral Research Associate to manage cultivation techniques for standardised marijuana. "Congress passed the Controlled Substance Act, making marijuana a Schedule-I drug." Dr. Coy Waller became director of RIPS.
1973 Congress established the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) as lead CSA enforcement agency.
1974 National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) established under the Alcohol, Drug Abuse, and Mental Health Administration.
1975 "NIDA and DEA collaborated to monitor the potency of illicit marijuana by establishing the Potency Monitoring Program as part of the contract." Dr. Mahmoud ElSohly joined as postdoctoral research associate.
1976 Outdoor cultivation expanded; "Over 100 varieties of cannabis seeds were planted this season." UM hosted the United Nations Narcotics Symposium in August.
1977 Because of potential health risks of smoking Mexican marijuana sprayed with herbicide paraquat, NIDA incorporated paraquat testing into the Potency Monitoring Program.
1978 Compassionate Investigational New Drug programme established to provide marijuana cigarettes for certain medical disorders in a limited number of patients.
1980 Tobacco drying barns installed at the garden for drying crops (previously sun-dried).
1981 Dr. Turner left UM to become Director of Drug Abuse Policy under President Reagan. Dr. ElSohly became director of the UM marijuana project.
1984 Experimental techniques developed to grow "sinsemilla" (only female plants allowed to mature, dense buds with high cannabinoid concentrations). "Today this is the predominate cultivation method for production of drug-type marijuana."
1989 Coy Waller Laboratory Complex constructed to provide dedicated laboratory and horticulture space.
1991 RIPS began development of a novel drug delivery system (suppository containing a THC derivative); developed a chemical "fingerprint" technique to identify country of origin of confiscated marijuana.
1992 NIDA became part of the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
1995 "The National Center for Natural Products Research (NCNPR) was established under RIPS with missions to improve human health and agricultural productivity through discovery, development and commercialization of natural products."
1999 NIDA Request for Proposals included Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) production requirements; NCNPR established new quality systems and hired additional personnel.
2000 Coy Waller Laboratory expanded: annex with indoor growing facility, second vault, plant processing laboratory.
2005 "NCNPR acquired an additional DEA Schedule-I bulk manufacturer to provide cannabis extract to pharmaceutical companies." 1,500 kg of marijuana produced in the outdoor garden; grow room renovated with new HVAC.
2006 NCNPR submitted Drug Master File "Cannabis Extract" to FDA; additional 1,500 kg produced for THC-rich cannabis extract.
2007 Over 300 kg of THC Cannabis Extract manufactured.
2012 School of Pharmacy researchers developed a transmucosal patch for THC delivery using THC prodrugs.
2014 Three cannabis varieties grown, yielding over 600 kg of marijuana of different chemical profiles for the NIDA Drug Supply Program; NIDA announced RFP; NCNPR/Nemus Bioscience collaborated on CBD analogues and THC prodrugs.
2015 Mississippi governor signed "Harper Grace's Law" to allow NCNPR and the University of Mississippi Medical Center (UMMC) to undertake a clinical study of CBD cannabis extract in paediatric epilepsy. "NCNPR won an award of a five-year NIDA contract, but Potency Monitoring Program was no longer included in the base contract."
2016 DEA announced new policy to allow marijuana growers outside the NIDA programme to provide materials for research. NCNPR submitted Drug Master Files "CBD Cannabis Extract" and "Cannabidiol" to FDA; developed "CBD Cannabis Extract Oral Solution" for the UMMC clinical study; grow room renovated with new lighting.
2017 UMMC paediatric neurologist Dr. Brad Ingram submitted an Investigational New Drug (IND) application to FDA for a clinical study of CBD Cannabis Extract Oral Solution in young epilepsy patients; FDA approved proceeding.
2018 UMMC Institutional Review Board approved beginning the CBD Cannabis Extract Oral Solution clinical study. 2018 Farm Bill signed, allowing cultivation of plants meeting the legal definition of "hemp."
2019 "At a location off-campus, NCNPR grew an experimental crop of hemp under federal farm bill regulations." "At the campus garden, NCNPR grew three varieties of cannabis for the NIDA Drug Supply Program." USDA published a final rule for hemp production in the United States.
2020 FDA approved extending the CBD Cannabis Extract Oral Solution clinical study for another two years at UMMC. Mississippi governor signed legislation to allow hemp cultivation in the state by farmers following USDA regulations. Mississippians voted to approve a ballot initiative for a medical marijuana programme. DEA published regulations to allow "Bulk Manufacturer" registrants to cultivate marijuana for research.
2021 NCNPR conducted a clinical study measuring pharmacokinetics of CBD Cannabis Extract Oral Solution in healthy volunteers. Mississippi Supreme Court ruled the ballot-initiative process outdated, effectively overturning the medical marijuana initiative. Two tunnel houses constructed in the UM Marijuana Garden to enhance outdoor production.

Source: University of Mississippi School of Pharmacy, "Marijuana Research | History" — https://pharm.olemiss.edu/marijuana/history/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026. The University page as opened ends at 2021; it does not carry the history forward to 2022–2026. Post-2021 history in this file therefore rests on NIDA/DEA sources and on clearly-labelled secondary reporting, not on the University timeline.

NIDA / DEA framework (official federal sources):

"Historically, the DEA has only issued a single registration for the cultivation of marijuana for research, to the University of Mississippi National Center for Natural Product Research, which is funded through a NIDA contract. In December 2020, the DEA finalized [a] rule which amended 21 Code of Federal Regulations 1318 to facilitate the cultivation of marijuana for research purposes. The DEA has since approved additional bulk manufacturer marijuana growers…"

"NIDA has a contract with the University of Mississippi to grow marijuana for use in research studies. The contract was renewed in 2023 under an open solicitation process. The University designates secure facilities where cannabis is cultivated and processed for research use, based on current and expected demand. This cannabis is grown, harvested, stored, and made available as homogenized plant material, cannabis cigarettes, or other purified elements of the cannabis plant to use for research."

Source: NIDA, "NIDA's Role in Providing Cannabis for Research" — https://nida.nih.gov/research/resources-grants-contracts/nidas-role-in-providing-cannabis-research — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

What the NIDA Drug Supply Program requires of a researcher (for context, not a Mississippi rule): Applicants (NIH-funded and non-NIH-funded) must provide a cover letter (products, amounts, NIH grant number, Project Officer), a statement acknowledging the NIDA Drug Supply Program in publications, a study protocol justifying quantity, IACUC approval (in vivo) or IRB approval (clinical trial), an IND number (human-subjects clinical trial), and a DEA Schedule I licence (as stated on the NIDA page as opened — the Schedule I licence reference is pre-rescheduling text and is [VERIFY] for post-April 2026 Schedule III medical research; see §11.9.2). Certificates of Analysis for NIDA-supplied material show cannabinoid content, water activity, heavy metals, pesticides, and bioburden. NIDA states it has supplied cannabis products through the Drug Supply Program "for over 40 years without any known health consequences from contaminants."

End of the sole-supplier era — stated precisely. The December 2020 DEA rule (21 CFR Part 1318 amendments) ended the de facto sole-registration position: DEA has since approved additional bulk-manufacturer marijuana growers. Ole Miss therefore no longer holds the only federal cultivation registration, even though it held the only one for over 50 years (1968–2020/21). Any statement that Ole Miss is "the only federally licensed grower" is outdated as of the post-2020 DEA approvals and must not be repeated as current.

11.9.2 Current status of the Ole Miss programme under Schedule III — [VERIFY]

No official statement was located in this run from the University of Mississippi, NIDA, NIH, or DEA addressing the current status of the Ole Miss NIDA cannabis-production programme as affected by Schedule III (given baseline: state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026, 91 FR 22714). Specifically, no official statement was located on any of the following:

  • Whether the NIDA contract (renewed 2023, per NIDA) remains in force, has been renewed again, has been allowed to lapse, or has been replaced by task orders, as of October 2026;
  • Whether Ole Miss's DEA bulk-manufacturer registration(s) have been amended, renewed, or reclassified in light of Schedule III;
  • Whether NIDA-supplied research material for state-licensed medical marijuana studies is now treated as Schedule III material for researcher licensing, ordering, or DEA quota purposes;
  • Whether the NIDA Drug Supply Program's "DEA Schedule 1 license" requirement (NIDA page as opened) has been updated to Schedule III for medical research.

Secondary reports that must not be treated as official statements (included only so the gap is visible):

  • A 2025 secondary report (Marijuana Moment, via search result) states that the Department of Government Efficiency touted cancellation of a $143,000 HHS contract for "potency monitoring of confiscated marijuana samples," a contract historically awarded to Ole Miss, and quotes a University spokesperson (Jacob Batte, director of news and media relations) as saying the School of Pharmacy "will continue to play a leading role… through [NCNPR], [NCCRE], and [R3CR]." Potency monitoring is a separate contract from cannabis production for the Drug Supply Program; its cancellation does not by itself establish the status of the production contract.
  • A 2026 secondary report (Beard Bros Pharms, summarising Cannabis Wire / Marijuana Moment) states: "NIDA has chosen not to award the current year task order to the University of Mississippi for cannabis production," while "the university maintains two years remaining on its federal contract through 2028, no new orders will be placed," and notes Ole Miss "recently opened a new Resource Center for Cannabis and Cannabinoid Research earlier this year." This report is secondary, single-sourced via trade press, and was not corroborated against a NIDA, NIH, DEA or University statement opened in this run. It is therefore marked [VERIFY] and is not adopted as the current status.
  • The NIH Resource Center for Cannabis and Cannabinoid Research (R3CR), launched April 2025 (secondary reporting: Marijuana Moment / Marijuana Herald, April 2025), is a separate initiative from NIDA production: Ole Miss (NCNPR) houses R3CR, partnering with Washington State University (research support) and the United States Pharmacopeia (research standards), with a National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) / NIH grant; Ole Miss leads the regulatory-guidance core, providing research information via website, webinars, seed funding and conferences. R3CR's launch does not by itself prove anything about NIDA production task orders.

Adopted position: [VERIFY] for all post-2023 production status and for all Schedule III effects. The only official positions adopted in this file are: (i) the University history to 2021; (ii) NIDA's statement of a 2023 contract renewal; (iii) the December 2020 DEA rule ending sole registration. Everything after 2023, and every Schedule III consequence for the Ole Miss programme, requires an official University/NIDA/DEA statement that was not located in this run.

11.9.3 MSDH research licence type — fees, university exemption, scope

Licence category. MSDH Rule 3.2.1(F):

"Cannabis Research License. Establishments licensed as medical cannabis research facilities/entities may engage in the following commercial cannabis activities: acquisition of cannabis or cannabis products from licensed cannabis cultivation facilities and licensed cannabis processing facilities in order to research cannabis, develop best practices for specific medical conditions, develop medicines and provide commercial access for medical use."

Definition. MSDH Rule 1.2.27:

"'Cannabis Research Facility Entity' or 'research facility entity' means a research facility entity at any university or college in this state or an independent entity licensed and registered by the Mississippi Department of Health pursuant to this chapter that acquires cannabis from cannabis cultivation facility entities and cannabis processing facility entities in order to research cannabis, develop best practices for specific medical conditions, develop medicines and provide commercial access for medical use."

Source: MSDH Title 15 Pt. 22, Rules 3.2.1(F), 1.2.27 — link as above — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Fees — verified against Run 1. MSDH Rule 3.2.2(H):

"Research Entity. One-time application fee of $10,000.00. Annual license fee of $15,000.00."

This confirms the Run 1 Part 4 figure ($10,000 application / $15,000 annual). It is corroborated by the MSDH FAQ application-fee list (Testing Establishment $10,000 is listed separately; the research application fee is stated in Rule 3.2.2(H) and in the SB 2095 fee schedule). No conflict was found on the research fee amounts.

University/college fee exemption — verified in statute, absent from the rule text opened. Miss. Code § 41-137-35(8) (as enacted by SB 2095, and carried verbatim in HB 1158 (2023), § (8)):

"Cannabis research facilities shall be subject to a one-time nonrefundable application fee of Ten Thousand Dollars ($10,000.00) and an annual license fee of Fifteen Thousand Dollars ($15,000.00). A research facility at any university or college in this state shall be exempt from all fees imposed under this section."

Source: SB 2095 fee schedule (via Scribd republication of the official bill text, lines 1300–1305) and HB 1158 (As Sent to Governor), 2023 Regular Session, § (8) — https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2023/html/HB/1100-1199/HB1158SG.htm — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Caveat on source type: the fee-exemption sentence was verified against bill texts (SB 2095 as sent to governor; HB 1158 as sent to governor), not against a current official Code extract opened in this run. The MSDH rule text opened (Rule 3.2.2(H)) states the fees without restating the exemption. Adopted position (see §0.3, C-6): the statutory exemption controls; a university/college research facility is fee-exempt; the rule's silence is not a repeal. A check against the current official § 41-137-35(8) is [VERIFY] for a filing that turns on the exemption, but the exemption is not treated as doubtful — it is in the enacted fee schedule in two successive bill texts.

What a research licence allows — on the text opened:

Allowed (express) Basis
Acquire cannabis / cannabis products from licensed cultivation facilities and licensed processing facilities Rules 3.2.1(F), 1.2.27
Research cannabis; develop best practices for specific medical conditions; develop medicines; provide commercial access for medical use Rules 3.2.1(F), 1.2.27
Produce cannabis concentrates, extractions or other cannabis products (research facilities are one of only two establishment types that may do so) § 41-137-39(6): "No medical cannabis establishment other than a cannabis processing facility or cannabis research facility may produce cannabis concentrates, cannabis extractions, or other cannabis products." (Justia 2025 republication — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-39/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026)
Hold a licence as a university/college facility or as an independent entity Rule 1.2.27 (both are "research facility entities")

What a research licence forbids / does not authorise — on the text opened:

Not authorised (or expressly limited) Basis / note
Cultivation as a primary activity The research licence is an acquisition licence (acquires from cultivators/processors). It is not a cultivation licence (Rule 3.2.1(A)) and does not authorise growing as a cultivator. A research facility that also wishes to cultivate needs a cultivation licence (and must meet cultivation requirements). Whether a research facility may grow small quantities for research under its research licence alone is not stated in Rules 3.2.1(F)/1.2.27 and is [VERIFY] — do not assume it. This is distinct from the federal Ole Miss NIDA cultivation programme (§11.9.1), which operates under federal DEA/NIDA authority, not under an MSDH research licence.
Retail dispensing to patients Not in Rule 3.2.1(F). "Provide commercial access for medical use" (Rules 3.2.1(F)/1.2.27) is ambiguous: it could mean providing research-derived products into the medical programme via licensed dispensaries, not direct retail sale by the research facility. Direct retail dispensing by a research facility is not expressly authorised and is [VERIFY]. A research facility that wishes to dispense needs an MDOR dispensary licence.
Sale to non-licensees / transfer outside the programme Not authorised. Transfers are within the licensed-establishment system (cultivators/processors → research facility; research facility → programme via licensed channels). The general rule (Rule 4.1.7, as opened) is that establishments "shall not acquire, possess, store, grow, cultivate, or harvest, manufacture, produce, or transport cannabis or cannabis products for any person or entity other than [those] authorized by this Part."
Human-subjects research without the SB 2888 / IRB guardrails (for programme-funded research) See §11.9.5: SB 2888 programme research involving human subjects must be IRB-reviewed/approved/overseen, and participants must be registered qualifying patient cardholders (or equivalent out-of-state certification). MSDH research-licence rules as opened do not restate IRB duties; the SB 2888 duties apply to the state programme, not necessarily to every independent MSDH research licensee. [VERIFY] whether MSDH imposes IRB/FDA-IND conditions on an individual research licence.
Exemption from work permits, background checks, seed-to-sale, testing, or waste rules No exemption was located. Research facilities are "medical cannabis establishments" (Rule 1.2.89) and are therefore subject to the general Part 22 duties (work permits for representatives, background checks, inspections, recordkeeping, seed-to-sale tracking, waste disposal via licensed entities, advertising limits) unless a specific rule exempts them. The only research-specific exemption located is the fee exemption for university/college facilities (§41-137-35(8)). Do not generalise the fee exemption into a compliance exemption.

Licence term and renewal. MSDH regular licences are valid for one year from issuance (Rule 3.7.1) and must be renewed annually (Rule 3.8.1), with renewal application within thirty (30) days prior to expiration, proof of continued compliance with local permits/licences, and payment of the renewal fee (Rule 3.8.3). No research-specific term or renewal period different from the general one-year term was located. Whether the university fee exemption extends to renewal fees as well as initial fees is answered by the statute's words — "exempt from all fees imposed under this section" — which on its face covers both application and annual fees. [VERIFY] only if MSDH has taken a contrary administrative position, which was not located.

11.9.4 Mississippi State University — hemp/cannabis research (extension, agronomy, USDA hemp trials)

What was found — and what was not. A search of Mississippi State University (MSU) official sources (Mississippi Agricultural and Forestry Experiment Station — MAFES — publications list and Extension materials) located no published industrial-hemp (Cannabis sativa) variety trial, agronomy trial, or USDA hemp trial report for Mississippi in this run. The MAFES publications list (accessed 25 Oct 2026, https://www.mafes.msstate.edu/publications/publist.php) shows, for 2024–2026, variety trials for corn, cotton, soybean, grain sorghum, wheat/oats, peanut, rice, bermudagrass, bedding plants and ornamentals, and cool-season forage crops — but no industrial-hemp trial publication. That absence is reported as a search result, not as proof that MSU has never conducted hemp work: unpublished, ongoing, or USDA-plan trial work would not necessarily appear in the publications list.

The sunn-hemp trap — do not conflate. The one MSU trial publication that a keyword search for "hemp" returns is:

"Mississippi Sunn Hemp Variety Trials, 2023, Mississippi Agricultural and Forestry Experiment Station, Mississippi State University" — https://www.mafes.msstate.edu/publications/information-bulletins/ib0586.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

"Sunn hemp" is Crotalaria juncea, a legume forage/cover crop in the pea family. It is not industrial hemp (Cannabis sativa), is not a cannabis product, and is not governed by hemp law. Its trials (planted June, 6 ft × 10 ft plots, randomised complete block, 25 lbs/acre, harvested ~45 days after planting, soil-tested, lime/P₂O₅/K₂O by soil-test recommendation) are forage trials. Citing the sunn-hemp bulletin as evidence of MSU industrial-hemp research would be a species error. This file cites it only to warn against that error.

MSU's hemp-adjacent history (secondary, pre-legalisation context only). Secondary reporting on the Mississippi Hemp Cultivation Task Force (2019, Mississippi Policy Institute summary) records MSU participation in hemp-policy discussion: Wes Burger (then associate director, Forest and Wildlife Research Center, MSU) is reported as saying hemp "has the potential to be a competitive crop in the state's agricultural mix, but that isn't a silver bullet," that markets and seed testing would be needed to find varieties suited to Mississippi's climate/soils, that there were no legal herbicides/pesticides for hemp, and that hemp's fibrous stems could damage combines. An MSU agricultural-economics estimate (Randy Little, Department of Agricultural Economics, via the same secondary summary) put hemp fibre/grain revenue near northeast-Mississippi corn and above Delta soybeans, but below cotton. These are 2019 policy-discussion estimates, not trial results, and are not relied on for any agronomic conclusion. Source (secondary): https://mspolicy.org/hemp-cultivation-task-force-holds-second-meeting/ and https://mspolicy.org/mississippi-farmers-want-the-opportunity-to-cultivate-hemp/ — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

MSU's role in CBD research law (statutory, historical). Under the pre-medical-programme CBD law (Harper Grace's Law framework, as amended by SB 2725 (2020)), the Mississippi Agricultural and Forestry Experiment Station at MSU and the NCNPR at Ole Miss were the only entities authorised to produce cannabis plants for cannabidiol research (SB 2725 (2020) § (2), and SB 2540 (2026, introduced, not enacted — cited only to show the provision's continued presence in bill drafts, not as law)). That authorisation concerned CBD-solution research under the pre-2022 framework, not the current MSDH research-licence regime, and it must not be cited as a current MSU hemp or medical-cannabis licence. Whether MSU currently holds an MSDH research licence, a DEA registration, or a USDA hemp licence was not located in this run and is [VERIFY] — no MSU licence was found in the sources opened, and none is asserted.

MSU Extension general agronomy — applicable by analogy only. MSU Extension provides general soil-testing, fertiliser-by-soil-test, variety-trial and forage guidance for Mississippi crops. None of that guidance located in this run is hemp-specific. A Mississippi hemp producer may use general Extension soil-testing and agronomy services as any farmer may, but there is no MSU Extension hemp production guide, hemp variety recommendation, or hemp pest-management guide located in this run to cite. [UNAVAILABLE] as an MSU hemp-specific publication.

Bottom line for MSU: [UNAVAILABLE] as a current, published MSU industrial-hemp/cannabis research programme in official sources opened for this run, apart from (a) the historical CBD-research authorisation (pre-2022 framework, above) and (b) general Extension/agronomy services that are not hemp-specific. Any claim of a current MSU hemp trial programme requires an MSU/MAFES/USDA source that was not located here.

11.9.5 Other university / state research programmes

Mississippi Medical Cannabis Research Program (SB 2888, 2024) — the state programme at Ole Miss. SB 2888 (2024 Regular Session, effective 1 July 2024, § 4) created:

"There is hereby created the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Research Program at the National Center for Cannabis Research and Education at the University of Mississippi."

Source: SB 2888 (As Sent to Governor), 2024 Regular Session, § 1(1) — http://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2024/html/SB/2800-2899/SB2888SG.htm — accessed 25 Oct 2026.

Duties (SB 2888, § 1(2), "Subject to funding"). The programme shall:

  • (a) seek state, federal and private funds to award grants for medical cannabis research;
  • (b) facilitate/support funding for research on health effects, including potential risks/side effects, of cannabis products;
  • (c) facilitate/support funding for research on efficacy and potential health effects of various delivery methods, including vaporising, ingesting, topical application, and combustion;
  • (d) support researchers in applying for/securing federal and private grant funding for expanding medical cannabis research;
  • (e) review current and future cannabis research literature, clinical studies and clinical trials;
  • (f) educate medical providers, lawmakers and the public about medical cannabis research advances;
  • (g) if requested, consult with researchers and eligible institutions seeking to conduct medical cannabis research regarding legal implications under state and federal law;
  • (h) monitor, to the extent appropriate and when sufficient data is available, patient outcomes in any state with a medicinal cannabis programme;
  • (i) (may) coordinate/share knowledge/best practices with a state that has a medical programme and is conducting cannabis research;
  • (j) (may) award/facilitate funding for grants to an eligible institution for medical cannabis research, including research regarding growing a medical-grade cannabis plant used for a cannabis product;
  • (k) (may) support a licensed cannabis cultivation facility to provide medical-grade cannabis products for research;
  • (l) make research outcomes publicly available (for research conducted by the programme);
  • (m) maintain a catalogue of all published scientific reports based on projects funded/managed by the programme;
  • (n) ensure that an individual who agrees to use a cannabis product as part of a programme/grantee research project: (i) is a registered, qualifying patient cardholder; or (ii) if included as a resident of another state, has the equivalent of such certification under that jurisdiction's laws;
  • (o) provide information to the Department of Health describing: (i) all grant-funded research projects, including the recipient institution; (ii) all programme-conducted projects; and (iii) adequacy of funding for the programme's duties.

Programme guardrails (SB 2888, § 1(3)). For research funded, conducted or facilitated by the programme, the programme must ensure the research (a) includes appropriate research development, testing and evaluation, and (b) if it involves human subjects, is reviewed, approved and overseen by an institutional review board. The University of Mississippi must provide staff for the programme (§ 1(4)).

Advisory board (SB 2888, § 2). The Medical Cannabis Research Advisory Board (11 members: 4 appointed by the Governor — 2 NCCRE medical cannabis researchers, 1 registered qualifying patient enrolled in Mississippi medical cannabis research, 1 Mississippi registered cannabis practitioner physician with 100+ cannabis patients; 4 appointed by the Lieutenant Governor — 1 medical cannabis research scientist, 1 MDOH representative involved in the Medical Cannabis Program, 1 advanced practice registered nurse registered cannabis practitioner with 100+ patients, 1 medical cannabis research technologist; 3 appointed by the Speaker — 1 physician experienced as a principal investigator in cannabinoid research/clinical trials, 1 epidemiologist, 1 patient care advocate) must meet at least every three months (or as often as necessary) to evaluate/make recommendations to the Legislature and MDOH/MDOR on evidence-based treatment guidance (per qualifying condition, risks/contraindications/side effects/adverse reactions, FDA-approved-medication interactions) and on educating providers, pharmacy providers, cardholders and the public. Board members serve terms concurrent with legislative terms, may be reappointed, serve without compensation (expenses reimbursed as authorised by law), and, subject to appropriation, receive per diem under § 25-3-69 and travel reimbursement under § 25-3-41. The chair is elected annually by voting members and may not serve more than two consecutive years. A majority constitutes a quorum; a majority of the quorum is required for action. MDOH and MDOR "shall act swiftly to assist the Advisory Board with any request" (§ 2(9)).

Reporting (SB 2888, § 3). By the November interim meeting each year beginning in 2024, the department (MDOH) must report to the Senate and House Public Health and Welfare Committees on information provided by the programme, without personally identifying information.

Funding — $1,500,000 (2024 appropriation). SB 3007 (2024), § 12 (As Sent to Governor):

"Of the funds appropriated in Section 1 of this act, One Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollars ($1,500,000.00) is hereby provided for the National Center for Cannabis Research and Education at the University of Mississippi - Research Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences for the purpose of data analysis, educational initiatives, and other activities in collaboration with the State Department of Health pursuant to Senate Bill 2888, Regular Session 2024."

Source: SB 3007 (As Sent to Governor), 2024, § 12 — https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2024/pdf/SB/3000-3099/SB3007SG.pdf — accessed 25 Oct 2026. Secondary reporting (Site Selection, Mississippi profile) states the programme began in July (2024), that over the next year $1.5 million was appropriated to School of Pharmacy researchers for five projects, the first being a website to share research findings and translation to modern healthcare practice, and quotes NCCRE Director Robert Welch as saying the SB 2888 programme is "totally separate from the NIDA project" and uses state funding to partner with MSDH's Medical Cannabis Program. That secondary account is consistent with the SB 2888/SB 3007 texts on funding and separation from NIDA, but project-level detail (five projects, website) rests on the secondary source, not on a programme publication opened in this run, and is [VERIFY] against an NCCRE programme publication.

PART 12 — CONSUMER AND SOCIAL RULES

Mississippi Cannabis & Hemp Research — Run 2, Part 12: Consumer and Social Rules

State: Mississippi only Run / Part: Run 2, Part 12 — Consumer and Social Rules Date accessed for all sources in this file: 25 October 2026 Scope note: This part covers only the ten items commissioned for Part 12. It does not re-research licensing, taxation, product testing, local opt-outs for dispensaries, or the federal baseline, except where a consumer/social rule turns on them.

Method, sourcing limits, and how to read this file

  • Official sources first. The Mississippi Legislature's bill-status site (billstatus.ls.state.ms.us), the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Program site (mmcp.ms.gov, Mississippi State Department of Health / MSDH), the Mississippi Department of Revenue (dor.ms.gov), and federal sources (ATF, HUD, FDA) were preferred. Where the official current Code text could not be opened in this research window, the report cites the closest indexed reproduction — principally Justia's Mississippi Code pages and the Legislature's own bill texts, which reproduce the statute — and marks the pinpoint [VERIFY] against the current official text on legislature.ms.gov.
  • A tool failure that affects sourcing — stated plainly. Three direct page-fetch attempts (browser.open) for Justia pages for §§ 41-137-13, 41-137-19 and 41-137-23 failed with a local-worker transport error, not with a page-not-found or login barrier. Those three requests were not repeated. The verbatim quotations below for those sections therefore rest on search-indexed reproductions of the same texts (Justia and Legislature bill texts) rather than on a directly opened page in this window, and are flagged [VERIFY] where the pinpoint matters. No other Part 12 conclusion depends solely on those three fetches; the same language is corroborated by Legislature bill texts reproduced in search results.
  • Verbatim quotes are in block quotes and are copied from the source cited immediately after them. Paraphrase is not presented as quotation.
  • [VERIFY] = a fact, pinpoint, amendment date, or current status that could not be confirmed against a current official source in this window and must be re-checked before reliance or outreach. [UNAVAILABLE] = no source was located in this window for that point; it is not asserted to be non-existent in law, only unlocated here.
  • Mississippi silence is not filled with another state's rule. Each of the ten items is structured as (i) what Mississippi law actually says, (ii) what is silent in Mississippi law, and (iii) what is federal law only. Where Mississippi is silent, the report says so and does not import, for example, another state's 21+ hemp age, another state's per se THC driving limit, or another state's automatic-expungement scheme.
  • No personal phone numbers or personal email addresses are included. Official programme contact pages are cited by URL only, without reproducing contact details.
  • Proposed bills are never presented as current law. Every bill discussed in this part is labelled introduced / died / committee / enrolled-as-brought-forward as its source shows, and its operative effect is stated as "would" not "does" unless it was enacted.
