Buffers 1,000 ft schools/churches/childcare (500 ft floor), 1,500 ft dispensary-to-dispensary Yes — location rule only Not a school-use rule. See §10 for the distinction.
No employment protection Yes in substance — citation corrected Run 1 cited § 41-137-13 for this. § 41-137-13 is the Limitations section (conduct the Act does not authorise). The employment provisions are § 41-137-15(5)–(6) (no private right of action; no change to the employer–employee relationship) and § 41-137-19(2) (nothing prohibits an employer from disciplining for ingesting in the workplace or working while under the influence). The substance — no employment protection — is unchanged; the pinpoint is corrected here and the Run 1 citation should not be reused.
MDAC issues NO hemp licences (USDA only, unfunded state plan); no hemp-derived product permit / age / testing / labelling statute located Yes Confirmed again in this part: no such statute was located. See §2.
AG opinion 11 Jun 2025 treats intoxicating hemp products outside the medical programme as prohibited — opinion, not statute Yes, and stressed The opinion itself says Mississippi law "does not specifically address" sale/possession of hemp products designed for human ingestion/consumption, and that a complete response is outside the scope of an official opinion because hemp cultivation is federally controlled. It must not be cited as a statute. See §2.
Non-patient possession penalties: ≤30 g first offence fine-only $100–$250 (summons-enforceable, not legalisation); 2nd within 2 years misdemeanour; 3rd+ misdemeanour; >30 g felony tiers to ≥5 kg; vehicle-occupant >1–30 g separate misdemeanour Yes Cross-referenced only; penalties are not re-researched in Part 12 except where paraphernalia (§1) and expungement (§4) turn on them.
Initiative 65 struck down in Butler v. Watson, 338 So. 3d 599 (14 May 2021); initiative process still broken; all 17 restoration measures in 2026 died/tabled Yes No Part 12 item depends on a restored initiative. No new initiative measure is asserted.
Choctaw Referendum 2025-01 authorised a feasibility study only, not sales Yes No Part 12 item asserts tribal sales. Tribal consumer rules are therefore [UNAVAILABLE] in this part.

Federal baseline — given, fixed, not re-researched

The following baseline was supplied for this run and is taken as fixed. Contradictions found in secondary sources are flagged, not used to rewrite the baseline:

  • Split scheduling: state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). Adult-use remains Schedule I.
  • Tax: IRS § 280E generally lifted for Schedule III medical; adult-use fully subject.
  • Hemp: PL 119-37 § 781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 § 2019 limits it until 11 December 2026. After 11 December 2026, the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply.
  • Hemp testing enforcement: USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp delayed to 31 December 2026.
  • Appropriations rider: federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider through 11 December 2026.
  • Banking: no federal cannabis banking law.

Contradiction flagged, baseline retained: Several secondary sources consulted in this window still describe cannabis as Schedule I across the board or describe rescheduling as merely proposed (e.g., a Mississippi guide stating "no final rule had been published as of early 2026"). Those sources pre-date, or do not reflect, the given 28 April 2026 Schedule III baseline and are not adopted where they conflict with it. Conversely, the given baseline does not by itself answer the firearms question in §8: whether a state-licensed medical user is an "unlawful user" under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) after Schedule III, and whether any ATF safe harbour exists, remains [VERIFY] — see §8 in full. Do not read the baseline as a firearms safe harbour.

1. Paraphernalia and smoke-shop rules

1(i) What Mississippi law actually says

Definition — § 41-29-105(v). "Paraphernalia" means, in the operative part:

"all products and materials of any kind which are used, intended for use, or designed for use in [planting, propagating, cultivating, growing, harvesting, manufacturing, compounding, converting, producing, processing, preparing, testing, analysing, packaging, repackaging, storing, containing, concealing, injecting, ingesting, inhaling or otherwise introducing into the human body] a controlled substance in violation of the Uniform Controlled Substances Law."

Source: Miss. Code § 41-29-105(v)(i), via Justia 2024 Code reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-29/article-3/section-41-29-105/ [VERIFY pinpoint against current official text; the definition language is stable across the 2010, 2019 and 2024 reproductions consulted.]

The definition then lists examples. The cannabis-specific list, § 41-29-105(v)(i)(12), covers:

"Objects used, intended for use or designed for use in ingesting, inhaling or otherwise introducing marijuana, cocaine, hashish or hashish oil into the human body, such as: a. Metal, wooden, acrylic, glass, stone, plastic or ceramic pipes with or without screens, permanent screens, hashish heads or punctured metal bowls; b. Water pipes; c. Carburetion tubes and devices; d. Smoking and carburetion masks; e. Roach clips…; f. Miniature cocaine spoons and cocaine vials; g. Chamber pipes; h. Carburetor pipes; i. Electric pipes; j. Air-driven pipes; k. Chillums; l. Bongs; and m. Ice pipes or chillers."

Source: same § 41-29-105(v) reproduction, via FindLaw/Justia, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://codes.findlaw.com/ms/title-41-public-health/ms-code-sect-41-29-105/

Whether an object is paraphernalia is not decided by the list alone. § 41-29-105(v)(ii) requires the court or authority to consider, "in addition to all other logically relevant factors," fourteen factors, including: statements by the owner/person in control about its use; prior controlled-substance convictions; proximity in time and space to a Uniform Controlled Substances Law violation and to controlled substances; residue; evidence of intent to deliver to persons who the owner knows or should reasonably know intend unlawful use (with the owner's own innocence as to a direct violation not preventing a finding); instructions and descriptive materials; national and local advertising; manner of display for sale; whether the owner is a legitimate supplier of like items (e.g., a licensed tobacco distributor/dealer); ratio of such sales to total business sales; legitimate uses in the community; and expert testimony. Source: § 41-29-105(v)(ii), Justia 2024 reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026. A 2024 addition, § 41-29-105(v)(iii), provides that "'Paraphernalia' does not include any materials used or intended for use in testing for the presence of fentanyl or a fentanyl analog in a substance" — i.e., fentanyl test strips are carved out; no equivalent carve-out for cannabis paraphernalia was located. [VERIFY the (v)(iii) amendment date and current lettering.]

Use / possession — § 41-29-139(d)(1). The medical-cannabis exception is built into the opening words:

"Except as otherwise provided under subsection (i) of this section for actions that are lawful under the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act and in compliance with rules and regulations adopted thereunder, it is unlawful for a person who is not authorized by the State Board of Medical Licensure, State Board of Pharmacy, or other lawful authority to use, or to possess with intent to use, paraphernalia to plant, propagate, cultivate, grow, harvest, manufacture, compound, convert, produce, process, prepare, test, analyze, pack, repack, store, contain, conceal, inject, ingest, inhale or otherwise introduce into the human body a controlled substance in violation of the Uniform Controlled Substances Law."

"Any person who violates this subsection (d)(1) is guilty of a misdemeanor and, upon conviction, may be confined in the county jail for not more than six (6) months, or fined not more than Five Hundred Dollars ($500.00), or both; however, no person shall be charged with a violation of this subsection when such person is also charged with the possession of thirty (30) grams or less of marijuana under subsection (c)(2)(A) of this section."

Source: § 41-29-139(d)(1), via search-indexed reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://arklegal.ai/state_statute/3392254/download.pdf (reproduction of § 41-29-139). The "no double charge" proviso is material: a person charged with ≤30 g marijuana possession under (c)(2)(A) cannot also be charged with (d)(1) paraphernalia use/possession on the same facts.

Sale / delivery / manufacture for sale — § 41-29-139(d)(2). As reproduced in the federal court's findings in Handy Pantry v. City of Hattiesburg (see §1, local rules below):

"(d) Paraphernalia. (2) It is unlawful for any person to deliver, sell, possess with intent to deliver or sell, or manufacture with intent to deliver or sell, paraphernalia, knowing, or under circumstances where one reasonably should know, that it will be used to … introduce into the human body a controlled substance in violation of the Uniform Controlled Substances Law. Except as provided in subsection (d)(3), a person who violates this subsection (d)(2) is guilty of a misdemeanor and, upon conviction, may be confined in the county jail for not more than six (6) months, or fined not more than Five Hundred Dollars ($500.00), or both."

Source: Miss. Code § 41-29-139(d)(2), quoted in Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, Handy Pantry et al. v. City of Hattiesburg, No. 2:2023cv00096 (S.D. Miss. 10 Apr 2025), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://cases.justia.com/federal/district-courts/mississippi/mssdce/2:2023cv00096/119201/48/0.pdf?ts=1744450194

Sale / delivery to a minor — § 41-29-139(d)(3). The rule is narrow and specific, and is the only paraphernalia-specific sale-to-minor rule located:

In substance: a person over the age of 18 who violates (d)(2) by delivering or selling paraphernalia to a person under 18 who is at least three years younger than the seller is guilty of a misdemeanour punishable by up to one year in county jail and a fine of up to $1,000.

Source: § 41-29-139(d)(3), as summarised in FindLaw's Mississippi controlled-substances tables, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.findlaw.com/state/mississippi-law/mississippi-cocaine-laws.html and https://www.findlaw.com/state/mississippi-law/mississippi-heroin-laws.html [VERIFY the verbatim (d)(3) text against the current official Code; the penalty (1 year / $1,000) and the "at least three years younger" element are consistent across both FindLaw tables.] Note the two cumulative conditions: the buyer must be under 18 and at least three years younger. A sale to a 17-year-old by a 19-year-old, for example, would not meet the age-gap element on the text as summarised — do not generalise this into a blanket "no sale to under-18s" paraphernalia ban.

Medical-cannabis carve-out — § 41-29-139(i) and § 41-137-9(2)(e). The (d)(1) exception quoted above points to subsection (i) "for actions that are lawful under the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act and in compliance with rules and regulations adopted thereunder." Separately, § 41-137-9(2) lists as lawful, subject to the Act's conditions and limitations, "(e) Providing or selling equipment used to ingest medical cannabis to a cardholder, nonresident cardholder or to a medical cannabis establishment." Source: § 41-137-9(2)(e), FindLaw reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://codes.findlaw.com/ms/title-41-public-health/ms-code-sect-41-137-9/ [VERIFY the (i) pinpoint and its full text; the cross-reference in (d)(1) is confirmed, but the full text of (i) was not reproduced in the sources consulted in this window.] Practical consequence, stated carefully: equipment sold to a cardholder for lawful medical use is within the Act's lawful-activity list; equipment sold to a non-cardholder for unlawful use is not, and remains within (d)(2). The statute does not create a general "smoke shop" safe harbour for sales to the public at large.

Local rules — Hattiesburg ordinance held void (2025). The City of Hattiesburg's Ordinance No. 3258 (enacted 18 Jun 2019), which attempted to create its own paraphernalia misdemeanour, was declared invalid and void on 10 April 2025:

"The Court finds the Ordinance was outside the authority of the City to enact because both Sections contradict state law and attempt to create a new criminal prohibition preempted by state law. Therefore, the Ordinance is void."

"Plaintiffs shall prevail in this action in so far as Ordinance No. 3258, enacted by the City of Hattiesburg on June 18, 2019, is declared invalid and void."

Source: Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, Handy Pantry et al. v. City of Hattiesburg, 10 Apr 2025, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://docs.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/mississippi/mssdce/2:2023cv00096/119201/48 — the court held the ordinance conflicted with the state statute both in its definition of "paraphernalia" and in lacking the state statute's knowledge / mens rea element, and also held it unconstitutionally vague. This is the only Mississippi local paraphernalia rule located in this window, and it was struck down. No surviving local paraphernalia licensing or ban scheme was located.

1(ii) What is silent in Mississippi law

  • No cannabis-specific smoke-shop / vape-shop licence was located. There is no statute or regulation found in this window that creates a "smoke shop licence," a "paraphernalia retailer licence," or a cannabis-accessories retail licence. That is a negative search result, not a positive statement that no licence of any kind is ever required: a shop remains subject to general business, tax, zoning and, where applicable, tobacco/ENDS requirements (see §1(iii) for the tobacco/ENDS distinction). Do not cite this section as authority that a paraphernalia-only shop needs no permission at all from any authority.
  • No state rule was located governing paraphernalia display, packaging, advertising to adults, online sale of paraphernalia, or a minimum age for possession of paraphernalia as such (as distinct from the (d)(3) sale-to-minor offence above). The fourteen § 41-29-105(v)(ii) factors (advertising, display, legitimate-supplier status) are evidentiary factors for deciding whether an object is paraphernalia, not freestanding advertising/display bans.
  • No rule was located distinguishing hemp-derived paraphernalia from marijuana paraphernalia. An object "designed for use" in introducing a controlled substance in violation of the Uniform Controlled Substances Law is paraphernalia on the statutory test; whether hemp-derived THC that is itself lawful under federal hemp law changes that analysis for a given object was not addressed by any Mississippi source located and is [VERIFY] — do not assume a hemp object is automatically excluded.
  • No paraphernalia-specific local delegation was located. The Act does not, in the sections consulted, delegate paraphernalia licensing to counties or municipalities, and the Hattiesburg decision points the other way for criminal paraphernalia ordinances that contradict state law.

1(iii) What is federal law only

  • Tobacco / nicotine retail permits are not cannabis paraphernalia licences, but they are the adjacent regime a smoke/vape shop will usually trigger. Mississippi Department of Revenue Notice 72-26-09 (22 Jun 2026) states that, pursuant to Miss. Code § 75-102-2, "each retailer, wholesaler or distributor of ENDS products are required to apply for and obtain an ENDS Permit from the Department of Revenue," with applications through Taxpayer Access Point (TAP); "ENDS products" are defined there as noncombustible products employing a heating element etc. to produce vapour from nicotine in solution, excluding products regulated as a drug/device under Chapter V of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Source: MDOR Notice 72-26-09, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.dor.ms.gov/sites/default/files/notices-technical-bulletins/72-26-09%20ENDS%20Permit.pdf — This is a state nicotine regime, cited here only to prevent confusion: an ENDS permit is for nicotine vapour products, not a licence to sell cannabis paraphernalia, and a cannabis vape device that is not a nicotine ENDS product does not become licensed by holding an ENDS permit. A separate secondary summary asserting a $10 tobacco retail licence under § 27-69-5 and annual renewal was not adopted as a verified statement because the primary MDOR source consulted addresses ENDS permits; the tobacco-permit fee and renewal details are [VERIFY] against MDOR.
  • Federal paraphernalia law (21 U.S.C. § 863, the federal drug-paraphernalia statute) is federal law only and is not analysed as Mississippi law in this part. No Mississippi source located in this window states that § 863 does or does not apply to a given Mississippi shop, and no conclusion is drawn on it here.
  • Proposed flavoured-vapour licensing is not law. HB 1486 (2025), which would have created a $250-per-location flavoured nicotine vapour licence, age-verification and 1,000-ft school/church restrictions, died in committee on 4 Feb 2025. Source: BillTrack50 summary of HB 1486, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.billtrack50.com/billdetail/1797264 — It is cited only to show that a vapour-shop licensing scheme was proposed and not enacted; it must not be cited as a current requirement.
Paraphernalia question Mississippi answer
Use / possess with intent to use (non-medical) Misdemeanour, ≤6 months county jail and/or ≤$500 — § 41-29-139(d)(1)
Sell / deliver / manufacture for sale, knowing or reasonably should know unlawful use Misdemeanour, ≤6 months and/or ≤$500 — § 41-29-139(d)(2)
Sell/deliver to under-18 at least 3 years younger (seller 18+) Misdemeanour, ≤1 year and/or ≤$1,000 — § 41-29-139(d)(3) [VERIFY verbatim text]
Double charge with ≤30 g possession Barred — § 41-29-139(d)(1) proviso
Lawful medical-cannabis equipment to a cardholder Lawful activity under § 41-137-9(2)(e); (d)(1) exception via (i)
State smoke-shop / paraphernalia licence None located — see §1(ii)
Local paraphernalia crime ordinance Hattiesburg Ord. 3258 held void 10 Apr 2025

2. Minimum age for hemp-derived THC products — and, separately, medical-programme age rules

2(i) What Mississippi law actually says

Hemp-derived THC: no Mississippi age rule was located — the Run 1 finding stands. No Mississippi statute or regulation located in this window sets a minimum age (18, 21, or any other) for purchasing, possessing, or using a hemp-derived THC product, and no hemp-derived product permit, testing, labelling, or age statute was located. This is not a gap in the search: the point was tested against (a) the failed 2025 hemp bills, (b) the AG opinion, and (c) secondary claims that assert an age rule, and none of them supplies a current statute.

  • HB 1502 (2025) died. The bill that would have regulated/banned intoxicating hemp products — and, in its various versions, would have created a 21-and-over rule for certain low-THC beverages and authorised MSDH to regulate CBD products — died on the calendar when the Legislature adjourned on 3 April 2025 (the AG opinion request itself notes HB 1502's death). It is proposed law only and creates no current age rule. Source: Cannabis Business Times report on the AG opinion (11 Jun 2025 opinion; HB 1502 context), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/us-states/mississippi/news/15748808/consumable-hemp-products-illegal-without-fda-approval-mississippi-ag-says
  • Conflicting secondary claims — none adopted. Secondary sources in this window assert, variously, that Mississippi requires 21+ for hemp-derived THC, that the age is 18+, and that Mississippi "currently places no age restriction" on hemp THC drinks while many retailers voluntarily enforce 21+. Examples: a 2025 local-news piece stating "Mississippi currently places no age restriction on purchasing these items, though many retailers choose to enforce a 21+ policy voluntarily" (Starkville Today, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://starkvilletoday.com/local-news/is-marijuana-legal-in-mississippi-2025-laws-medical-use-penalties/); a student-news piece stating the House and Senate "each passed different versions of a bill that would have banned high-potency hemp products, capped THC levels in beverages and created a 21-and-over purchase requirement. But lawmakers could not reconcile the differences, and the legislation died in conference committee" (RHCJC News, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://rhcjcnews.com/4573/what-is-true/thc-drinks-raise-concern-but-facts-are-mixed/). The 21+ and 18+ claims that cite "Mississippi Law" without a statute citation are not adopted. The only proposition supported by the legislative record is the negative one: no age statute was enacted. A retailer's voluntary 21+ policy is a private business policy, not law, and must not be reported as a legal requirement.
  • The AG opinion does not set an age. Attorney General Opinion (11 Jun 2025, on request of Rep. Lee Yancey) answers three questions — whether sale, and whether possession, of non-FDA-approved hemp-derived products designed for human ingestion/consumption is prohibited, and whether municipalities may prohibit/penalise sale/possession — by concluding, in reliance on the Uniform Controlled Substances Law, that sale and possession are prohibited except for products sold through a duly licensed medical cannabis dispensary in strict accordance with the Medical Cannabis Act. The opinion's own limiting language, quoted in secondary reporting, is:

"Except for products sold through a duly licensed medical cannabis dispensary and in strict accordance with the provisions of the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act, the sale of a product derived from the hemp plant designed for human ingestion and/or consumption that is not approved by the United States FDA is prohibited under Mississippi's Uniform Controlled Substances Law."

"Mississippi law does not specifically address the possession or sale of products derived from the hemp plant designed for human ingestion and/or consumption."

"Because the cultivation of hemp in Mississippi is legalized, licensed, and controlled by federal law, a complete response to your request is outside the scope of an official opinion."

Sources: Budding Trends analysis of the 11 Jun 2025 opinion, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.buddingtrendsblog.com/2025/06/maybe-so-maybe-not-mississippi-ags-office-opines-that-mississippi-law-prohibits-most-consumable-hemp-products-while-recognizing-opinions-limitations/ ; Enterprise Journal / Star Herald reporting of Jackson County Sheriff enforcement letters relying on the opinion, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.enterprise-journal.com/law-enforcement-agencies-issuing-letters-removal-non-fda-approved-hemp-products-689671fe3508b — Status warning: an AG opinion is advisory to government officials; it is not a statute, not a regulation, and its own text acknowledges its federal-law limits. Enforcement letters from Gulf Coast sheriffs in 2025 (e.g., Jackson County, 48-hour removal notices) are enforcement practice relying on the opinion, not a new age rule and not a statute. No age element appears in the opinion's holding as reported.

Medical programme age rules — these are separate and are statutory. Do not conflate them with hemp:

  • No minimum age to qualify as a patient. MMCP's August 2026 Patient's Rights toolkit states: "There is no minimum age requirement to qualify for medical cannabis in Mississippi. However, patients under the age of 18 must have a parent or legal guardian registered as their caregiver and responsible for administration and dosage." Source: MSDH/MMCP Patient's Rights toolkit (Aug 2026), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/sites/default/files/2026/MMCP%20Tool%20Kit%20-%20August%202026/MSDH_Medical_Cannabis_Patient%27s%20Rights.pdf
  • Minors — certification. § 41-137-5(2)(d): a written certification may "Only be issued on behalf of a minor when the minor's parent or guardian is present and provides signed consent." § 41-137-5(8): "Only physicians and doctors of osteopathic medicine may issue written certifications to registered qualifying patients who are minors." Source: § 41-137-5, Justia 2025 reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-5/
  • Designated caregivers — 21, with a parent/guardian exception. The Act's definition (as reproduced in HB 1158, 2023, and SB 2438, 2026, bringing forward the definitions) provides a designated caregiver "(iii) Is at least twenty-one (21) years of age unless the person is the parent or legal guardian of each qualifying patient the person assists." Source: definitions reproduced in HB 1158 (As Sent to Governor, 2023), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2023/html/HB/1100-1199/HB1158SG.htm [VERIFY the current § 41-137-3 lettering for "designated caregiver."]
  • Patients aged 18–25 — two-practitioner rule. § 41-137-39(16) (as amended by HB 1158, 2023) provides in substance that a patient between 18 and 25 years of age is not eligible for a registry identification card unless two practitioners from separate medical practices have diagnosed the patient after an in-person consultation, one of whom must be a physician or doctor of osteopathic medicine; the separate-practices requirement does not apply if the patient is homebound or held a card before age 18. Source: § 41-137-39(16), reproduced in HB 1158 and in HB 895 (2026, committee substitute bringing forward § 41-137-39), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://legiscan.com/MS/text/HB895/id/3335658/Mississippi-2026-HB895-Comm_Sub.html [VERIFY whether § 41-137-39(16) was amended after 2023; HB 895 (2026) is a brought-forward text, not proof of amendment.]
  • Dispensary / establishment entry — under 21. § 41-137-39(17): "Except as otherwise provided in this section, a medical cannabis establishment shall not allow an individual who is younger than twenty-one (21) years old to enter the premises of the establishment unless the individual possesses a registry identification card and is accompanied by his or her legal guardian." Source: § 41-137-39(17), HB 1158 / HB 895 reproductions, accessed 25 Oct 2026. Note the wording is "legal guardian," not "parent or caregiver" generally; a 19-year-old cardholder unaccompanied by a legal guardian is, on the text, barred from entry. MMCP's summary phrase "Entry into dispensaries by patients under 21 without a parent or legal guardian present" is consistent in substance.
  • Topicals — the only non-cardholder sale, and it is 21+. § 41-137-39(21): a topical cannabis product purchased by a dispensary from a licensed processor, "that is not ingested by the liver, may be sold to a cardholder or any person over the age of twenty-one (21) years old who is not a cardholder," and such products must be placed in an area of the dispensary that does not require access with a registry identification card. Source: § 41-137-39(21), Justia 2023 reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/2023/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-39/ — This 21+ rule is for dispensary topicals, not for hemp products sold elsewhere. Do not generalise it into a hemp age rule.

2(ii) What is silent in Mississippi law

  • No age for hemp-derived THC purchase, possession, or use; no age for hemp-derived CBD; no age-verification, ID-check, or signage duty for hemp sellers; no hemp-specific sale-to-minor offence. The only sale-to-minor offences located that touch this area are (a) the paraphernalia offence in § 41-29-139(d)(3) (§1 above) and (b) tobacco/alternative-nicotine sale-to-minor rules (see §2(iii)), neither of which is a hemp-THC age rule.
  • No Mississippi rule was located addressing a minor's possession of a hemp-derived THC product as such, as distinct from the general controlled-substances and medical-programme rules. Whether a given hemp product is a "controlled substance" for § 41-29-139 purposes on its THC content is the same unresolved question as in the AG opinion and is [VERIFY] product-by-product; no blanket answer is given here.
  • No rule was located on age for giving (as opposed to selling) a hemp product to a minor, or on parental consent for hemp products. Do not import another state's parental-consent or gift rule.

2(iii) What is federal law only

  • Federal hemp law sets no minimum age. The 2018 Farm Bill hemp definition (0.3% delta-9 THC on a dry-weight basis) contains no purchase-age provision; the post-11 December 2026 federal definition and 0.4 mg/container cap in the given baseline likewise contain no age element. Any "21+" seen on a hemp product label or a retailer's door is, in Mississippi, a private policy or another jurisdiction's rule unless a Mississippi statute is produced.
  • Tobacco 21+ is not hemp 21+. Federal Tobacco 21 (21 U.S.C. § 387f(d) / FDA enforcement) and Mississippi's tobacco/alternative-nicotine provisions (e.g., § 97-32-51 advertising and sale provisions discussed in secondary summaries) apply to tobacco and nicotine products. They do not, on any source located, extend to hemp-derived THC. The ENDS permit regime (§1(iii)) is likewise nicotine-specific.
  • FDA approval status is federal. The AG opinion's FDA-approval pivot turns on federal FDA approval, not on a Mississippi age or licensing decision. No FDA-approved hemp-derived THC product for general consumer sale was identified in this window, and no conclusion is drawn on whether any specific product is FDA-approved.

3. THC driving limits and impairment testing

3(i) What Mississippi law actually says

No per se THC driving limit — Run 1 position verified. Mississippi has no statute setting a blood-THC concentration (ng/mL) above which driving is per se unlawful, for any driver class. § 63-11-30 sets alcohol concentrations only — 0.08% for persons above the legal age to purchase alcohol, 0.02% for persons below that age, 0.04% for commercial-vehicle operators — and contains no THC figure. The absence is structural, not an oversight in one version: it is present in the 2010, 2012 and 2015 reproductions and in the 2026 bill text bringing forward § 63-11-30.

The DUI statute — § 63-11-30(1). In its current-form wording (2015 reproduction, renumbering as in that version):

"It is unlawful for a person to drive or otherwise operate a vehicle within this state if the person: (a) Is under the influence of intoxicating liquor; (b) Is under the influence of any other substance that has impaired the person's ability to operate a motor vehicle; (c) Is under the influence of any drug or controlled substance, the possession of which is unlawful under the Mississippi Controlled Substances Law; or (d) Has an alcohol concentration in the person's blood [of 0.08% / 0.02% / 0.04% as above], as shown by a chemical analysis of the person's breath, blood or urine administered as authorized by this chapter…"

Source: § 63-11-30(1), Justia 2015 reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/2015/title-63/chapter-11/section-63-11-30/ [VERIFY the current subsection lettering: the 2010/2012 reproductions letter the drug prong as (d) and the alcohol prong as (c)/(e); the substance is the same.]

Two consequences follow from the text and must both be stated:

  1. Impairment prong (b) catches lawful medical use if it impairs. Prong (b) — "any other substance that has impaired the person's ability to operate a motor vehicle" — does not require unlawful possession. A registered patient who drives while impaired by medical cannabis can therefore be prosecuted under (b) even though the cannabis itself was lawfully possessed. This is reinforced by § 41-137-13(2)(d) (see §5), which preserves penalties for operating/navigating/being in actual physical control of a vehicle, aircraft, train, motorboat or other conveyance in a manner violating § 63-11-30 (or § 59-23-7 for boating, or federal law) as a result of medical use.
  2. Unlawful-possession prong (c)/(d) is narrower for lawful patients — but do not over-read it. Prong (c)/(d) requires a drug "the possession of which is unlawful under the Mississippi Controlled Substances Law." Medical cannabis possessed within the Act's allowable amount is not unlawful possession under state law (see § 41-137-9). Whether a prosecutor could still proceed on (c)/(d) for a patient who exceeds the allowable amount, or for a non-patient, is a charging question not answered by the statute text alone and is [VERIFY] against charging practice; the safe statement is that (b) is the prong that does not depend on lawfulness.

"Actual physical control" — broader than driving. § 41-137-13(2)(d) and § 63-11-30 both reach a person "in actual physical control" of a vehicle, not only a person driving it. Secondary legal Q&A in this window summarises Mississippi courts as treating driver's-seat occupancy with immediate access to the ignition (e.g., keys present) as presumptive actual physical control even if the vehicle is stationary. That summary is not adopted as a holding; it is noted only to flag that "I wasn't driving, I was parked" is not, on the statutory words, a complete answer. The precise Mississippi case law on actual physical control and cannabis impairment was not located in this window and is [VERIFY].

Implied consent and chemical testing — § 63-11-5. In substance:

  • Any person driving on Mississippi public highways/roads/streets is deemed to have given consent to chemical tests of breath, blood, or urine to determine alcohol concentration or the presence of impairing substances, where an officer has reasonable grounds and probable cause to believe the person was driving under the influence.
  • The officer must inform the person that failure to submit to a breath test will result in suspension of driving privileges for 90 days if the person has not previously been convicted under § 63-11-30, or for one (1) year if there is a previous § 63-11-30 conviction.
  • Refusal evidence is admissible in a criminal action (§ 63-11-41, as summarised in secondary sources — [VERIFY] pinpoint).
  • A person tested may, at their own expense, obtain an additional test by a qualified person of their choosing (secondary summary of § 63-11-5 — [VERIFY] verbatim text).

Source: § 63-11-5, Justia 2017 reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/2017/title-63/chapter-11/section-63-11-5/ ; corroborated by Grace Law Firm implied-consent summary, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.gracelawfirm.com/blog/driving-under-the-influence-and-implied-consent

Penalties (summary, for context only — not re-researched in full). First offence under § 63-11-30: fine $250–$1,000 and/or up to 48 hours' jail, alcohol safety education programme, and a 90-day licence suspension (with ignition-interlock restricted-licence alternative in the 2015 text). Second offence within five years and third offence (felony) escalate sharply. These figures are taken from the 2015 § 63-11-30 reproduction and secondary summaries; the current penalty schedule, including any 2026 amendment, is [VERIFY] before citation in advice. The key Part 12 point is not the fine schedule but that no THC tier exists within it.

Medical-cannabis DUI applicability — a 2026 bill text that must not be mistaken for current law. SB 2675 (2026, as introduced, "Expungement of state criminal records" bill that also brings forward § 63-11-30) reproduces a subsection (15) stating: "The provisions of this section are fully applicable to any person who is under the influence of medical cannabis that is lawful under the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act and in compliance with rules and regulations adopted thereunder which has impaired the person's ability to operate a motor vehicle." Source: SB 2675 (2026, as introduced), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2026/dt/SB/2600-2699/SB2675IN.pdf — Status: introduced bill text bringing forward § 63-11-30; whether subsection (15) in that form is already current law or is proposed by SB 2675 is [VERIFY]. It is consistent with the (b) impairment analysis above, but it is not cited here as current law.

3(ii) What is silent in Mississippi law

  • No per se THC limit (any ng/mL figure, any "5 ng/mL" or similar rule — none exists in Mississippi; do not import Colorado/Washington-style limits).
  • No Mississippi-specific impairment-testing rule for cannabis was located: no statute or regulation adopting oral-fluid testing, Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) protocols, roadside THC screening devices, or a THC-specific blood-draw procedure. The general implied-consent machinery (breath/blood/urine "as authorized by this chapter") is the only testing framework located.
  • No rule was located on how long after use impairment is presumed, on metabolite-only presence (THC-COOH without impairment) as an offence, or on a medical-patient defence to a (b) charge based solely on lawful use. The converse — that lawful use is not a defence to an impairment charge — follows from (b)'s wording and § 41-137-13(2)(d), but no case holding to that effect was located in this window [VERIFY].
  • No Mississippi rule was located on cannabis impairment for boating (§ 59-23-7 is cross-referenced in § 41-137-13(2)(d) but its THC content was not examined in this part — [UNAVAILABLE] here), aviation, or commercial driving beyond the general § 63-11-30 framework and the 0.04% alcohol figure for commercial operators.
  • No "open container" offence for medical cannabis was located as current law. HB 1572 (2024) proposed to prohibit possession of an open container of medical cannabis while operating a motor vehicle on a public street, in a public place, on dispensary premises, or on a public street/sidewalk, with a sealed-manufacturer-container exception. It is a 2024 proposal, not current law, and must not be cited as an offence. Source: HB 1572 (2024) summary, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://pluralpolicy.com/app/legislative-tracking/bill/details/state-ms-2024-hb1572

3(iii) What is federal law only

  • Federal drug-testing / DOT rules (e.g., U.S. Department of Transportation drug testing for safety-sensitive transportation employees, and the federal oral-fluid rule whose implementation awaits HHS certification of laboratories, as noted in federal Run 2 research) are federal law only. They do not create a Mississippi per se THC driving limit and do not displace § 63-11-30 for ordinary Mississippi drivers.
  • No federal per se THC driving limit was identified in this window either; federal impaired-driving law for ordinary drivers is state law. Do not present any federal ng/mL figure as a Mississippi limit.

4. Expungement and record clearing for marijuana offences

4(i) What Mississippi law actually says

Mississippi has no cannabis-specific expungement statute and no automatic expungement for any marijuana offence. What exists is (a) the general expungement statute § 99-19-71, which includes certain drug-possession offences in its lists, and (b) the first-offender deferred-adjudication route in § 41-29-150. Both are petition-based, court-granted, and one-time in the ways stated below. Nothing in this section is self-executing.

A. General expungement — § 99-19-71.

  • Misdemeanour, first offender — § 99-19-71(1):

"Any person who has been convicted of a misdemeanor that is not a traffic violation, and who is a first offender, may petition the justice, county, circuit or municipal court in which the conviction was had for an order to expunge any such conviction from all public records."

Source: § 99-19-71(1), Justia 2015 reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/2015/title-99/chapter-19/in-general/section-99-19-71/ — Note what the text does not say: it states no waiting period for this misdemeanour path. A secondary drug-policy summary in this window claims a "commonly cited" two-year wait for a misdemeanour marijuana-possession path and expungement of a "first or second" misdemeanour. That secondary claim is not adopted: the statute text as reproduced says "first offender" (singular) and states no two-year period for subsection (1). Whether a two-year practice exists under a different subsection, a local rule, or a later amendment is [VERIFY] against the current official § 99-19-71; do not cite the two-year figure from the secondary summary.

  • One listed felony, five years — § 99-19-71(2)(a):

"Any person who has been convicted of one (1) of the following felonies may petition the court in which the conviction was had for an order to expunge one (1) conviction from all public records five (5) years after the successful completion of all terms and conditions of the sentence for the conviction: a bad check offense under Section 97-19-55; possession of a controlled substance or paraphernalia under Section 41-29-139(c) or (d); false pretense under Section 97-19-39; larceny under Section 97-17-41; malicious mischief under Section 97-17-67; or shoplifting under Section 97-23-93. A person is eligible for only one (1) felony expunction under this paragraph."

Source: § 99-19-71(2)(a), same Justia reproduction. For marijuana, this is the key felony path: possession under § 41-29-139(c) and paraphernalia under (d) are expressly listed. Two limits matter: (1) it is possession/paraphernalia, not sale, manufacture, distribution, or possession with intent — those (a)-subsection offences are not in the (2)(a) list; (2) it is one felony expunction per person under this paragraph, five years after successful completion of all terms and conditions of the sentence (including, on the text, fines/costs — see the 2019 bill text's "paid all criminal fines and costs" formulation for the same paragraph [VERIFY] whether that fines-paid language is in the current text or was a proposed addition).

  • Under-21 felony — § 99-19-71(2)(b):

In substance: a person who was under 21 when they committed a felony may petition for one expunction five years after successful completion of all sentence terms; eligibility does not apply to a felony classified as a crime of violence under § 97-3-2, nor to a felony that, in the circuit court's determination, is related to distribution of a controlled substance and in the court's discretion should not be expunged. One expunction per person under this paragraph.

Source: § 99-19-71(2)(b), 2019 SB 2662 reproduction of the same paragraph, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — http://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2019/html/SB/2600-2699/SB2662IN.htm [VERIFY the current (2)(b) age threshold: a 2013 version used "under 18," later versions use "under 21"; the under-21 version is adopted here as the later text, but the current official text must be confirmed.]

  • Procedure — notice and effect. The petitioner must give ten (10) days' written notice to the district attorney before any hearing on the petition ( § 99-19-71(2)(c), as reproduced in the 2019 bill text). The court may grant the petition if it determines, on the record or in writing, as provided in the statute (the full grant standard was not reproduced in the sources consulted — [VERIFY]). On entry of an expunction order, a nonpublic record is retained by the court and by the Mississippi Criminal Information Center solely to determine first-offender status in subsequent proceedings; the effect is to restore the person, in contemplation of law, to the status occupied before the arrest, and the person is not guilty of perjury/false statement by failing to recite the arrest/conviction in response to an inquiry for any purpose, except to determine first-offender status in a subsequent proceeding under the section. Source: § 99-19-71(1) effect language, 2008/2019 reproductions, accessed 25 Oct 2026.

  • Arrest without conviction — court shall expunge. Upon petition, the court shall expunge the record of a case in which an arrest was made, the person was released and the case was dismissed or charges dropped, there was no disposition, or the person was acquitted/found not guilty at trial. Source: § 99-19-71(2) (arrest-expunction paragraph), SB 2662 (2019) reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026. This path is distinct from conviction expungement and has no five-year wait on the text as reproduced. [VERIFY] the current paragraph numbering, because later amendments have renumbered § 99-19-71 subsections.

B. First-offender deferred adjudication — § 41-29-150(d). This is the route most relevant to a first marijuana-possession/paraphernalia case, and it is not expungement at the moment of sentencing — it is deferral, then dismissal, then a separate expunction application:

"If any person who has not previously been convicted of violating Section 41-29-139, or the laws of the United States or of another state relating to narcotic drugs, stimulant or depressant substances, other controlled substances or marihuana is found to be guilty of a violation of subsection (c) or (d) of Section 41-29-139, after trial or upon a plea of guilty, the court may, without entering a judgment of guilty and with the consent of such person, defer further proceedings and place him on probation upon such reasonable conditions as it may require and for such period, not to exceed three (3) years, as the court may prescribe."

"If during the period of his probation such person does not violate any of the conditions of the probation, then upon expiration of such period the court shall discharge such person and dismiss the proceedings against him. Discharge and dismissal under this subsection shall be without court adjudication of guilt, but a nonpublic record thereof shall be retained by the bureau solely for the purpose of use by the courts in determining whether or not, in subsequent proceedings, such person qualifies under this subsection. Such discharge or dismissal shall not be deemed a conviction for purposes of disqualifications or disabilities imposed by law upon conviction of a crime, including the penalties prescribed under this article for second or subsequent conviction, or for any other purpose."

"Discharge and dismissal under this subsection may occur only once with respect to any person…"

"Upon the dismissal of a person and discharge of proceedings against him under paragraph (1) of this subsection, the person may apply to the court for an order to expunge from all official records, other than the nonpublic records to be retained by the bureau…, all recordation relating to his arrest, indictment, trial, finding of guilt, and dismissal and discharge pursuant to this section."

Source: § 41-29-150(d), FindLaw reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://codes.findlaw.com/ms/title-41-public-health/ms-code-sect-41-29-150/ ; corroborated by Justia 2025 reproduction — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-29/article-3/section-41-29-150/

Note the eligibility limits in the text: no previous conviction for violating § 41-29-139 or equivalent U.S./other-state drug laws; only (c) (possession) or (d) (paraphernalia) violations of § 41-29-139; probation up to three years; dismissal only once per person. A second (c)/(d) case cannot use this route again.

C. What is not eligible — stated from the lists, not assumed. Sale, transfer, manufacture, distribution, dispensing, and possession with intent under § 41-29-139(a) are not in the § 99-19-71(2)(a) list and are not within § 41-29-150(d) (which covers only (c)/(d)). The under-21 felony path in (2)(b) expressly excludes distribution-related felonies in the court's discretion. DUI / implied-consent violations are separately excluded from expunction in the 2026 SB 2792/SB 2675 bill texts ("no expunction of any implied consent violations shall be allowed" — proposed bill language, [VERIFY] whether that exclusion is already current law under § 63-11-30 or is proposed). Do not present any of these as expungeable under the possession paths.

4(ii) What is silent in Mississippi law

  • No automatic (system-initiated, no-petition) expungement or sealing for any marijuana offence, and no cannabis-specific expungement, resentencing, or record-clearing programme. Run 1's "none asserted" for automatic expungement is confirmed as a negative finding in this window: no automatic scheme was located.
  • No statute was located providing expungement because conduct is now lawful under the Medical Cannabis Act (e.g., a pre-2022 possession conviction for an amount now within the medical allowable amount is not automatically expungeable by virtue of the Act). The Act contains no retroactive record-clearing provision located in this window.
  • No waiting-period, fee, or form rule specific to marijuana expungement was located beyond the general § 99-19-71 / § 41-29-150 framework above. Court costs, filing fees, and the treatment of a first-offence ≤30 g civil fine (see Run 1 penalties) as a "conviction" for expungement purposes are [VERIFY] — the fine-only first-offence scheme's interaction with § 99-19-71 was not addressed by any source located.
  • No rule was located on expungement of a nonresident or juvenile marijuana record beyond the general statutes; juvenile expungement procedure (petition to the court with proper jurisdiction) is noted in secondary guides but its current statutory basis was not verified here [VERIFY].

4(iii) Cannabis-specific bills — proposed only, with status

Not enacted on any source located. Source: SB 2266 (2023, as introduced), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2023/dt/SB/2200-2299/SB2266IN.pdf

Not enacted on any source located; automatic-expungement language is in the bill, not in current law. A secondary 2026 drug-policy brief's summary — "Cannabis expungement-expansion bills died in 2026" and "There is no automatic record-clearing for cannabis offenses; expungement is petition-based" — is consistent with the bill record above and is adopted only for that negative proposition. Source: Drug Policy Watch, Mississippi 2026 brief, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — http://drugpolicywatch.info/states/mississippi.html

4(iv) Federal law only

  • Federal expungement / record-clearing for federal marijuana convictions is federal law only and is not covered by § 99-19-71 or § 41-29-150, which are state-court statutes. No federal automatic-expungement scheme for state convictions exists, and no conclusion is drawn here on federal pardon or federal record relief. A Mississippi state expunction order does not, by itself, erase a federal record or restore federal firearms rights — see §8 for the firearms interaction, which is [VERIFY] in its post-Schedule III form.

5. Consumption rules

5(i) What Mississippi law actually says

The controlling limitations section — § 41-137-13(2). The Act "does not authorize any individual to engage in, and does not prevent the imposition of any civil, criminal or other penalties for engaging in, the following conduct":

"(a) Acting with negligence, gross negligence, recklessness, in breach of any applicable professional or occupational standard of care, or to effect an intentional wrong, as a result, in whole or in part, of that individual's medical use of medical cannabis; (b) Possessing medical cannabis or otherwise engaging in the medical use of medical cannabis in any correctional facility, unless the correctional facility has elected to allow the cardholder to engage in the use of medical cannabis; (c) Smoking medical cannabis in a public place or in a motor vehicle; for purposes of this paragraph (c), the term 'smoking' includes vaping and any other method of inhalation of medical cannabis; (d) Operating, navigating, or being in actual physical control of any motor vehicle, aircraft, train, motorboat or other conveyance in a manner that would violate Section 59-23-7, Section 63-11-30 or federal law as a result, in whole or in part, of that individual's medical use of medical cannabis; (e) Possessing medical cannabis in excess of the allowable amount of medical cannabis; or (f) Consumption, by a registered designated caregiver, of cannabis provided for use to a registered qualifying patient."

Source: § 41-137-13(2), Justia 2025 reproduction (search-indexed; direct fetch failed — see Method note), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-13/ [VERIFY against current official text.]

"Public place" — § 41-137-3 definition. As reproduced in SB 2095 (as sent to Governor):

"'Public place' means a church or any area to which the general public is invited or in which the general public is permitted, regardless of the ownership of the area, and any area owned or controlled by a municipality, county, state or federal government, including, but not limited to, streets, sidewalks or other forms of public transportation. Such term shall not mean a private residential dwelling."

Source: § 41-137-3(dd) definition, SB 2095 reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.scribd.com/document/568505039/Mississippi-Medical-Cannabis-Act [VERIFY the current § 41-137-3 lettering.]

Workplace. § 41-137-19(2) (see §7) and § 41-137-15(5)–(6) together mean: nothing prohibits an employer from disciplining for ingesting in the workplace or working while under the influence; no private right of action against an employer is created; the Act does not change the existing employer–employee legal relationship. MMCP's summary adds the practical gloss that operating a vehicle, boat, aircraft, train, or performing tasks that may constitute negligence/professional malpractice while under the influence is prohibited — consistent with § 41-137-13(2)(a) and (d).

Where a patient may consume — by exclusion, not by a positive list. The Act contains no "consumption lounge" provision, no "consumption area" licence, and no list of permitted public consumption sites. The lawful-consumption space that the statute affirmatively leaves alone is, in effect: (1) a private residential dwelling (expressly excluded from "public place"); and (2) property where the person in lawful possession of the property allows use — § 41-137-19(3): "Any person or establishment that is in lawful possession of property may allow a guest, client, customer or other visitor to use medical cannabis on or in that property as authorized under this chapter." Source: § 41-137-19(3), Justia 2025 reproduction (search-indexed), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-19/ [VERIFY.] That permission is permissive for the property holder, not a right for the patient: a holder may allow, and may equally refuse.

Smoking vs. edibles vs. vaping — the textual distinction that matters.

Form Public place / motor vehicle Basis
Smoking Prohibited § 41-137-13(2)(c)
Vaping Prohibited — expressly included in "smoking" § 41-137-13(2)(c): "'smoking' includes vaping and any other method of inhalation"
Any other inhalation (e.g., dabbing, inhaler-type device) Prohibited — same inclusion § 41-137-13(2)(c)
Eating an edible / ingesting a tincture / applying a topical in a public place Not prohibited by § 41-137-13(2)(c) on its words — the paragraph bans smoking (as defined) only Textual gap — see warning below
Any form while driving / in actual physical control, if impaired Prohibited via § 63-11-30 / § 41-137-13(2)(d) §3 above

Warning on the edible gap — read this before relying on it. The fact that (2)(c) does not name edibles in a public place is not a permission to eat edibles anywhere. Other rules may still apply: workplace discipline (§ 41-137-19(2)), school/correctional-facility rules (§§ 41-137-13(2)(b), 10 below), a property holder's refusal (§ 41-137-19(3)), a lease ban (§7), and federal rules on federal property. No Mississippi source located in this window affirmatively authorises public edible consumption, and no case or MSDH guidance was located blessing it. The correct statement is narrow: § 41-137-13(2)(c) as written bans inhalation in public/vehicles; it does not, on its face, ban non-inhaled consumption in a public place; whether any other law bans it in a given place is [VERIFY] place-by-place. Do not summarise this as "edibles are legal in public in Mississippi."

Correctional facilities. § 41-137-13(2)(b) preserves penalties for possessing/using in a correctional facility unless the facility has elected to allow it. No list of electing facilities was located [UNAVAILABLE].

Caregiver consumption. § 41-137-13(2)(f) preserves penalties for consumption by a registered designated caregiver of cannabis provided for a registered qualifying patient. A caregiver may purchase/transport/administer for the patient; the caregiver may not consume the patient's supply.

Rental property — cross-reference. Consumption in a rental home sits at the intersection of the "private residential dwelling" exclusion and the landlord's § 41-137-19(4) power to refuse to allow use (see §7). The dwelling exclusion answers the public-place question; it does not override a lease ban.

5(ii) What is silent in Mississippi law

  • No consumption-lounge, social-use, or on-site consumption licence or rule.
  • No rule on consumption in hotels, short-term rentals, or other temporary lodging as such — the property-holder permission in § 41-137-19(3) and any lease/house-rule ban are the only frameworks located; a hotel's own policy is private, not statute.
  • No rule on consumption on private property open to the public (e.g., a private business that invites the public in) beyond the "public place" definition, which expressly covers areas "to which the general public is invited or in which the general public is permitted, regardless of the ownership of the area." A private business that invites the public is therefore a "public place" for (2)(c) purposes on the definition's words — but no guidance or case applying that definition to a specific business type was located [VERIFY].
  • No rule on secondhand-smoke exposure, odour nuisance as a standalone cannabis offence, or a distance rule for smoking near another person/property (as distinct from the dispensary location buffers in Run 1). General nuisance/lease law may apply but was not researched as a cannabis rule here.
  • No rule on consumption by a patient in a vehicle as a passenger (as distinct from smoking in a motor vehicle, which (2)(c) bans regardless of driver/passenger status on its words, and driving while impaired, which § 63-11-30 bans). The (2)(c) ban says "in a motor vehicle," not "while driving a motor vehicle" — on its words it covers passengers who smoke/vape in the vehicle too. No exception for a parked vehicle was located.
  • No local consumption delegation was located: the Act does not, in the sections consulted, authorise counties/municipalities to create their own public-consumption bans or permits beyond general police powers, and no surviving local consumption ordinance was located. (Contrast the struck-down Hattiesburg paraphernalia ordinance in §1.)

5(iii) What is federal law only

  • Federal property / federal law. § 41-137-13(2)(d) expressly preserves federal-law violations for operating conveyances, and the "public place" definition includes areas owned/controlled by the federal government. Possession/use on federal property is governed by federal law, not by the Mississippi Act's protections. After the given Schedule III baseline, whether state-licensed medical possession on federal property is treated differently is [VERIFY] — no post-28 April 2026 federal-property guidance was located in this window, and no safe harbour is asserted here.
  • No federal "public consumption" permission exists that would override Mississippi's (2)(c) ban. Federal law does not create a right to consume in public in Mississippi.

6. Visitor and out-of-state patient rules

6(i) What Mississippi law actually says

No reciprocity — Run 1 position verified. Mississippi does not accept another state's medical cannabis card for direct purchase at a Mississippi dispensary. An out-of-state card is a prerequisite for, not a substitute for, a Mississippi nonresident registration. MMCP states this directly: out-of-state visitors "may apply for a temporary Mississippi medical cannabis card if they meet the medical eligibility requirements and hold an active medical cannabis card from their home state," with applications up to 30 days before arrival and cards valid for a maximum of two 15-day periods in a 365-day year. Source: MSDH/MMCP Programme Overview toolkit (Aug 2026), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/sites/default/files/2026/MMCP%20Tool%20Kit%20-%20August%202026/MSDH_Medical_Cannabis_Program%20Overview.pdf — Corroborated by LegalClarity's Mississippi guide (secondary, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://legalclarity.org/does-mississippi-accept-out-of-state-medical-cards/), which states Mississippi "does not honor out-of-state medical cannabis cards for direct purchases" and that the nonresident card "is the only document dispensaries will accept."

Definition — "nonresident cardholder." As reproduced in HB 1158 (2023), a nonresident cardholder means a person who: (i) has been diagnosed with a debilitating medical condition by a practitioner in their respective state or territory, or is the parent, guardian, conservator or other person with authority to consent to medical use by a person so diagnosed; (ii) is not a resident of Mississippi or has been a resident for less than forty-five (45) days; and (iii) has submitted documentation required by MDOH rules and received confirmation of registration. Source: HB 1158 definitions, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/documents/2023/html/HB/1100-1199/HB1158SG.htm [VERIFY the current § 41-137-3 lettering; the 45-day element is consistent across SB 2095 and HB 1158 reproductions.] The Act's registration procedure for nonresidents, § 41-137-41(xviii) (rulemaking), must require submission of (1) a practitioner's statement confirming a debilitating medical condition and (2) documentation demonstrating the nonresident is allowed to possess medical cannabis/cannabis preparations in their home jurisdiction. Source: § 41-137-41, FindLaw reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://codes.findlaw.com/ms/title-41-public-health/ms-code-sect-41-137-41/

Purchase, possession, and validity — § 41-137-39(12)–(14), verified against Run 1. The Run 1 figures are confirmed verbatim by the § 41-137-39 text reproduced in SB 2095 and in HB 895 (2026, committee substitute):

"(13) A nonresident cardholder shall not obtain more than a total of six (6) MMCEUs of allowable medical cannabis in a week from a dispensary or a combination of dispensaries. A nonresident cardholder shall not obtain more than a total of twelve (12) MMCEUs of allowable cannabis from a dispensary or a combination of dispensaries in a fifteen-day period."

"(14) A nonresident may apply to receive a nonresident registry identification card up to thirty (30) days before arriving in Mississippi. A nonresident registry identification card shall be valid for fifteen (15) days. After the expiration of the card, a nonresident may apply for a renewal of the card and may be granted another card which shall be valid for another fifteen-day period. A nonresident registry identification card shall only be valid, at a maximum, for two (2) separate periods of fifteen (15) days in a three-hundred-sixty-five-day period. An applicant may indicate on his or her application the specific time period that he or she wishes for the card to be valid. The possession limit of the allowable amount of medical cannabis for nonresident cardholders shall be fourteen (14) MMCEUs."

Sources: § 41-137-39(13)–(14), SB 2095 reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.scribd.com/document/568505039/Mississippi-Medical-Cannabis-Act ; HB 895 (2026) committee substitute reproducing the same subsections, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://legiscan.com/MS/text/HB895/id/3335658/Mississippi-2026-HB895-Comm_Sub.html ; MMCP FAQ allotment guidance (same 6 / 12 figures), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/node/161 and https://www.mmcp.ms.gov/faq?os=app&

Run 1 citation note. The task brief cited "§ 41-137-23 / § 41-137-5" for nonresident registration. The operative purchase/possession/validity rules are in § 41-137-39(13)–(14) (dispensary requirements), while § 41-137-23 governs issuance/denial of registry cards generally and § 41-137-5 governs authorisation/certification. The figures themselves (6/week, 12/15 days, 14 possession, 15-day card, max two per 365 days, apply up to 30 days before arrival) are confirmed; the pinpoint is corrected to § 41-137-39 for the limits. Whether § 41-137-23 contains a separate nonresident issuance paragraph was not confirmed from a directly opened text in this window [VERIFY] — do not cite § 41-137-23 alone for the limits.

Fee — secondary only, flagged. Secondary sources state a $75 nonresident card fee. No official MMCP fee schedule was opened in this window confirming $75 as the current fee, so the fee is [VERIFY] and is not stated here as a confirmed fact. Do not quote $75 as verified.

Visitors who are not patients — no legal purchase or use. A visitor without (a) a home-state qualifying diagnosis/card and (b) a Mississippi nonresident registration has no lawful route to purchase at a Mississippi dispensary (§ 41-137-39(12): dispensaries may not dispense more than the allowable amount to a registered qualifying patient or nonresident cardholder; § 41-137-39(21): sales only to cardholders inside the dispensary, except the 21+ topical exception in §2 above) and no lawful route to possess/use medical cannabis in Mississippi. Recreational use remains unlawful (see Run 1 penalties). Transporting medical cannabis into Mississippi from another state, or out of Mississippi, is also outside the Act: § 41-137-39(18) provides a medical cannabis establishment shall only purchase/grow/cultivate/use cannabis grown in Mississippi and "Any medical cannabis that is grown and cultivated in this state shall not be transported outside of this state" — and no provision authorises a patient to import another state's product. Interstate transport is additionally a federal offence (federal law only, see §6(iii)).

6(ii) What is silent in Mississippi law

  • No list of "recognised" home states, and no rule that a home-state card from a state with a different qualifying-conditions list is or is not sufficient beyond the practitioner's-statement + home-possession-documentation requirements in § 41-137-41(xviii). Whether a condition that qualifies in the home state but is not listed in § 41-137-3 qualifies in Mississippi for nonresident purposes is [VERIFY] — the statute's nonresident definition says "diagnosed with a debilitating medical condition by a practitioner in his or her respective state," which on its words points to the home-state diagnosis, but no MSDH guidance resolving a conditions-list mismatch was located.
  • No rule was located on a nonresident designated caregiver (e.g., whether a visitor's home-state caregiver may purchase in Mississippi, or whether a Mississippi caregiver may be designated by a nonresident). The nonresident definition includes a parent/guardian/conservator as the nonresident cardholder for a diagnosed person, but a separate nonresident-caregiver purchase rule was not located [VERIFY].
  • No rule was located on what happens to unused nonresident product at the end of the 15-day period, on renewal timing beyond "after expiration… may apply for a renewal," or on whether the two 15-day periods must be consecutive or may be split across the 365 days beyond the "two separate periods" wording.
  • No Mississippi rule was located giving a Mississippi resident cardholder any right to purchase in another state (that is the other state's law), and no Mississippi rule was located on a Mississippi cardholder's possession while temporarily outside Mississippi.

6(iii) What is federal law only

  • Interstate transport is a federal offence regardless of whether both states have medical programmes, and there is no federal reciprocity exception. This is federal law (Controlled Substances Act) and is not a Mississippi rule, but it is the reason a visitor cannot lawfully drive their home-state product into Mississippi and rely on it, even if they later obtain a Mississippi nonresident card for Mississippi-dispensary product.
  • Federal Schedule III baseline does not create reciprocity. State-licensed medical status in one state does not, on the given baseline, confer federal authorisation to possess in another state or to transport across state lines. No federal reciprocity rule was located.

Does Mississippi accept my home-state card at the dispensary? No — must obtain a Mississippi nonresident card
Apply how early? Up to 30 days before arriving
Valid how long? 15 days; one renewal for another 15 days; max two 15-day periods per 365 days
Purchase limits 6 MMCEUs/week; 12 MMCEUs/15 days (all dispensaries combined)
Possession limit 14 MMCEUs
Who qualifies? Home-state diagnosis by home-state practitioner + home-possession documentation + MDOH registration; non-resident or <45 days' Mississippi residence
Non-patient visitor purchase/use? No lawful route
