7. Landlord and tenant rules

7(i) What Mississippi law actually says

The landlord provision — § 41-137-19(4). This is the whole of the Medical Cannabis Act's landlord rule, and it is permissive, not protective of a tenant's right to use:

"A landlord may, but shall not be required to, allow the lawful cultivation, processing, testing, research, sale or use of medical cannabis on rental property as authorized under this chapter."

Source: § 41-137-19(4), Justia 2025 reproduction (search-indexed; direct fetch failed — see Method note), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-41/chapter-137/section-41-137-19/ — Laws 2022, ch. 303, § 10, eff. 2 Feb 2022.

The companion property-holder provision — § 41-137-19(3):

"Any person or establishment that is in lawful possession of property may allow a guest, client, customer or other visitor to use medical cannabis on or in that property as authorized under this chapter."

Source: same § 41-137-19 reproduction. A landlord is a person in lawful possession; (3) and (4) together mean a landlord may allow use, and need not.

The anti-penalty provision — § 41-137-15(2) — protects the landlord, not the tenant's use:

"No school, landlord or employer may be penalized or denied any benefit under state law for enrolling, leasing to or employing a cardholder."

Source: § 41-137-15(2), as brought forward in HB 1753 (2026, as introduced), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://legiscan.com/MS/text/HB1753/2026 [VERIFY the current § 41-137-15 text; HB 1753 is a brought-forward bill text, not an amendment, so it reproduces the current section as of introduction.] Read carefully: this bars the state from penalising a landlord for leasing to a cardholder. It does not bar a landlord from banning use in the lease, and it does not create a tenant right to use despite a ban. Conflating (2) with a tenant protection is a common misreading and must be avoided.

Custody/visitation — adjacent, not housing. § 41-137-15(1): "A person shall not be denied custody of or visitation rights or parenting time with a minor solely for the person's status as a cardholder." This is a family-law protection, not a housing rule, and is noted here only to prevent it being cited as a housing protection.

Care facilities — § 41-137-21 (facility restrictions) [VERIFY section number]. Secondary summaries of SB 2095 § 11 (the facility-restrictions section) state that a nursing facility, hospital, hospice, assisted living facility, personal care home, adult day care facility, or adult foster care facility may adopt reasonable restrictions on use by patients receiving healthcare/residential/day-care services from the facility, including that the facility will not store/maintain the patient's supply and is not responsible for providing it, but may not deny a qualifying patient or unreasonably limit access/use unless failing to do so would cause the facility to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law or regulations. Source: Bradley LLP summary of SB 2095 (Jan 2022), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.bradley.com/insights/publications/2022/01/medical-cannabis-program-oh-so-close-in-mississippi-after-house-sends-legislation-to-governor — The section number (§ 41-137-21) and the "unless federal benefit loss" proviso are [VERIFY] against the current official text; the substance is stated here from a reputable secondary summary, not from a directly opened statute. Care facilities are not ordinary rental housing, and this provision must not be generalised to private landlords.

Eviction — general landlord-tenant law, not a cannabis rule. The Mississippi Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Title 89, Chapter 8, governs eviction generally. Secondary eviction guides summarise the framework as: non-payment — 3-day notice; lease violation — 14-day notice to remedy or quit (the guides differ on 7-day vs. 14-day notice forms for noncompliance, so the notice period is [VERIFY] against §§ 89-8-13 / 89-8-31); illegal activity on the premises — immediate eviction without a remedy opportunity on the guides' summary. No cannabis-specific eviction ground, notice period, or procedure was located in Chapter 8. The practical consequence is that eviction for cannabis use in a rental will, in practice, turn on (a) whether the lease bans use/smoking/cultivation (a lease violation), (b) whether the use is unlawful use (e.g., non-medical use, or cultivation, which is unlawful for a patient in any event — see Run 1: no home grow), or (c) general health/safety/damage provisions — not on a cannabis-specific eviction statute. Whether a landlord may evict solely for lawful medical use that the lease does not ban is not answered by any statute located and is [VERIFY] — do not assert either that they may or that they may not on the basis of § 41-137-19(4) alone, because (4) addresses allowing use, not the eviction standard.

Cultivation in a rental — doubly barred. Even if a landlord were willing to allow use, cultivation by a patient is not lawful medical use at all: § 41-137-3's definition of "medical use" excludes cultivation unless done by a cultivation facility, and Run 1 confirms no home grow for patients or caregivers. A landlord's permission under § 41-137-19(4) cannot authorise patient cultivation, because (4) allows only use "as authorized under this chapter."

7(ii) What is silent in Mississippi law

  • No tenant right to use medical cannabis in a rental despite a lease ban; no "reasonable accommodation" duty for private landlords; no rule requiring a landlord to permit non-smoked forms (edibles/tinctures/topicals) even if smoking is banned — the Act's landlord provision does not distinguish forms. (Contrast the rejected 2020 HB 1213 draft language, which would have barred a landlord from prohibiting non-smoking medical use — that language was not enacted in SB 2095 and must not be cited as law.)
  • No rule on smoking vs. non-smoking distinctions in leases for cannabis, on odour as a lease violation, on a landlord's right to enter/inspect for cannabis, or on a landlord's liability for a tenant's lawful use.
  • No rule on eviction procedure, notice, or defences specific to a cardholder tenant, and no rule on whether a cardholder's status alone (without use on the premises) is a lawful eviction ground. § 41-137-15(2) bars state penalisation of the landlord for leasing to a cardholder; it does not, on its words, bar a private landlord from declining to lease to a cardholder in the first place — that question is [VERIFY] and must not be answered by analogy to employment or school-enrolment protections.
  • No Mississippi public-housing-specific statute was located. Public housing in Mississippi is governed by the federal framework in §7(iii) and by each housing authority's own admissions policy.

7(iii) What is federal law only — federally assisted housing

This is federal law only and is labelled as such throughout. It is not Mississippi law, and the given Schedule III baseline does not, on any source located, change it as of 25 October 2026:

  • HUD policy (pre-baseline, not updated in sources consulted): HUD requires owners of federally assisted properties to deny admission to applicants the owner determines are currently using a substance illegal under federal law, and permits eviction of current tenants for cannabis use on a case-by-case basis. HUD has stated that public housing agencies may not make reasonable accommodations for medical marijuana, even in states where it is legal. Sources (secondary summaries of HUD guidance, accessed 25 Oct 2026): LegalClarity Mississippi guide — https://legalclarity.org/mississippi-medical-cannabis-act-rules-and-compliance-guide/ ; LegalClarity eviction guide — http://legalclarity.org/can-i-get-evicted-for-smoking-weed-in-my-apartment/ — Both summaries describe cannabis as Schedule I; they pre-date or do not reflect the given 28 April 2026 Schedule III baseline for state-licensed medical use, so whether HUD has updated its guidance after that date is [VERIFY] against current HUD guidance. No post-baseline HUD update was located in this window, and no conclusion is drawn that HUD policy has changed.
  • Statutory framework (federal): 42 U.S.C. §§ 1437d(l)(9), 1437f, 13661–13664 (U.S. Housing Act of 1937; Quality Housing and Work Responsibility Act of 1998) — lease termination for drug-related criminal activity, screening/denial of admission for current illegal-drug use, and the "one-strike" eviction authority confirmed in HUD v. Rucker, 535 U.S. 125 (2002) (eviction permitted for drug activity by household members/guests even without the tenant's knowledge, subject to notice and hearing). Whether "drug-related criminal activity" after Schedule III still captures state-licensed medical use is [VERIFY] — it turns on federal interpretation after 28 April 2026 that was not located here.
  • Proposed federal housing protection is not law. Appropriations amendments that would bar HUD funds from being used to enforce the housing prohibitions on medical-marijuana possession/use in listed states including Mississippi (e.g., the § 420 amendment filed in 2022) were proposed amendments, not enacted law on sources located. They must not be cited as a housing protection.

Bottom line for §7: Private rental — landlord may allow, need not allow; no tenant use-right located; eviction turns on the lease and general Chapter 8 law, not a cannabis eviction statute. Federally assisted housing — federal HUD framework, labelled federal-only, with post-Schedule III HUD treatment [VERIFY].

8. Gun ownership conflicts for patients

8(i) What Mississippi law actually says

State protection — § 41-137-15(3). As brought forward in HB 1753 (2026):

"(3) A registered qualifying patient or registered designated caregiver shall not be denied the right to own, purchase or possess a firearm, firearm accessory or ammunition based solely on his or her status as a registered qualifying patient or registered designated caregiver. No state or local agency, municipal or county governing authority shall restrict, revoke, suspend or otherwise infringe upon the right of a person to own, purchase or possess a firearm, firearm accessory or ammunition or any related firearms license or certification based solely on his or her status as a registered qualifying patient or registered designated caregiver."

Source: § 41-137-15(3), HB 1753 (2026, as introduced, bringing forward § 41-137-15), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://legiscan.com/MS/text/HB1753/2026 [VERIFY the current official § 41-137-15(3) text; the brought-forward reproduction is consistent with SB 2095 § 8 summaries.]

The protection is expressly limited by "based solely on … status." It does not, on its words, protect a person who is independently prohibited (e.g., by a felony conviction, a domestic-violence order, or federal law as applied to use rather than status), and it does not bind the federal government or a federal firearms licensee (FFL) applying federal law.

Permitless carry — § 45-9-101(24) proviso. Mississippi's permitless-carry provision provides that no licence is required for a loaded/unloaded pistol or revolver carried in a sheath, belt/shoulder holster, purse, handbag, satchel, similar bag/briefcase, or fully enclosed case, if the person is not engaged in criminal activity other than a misdemeanour traffic offence, is not otherwise prohibited from possessing a pistol/revolver under state or federal law, and is not in a location prohibited under § 45-9-101(13). It then adds a narrow proviso:

"However, the medical use of medical cannabis by a cardholder who is a registered qualifying patient which is lawful under the provisions of the Mississippi Medical Cannabis Act and in compliance with rules and regulations adopted thereunder shall not disqualify a person under this subsection (24) solely because the person is prohibited from possessing a firearm under 18 USCS Section 922(g)(3) due to such medical use of medical cannabis."

Source: § 45-9-101(24), Justia 2025 reproduction, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://law.justia.com/codes/mississippi/title-45/chapter-9/license-to-carry-concealed-pistol-or-revolver/section-45-9-101/ — Amended by Laws 2022, ch. 303, SB 2095, § 64, eff. 2 Feb 2022.

Read the proviso's limits precisely: (1) it operates only "under this subsection (24)" — i.e., for the permitless-carry licence exemption; (2) it disapplies only the § 922(g)(3) disqualification solely because of lawful medical use; (3) it does not say the person is not prohibited under federal law, and it does not authorise a federally prohibited purchase or possession. A person who is "otherwise prohibited … under state or federal law" on any other ground is still disqualified under (24)'s main text.

Licensed (enhanced / concealed) carry — no patient-specific rule located. § 45-9-101's licensing provisions (application, fees, exemptions, prohibited locations under subsection (13)) contain no patient-specific eligibility rule located in this window beyond the (24) proviso. Whether lawful medical use affects a licence application (as opposed to permitless carry) is [VERIFY] against the current § 45-9-101 licensing subsections and DPS practice; do not assume the (24) proviso extends to licensing.

State firearm prohibitions independent of cannabis — silent as to patients. No Mississippi statute was located that independently bars a medical cannabis patient from owning/possessing a firearm because of cannabis use, beyond the general state/federal prohibited-persons framework. Mississippi law is therefore, on the sources located, silent as an independent bar and protective as to status ( § 41-137-15(3)) and as to (24) permitless carry — but that state protection does not resolve the federal question below.

8(ii) What is federal law, and what is unresolved after Schedule III — read with care

The federal statute as written — 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3). It is unlawful for any person "who is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance" to ship, transport, possess, or receive firearms or ammunition. The statute's text turns on "unlawful user," not on "cardholder" and not on "marijuana" by name. Whether a state-licensed medical user, after medical marijuana moved to Schedule III, is an "unlawful user" is the unresolved question — the statute was not amended in the sources consulted, and no ATF safe harbour for state-licensed medical users was located.

Form 4473 — current form vs. draft form (the distinction is the whole point).

  • Current (still operative) form: Question 21.f (numbered 21.e in older forms — the numbering differs by form version; do not treat the letter as substantive) asks: "Are you an unlawful user of, or addicted to, marijuana or any depressant, stimulant, narcotic drug, or any other controlled substance?" with the warning: "The use or possession of marijuana remains unlawful under Federal law regardless of whether it has been legalized or decriminalized for medicinal or recreational purposes in the state where you reside." On that form, a "Yes" requires the FFL to stop the transfer, and a "No" while actively using is a false statement (18 U.S.C. § 1001 / § 922(a)(6) exposure). Source: U.S. Law Shield summary of the current form, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://educate.uslawshield.com/what-rescheduling-marijuana-to-schedule-iii-means-for-gun-owners/
  • Draft form (May 2026, NOT final): On 8 May 2026 ATF published a draft revision to Form 4473 (Federal Register document 2026-09182, comment period through August 2026 on one summary / through 7 July 2026 on another — the comment deadline discrepancy is [VERIFY] against the Federal Register notice itself). The draft recasts the warning to: "You can be an unlawful user under federal law, even if your possession is legal under state law. Federal law does not permit the use or possession of marijuana for recreational purposes." — omitting the prior blanket reference to medicinal use. Secondary analyses (NORML, Marijuana Moment, U.S. Law Shield, Central Law) all agree on one point: the draft is not yet legally operative; FFLs must continue using the current form until ATF completes rulemaking and publishes a final revised form. Sources, accessed 25 Oct 2026: https://norml.org/blog/2026/05/12/atf-posts-draft-document-acknowledging-medical-cannabis-scheduling-change/ ; https://www.marijuanamoment.net/new-atf-gun-form-recognizes-medical-marijuanas-federally-legal-status-under-trumps-rescheduling-move/ ; https://educate.uslawshield.com/what-rescheduling-marijuana-to-schedule-iii-means-for-gun-owners/ ; https://www.centrallaw.com/blog/atf-form-4473/

Therefore, the following are all [VERIFY] and must not be asserted as settled:

  1. Whether, after 28 April 2026, a person who exclusively uses state-licensed medical cannabis (Schedule III) is an "unlawful user" under § 922(g)(3). The draft Form 4473 points toward ATF treating such use as not unlawful, but a draft form is not a regulation, not a safe harbour, and not a statutory amendment.
  2. Whether ATF's January 2026 interim final rule rewriting 27 C.F.R. § 478.11 (requiring "regular use continuing into the present" for unlawful-user status, as noted in federal Run 2 research for other states) changes the analysis for Mississippi medical patients, and whether that rule has been applied to Schedule III medical use. No Mississippi-specific ATF guidance was located [VERIFY].
  3. Whether U.S. v. Hemani (federal Second Amendment as-applied holding, noted in federal Run 2 research) or the November 2025 Fifth Circuit panel decision reported as in United States v. Mitchell, No. 24-60607 (5th Cir. 21 Nov 2025), holding 922(g)(1) unconstitutional as applied to Mitchell, whose predicate was a prior 922(g)(3) conviction without shown contemporaneous intoxication - NOT a 922(g)(3) invalidation and NOT a medical-patient holding (Law360, 24 Nov 2025 — paywalled summary, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.law360.co.uk/personal-injury-medical-malpractice/articles/2414976/5th-circ-finds-gun-ban-for-pot-users-unconstitutional-) helps any particular Mississippi patient. Both are as-applied, fact-specific holdings, not a general safe harbour, and the Fifth Circuit report was not verified against the slip opinion here [VERIFY — do not cite the Fifth Circuit holding without the opinion].
  4. Whether answering Form 4473 after Schedule III, while the current form remains operative, exposes a medical patient to false-statement liability. On the current form's warning language, the risk cannot be dismissed; on the draft form's language, it would be narrowed — but the draft is not the form in use. No safe harbour is asserted in this report.

Hemp-derived CBD and firearms — narrow point. Hemp-derived CBD containing less than 0.3% THC is federally legal under the 2018 Farm Bill definition and is not, by itself, marijuana use for § 922(g)(3) purposes on secondary analyses. That proposition is not a safe harbour for a medical cardholder who also uses marijuana-derived products, and the distinction between hemp-derived and marijuana-derived CBD is product-specific [VERIFY].

Concealed-carry permit interaction — summary. State law: § 41-137-15(3) bars state/local denial based solely on status; § 45-9-101(24) proviso bars (24) disqualification solely because of § 922(g)(3) status from lawful medical use. Federal law: an FFL transfer still requires the current Form 4473, and federal prohibited-person status is determined by federal law, not by § 41-137-15(3). A Mississippi patient therefore faces a state-protective / federally-unresolved split, not a clean "you may buy" answer.

Hunting / federal lands — [UNAVAILABLE] / [VERIFY]. No Mississippi statute, Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks rule, or federal-land guidance specific to a Mississippi medical patient's possession of a firearm while hunting, or possession of medical cannabis on federal lands in Mississippi, was located in this window. General principles that would need verification before any statement: (a) federal lands are federal jurisdiction (see §5(iii)); (b) hunting while impaired may violate state/federal hunting and DUI-adjacent rules, but no cannabis-specific hunting-impairment rule was located; (c) a federal firearms prohibition, if it applies, applies on federal lands regardless of state carry law. No hunting or federal-lands conclusion is given here beyond [UNAVAILABLE].

8(iii) What is silent in Mississippi law

  • No Mississippi rule on disclosure of cardholder status to DPS, to an FFL, or on a background-check form; no rule on whether MSDH registry data is shared with NICS (secondary sources state registries are generally confidential and not directly NICS-accessible, but no Mississippi-specific data-sharing rule was located [VERIFY]).
  • No Mississippi rule on firearms storage, transport with medical cannabis in the same vehicle, or on a patient's possession of a firearm while using medical cannabis (as distinct from status-based ownership). The (24) proviso addresses disqualification, not contemporaneous use-and-carry.
  • No Mississippi rule on nonresident cardholders and firearms (whether § 41-137-15(3)'s "registered qualifying patient" includes a nonresident cardholder for firearms purposes is [VERIFY] — the section says "registered qualifying patient or registered designated caregiver" without expressly naming nonresident cardholders).

9. Pet and veterinary products

9(i) What Mississippi law actually says

No Mississippi veterinary-cannabis rule was located. No Mississippi statute, Mississippi Board of Veterinary Medicine rule, MDAC rule, or MSDH rule was located in this window that: authorises, prohibits, or regulates CBD/hemp products for animals; authorises a Mississippi veterinarian to prescribe, recommend, dispense, or discuss cannabis/CBD for an animal patient; sets a THC/CBD limit, labelling, or testing rule for pet products; or creates a Mississippi pet-product licence or registration. The Mississippi Board of Veterinary Medicine was noted in secondary news only for an unrelated rule (diagnosis of livestock pregnancy by licensed veterinarians) — no cannabis position was located. This is a negative finding: Mississippi law, on the sources consulted, is silent on veterinary cannabis/CBD.

What does exist in Mississippi law that touches animals only tangentially:

  • The Uniform Controlled Substances Law definition of "ultimate user" (§ 41-29-105(cc)) includes a person who lawfully possesses a controlled substance "for administering to an animal owned by him or by a member of his household" — but that definition operates within the controlled-substances framework and does not authorise veterinary cannabis, because medical cannabis under the Act is for registered qualifying patients (humans) and the Act contains no animal-patient provision.
  • The Medical Cannabis Act contains no animal, veterinary, or pet provision located in this window. A pet owner cannot obtain medical cannabis for a pet through the programme, and a veterinarian cannot certify an animal patient.
  • Hemp cultivation in Mississippi is USDA-licensed only (Run 1: MDAC issues no licences, unfunded state plan). That cultivation framework governs growing hemp, not manufacturing or selling pet CBD products, and it sets no pet-product rule.

9(ii) What is silent in Mississippi law

  • Whether a Mississippi veterinarian may discuss CBD/hemp with a pet owner without discipline; whether discussion vs. recommendation vs. dispensing are treated differently by the Board; whether a veterinarian faces discipline for recommending an unapproved animal drug — all [UNAVAILABLE] as Mississippi-specific positions. Do not import California's (or any other state's) veterinary-cannabis discussion-protection statute (e.g., California AB 221 / AB 1999-type protections) into Mississippi; no equivalent Mississippi statute was located.
  • No Mississippi rule on pet-product labelling, THC limits for pets, species-specific dosing, or adverse-event reporting.
  • No Mississippi rule on hemp seed oil vs. CBD extract for animals, on "pet treats" as feed vs. drug, or on retail sale of pet CBD in Mississippi shops (beyond the general hemp/AG-opinion uncertainty in §2, which addresses human ingestion/consumption products and does not address animal products).

9(iii) What is federal law / federal guidance only

  • FDA position (federal, not Mississippi): "The FDA has not approved cannabis for any use in animals and cannot ensure the safety or effectiveness of cannabis products marketed for them, and it recommends that pet owners talk with their veterinarian." The FDA has approved one cannabis-derived human drug (Epidiolex) and three cannabis-related human drugs (Marinol, Syndros, Cesamet); none is an animal approval. Federal extralabel-use rules allow veterinarians to prescribe approved human/animal drugs under specific conditions, but those rules apply only to approved drugs — they do not authorise extralabel use of an unapproved CBD product. In January 2023 FDA concluded its existing food/dietary-supplement frameworks were not appropriate for CBD and a new regulatory pathway was needed; in January 2025 FDA's Center for Veterinary Medicine asked veterinarians to share experience with cannabis-derived products in animals, including adverse events and interactions. Source: dvm360 summary of FDA/CVM positions, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.dvm360.com/view/new-maryland-law-limits-board-action-against-veterinarians-who-discuss-cannabis-and-cbd
  • AVMA position (professional guidance, not law): Products for animals for which therapeutic claims are made that have not been evaluated/approved by FDA are unapproved animal drugs, considered "unsafe" under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act because safety/efficacy have not been shown; marketing such products may lead owners to forgo approved therapies. Source: JD Supra summary of AVMA/FDA positions, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/six-things-you-need-to-know-about-cbd-8224136/
  • Practical federal consequences that are often confused with Mississippi law: A pet CBD product marketed with disease claims (arthritis, anxiety, seizures, pain) is, under federal law, an unapproved new animal drug regardless of its Mississippi retail availability; a product marketed without disease claims still faces the FDA's position that CBD cannot lawfully be marketed as a dietary supplement (human or animal) where CBD is an active ingredient in an approved/investigational drug. None of this is a Mississippi statute, and none of it creates a Mississippi enforcement rule located here.
  • Post-11 December 2026 federal hemp cap (given baseline): The 0.4 mg total THC per container cap, when it applies, is a federal hemp-definition rule. Whether it applies differently to pet products vs. human products was not addressed in the given baseline and is [VERIFY] — do not assume pet products are exempt from or covered by the cap on the baseline alone.

Bottom line for §9: Mississippi: silent. Federal: no FDA approval for any cannabis use in animals; veterinarian discussion/recommendation risk is a federal unapproved-drug question, not a Mississippi rule located here. Pet owners and veterinarians in Mississippi therefore have no Mississippi veterinary-cannabis safe harbour to cite, and no Mississippi prohibition to cite either — the operative guidance is federal FDA/AVMA guidance, labelled as such.

10. Medical cannabis in schools

10(i) What Mississippi law actually says

The school-administration permission — § 41-137-15(4). This is the Act's school provision, and it is broader than "silent" — but it is also thinner than a school-use procedure:

"(4) Facilities such as schools, child care facilities and temporary care providers shall be allowed to administer medical cannabis in the same manner as with medical prescriptions."

Source: § 41-137-15(4), as brought forward in HB 1753 (2026, as introduced), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://legiscan.com/MS/text/HB1753/2026 ; corroborated by Grace Law Firm summary ("Facilities such as schools, child care facilities and temporary care providers shall be allowed to administer medical cannabis in the same manner as with medical prescriptions. (Section 41-137-15…)"), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.gracelawfirm.com/blog/medical-cannabis-in-mississippi ; and Bradley LLP SB 2095 summary ("Schools, childcare facilities, and temporary care providers can administer medical cannabis just like any medical prescription."), accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://www.bradley.com/insights/publications/2022/01/medical-cannabis-program-oh-so-close-in-mississippi-after-house-sends-legislation-to-governor [VERIFY the current official § 41-137-15(4) text and its subsection lettering.]

What (4) does and does not do — stated precisely:

  • Does: It allows a school (and childcare facility / temporary care provider) to administer medical cannabis "in the same manner as with medical prescriptions." The natural reading is that a school is not barred by the Act from administering a student's medical cannabis as it would a prescription medicine, and that administration by the school is within the Act's contemplated activities.
  • Does not, on its words: Require any school to administer; specify who administers (school nurse? designated unlicensed personnel? parent/caregiver on site?); specify form (does it include smoked/vaped product, or only non-inhaled forms? — the Act elsewhere bans smoking in a public place, and a school is a public place on the § 41-137-3 definition, so smoked administration at school would collide with § 41-137-13(2)(c) — see below); specify storage, documentation, parental-consent forms, dosage control, or what happens if a school declines; or override federal Drug-Free Schools / federal funding conditions (see §10(iii)).
  • Does not authorise a student to self-possess, self-administer, or use on school property as of right. The subject of (4) is the facility administering, not the student possessing. A student-patient's own possession/use at school is a separate question (see below).

Student possession/use at school — no affirmative student-use rule located, and a colliding expulsion statute.

  • Expulsion — § 37-11-18(1): "Any student in any school who possesses any controlled substance in violation of the Uniform Controlled Substances Law, a knife, handgun, other firearm or any other instrument considered to be dangerous and capable of causing bodily harm or who commits a violent act on educational property… shall be subject to automatic expulsion for a calendar year by the superintendent or principal of the school in which the student is enrolled; provided, however, that the superintendent… shall be authorized to modify the period of time for such expulsion on a case by case basis. Such expulsion shall take effect immediately subject to the constitutional rights of due process, which shall include the student's right to appeal to the local school board." Source: § 37-11-18, via Mississippi Bar school-consequences brochure and OCR resolution letter reproducing the statute, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://msbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Consequences-Of-Misconduct-In-School-Brochure.pdf ; https://www.ed.gov/media/document/case-resolution-letter-tupelo-public-schools-06-11-5002-2014-rescinded-44352.pdf — The italicised qualifier matters: expulsion is for possession "in violation of" the Uniform Controlled Substances Law. Medical cannabis possessed lawfully under the Act (within the allowable amount, by a cardholder) is, by § 41-137-9, lawful activity, not a UCSL violation. Whether a school district in practice treats any on-campus cannabis possession as a § 37-11-18 violation regardless of cardholder status, and whether a district's code of conduct does so, is a district-policy question [VERIFY district by district] — the statute's qualifier points against automatic expulsion for lawful medical possession, but no case or MSDH/MDE guidance resolving the collision was located.
  • A secondary claim that must not be overstated. A secondary Mississippi guide states: "possession or use of medical cannabis that is lawful under the act does not count as possession of a 'controlled substance' for purposes of school discipline policies" (citing SB 2095 as sent to Governor). Source: LegalClarity Mississippi guide, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://legalclarity.org/mississippi-medical-cannabis-act-rules-and-compliance-guide/ — This proposition was not verified against a directly opened § 41-137-9 or § 41-137-15 text in this window and is [VERIFY]. It is consistent with the § 37-11-18 "in violation of" qualifier, but it is not quoted here as a verified statutory sentence. Do not cite it as a holding.
  • Minor-patient framework (from §2, applied to schools): A minor patient must have a parent/guardian as designated caregiver responsible for acquisition, dosage, and frequency of use, with parent/guardian present and signed consent for certification, and only an MD/DO may certify a minor. That caregiver framework is the most plausible who administers answer for a minor at school (parent/guardian-caregiver administers, or school administers under (4) as with a prescription), but the Act does not expressly say a parent/caregiver may enter school property to administer, nor that a school must admit them for that purpose. Both are [VERIFY].

School-board / nurse administration rules — none located as a statewide procedure. No Mississippi Department of Education (MDE) guidance, rule, or model policy specifically addressing medical-cannabis administration in schools was located in this window. MDE's Medication Safety Guidelines: Procedures & Standards in the School Setting (revised 2026) address controlled substances generally — identification, secure storage per Board of Pharmacy Article XXIV, documentation of receipt/number/return with signatures of the adult bringing medication and school personnel receiving/counting it, a rule that "no medication should be brought to school by the student," and reporting of discrepancies to the school nurse, principal, and other authorities — but the guidelines as indexed do not address medical cannabis specifically, and the full text was not opened in this window. Source: MDE Medication Safety Guidelines (revised 2026), indexed summary, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://mdek12.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/24/2026/09/Medication-Safety-Guidelines-.-Procedures-Standards-in-the-School-Setting-Revised-2026-.pdf [VERIFY whether the current MDE guidelines mention cannabis at all; do not cite the general controlled-substances procedures as a cannabis procedure.] The "no medication brought by the student" general rule, if applied to cannabis, would point toward adult-delivered, school-stored administration — but that is an inference from a general guideline, not a cannabis rule, and is flagged as such.

Distinction required by the brief — buffer vs. school use. The 1,000-ft dispensary buffer (Run 1: schools/churches/childcare, 500-ft floor) is a location rule for where a dispensary may be sited. It has nothing to do with whether a student may possess or use, or a school may administer, medical cannabis on school property. A school that is within a buffer zone for dispensary siting is not thereby barred from (4) administration, and a school outside any buffer is not thereby authorised to permit student smoking. The two rules must not be conflated.

Smoking at school — collision noted. A school is, on the § 41-137-3 "public place" definition (area to which the general public is invited/permitted, and government-owned/controlled area), a public place, and § 41-137-13(2)(c) bans smoking (including vaping/inhalation) in a public place. Section 41-137-15(4) ("in the same manner as with medical prescriptions") does not, on its words, carve smoking out of (2)(c). The coherent reading — [VERIFY] against any MSDH/MDE guidance — is that (4) administration, if it occurs at school, would be by a non-inhaled form (edible, tincture, topical) or by a method that does not constitute "smoking" under (2)(c); smoked/vaped administration at school would still violate (2)(c). No source located resolves this collision expressly.

10(ii) What is silent in Mississippi law

  • No statewide school-cannabis procedure: no designated-administrator qualifications, training, storage (locked cabinet? nurse's office?), documentation, parental authorisation form, emergency protocol, or refusal procedure specific to cannabis.
  • No rule on a student-patient's self-carry, self-administration, or possession in a backpack/locker, on a school bus, on a field trip, or at a school-sponsored event off campus.
  • No rule on a school's duty to notify or permit a parent/caregiver to come on site to administer, or on a school's liability for administering or refusing.
  • No rule on university/college students (the Act's (4) says "schools" without distinguishing K-12 vs. post-secondary; a university's own drug policy — e.g., the University of Mississippi Medical Center student drug/alcohol policy stating cannabis use/possession/distribution on UMMC property is prohibited even if approved under the Act, by reference to federal law — is an institutional/federal policy, not a statewide K-12 rule, and must not be generalised to K-12 schools). Source for the UMMC example (institutional policy only): UMMC Student Drug and Alcohol Prevention Program, accessed 25 Oct 2026 — https://UMC.EDU/Office of Academic Affairs/About-Academic-Affairs/Academic-Support/Student-Drug-and-Alcohol-Prevention-Program.html
  • No MDE guidance specific to medical cannabis was located [UNAVAILABLE in this window — not asserted to be non-existent; MDE guidance may exist under a different title and should be searched by title before outreach].

10(iii) What is federal law only

  • Drug-Free Schools and Communities Act / federal funding conditions: Federal law conditions certain education funding on drug-free-school policies, and cannabis remains a controlled substance under federal law for adult-use and, for medical use, is Schedule III only for state-licensed medical use under the given baseline — whether that baseline changes a school's federal obligations is [VERIFY] against current U.S. Department of Education guidance. No post-baseline federal school guidance was located. A school that administers under § 41-137-15(4) may still face a federal-funding question that Mississippi law does not answer.
  • Federal disability / accommodation law (Section 504, ADA, IDEA) does not, on any source located, create a federal right to cannabis administration at school, and no conclusion is drawn here on whether a student's individualised plan could include cannabis administration. That is a federal-law question beyond the Mississippi sources consulted.

  • Hemp waste: no Mississippi disposal entity or product-waste rule; USDA 7 CFR §990.27 still says "Schedule I" on its face — flagged as a text-vs-baseline tension; no finished-product container-cap destruction procedure located.
  • USDA 10-year felony ban for controlled-substance felonies only (§990.20(b)), key participants only; no hemp age/drug-test/employee rule located, no MDAC hemp-employee rule.

Part 12 gaps (R2-12-01 to R2-12-10, full notes in part12.md)

  • No cannabis smoke-shop licence located; Hattiesburg Ord. 3258 held void 10 April 2025.
  • No Mississippi age statute for hemp-derived THC products located — conflicting secondary 21+/18+ claims not adopted; voluntary retailer 21+ is private policy.
  • No per se THC driving limit verified — impairment prong §63-11-30(1)(b) applies even to lawful patients; no Mississippi cannabis-specific impairment-testing rule located.
  • Expungement is petition-only, no automatic, no cannabis-specific statute; §99-19-71(1) misdemeanour first-offender, one listed felony after 5 years, §41-29-150(d) deferred dismissal once only; SB 2266 (2023) and HB 940 (2025) proposals not enacted.
  • Consumption: §41-137-13(2)(c) bans smoking/vaping/any inhalation in public places and vehicles; private dwelling excluded from "public place"; edibles not named in (2)(c) — flagged as a textual gap, not a permission; no lounges.
  • No reciprocity verified; nonresident card per §41-137-39(13)–(14); fee $75 secondary-only [VERIFY].
  • Landlord: §41-137-19(4) — landlord may, need not, allow use; §41-137-15(2) protects the landlord from state penalty for leasing to a cardholder, not a tenant use-right; federally assisted housing is federal HUD law only, post-Schedule III HUD treatment [VERIFY].
  • Guns: state protection §41-137-15(3) (status only) + §45-9-101(24) permitless-carry proviso, but federal §922(g)(3) unresolved (see cross-cutting cautions); hunting/federal lands [UNAVAILABLE].
  • Pets: no Mississippi veterinary-cannabis rule located; federal FDA position only — no cannabis approved for any animal use.
  • Schools: §41-137-15(4) allows schools/childcare/temporary care to administer "as with prescriptions", but no statewide procedure, nurse rule or MDE cannabis guidance located; §37-11-18 expulsion applies only to possession "in violation of" the UCSL; smoking-at-school collision with §41-137-13(2)(c) flagged. The 1,000 ft dispensary buffer is a location rule, not a school-use rule.

Conflicts with Run 1 — summary (see cover for full list)

Substance: none overturned. Pinpoints corrected: employment-protection provisions (§41-137-15(5)–(6), §41-137-19(2) rather than §41-137-13 alone); nonresident-card pinpoint (§41-137-39(13)–(14)). Text conflict resolved in favour of Run 1: MMCEU 1 g total THC (SB 2748, from 1 July 2025) over the 100 mg figure in the 2023 MSDH consolidation. Unresolved Run 1 conflicts carried forward unchanged: Tier 6 canopy (FAQ vs rule), Metrc vendor (secondary only), tribal "state-licensed" status for Schedule III [VERIFY].
